template_adherence.title: ADR 001: Screen Controllers
template_adherence.context: We don’t want to put business logic inside Android framework classes (like an `Activity` or `Fragment`) because those cannot be unit tested. To enable a fast feedback loop (i.e. tests that run on the JVM and not Android VM), we separate screens and controllers using the MVI architecture pattern.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to separate business logic from Android framework classes to enable unit testing.
- Desire for a fast feedback loop with JVM tests.
- Use of MVI architecture pattern to separate concerns.
- Handling user events and UI changes in a unidirectional data flow.
- Efficient event stream management to avoid redundant subscriptions.
template_adherence.decision: Every screen has one controller that consumes user events, performs business logic with the help of data repositories and communicates UI changes back to the screen. User interactions are abstracted as UiEvent data classes flowing to the controller via RxJava streams. The controller transforms UiEvents into UiChanges, which are lambda functions applied to the screen interface. Event streams are merged and shared using RxJava operators like merge(), replay(), and refCount() to maintain a unidirectional data flow and efficient event handling.
template_adherence.consequences:
- UiChange functions must subscribe to events exactly once and immediately when the controller is constructed to avoid replay issues.
- Incorrect subscription patterns (e.g., subscribing inside flatMap) can cause events to be replayed multiple times leading to stale data.
- Proper use of RxJava operators like withLatestFrom ensures correct event handling.
- The architecture enforces separation of concerns and testability but requires careful implementation of event streams.

alternatives.description: Keep business logic inside Android framework classes like Activity or Fragment.
pros: Simpler initial implementation without additional abstraction.
Less code to manage separate controllers.
cons: Business logic tightly coupled with Android framework classes.
Difficult to unit test business logic as it requires Android VM.
Slower feedback loop due to reliance on instrumentation tests.

alternatives.description: Use MVP (Model-View-Presenter) architecture instead of MVI.
pros: Well-known and widely used pattern.
Clear separation of concerns between View and Presenter.
Easier to understand for teams familiar with MVP.
cons: May not leverage reactive streams as effectively as MVI.
Potentially more boilerplate code.
Less unidirectional data flow compared to MVI.

template_adherence.title: Using Activity for bottom sheets instead of Fragment
template_adherence.context: For displaying non-persistent bottom sheets, Material.io recommends using BottomSheetDialogFragment. Unfortunately it doesn’t play very nicely with the on-screen keyboard when the sheet includes input text fields. When the on-screen keyboard is shown, it aligns itself with the bottom edge of the field. Everything beneath the focused text field gets covered by the keyboard. This is standard behavior of the on-screen keyboard, but Activities have worked around this by panning or resizing the layout whenever the keyboard is shown. For some reason, changing the softInputMode on the dialog doesn’t have any affect on dialogs. To be able to align the entire sheet above the keyboard, an Activity called BottomSheetActivity is used instead of BottomSheetDialogFragment that mimics a modal sheet with a translucent background.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to display non-persistent bottom sheets.
- BottomSheetDialogFragment recommended by Material.io but has issues with on-screen keyboard covering input fields.
- Standard keyboard behavior covers content beneath focused text field.
- Activities can pan or resize layout to avoid keyboard overlap, but dialogs cannot.
- Desire to align entire sheet above keyboard.
- Need for a solution that works better with keyboard input fields in bottom sheets.
template_adherence.decision: Use an Activity called BottomSheetActivity instead of BottomSheetDialogFragment to display bottom sheets. This Activity mimics a modal sheet with a translucent background and allows the entire sheet to be aligned above the keyboard, avoiding the issue of the keyboard covering input fields.
template_adherence.consequences: BottomSheetActivity doesn’t support drag-to-dismissing. There is a possibility to use BottomSheetBehavior in the future to add support for drag-to-dismiss functionality.

alternatives.description: Continue using BottomSheetDialogFragment as recommended by Material.io.
pros: Officially recommended by Material.io.
Standard approach for bottom sheets in Android.
cons: Does not handle on-screen keyboard well when input fields are present.
Keyboard covers content beneath focused text field.
Changing softInputMode on dialog has no effect.

alternatives.description: Use an Activity (BottomSheetActivity) to mimic a modal sheet with translucent background.
pros: Allows aligning entire sheet above keyboard.
Works around keyboard covering input fields issue.
Leverages Activity's ability to pan or resize layout with keyboard.
cons: Does not support drag-to-dismiss functionality currently.

template_adherence.title: ADR 003: Weak references (no foreign keys) between SQLite tables
template_adherence.context: Strong references between SQL tables using foreign keys are useful for maintaining data integrity. They introduce safeguards against orphaned records by making it impossible to create data records that do not fulfill relation and deleting referenced records in a cascading fashion when the root dependent record is deleted. In the context of Simple, a good example would be the `Patient` and `BloodPressureMeasurement` tables. In real world, it’s impossible to record a blood pressure for a non-existent patient. Likewise, maintaining a strong reference between these two tables in SQL would have ensured that blood pressures do not get created either unless the associated patient already exists in the database. Additionally, if the patient ever gets deleted, SQLite would have handled deletion of all their blood pressures automatically. Unfortunately, strong references work only when the data storage is centralized. Because Simple’s data is distributed across many devices, it’s impossible to guarantee the existence of all data records at the same time due to its offline by default nature. For instance, it’s easy to imagine a scenario where the app receives some blood pressures from the server, but fails to receive their associated patients because of bad network connectivity. This is expected behavior and we do not want the app to fail because of a foreign key integrity failure.
template_adherence.decision: SQL tables in Simple will not keep strong references using foreign keys unless they can be synced **together** in the same network call with the server.
template_adherence.consequences: We are intentionally making a trade-off by letting go of data integrity on the database level. We’ll have to rely on the user interface to ensure safety against the creation of orphaned records. For instance, the user interface should make it impossible to record a blood pressure if the patient does not exist.

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: treating the client app as the source of truth
template_adherence.context: Unlike an online-only app that can depend on the server to create unique record IDs, Simple is designed to work completely offline. It needs to create data locally and perform two-way syncing of data with the server whenever possible. This brings two kinds of challenges, 1. Resolving conflicts when merging data from the server with its local copy. 2. Generating IDs that are universally unique.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the context and decision sections imply drivers such as the need for offline functionality, conflict resolution, and unique ID generation.
template_adherence.decision: Simple is primarily an app-only service, therefore the client app is considered as the source of truth for all Protected Health Information (PHI). Conflict resolution favors the local dirty copy over the server copy. UUID v4 is used for generating unique IDs due to its near-zero collision probability and convenience, as opposed to database-generated IDs or other random methods.
template_adherence.consequences: 1. When discarding a server record in favor of a dirty local copy, additional data in the server record will be lost. 2. Using UUIDs as primary keys in SQLite tables requires more storage and results in slower queries compared to primitives.

alternatives.description: Letting the database handle generation of IDs using auto-incrementing integer IDs.
pros: Simple to implement.
Efficient storage and querying.
cons: SQLite only supports auto-incrementing integers, which are not universally unique.
Not suitable for offline-first apps needing unique IDs across client and server.

alternatives.description: Using Random.nextLong for ID generation.
pros: Simple to implement.
cons: Random.nextLong space is not large enough to guarantee near uniqueness.
Higher risk of ID collisions.

template_adherence.title: ADR 005: A single activity, view-based screen navigation system
template_adherence.context:
Fragments were introduced in Android API 11, as a way to model behavior or a portion of the user interface. Fragments can be shared between multiple Activities, and can be replaced by other Fragments without affecting the parent Activity.

However, Fragments have a lifecycle that, although part of the Activity lifecycle, is slightly different and the two are not sychronous. This has created a class of bugs, of which many are common in Android apps; e.g.:

- Fragments are usually created after `Activity#onCreate()` has been called. But during state restoration, Fragments get created
in `Activity#onCreate()` when the Activity’s properties may not have been initialised.
- When exchanging data between Activities, the `Activity#onActivityResult()` gets called before the Activity is resumed, and creating a Fragment when
a result is received will crash the app.
- Fragments are not resumed when `Activity#onResume()` is called. The documentation recommends using `Activty#onResumeFragments()` instead.
- Fragment lifecycle events are not synchronised with Activity lifecycle, and trying to do this introduces an extra layer of complexity. Race
conditions are difficult to avoid with an asynchronous lifecycle
causing [pain, suffering and misery](https://www.google.com/search?q=illegal+state+exception+fragment+android).
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers are the problems and complexities caused by the asynchronous lifecycle of Fragments compared to Activities, leading to bugs and race conditions. The desire to reduce complexity, avoid race conditions, and have synchronous UI state management are key drivers. Also, the need for easy animations and a manageable back stack for navigation are drivers. The trade-offs include reliance on a third-party library and loss of some built-in Android features like Activity-based data sharing.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a single Activity to hold all screens and avoid using Fragment classes entirely. Navigation between screens will be handled by the Flow library, which uses View classes for screens and provides a view-based backstack. This approach reduces complexity and race conditions by using synchronous View inflation and simplifies animations.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include adopting an unusual architecture that relies on a third-party library (Flow), which may require maintenance if neglected. The common community support for Fragment and Activity usage is lost. Also, the inability to use Android's built-in Activity data sharing mechanisms requires building and maintaining a custom solution.

alternatives.description: Continue using Fragments and Activities as per standard Android architecture.
pros: Standard approach with wide community support.
Built-in lifecycle management and back stack.
Android framework support for data sharing between Activities.
cons: Complex and asynchronous lifecycle leading to bugs and race conditions.
Difficulties in synchronizing Fragment and Activity lifecycles.
Harder to manage animations and transitions.

alternatives.description: Use multiple Activities for each screen instead of a single Activity with Views.
pros: Leverages Android's native Activity lifecycle and back stack.
Built-in support for data sharing between Activities.
cons: More complex transitions and animations between Activities.
Potentially higher resource usage due to multiple Activities.
Does not solve Fragment lifecycle complexity if Fragments are still used.

template_adherence.title: Forward compatibility for persistable enums from Server responses
template_adherence.context:
RESTful APIs tend to return enumerated values to represent properties with a fixed number of well-defined values. These are usually represented as `enum` classes on the client. When new business use cases are introduced, there could be additions to these values. If these values are consumed on the fly and are not persisted on the client, they could simply be treated as a special case (unknown) or ignored all together.

Simple is an "offline-first" application and some of these values have to be persisted to the database. Hence, these enumerated values cannot be represented using a Kotlin `enum` class. Offline-first means, there are some unique constraints that we have to deal with.

Apps on an older app version should be able to handle new enum values added to a type even though they don't know how to interpret the new value. This could be solved by adding an UNKNOWN fallback value which the server adds as well. Except,

* Records are shared between different users and thus, between different app versions. A newer app version that understands the new enum value could create a record with the new value and upload it, but an older app version that does not know the new value will overwrite it with UNKNOWN and this value will overwrite the actual value on the server as well when it syncs.

* An app on an older version could have a degraded, fallback experience for enum values it does not understand, but as soon as it updates, the app should be able to interpret the new values as if it was synced afresh.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle forward compatibility for enum values in an offline-first app.
- Enumerated values must be persisted to the database.
- Older app versions must not overwrite newer enum values with UNKNOWN.
- Ability to send unknown enum values back to the server during sync.
- Maintain data integrity across app versions and server.
- Developer awareness and enforcement of this pattern.
template_adherence.decision:
To maintain forward-compatibility with enum values, we have to roll out our own infrastructure. To accommodate, we use sealed classes to represent enumerated values so that,

- We could save these values to the database.
- Use these values in newer versions of the app.
- Send the same enum values back to the server during sync even though the current version of the app cannot interpret these values during runtime.

In order or achieve this, we require 4 classes.

1. A sealed class hierarchy that is used to represent the enumerated values. Which also includes an `Unknown(val actualValue: String)` data class which is used to capture and handle newly introduced values.
2. An implementation of the `SafeEnumTypeAdapter` class.
3. A `RoomTypeConverter` to safely store and retrieve newly added enum values.
4. A `MoshiTypeAdapter` to serialize and deserialize newly added enum values.

The `SafeEnumTypeAdapter` class is designed to map known enum values and handle unknown values gracefully.
template_adherence.consequences:

template_adherence.title: Material Design Components (MDC) Migration
template_adherence.context:
We have been using `Theme.Design.*` theme from the start, while that worked perfectly it did not allow us to use new material components because those are dependent on `Theme.MaterialComponents.*` app theme. Using new material components allows us to have much more control over component theming like text styles, icon & icon gravity, strokes, corners, etc.

- Right now we are using 3 different kind of buttons to satisfy various design requirements `Button`, `OmegaCenterIconButton` & `PrimarySolidButton`.
- Since all our Figma designs are made using material specs/material components, the design specs for certain components didn’t translate properly to appcompat variants or there are no components available in appcompat at all. Moving to MDC will make the design to layout/style much easier.

You can find more information on setting up MDC Android [here](https://material.io/develop/android/docs/getting-started/).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to use new material components that depend on `Theme.MaterialComponents.*` app theme.
- Desire for more control over component theming such as text styles, icon positioning, strokes, corners.
- Current use of multiple button types to satisfy design requirements is complex.
- Alignment with Figma designs that use material specs/components.
- Simplify design to layout/style translation by moving to MDC.
template_adherence.decision: Moving to MDC will allow us to use `MaterialButton` & other material components if needed. We will replace the current three button types (`Button`, `OmegaCenterIconButton`, `PrimarySolidButton`) with `MaterialButton`. This migration enables better theming support (corner radius, strokes, shapes) and icon support (icon, icon gravity, icon tint). The app theme will extend `Theme.MaterialComponents.Light.NoActionBar` and define styles for buttons accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Some component styles may break partially or completely due to the theme switch.
- Material theme will automatically convert any `Button` to `MaterialButton` internally using a custom inflater, which may break styles of components extending `Button` like `RadioButton`.
- Simplifies theming and aligns app components with material design specifications.
- Reduces complexity by removing multiple button types in favor of `MaterialButton`.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing `Theme.Design.*` theme and current button implementations without migrating to MDC.
pros: No immediate changes required to existing codebase.
Avoids risk of breaking component styles due to theme migration.
cons: Cannot use new material components dependent on `Theme.MaterialComponents.*`.
Limited control over component theming (text styles, icon positioning, strokes, corners).
Design specs from Figma do not translate properly to appcompat variants.
Maintaining multiple button types increases complexity.

template_adherence.title: ADR 010: Dagger Qualifier Migration
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for type safety when defining dependencies with the same return type.
- Avoiding developer errors such as typos in `@Named` values.
- Maintaining build performance with no additional overhead.
- Gradual migration strategy to avoid breaking existing code.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to migrate from using `@Named` annotations to using custom `@Qualifier` annotations from the `javax.inject` package for providing and injecting dependencies with the same return type. This approach improves type safety and reduces errors. Since `@Named` is itself a `@Qualifier`, both behave the same internally, so no build overhead is introduced. The migration will be gradual: new dependencies will use `Qualifier`s, and existing `Named` usages will be converted when modified or newly injected.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The codebase will temporarily contain both `Named` and `Qualifier` annotations during the migration period.
- Improved type safety and reduced risk of errors in dependency injection.
- No additional build overhead.
- Requires developers to adopt new `Qualifier` annotations for new or modified dependencies.

alternatives.description: Continue using `@Named` annotations for all dependencies with the same return type.
pros: No changes required to existing codebase.
Developers are already familiar with `@Named`.
No migration effort needed.
cons: Prone to developer errors such as typos in string values.
Lacks type safety.
Errors only detected at build time after Dagger graph generation.

alternatives.description: Use a different mechanism other than `@Qualifier` or `@Named` for distinguishing dependencies, such as custom wrapper classes or different types.
pros: Could enforce type safety through different types.
May provide clearer semantics depending on implementation.
cons: Requires significant refactoring.
May introduce complexity and overhead.
Not aligned with standard Dagger practices.

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: SQL Performance Profiling
template_adherence.context: The Simple Android app relies heavily on a local database, which can cause performance issues when running expensive queries on large data sets. Historically, performance optimization was reactive, occurring after production issues were reported, leading to degraded user experience and team stress.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to proactively collect SQL query performance data in production to identify and fix issues before they impact users; challenges posed by Room database abstraction and reactive query types; desire to minimize performance impact of instrumentation; maintainability and complexity of instrumentation approach; compatibility with build and minification tooling; handling of overloaded methods and paging library limitations.
template_adherence.decision: Adopted an approach combining Java Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) processing and runtime stacktrace analysis. This involves generating metadata about Room-generated DAO methods during build time using Javaparser, embedding this metadata in the APK, and at runtime, wrapping the SQLite helper to capture stacktraces and map query execution to DAO methods for performance tracking. This approach was chosen over bytecode manipulation due to complexity and maintainability concerns.
template_adherence.consequences: Performance impact is minimal, with stacktrace capture taking about 1 ms on low-end devices and sampling reducing overhead. Limitations include dependency on minification tooling preserving line numbers and no obfuscation, inability to track queries from the Paging library, and challenges with overloaded DAO methods which are handled by failing the build if detected. The approach enables proactive performance monitoring but requires awareness of these constraints.

alternatives.description: Bytecode processing using Javassist to insert profiling code into generated DAO implementations.
pros: Direct instrumentation of generated code.
Potentially comprehensive coverage of queries.
cons: High complexity and maintenance burden.
Tightly coupled to Room library version and generated bytecode structure.
Requires developers to understand JVM bytecode.
Deemed too expensive and complex for practical use.

template_adherence.title: The MVP will pass complex datatypes over the FFI using simple, explicit serialization
template_adherence.context:
Passing complex data-types from Rust to foreign-language code and back again can be, well, *complex*.
Given a Rust struct with named fields, and a corresponding autogenerated data class in the foreign language
bindings, how does one turn into the other?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Ensuring safety of the generated code.
* Fitting with our [MVP goal](./0001-mvp-webidl.md) of favouring initial-time-to-ship over performance.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option:
* **Option C: Implement a simple direct serialization scheme, pass them as serialized bytes.**

The choice here comes down to simplicity and safety for the MVP.

Serializing complex datatypes into a bytebuffer makes it easier for us to pass the data safely across the FFI,
because it strictly controls shared access to memory on each side of the boundary. Using our own simple
serialization scheme reducing the number of moving parts relative to third-party serialization libraries.

This choice comes with non-trivial performance costs, but that's acceptable for MVP.
We are likely to ***revisit this choice*** if the MVP of the tool proves successful
and expect that we can do so incrementally without changing the consumer-facing experience.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision prioritizes simplicity and safety over performance for the MVP, accepting some performance overhead due to serialization. It allows safe passing of complex data types across the FFI boundary with controlled memory access. The approach can be revisited and improved incrementally post-MVP without affecting the consumer-facing API.

alternatives.description: Declare complex datatypes using Protocol Buffers, pass them as serialized bytes.
pros: Familiar approach from existing components.
Good tooling for generating serialization code in various target languages.
Hard to mishandle data causing memory-safety issues.
cons: Complex setup due to calling protobuf code-generator inside own code-generator.

template_adherence.title: Let consumers opt out of HandleMap locking if their interface is threadsafe
template_adherence.context: Uniffi currently uses a very coarse locking strategy for managing concurrent access to object instances, which has caused us to accidentally ship code in a product that blocked the main thread on network I/O. We need to enable finer-grained concurrency control in order to provide the desired API for a key consumer. Currently, every interface has a corresponding ffi_support::ConcurrentHandleMap that is responsible for owning all instances of that interface and for handing out references to them in a mutability-safe and threadsafe manner. This ensures that the generated code is safe in the face of concurrent operations, but has a substantial runtime cost: only one method call can be executed on an instance at any time. Any attempt to call an object method while a concurrent method is already executing, will block until the previous call has completed. The desired API for Project Nimbus includes methods that will be called synchronously from the main thread, and hence must not block on network or disk I/O. Such an API cannot be built with uniffi as currently implemented.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Enabling consumers to control the potential blocking behaviour of their generated APIs. Ensure safety of the generated code. Ship a solution in a timely manner to unblock Project Nimbus.
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: Option B: Let consumers mark interface definitions as threadsafe to opt in to a less-locking handlemap. The choice here comes down to safety and simplicity. By making a more-concurrency-friendly handlemap we can maintain the current strict enforcement of Rust's mutability-safety and thread-safety guarantees, even in the face of errors in the generated bindings. It seems to be a relatively small change, and by making it opt-in we avoid creating busywork for other consumers who are not urgently facing this problem. One downside is that consumers need to opt-in to the fix, meaning that the default behavior may still be surprising to new consumers. We'll mitigate this with docs and will consider revisiting the default behaviour if the majority of consumers adopt the new approach. This choice does also punt some potential performance improvements to future work, but that seems in keeping with where we are in the project's lifecycle.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision enables consumers to opt in to a less-locking handlemap, improving concurrency and reducing blocking on the main thread for threadsafe interfaces. It maintains safety guarantees and is a relatively small change, but requires consumers to opt in, so the default behavior remains with the existing locking. It also introduces maintenance overhead for two handlemap variants and may cause some surprise for new consumers due to hidden mutexes in the default behavior. The decision punts some performance improvements to future work.

template_adherence.title: Use raw `Arc<T>` pointers to pass objects across the FFI
template_adherence.context:
UniFFI currently manages object instances using the `HandleMap` struct in the ffi-support crate. This means that external consumers of UniFFI-wrapped interfaces never see any pointers to structs - instead, they get what is (roughly) an index into an array, with the struct being stored in (and owned by) that array.

This has a number of safety characteristics which are particularly important for hand-written FFI interfaces, but it does cause some issues in evolving UniFFI in directions we consider important. In addition to the slight performance overhead, the use of `HandleMap`s makes it difficult to support:

* Passing object instances as arguments ([#40](https://github.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/issues/40)). Getting objects out of a `HandleMap` involves a closure, so accepting multiple object-typed arguments would involve code-generating nested closures.
* Returning object instances from functions ([#197](https://github.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs/issues/197)). Does the returned object already exist in the handlemap? If so, what is its handle? How will we manage the lifetime of multiple references to the object?

These restrictions mean that UniFFI's `Object` type is currently only suitable as the `self` argument for method calls, and is forbidden in argument position, as record fields, etc.

This ADR considers ways to evolve the handling of object instances and their lifetimes, so that references to structs can be used more widely than currently allowed.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* We desire the ability to have more flexible lifetimes for object interfaces, so they can be stored in dictionaries or other interfaces, and be returned by functions or methods other than constructors.

* We would like to keep the UniFFI implementation as simple as possible while providing a suitable degree of safety - in particular, a promise that it should be impossible to misuse the generated bindings in a way that triggers Rust's "undefined behavior" or otherwise defeats Rust's safety characteristics and ownership model (and in particular, avoiding things like use-after-free issues).

* We would like to keep the overhead of UniFFI as small as possible so that it is a viable solution to more use-cases.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option:

* **[Option 2] We replace `HandleMap<T>` with raw pointers to Rust's builtin `Arc<T>`**

This decision is taken because:

* We believe the additional safety offered by `HandleMap`s is far less important for this use-case, because the code using these pointers is generated instead of hand-written.

* Correctly implementing better lifetime management in a thread-safe way is not trivial and subtle errors there would defeat all the safety mechanisms the `HandleMap`s offer. Ultimately we'd just end up reimplementing `Arc<>` anyway, and the one in the stdlib is far more likely to be correct.

* There are usability and familiarity benefits to using the stdlib `Arc<>` rather than a special-purpose container like `triomphe::Arc`, and the way we currently do codegen means we're unlikely to notice any potential performance improvements from using a more specialized type.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive Consequences

* There will be less overhead in our generated code - both performance overhead and cognitive overload - it will be much easier to rationalize about how the generated code actually works and performs.

### Negative Consequences

* Errors in our generated code might cause pointer misuse and lead to "use after free" type issues.

* Misuse of generated APIs may be able to create reference cycles between Rust objects that cannot be deallocated, and consumers coming from a garbage-collected language may assume that such cycles will be collected.

alternatives.description: We extend the `HandleMap` abstraction to track lifetimes and support easier codegen
pros: Raw pointers aren't handed out anywhere, increasing safety.
cons: Need to reimplement safe reference counting or garbage collection.
Code generation is likely to remain somewhat complex.

alternatives.description: We replace `HandleMap<T>` with raw pointers to Rust's builtin `Arc<T>`
pros: Code generated by UniFFI is clearer and easier to understand.
Reuse the Rust standard library and have confidence in its implementation.
cons: Handing raw pointers around means bugs in the generated code or intentional misuse of the bindings might cause vulnerabilities.

alternatives.description: We replace `HandleMap<T>` with raw pointers to a special-purpose reference container
pros: Code generated by UniFFI is clearer and easier to understand.
Reuse an existing well-tested container type like `triomphe:Arc`.
The special-purpose container type may be more performant than the default implementation in the Rust stdlib.
cons: Handing raw pointers around means bugs in the generated code or intentional misuse of the bindings might cause vulnerabilities.
The special-purpose container may "leak" into the implementation of the UniFFI-wrapped Rust code, adding cognitive overhead for consumers.

template_adherence.title: Update the code or update the template wrappers?
template_adherence.context:
UniFFI was not able to support types from external crates because Rust's orphan rule prevents implementing the `ViaFfi` trait. In order to add support we needed to choose between updating the `uniffi` traits or updating the `lift_py` and `lower_py` scaffolding functions.

The same general question comes up often. When adding new features we often need to choose between two paths:

* Updating the code in the target language
* Updating the template wrapping code

This ADR discusses this particular decision and also the general pros and cons of each path.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: * We wanted to support external crates that define new types by wrapping an UniFFI primitive type. For example supporting `serde_json::Value` that wraps `string` or a `Handle` that wraps `int32`. We wanted this kind of wrapping code to exist outside of `uniffi` to allow for more experimentation with wrapped types and to support types that were specific to particular libraries (for example the application-services `Guid` type).
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option:

* **[Option 2] Update the `uniffi` code and generalize the `ViaFfi` trait**

This decision is taken because:

* It was relatively easy to implement wrapper types by allowing the external crates to add custom scaffolding code. This code could wrap primitive types because all lifting/lowering/reading/writing was handled by Rust code. If we had gone with option 1, then the wrapping code would need to hook into the template functions (`lift_rs`, `lower_rs`, etc.). We couldn't see a simple way to implement this.

* Updating the code in the target language results in more readable generated code. The newtype pattern makes the generated code more difficult to read, especially when types are wrapped in `Option<>`, `Vec<>`, etc.

* The same pattern could be used to implement wrapping on the bindings side.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive Consequences

* Paved the way for wrapper types.
* Simplified the template code.

### Negative Consequences

* Implementing wrapping with template functions can lead to more direct code. For example, lifting a integer value is a no-op, but we still generate a function call to do it. This is not an issue with Rust, since the compiler will optimize the call away, but it could be an issue for the bindings code. If we decide that it is an issue, we could go with a hybrid solution: generate the lifting/lowering code in the target language, but also have lift/lower filter functions that exist solely to optimize lifting/lowering simple types.

alternatives.description: Extend the template code to wrap the type
pros: Allows wrapping external types using the newtype pattern in the template code.
Generates code in filters to wrap lift/lower/read/write functions.
cons: Wrapping code would need to hook into template functions like `lift_rs`, `lower_rs`, which is complex.
Generated code can be more difficult to read due to newtype pattern especially with nested types.

alternatives.description: Update the `uniffi` code and generalize the `ViaFfi` trait
pros: Easier to implement wrapper types by allowing external crates to add custom scaffolding code.
All lifting/lowering/reading/writing handled by Rust code directly, simplifying template code.
Results in more readable generated code.
Pattern can be used on bindings side as well.
cons: Implementing wrapping with template functions can lead to more direct code and potential inefficiencies (e.g., unnecessary function calls).
Potential performance issues in bindings code if not optimized.

template_adherence.title: Event Subscription
template_adherence.context: In the light client (or any other client), the user may want to subscribe to a subset of transactions (rather than all of them) using `/subscribe?event=X`. For example, I want to subscribe for all transactions associated with a particular account. Same for fetching. The user may want to fetch transactions based on some filter (rather than fetching all the blocks). For example, I want to get all transactions for a particular account in the last two weeks (`tx's block time >= '2017-06-05'`). Now you can't even subscribe to "all txs" in Tendermint. The goal is a simple and easy to use API for doing that.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for users to subscribe to a subset of transactions rather than all.
- Desire for a simple and easy to use API.
- Support for fetching transactions based on filters.
- Limitations in current Tendermint subscription capabilities.
- Need to support multiple indexers with different APIs.
- Performance considerations for matching queries with many subscribers.
template_adherence.decision: ABCI app returns tags with a `DeliverTx` response inside the `data` field (for now, later possibly a separate field). Tags are a list of key-value pairs, protobuf encoded. These tags are parsed and matched with current queries (subscribers). If the query matches the tags, the subscriber receives the transaction event. A new package will be developed to replace the current `events` package to allow clients to subscribe to different types of events in the future. For fetching transactions, an indexing storage (Postgres, SQLite, etc.) will be needed for historic queries.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Same format for event notifications and search APIs.
- Powerful enough query capabilities.

Negative:
- Performance concerns with the `match` function when there are many queries/subscribers.
- Potential issues with too many transactions in the database.

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated.)

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implied alternatives include continuing with the current Tendermint subscription model which does not support subscribing to all transactions or filtered subsets.
pros: Simplicity of existing system.
No need to develop new packages or indexing storage.
cons: Does not support subscribing to subsets of transactions.
Limited querying and fetching capabilities.
Not user-friendly for filtered subscriptions.

template_adherence.title: Must an ABCI-app have an RPC server?
template_adherence.context:
ABCI-server could expose its own RPC-server and act as a proxy to Tendermint.

The idea was for the Tendermint RPC to just be a transparent proxy to the app.
Clients need to talk to Tendermint for proofs, unless we burden all app devs
with exposing Tendermint proof stuff. Also seems less complex to lock down one
server than two, but granted it makes querying a bit more kludgy since it needs
to be passed as a `Query`. Also, **having a very standard rpc interface means
the light-client can work with all apps and handle proofs**. The only
app-specific logic is decoding the binary data to a more readable form (eg.
json). This is a huge advantage for code-reuse and standardization.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a unified and standard RPC interface for all apps.
- Desire to avoid burdening app developers with exposing Tendermint proof logic.
- Complexity considerations in managing one server versus two.
- Importance of code reuse and standardization for light-client compatibility.
template_adherence.decision: We dont expose an RPC server on any of our ABCI-apps.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Unified interface for all apps

Negative:
- `Query` interface

Neutral:
- (No details provided)

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: Historical Validators
template_adherence.context:
Right now, we can query the present validator set, but there is no history.
If you were offline for a long time, there is no way to reconstruct past validators. This is needed for the light client and we agreed needs enhancement of the API.
template_adherence.decision:
For every block, store a new structure that contains either the latest validator set,
or the height of the last block for which the validator set changed. Note this is not
the height of the block which returned the validator set change itself, but the next block,
ie. the first block it comes into effect for.

Storing the validators will be handled by the `state` package.

At some point in the future, we may consider more efficient storage in the case where the validators
are updated frequently - for instance by only saving the diffs, rather than the whole set.

An alternative approach suggested keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
While it might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed, it would be more complex,
and likely less efficient.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Can query old validator sets, with proof.

### Negative

- Writes an extra structure to disk with every block.

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 005: Consensus Params
template_adherence.context: Consensus critical parameters controlling blockchain capacity have until now been hard coded, loaded from a local config, or neglected. Since they may be need to be different in different networks, and potentially to evolve over time within networks, we seek to initialize them in a genesis file, and expose them through the ABCI. While we have some specific parameters now, like maximum block and transaction size, we expect to have more in the future, such as a period over which evidence is valid, or the frequency of checkpoints.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have consensus critical parameters configurable per network and evolvable over time, avoiding hard coding or local config files. The parameters must be accessible and modifiable through the ABCI interface, and must support default values and special values (0 and -1) to indicate undefined or non-applicable parameters. The solution must maintain sanity checks and allow future extensibility.
template_adherence.decision: Consensus critical parameters should not be in the config.toml but optionally included in the genesis.json file and loaded into the State. Parameters not included get default values; 0 means undefined, -1 means not applicable. Parameters are used to validate blocks and transactions. The ConsensusParams struct can evolve by adding new structs. Enforcement rules apply to certain parameters. The ABCI interface (InitChain and EndBlock) is extended to handle ConsensusParams accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Allows specifying alternative capacity limits and consensus parameters without recompilation; parameters can change over time under application control. Negative: Increased complexity due to more exposed parameters; varying rules at different blockchain heights complicate fast sync. Neutral: Potential conflicts between TxSize validity checks and config's max_block_size_tx proposal sizes.

alternatives.description: Keep consensus parameters hard coded or loaded from local config files only.
pros: Simplicity in implementation.
No need to extend genesis or ABCI interfaces.
cons: Lack of flexibility to change parameters per network or over time.
Requires recompilation or manual config changes for parameter updates.

alternatives.description: Include all consensus parameters directly in the ABCI InitChain call.
pros: Centralizes all parameters in one place.
Potentially simplifies parameter passing at chain start.
cons: May expose parameters that the application shouldn't know about.
Could complicate the InitChain interface and increase coupling.

template_adherence.title: ADR 009: ABCI UX Improvements
template_adherence.context: The ABCI was first introduced in late 2015 as a generic interface between state machines and their replication engines, designed to be language- and replication-engine-agnostic. Recent community discussions identified pain points such as Amino encoded types, managing validator sets, and protobuf imports, which affect developer experience and compatibility.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to improve developer experience, maintain compatibility across languages and consensus engines, reduce dependencies and complexity (e.g., moving away from gogoproto and Amino), and ensure efficient and clear handling of public keys, addresses, validators, and blockchain headers.
template_adherence.decision: The ADR decides to move away from gogoproto in the short term by maintaining a second protobuf file without gogoproto annotations, and in the long term to use Amino. Amino will be removed from ABCI in the short term to simplify development, with plans to improve it as proto4. PubKey encoding will use a type string and bytes data without enums or oneof. Addresses will be simplified to SHA256-based computation. Validator messages will include addresses. RequestBeginBlock will include complete validator sets with voting info but exclude public keys. ResponseEndBlock will include validator addresses. RequestInitChain and ResponseInitChain will be extended to include full genesis info and allow app control over initial validators and consensus parameters. The Header will match Tendermint's header exactly for serialization compatibility.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include easier development on ABCI and identical serialization of ABCI and Tendermint headers. Negative consequences include maintenance overhead of alternative encoding schemes and duplicate types, and performance overhead of passing all validator info every block (though only addresses, not pubkeys). Neutral consequence is that ABCI developers must understand validator addresses.

alternatives.description: Continue using gogoproto and Amino as is without changes.
pros: No immediate changes required.
Maintains current compatibility and encoding schemes.
cons: Developer pain points remain unaddressed.
Continued complexity and dependency on gogoproto and Amino.
Potential incompatibility with other languages and tools.

alternatives.description: Adopt a single encoding scheme immediately, such as fully switching to Amino or protobuf without backward compatibility.
pros: Simplifies encoding scheme to one standard.
Potentially reduces maintenance overhead in the long term.
cons: High risk and effort to migrate existing systems.
May break compatibility with existing applications and tools.
Could alienate parts of the developer community.

template_adherence.title: ADR 010: Crypto Changes
template_adherence.context:
Tendermint is a cryptographic protocol that uses and composes a variety of cryptographic primitives.

After nearly 4 years of development, Tendermint has recently undergone multiple security reviews to search for vulnerabilities and to assess the the use and composition of cryptographic primitives.

### Hash Functions

Tendermint uses RIPEMD160 universally as a hash function, most notably in its Merkle tree implementation.

RIPEMD160 was chosen because it provides the shortest fingerprint that is long enough to be considered secure (ie. birthday bound of 80-bits).
It was also developed in the open academic community, unlike NSA-designed algorithms like SHA256.

That said, the cryptographic community appears to unanimously agree on the security of SHA256. It has become a universal standard, especially now that SHA1 is broken, being required in TLS connections and having optimized support in hardware.

### Merkle Trees

Tendermint uses a simple Merkle tree to compute digests of large structures like transaction batches
and even blockchain headers. The Merkle tree length prefixes byte arrays before concatenating and hashing them.
It uses RIPEMD160.

### Addresses

ED25519 addresses are computed using the RIPEMD160 of the Amino encoding of the public key.
RIPEMD160 is generally considered an outdated hash function, and is much slower
than more modern functions like SHA256 or Blake2.

### Authenticated Encryption

Tendermint P2P connections use authenticated encryption to provide privacy and authentication in the communications.
This is done using the simple Station-to-Station protocol with the NaCL Ed25519 library.

While there have been no vulnerabilities found in the implementation, there are some concerns:

- NaCL uses Salsa20, a not-widely used and relatively out-dated stream cipher that has been obsoleted by ChaCha20
- Connections use RIPEMD160 to compute a value that is used for the encryption nonce with subtle requirements on how it's used
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Security reviews identified potential vulnerabilities and outdated cryptographic primitives.
Desire to use more modern, widely adopted, and hardware-accelerated cryptographic functions.
Concerns about the use of RIPEMD160 and Salsa20 in current implementations.
Need to improve cryptographic security and performance while maintaining compatibility.
template_adherence.decision:
Use the first 20-bytes of the SHA256 hash instead of RIPEMD160 for all hashing purposes.
Compute ED25519 addresses as the first 20-bytes of the SHA256 of the raw 32-byte public key.
Replace xSalsa20 with xChaCha20 for authenticated encryption.
Use an HKDF instead of RIPEMD160 to compute nonces for encryption.
Note: The decision for Merkle Trees is marked as TODO, indicating incomplete decision documentation in that area.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Adoption of more modern and standard cryptographic functions with wider adoption and hardware acceleration.

Negative:
- The exact authenticated encryption construction is not already provided in a well-used library, potentially increasing implementation complexity.

Neutral:
- No specific neutral consequences detailed.

alternatives.description: Continue using RIPEMD160 and Salsa20 as currently implemented.
pros: No immediate changes required, maintaining current system stability.
Avoids potential risks associated with changing cryptographic primitives.
cons: Uses outdated and less secure cryptographic primitives.
Lacks hardware acceleration and wider adoption benefits.
Potentially vulnerable to future cryptographic attacks.

alternatives.description: Adopt SHA256 and ChaCha20-based constructions as proposed.
pros: More modern and widely accepted cryptographic standards.
Better hardware support and performance.
Addresses security concerns identified in reviews.
cons: Requires changes to existing implementations.

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: PeerTransport
template_adherence.context: One of the more apparent problems with the current architecture in the p2p package is that there is no clear separation of concerns between different components. Most notably the `Switch` is currently doing physical connection handling. An artifact is the dependency of the Switch on `config.P2PConfig`.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to separate concerns between components, reduce dependencies of Switch on configuration, simplify implementation and testing, and allow pluggable transport implementations.
template_adherence.decision: Transport concerns will be handled by a new component (`PeerTransport`) which will provide Peers at its boundary to the caller. The Switch will use this new component to accept new Peers and dial them based on NetAddress. This removes transport concerns from Switch and its dependency on P2PConfig.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include freeing Switch from transport concerns, enabling pluggable transport implementations, and removing Switch dependency on P2PConfig, making testing easier. Negative consequences include more setup required for tests depending on Switch. Neutral consequence is that multiplexed transport will be the default implementation.

alternatives.description: Keep the current architecture where Switch handles physical connection and depends on P2PConfig.
pros: No additional component or refactoring needed.

cons: Switch has mixed responsibilities, violating separation of concerns.

template_adherence.title: Secp256k1 Signature Malleability
template_adherence.context:
Secp256k1 has two layers of malleability. The signer has a random nonce, and thus can produce many different valid signatures. This ADR is not concerned with that. The second layer of malleability basically allows one who is given a signature to produce exactly one more valid signature for the same message from the same public key. (They don't even have to know the message!) The math behind this will be explained in the subsequent section.

Note that in many downstream applications, signatures will appear in a transaction, and therefore in the tx hash. This means that if someone broadcasts a transaction with secp256k1 signature, the signature can be altered into the other form by anyone in the p2p network. Thus the tx hash will change, and this altered tx hash may be committed instead. This breaks the assumption that you can broadcast a valid transaction and just wait for its hash to be included on chain. One example is if you are broadcasting a tx in cosmos, and you wait for it to appear on chain before incrementing your sequence number. You may never increment your sequence number if a different tx hash got committed. Removing this second layer of signature malleability concerns could ease downstream development.

### ECDSA context

Secp256k1 is ECDSA over a particular curve. The signature is of the form `(r, s)`, where `s` is a field element. (The particular field is the `Z_n`, where the elliptic curve has order `n`) However `(r, -s)` is also another valid solution. Note that anyone can negate a group element, and therefore can get this second signature.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to remove the second layer of signature malleability to ease downstream development.
- Desire to maintain the ability to expect a transaction hash to appear in the blockchain.
- Simplicity and ease of checking the canonical form.
- Alignment with existing solutions like Ethereum's approach.
- Consideration of implementation effort and maintenance overhead (forking a library).
template_adherence.decision:
We can just distinguish a canonical form for the ECDSA signatures. Then we require that all ECDSA signatures be in the form which we defined as canonical. We reject signatures in non-canonical form.

A canonical form is rather easy to define and check. It would just be the smaller of the two values for `s`, defined lexicographically. This is a simple check, instead of checking if `s < n`, instead check `s <= (n - 1)/2`. An example of another cryptosystem using this is the parity definition here https://github.com/zkcrypto/pairing/pull/30#issuecomment-372910663.

This is the same solution Ethereum has chosen for solving secp malleability.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Lets us maintain the ability to expect a tx hash to appear in the blockchain.

Negative:
- More work in all future implementations (Though this is a very simple check)
- Requires us to maintain another fork

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated)

template_adherence.title: Limiting txs size inside a block
template_adherence.context: We currently use MaxTxs to reap txs from the mempool when proposing a block, but enforce MaxBytes when unmarshaling a block, so we could easily propose a block thats too large to be valid. We should just remove MaxTxs all together and stick with MaxBytes, and have a `mempool.ReapMaxBytes`. But we can't just reap BlockSize.MaxBytes, since MaxBytes is for the entire block, not for the txs inside the block. There's extra amino overhead + the actual headers on top of the actual transactions + evidence + last commit. We could also consider using a MaxDataBytes instead of or in addition to MaxBytes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid proposing blocks that are too large to be valid.
- Desire to simplify configuration by removing MaxTxs.
- Need to account for overheads beyond just transaction bytes (headers, evidence, last commit).
- Consideration of MaxBytes vs MaxDataBytes for bounding block size.
- Maintainability concerns regarding constants if underlying structs change.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to remove MaxTxs entirely and rely solely on MaxBytes (renamed from MaxTxsBytes). When reaping transactions from the mempool, calculate the upper bound for transaction bytes by subtracting overheads (amino overhead, last commit bytes, evidence bytes, header bytes) from MaxBytes. Constants for overhead sizes are defined in the types package. ChainID length is bounded to 50 symbols. A test should be written to ensure constants remain accurate if underlying structs change.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Provides a clear way to limit block size.
- Reduces the number of configuration variables.
Negative:
- Requires maintenance of constants if underlying data structures change.
Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Continue using MaxTxs and MaxBytes separately.
pros: Familiar approach, no immediate changes needed.
cons: Risk of proposing blocks too large to be valid.
More configuration variables to manage.

alternatives.description: Use both MaxBytes and MaxDataBytes for finer control.
pros: More granular control over block and transaction sizes.
cons: Increased complexity.
Potential confusion over which limit applies when.

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: ABCI Events
template_adherence.context: ABCI tags were first described in ADR 002. They are key-value pairs used to index transactions. Currently, ABCI messages return a list of tags describing an event during Check/DeliverTx/Begin/EndBlock, with each tag referring to a property of the event. Since there is only one list of tags, recording data for multiple events in a single message must be done using prefixes in the key space. Alternatively, groups of tags can be separated by a special tag to denote breaks between events, allowing encoding of multiple events without prefixing, at the cost of special tags.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to represent multiple distinct events within a single ABCI message and improve the clarity and power of event indexing and querying, while balancing complexity in query syntax and implementation.
template_adherence.decision: Instead of returning a list of tags, return a list of events, where each event is a list of tags, naturally capturing multiple events during a single ABCI message.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to track distinct events separate from ABCI calls and more powerful query abilities. Negative consequences include more complex query syntax and more complex search implementation. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using a single list of tags with prefixes to distinguish multiple events.
pros: Simple existing implementation.
No changes to indexing or querying logic.
cons: Requires prefixing keys, which can be cumbersome.
Less clear separation of events.

alternatives.description: Use special tags to separate groups of tags constituting different events within a single list.
pros: Allows encoding multiple events without prefixing.
Maintains a single list structure.
cons: Requires special tags to separate events.
Adds complexity in encoding and decoding events.

template_adherence.title: ADR 024: SignBytes and validator types in privval
template_adherence.context: Currently, the messages exchanged between tendermint and a (potentially remote) signer/validator, namely votes, proposals, and heartbeats, are encoded as a JSON string (e.g., via `Vote.SignBytes(...)`) and then signed. JSON encoding is sub-optimal for both hardware wallets and for usage in ethereum smart contracts. Both issues are detailed in issue#1622. Additionally, there are no differences between sign-request and -replies, and no possibility for a remote signer to include an error code or message if something went wrong. The messages exchanged currently live in privval/socket.go and encapsulate corresponding types in types.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a binary encoding format easily parseable by hardware devices and smart contracts.
- Clear separation between sign-requests and sign-replies.
- Ability to include error codes and messages in responses.
- Compatibility with existing code and interfaces.
- Consideration of key management system (KMS) use cases.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to restructure vote, proposal, and heartbeat messages to use a binary encoding format (amino), split messages into requests and responses, and include an error type in responses. The ADR proposes specific protobuf-like message structures for Vote, Proposal, and Heartbeat, with corresponding SignXRequest and SignedXReply types. The SignBytes interface is updated to not require a ChainID parameter and to marshal the message using binary encoding. The ADR also notes that the public key handling and KMS considerations require further thought.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include easier parsing by hardware modules and smart contracts, clearer separation between requests and responses, and improved error handling due to error messages. Negative consequences include a relatively large refactoring effort touching many parts of the codebase and the need to modify interfaces that assume a Vote with an included signature. Neutral consequences are humorously noted but not substantive.

alternatives.description: Continue using JSON encoding for messages and keep the current message structure without separating requests and responses or including error codes.
pros: No changes required to existing codebase.
Maintains current interface assumptions.
cons: JSON encoding is sub-optimal for hardware wallets and smart contracts.
No error codes or messages in responses, limiting error handling.
No clear separation between requests and responses, potentially causing confusion.

alternatives.description: Use a different binary encoding format other than amino for message serialization.
pros: Potentially better performance or compatibility depending on chosen format.
cons: Requires evaluation and integration effort.
May not be as well supported or integrated as amino in the current ecosystem.

template_adherence.title: ADR 025 Commit
template_adherence.context:
Currently the `Commit` structure contains a lot of potentially redundant or unnecessary data. It contains a list of precommits from every validator, where the precommit includes the whole `Vote` structure. Thus each of the commit height, round, type, and blockID are repeated for every validator, and could be deduplicated, leading to very significant savings in block size.

The original tracking issue for this is #1648. We have discussed replacing the `Vote` type in `Commit` with a new `CommitSig` type, which includes at minimum the vote signature. The `Vote` type will continue to be used in the consensus reactor and elsewhere.

A primary question is what should be included in the `CommitSig` beyond the signature. One current constraint is that we must include a timestamp, since this is how we calculuate BFT time, though we may be able to change this in the future.

Other concerns include whether to include Validator Address, how to represent absent votes, and how to represent votes for nil and other block IDs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to reduce redundancy and block size by deduplicating repeated fields in the `Commit` structure, maintain necessary information for BFT time calculation (timestamp), ergonomic and debugging advantages of including ValidatorAddress, handling absent votes explicitly to resolve serialization issues, and clarifying representation of votes for nil and other block IDs. Also, considerations about future changes and backward compatibility influence the decision.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to deduplicate the fields and introduce a new `CommitSig` type in the `Commit` structure. The `Commit` struct will have Height, Round, BlockID, and a slice of `CommitSig` for Precommits. The `CommitSig` includes BlockIDFlag, ValidatorAddress, Timestamp, and Signature.

Timestamp is kept for now to maintain BFT time calculation. ValidatorAddress is included for ergonomic and debugging benefits despite increasing block size. Absent votes are included explicitly with no Signature or Timestamp but with ValidatorAddress to resolve serialization issues. Only three BlockIDFlag values are allowed (Absent, Commit, Nil), disallowing votes for other block IDs currently. Future support for other block IDs may be considered.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include significant savings in block size (up to 8kB per block for 100 validators) by removing redundant fields.

Negative consequences include a large breaking change to the block and commit structure and added complexity in code to differentiate between Vote and CommitSig objects.

Neutral consequence is that Commit.Precommits no longer contains nil values.

alternatives.description: Keep the existing `Commit` structure with full `Vote` objects for each precommit, accepting redundancy and larger block sizes.
pros: No breaking changes to existing structures.
Simpler code as no differentiation between Vote and CommitSig is needed.
cons: Larger block sizes due to redundant data.
Inefficient serialization and bandwidth usage.

alternatives.description: Remove the timestamp from `CommitSig` to reduce size further, switching to proposer-based time for BFT time calculation.
pros: Further reduces block size.
Simplifies `CommitSig` structure.
cons: Requires more analysis and work to change BFT time calculation.
Potentially breaks existing assumptions and requires a breaking change.

alternatives.description: Exclude ValidatorAddress from `CommitSig` to save 20 bytes per validator.
pros: Reduces block size further.
Simplifies `CommitSig` structure.
cons: Loses ergonomic and debugging advantages.
Lite clients cannot verify commits without downloading validator set.
Requires access to ValidatorSet to reconstruct votes.

template_adherence.title: ADR 029: Check block txs before prevote
template_adherence.context:
We currently check a tx's validity through 2 ways.

1. Through checkTx in mempool connection.
2. Through deliverTx in consensus connection.

The 1st is called when external tx comes in, so the node should be a proposer this time. The 2nd is called when external block comes in and reach the commit phase, the node doesn't need to be the proposer of the block, however it should check the txs in that block.

In the 2nd situation, if there are many invalid txs in the block, it would be too late for all nodes to discover that most txs in the block are invalid, and we'd better not record invalid txs in the blockchain too.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to detect invalid transactions earlier in the consensus process to avoid committing invalid txs.
- Maintain consistency and correctness of the blockchain.
- Minimize performance impact and avoid redundant validations.
- Ensure application logic can adapt to new interface methods.
- Consider network overhead of sending tx data multiple times.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to reject the proposed solution of checking all transactions in a block before sending a prevote due to the performance impact being too great, as referenced in issue #2384.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- More robust defense against adversaries proposing blocks full of invalid transactions.

Negative:
- Requires adding a new interface method, necessitating changes in application logic.
- Increases network load by sending all transaction data twice over ABCI.
- Causes potentially redundant validations (e.g., signature checks in both CheckBlock and DeliverTx).

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated.)

alternatives.description: Implement a method in BlockExecutor to check all transactions' validity in a block before prevote, using a new interface method checkBlock in Application to share the same state as deliverTx.
pros: Early detection of invalid transactions before prevote phase.
Prevents committing invalid transactions to the blockchain.
Improves robustness against adversarial blocks.
cons: Performance impact is significant.
Requires adding a new interface method, increasing complexity.
Increases network traffic by sending transaction data twice.
Potentially redundant validations leading to inefficiency.

template_adherence.title: ADR 030: Consensus Refactor
template_adherence.context:
One of the biggest challenges this project faces is to proof that the implementations of the specifications are correct, much like we strive to formaly verify our alogrithms and protocols we should work towards high confidence about the correctness of our program code. One of those is the core of Tendermint - Consensus - which currently resides in the `consensus` package. Over time there has been high friction making changes to the package due to the algorithm being scattered in a side-effectful container (the current `ConsensusState`). In order to test the algorithm a large object-graph needs to be set up and even than the non-deterministic parts of the container makes will prevent high certainty. Where ideally we have a 1-to-1 representation of the [spec](https://github.com/tendermint/spec), ready and easy to test for domain experts.

Addresses:

- [#1495](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1495)
- [#1692](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1692)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to prove correctness of the consensus algorithm implementation.
- Current implementation is scattered and side-effectful, making testing and confidence difficult.
- Desire for a 1-to-1 representation of the spec for easier testing and reasoning.
- Need for improved testability and separation of concerns.
template_adherence.decision: To remedy these issues we plan a gradual, non-invasive refactoring of the `consensus` package. Starting of by isolating the consensus algorithm into a pure function and a finite state machine to address the most pressuring issue of lack of confidence. Doing so while leaving the rest of the package intact and have follow-up optional changes to improve the separation of concerns.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Isolated implementation of the algorithm.
- Improved testability - simpler to prove correctness.
- Clearer separation of concerns - easier to reason.

Negative:
- None explicitly stated.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Keep the current implementation without refactoring.
pros: No immediate development effort required.
No risk of introducing new bugs due to refactoring.
cons: Continued difficulty in testing and proving correctness.
High friction in making changes to the consensus package.
Algorithm remains scattered and side-effectful, reducing confidence.

alternatives.description: Rewrite the consensus algorithm from scratch.
pros: Potentially cleaner and more modern implementation.
Opportunity to redesign with best practices from the start.
cons: High development effort and risk.
Longer time before benefits are realized.
Potential for introducing new bugs and regressions.

template_adherence.title: ADR 033: pubsub 2.0
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses issues in the initial pubsub design, including performance problems, ordering guarantees, blocking behavior, and interface design. It discusses the trade-offs between synchronous and asynchronous message delivery, blocking vs non-blocking sends, and the use of channels vs callbacks for message transmission.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for strict ordering of events, avoiding the slow client problem, ensuring idiomatic Go interface design, and providing subscribers with information about message tags and subscription cancellation reasons.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a MsgAndTags struct for messages, change Subscribe() to return a Subscription struct with Out(), Canceled(), and Err() methods, use buffered channels with capacity 1 by default for Out(), treat buffered and unbuffered channels differently in publishing, and terminate slow subscribers. This design aims to solve deadlock issues, provide more information to subscribers, and maintain strict ordering.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a more idiomatic interface, subscribers knowing message tags, and awareness of subscription cancellation reasons. Negative consequences include no concurrency in publishing messages since version 1. Neutral consequences are not explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Use goroutines per subscriber or per message to achieve asynchronous publishing.
pros: Improves performance by avoiding blocking on slow subscribers.
Allows concurrent message delivery.
cons: Complicates implementation due to managing many goroutines and channels.
May not guarantee strict ordering of events.
Potential uncontrolled memory growth.

alternatives.description: Use non-blocking sends with select default to avoid blocking on slow subscribers.
pros: Prevents system from halting due to slow or unresponsive clients.
Simplifies handling of slow clients by skipping messages.
cons: Slow clients may miss messages without notification.
Requires developers to ensure subscriber handling code does not block, which is difficult.

alternatives.description: Use callback functions instead of channels for message transmission.
pros: Gives subscribers more flexibility in handling messages.
Allows use of mutexes, channels, goroutines as needed.
cons: Can cause memory leaks or increased memory usage due to local scope.
Less idiomatic in Go compared to channels.

template_adherence.title: ADR 034: PrivValidator file structure
template_adherence.context:
For now, the PrivValidator file `priv_validator.json` contains mutable and immutable parts. Even in an insecure mode which does not encrypt private key on disk, it is reasonable to separate the mutable part and immutable part.

References:
[#1181](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1181)
[#2657](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2657)
[#2313](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2313)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to separate mutable and immutable parts of the PrivValidator file to improve structure and security considerations, and to specify file paths in configuration.
template_adherence.decision: Split the PrivValidator file into two structs: `FilePVKey` for immutable parts and `FilePVLastSignState` for mutable parts, then combine them into `FilePV`. Store `FilePV` in `config` and `FilePVLastSignState` in `data`, with file paths specified in `config.yml`.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Separation of mutable and immutable parts of PrivValidator.
Negative:
- Additional configuration needed for file paths.
Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences listed)

alternatives.description: Keep the PrivValidator file as a single structure without separating mutable and immutable parts.
pros: Simpler file structure.
No need to change existing methods or configuration.
cons: Less clear separation of concerns.
Potential security and maintainability issues due to mixing mutable and immutable data.

alternatives.description: Encrypt the private key on disk instead of separating mutable and immutable parts.
pros: Improves security by encrypting sensitive data.
Keeps file structure simpler.
cons: Requires encryption/decryption logic.
Does not address separation of mutable and immutable data concerns.

template_adherence.title: ADR 035: Documentation
template_adherence.context: The Tendermint documentation has undergone several changes until settling on the current model. Originally, the documentation was hosted on the website and had to be updated asynchronously from the code. Along with the other repositories requiring documentation, the whole stack moved to using Read The Docs to automatically generate, publish, and host the documentation. This, however, was insufficient; the RTD site had advertisement, it wasn't easily accessible to devs, didn't collect metrics, was another set of external links, etc.
template_adherence.decision:
For two reasons, the decision was made to use VuePress:

1) ability to get metrics (implemented on both Tendermint and SDK)
2) host the documentation on the website as a `/docs` endpoint.

This is done while maintaining synchrony between the docs and code, i.e., the website is built whenever the docs are updated.
template_adherence.consequences:
Because of the organizational seperation between Tendermint & Cosmos, there is a challenge of "what goes where" for certain aspects of documentation.

### Positive

This architecture is largely positive relative to prior docs arrangements.

### Negative

A significant portion of the docs automation / build process is in private repos with limited access/visibility to devs. However, these tasks are handled by the SRE team.

### Neutral
