template_adherence.title: Deliver Block
template_adherence.context: Some applications can handle transactions in parallel, or at least some part of tx processing can be parallelized. Now it is not possible for developer to execute txs in parallel because Tendermint delivers them consequentially.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to allow applications to decide how to execute transactions (in parallel or consequentially), simplify and speed up communications between application and Tendermint, and address the limitations of the current ABCI interface.
template_adherence.decision: Merge the existing ABCI steps (BeginBlock, EndBlock, Commit, DeliverTx) into one DeliverBlock step, introducing a new ABCI type to support this change while maintaining compatibility.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include simpler introduction and tutorials for new developers, ability to handle transactions in parallel, simpler interface, and faster communications between Tendermint and application. Negative consequence is that Tendermint should now support 2 kinds of ABCI.

alternatives.description: Keep the current ABCI interface with separate steps BeginBlock, DeliverTx, EndBlock, and Commit.
pros: No need to change existing applications.
Maintains current compatibility.
cons: Does not allow parallel transaction processing.
More complex interface with multiple methods.
Slower communication between Tendermint and application.

alternatives.description: Introduce a new ABCI type with DeliverBlock step while keeping the existing ABCI interface for backward compatibility.
pros: Allows applications to choose execution model.
Simplifies interface for new applications.
Enables parallel transaction processing.
Speeds up communication.
cons: Requires Tendermint to support two kinds of ABCI.
Applications need to change implementation to use new ABCI type.

template_adherence.title: ADR 039: Peer Behaviour Interface
template_adherence.context: The responsibility for signaling and acting upon peer behaviour lacks a single owning component and is heavily coupled with the network stack. Reactors maintain a reference to the `p2p.Switch` which they use to call `switch.StopPeerForError(...)` when a peer misbehaves and `switch.MarkAsGood(...)` when a peer contributes in some meaningful way. While the switch handles `StopPeerForError` internally, the `MarkAsGood` method delegates to another component, `p2p.AddrBook`. This scheme of delegation across Switch obscures the responsibility for handling peer behaviour and ties up the reactors in a larger dependency graph when testing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to decouple signaling peer behaviour from acting upon it.
- Reduce coupling between reactors and the network stack.
- Improve testability by reducing dependencies.
- Centralize responsibility for managing peer behaviour.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce a `PeerBehaviour` interface and concrete implementations which provide methods for reactors to signal peer behaviour without direct coupling to `p2p.Switch`. Introduce `ErrorBehaviourPeer` and `GoodBehaviourPeer` types to provide concrete reasons for stopping peers and ways peers contribute, respectively. Provide a concrete implementation wrapping the switch and another for testing purposes.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Decouples signaling from acting upon peer behaviour.
- Reduces coupling of reactors and the Switch and the network stack.
- Centralizes responsibility for managing peer behaviour.

Negative:
- Initial implementation adds a level of indirection by wrapping the Switch.

Neutral:
- None specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing approach where reactors directly call methods on `p2p.Switch` and `p2p.AddrBook` to signal peer behaviour.
pros: No additional abstraction or interface needed.
No changes to existing codebase structure.
cons: High coupling between reactors and network stack.
Responsibility for peer behaviour is split and unclear.
Difficult to unit test reactors due to large dependency graph.

alternatives.description: Introduce a different interface or abstraction with different method signatures or design patterns (e.g., event-driven or observer pattern) to handle peer behaviour signaling.
pros: Potentially more flexible or extensible design.
Could better fit certain architectural styles.
cons: More complex design and implementation.
May require more extensive refactoring.
Not chosen due to simplicity and sufficiency of the chosen interface.

template_adherence.title: ADR 042: State Sync Design
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the need for a StateSync feature to allow new nodes to receive a snapshot of the application state quickly without downloading blocks or going through consensus, facilitating faster node setup.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include performance (speed), safety, liveness, and implementation effort. Considerations include snapshot format, validation methods, performance characteristics, and security models (light client validation vs majority of peers).
template_adherence.decision: The chosen decision is to implement an eager StateSync approach with per chunk light client validation. This approach pre-computes efficient snapshots for sequential IO streaming and uses light client validation to avoid eclipse attacks inherent in majority peer validation.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a safe and performant design with real-world implementation experience, general interfaces for application-specific innovation, and a parallelizable implementation path with reasonable effort. Negative consequences include static scheduling lacking real-time chunk availability optimizations.

alternatives.description: Lazy StateSync: Snapshots are produced dynamically at request time using existing data structures, with chunking done lazily and dynamically. Validation tends to be per chunk using existing tree structures.
pros: Uses existing data structures without auxiliary data structures.
Per chunk validation aligns naturally with existing tree structures.
cons: Performance concerns with random reads and iterating through trees.
Potentially less efficient compression and snapshot serving.
More complex scheduling and chunk management.

alternatives.description: Eager StateSync: Snapshots are produced periodically and served from disk using auxiliary data structures optimized for batch read/writes. Requires honest majority of peers for manifest validation.
pros: Efficient compression and serving of snapshots.
Sequential IO optimizations.
Simpler snapshot serving once produced.
cons: Requires honest majority of peers for manifest validation, vulnerable to eclipse attacks.
Potential burden on block proposers if snapshot creation is synchronized with block creation.

template_adherence.title: ADR 044: Lite Client with Weak Subjectivity
template_adherence.context:
The concept of light clients was introduced in the Bitcoin white paper. It describes a watcher of distributed consensus process that only validates the consensus algorithm and not the state machine transactions within.

Tendermint light clients allow bandwidth & compute-constrained devices, such as smartphones, low-power embedded chips, or other blockchains to efficiently verify the consensus of a Tendermint blockchain. This forms the basis of safe and efficient state synchronization for new network nodes and inter-blockchain communication (where a light client of one Tendermint instance runs in another chain's state machine).

In a network that is expected to reliably punish validators for misbehavior by slashing bonded stake and where the validator set changes infrequently, clients can take advantage of this assumption to safely synchronize a lite client without downloading the intervening headers.

Light clients (and full nodes) operating in the Proof Of Stake context need a trusted block height from a trusted source that is no older than 1 unbonding window plus a configurable evidence submission synchrony bound. This is called “weak subjectivity”.

Weak subjectivity is required in Proof of Stake blockchains because it is costless for an attacker to buy up voting keys that are no longer bonded and fork the network at some point in its prior history. See Vitalik’s post at Proof of Stake: How I Learned to Love Weak Subjectivity.

Currently, Tendermint provides a lite client implementation in the light package. This lite client implements a bisection algorithm that tries to use a binary search to find the minimum number of block headers where the validator set voting power changes are less than < 1/3rd. This interface does not support weak subjectivity at this time. The Cosmos SDK also does not support counterfactual slashing, nor does the lite client have any capacity to report evidence making these systems theoretically unsafe.

NOTE: Tendermint provides a somewhat different (stronger) light client model than Bitcoin under eclipse, since the eclipsing node(s) can only fool the light client if they have two-thirds of the private keys from the last root-of-trust.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a safe and efficient light client that supports weak subjectivity in Proof of Stake blockchains.
- Limitations of the current Tendermint light client implementation which lacks weak subjectivity support.
- Desire to enable light clients to synchronize safely even after being offline for longer than the unbonding period.
- Trade-offs between bandwidth/computation efficiency and security in verification algorithms.
- Requirement to handle potential forged headers and evidence submission.
- User experience considerations for obtaining trust information from trusted sources.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to add the weak subjectivity interface for new or offline light clients, requiring initialization of a TrustOptions structure with trust period, trust height, trust hash, and optional callback for confirmation.

Two verification algorithms are described:

1. Linear Verification: Downloads all headers between TrustHeight and LatestHeight and verifies each.

2. Bisecting Verification: Uses a bisection algorithm to minimize downloaded headers, verifying headers recursively at midpoints until synchronization is achieved.

The client should submit evidence of forged headers to full nodes and retry with other nodes if necessary. Caching trusted headers is recommended to minimize network usage.

This approach balances safety, efficiency, and user trust assumptions in the light client design.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Provides a light client that is safe to use, allowing offline operation within limits.

Negative:
- Introduces complexity in the bisection verification algorithm.

Neutral:
- Social consensus mechanisms for trust establishment can be prone to errors when new clients join or after long offline periods.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing Tendermint light client implementation without weak subjectivity support.
pros: Simplicity: No additional complexity added to the client.
No changes required to existing systems.
cons: The client is theoretically unsafe as it lacks weak subjectivity support.
Cannot safely synchronize after long offline periods.
No mechanism to report evidence of misbehavior.

template_adherence.title: ABCI Evidence Handling
template_adherence.context:
Evidence is a distinct component in a Tendermint block and has its own reactor for high priority gossipping. Currently, Tendermint supports only a single form of evidence, an explicit equivocation, where a validator signs conflicting blocks at the same height/round. It is detected in real-time in the consensus reactor, and gossiped through the evidence reactor. Evidence can also be submitted through the RPC.

Currently, Tendermint does not gracefully handle a fork on the main chain. If a fork is detected, the node panics. At this point manual intervention and social consensus are required to reconfigure. We'd like to do something more graceful here, but that's for another day.

It's possible to fool lite clients without there being a fork on the main chain - so called Fork-Lite. See the fork accountability document for more details. For a sequential lite client, this can happen via equivocation or amnesia attacks. For a skipping lite client this can also happen via lunatic validator attacks. There must be some way for applications to punish all forms of misbehaviour.

The essential question is whether Tendermint should manage the evidence verification, or whether it should treat evidence more like a transaction (ie. arbitrary bytes) and let the application handle it (including all the signature checking).

Currently, evidence verification is handled by Tendermint. Once committed, evidence is passed over ABCI in BeginBlock in a reduced form that includes only the type of evidence, its height and timestamp, the validator it's from, and the total voting power of the validator set at the height. The app trusts Tendermint to perform the evidence verification, as the ABCI evidence does not contain the signatures and additional data for the app to verify itself.

Arguments in favor of leaving evidence handling in Tendermint:
1) Attacks on full nodes must be detectable by full nodes in real time, ie. within the consensus reactor. So at the very least, any evidence involved in something that could fool a full node must be handled natively by Tendermint as there would otherwise be no way for the ABCI app to detect it (ie. we don't send all votes we receive during consensus to the app ... ).
2) Amensia attacks can not be easily detected - they require an interactive protocol among all the validators to submit justification for their past votes. Our best notion of how to do this currently is via a centralized monitor service that is trusted for liveness to aggregate data from current and past validators, but which produces a proof of misbehaviour (ie. via amnesia) that can be verified by anyone, including the blockchain. Validators must submit all the votes they saw for the relevant consensus height to justify their precommits. This is quite specific to the Tendermint protocol and may change if the protocol is upgraded. Hence it would be awkward to co-ordinate this from the app.
3) Evidence gossipping is similar to tx gossipping, but it should be higher priority. Since the mempool does not support any notion of priority yet, evidence is gossipped through a distinct Evidence reactor. If we just treated evidence like any other transaction, leaving it entirely to the application, Tendermint would have no way to know how to prioritize it, unless/until we significantly upgrade the mempool. Thus we would need to continue to treat evidence distinctly and update the ABCI to either support sending Evidence through CheckTx/DeliverTx, or to introduce new CheckEvidence/DeliverEvidence methods. In either case we'd need to make more changes to ABCI then if Tendermint handled things and we just added support for another evidence type that could be included in BeginBlock.
4) All ABCI application frameworks will benefit from most of the heavy lifting being handled by Tendermint, rather than each of them needing to re-implement all the evidence verification logic in each language.

Arguments in favor of moving evidence handling to the application:
5) Skipping lite clients require us to track the set of all validators that were bonded over some period in case validators that are unbonding but still slashable sign invalid headers to fool lite clients. The Cosmos-SDK staking/slashing modules track this, as it's used for slashing. Tendermint does not currently track this, though it does keep track of the validator set at every height. This leans in favour of managing evidence in the app to avoid redundantly managing the historical validator set data in Tendermint
6) Applications supporting cross-chain validation will be required to process evidence from other chains. This data will come in the form of a transaction, but it means the app will be required to have all the functionality to process evidence, even if the evidence for its own chain is handled directly by Tendermint.
7) Evidence from lite clients may be large and constitute some form of DoS vector against full nodes. Putting it in transactions allows it to engage the application's fee mechanism to pay for cost of executions in the event the evidence is false. This means the evidence submitter must be able to afford the fees for the submission, but of course it should be refunded if the evidence is valid. That said, the burden is mostly on full nodes, which don't necessarily benefit from fees.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for real-time detection of attacks on full nodes, the complexity of detecting amnesia attacks requiring interactive protocols, the priority handling of evidence gossiping, the benefit of centralized evidence verification logic in Tendermint, the need to track historical validator sets for skipping lite clients, cross-chain validation requirements, and concerns about denial of service vectors from large evidence submissions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is that evidence detection belongs in Tendermint. Arguments (5) and (6) do not impose large obligations on Tendermint and can be managed by the app using Tendermint libraries. Although (7) raises concerns about DoS attacks, these can be mitigated out of band, for example by banning client IPs or using payment channels. A separate ADR will describe how Tendermint will handle new forms of evidence, including monitoring protocols and DoS management.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include no real changes to ABCI and Tendermint handling evidence for all apps. Neutral consequences include the need to be careful about denial of service on the Tendermint RPC. Negative consequences include Tendermint duplicating data by tracking all pubkeys that were validators during the unbonding period.

alternatives.description: Leaving evidence handling in Tendermint.
pros: Attacks on full nodes can be detected in real time within the consensus reactor.
Amnesia attacks detection is specific to Tendermint protocol and better handled internally.
Evidence gossiping can be prioritized via a distinct Evidence reactor.
All ABCI application frameworks benefit from centralized evidence verification logic.
cons: Tendermint duplicates data by tracking all pubkeys that were validators during the unbonding period.
Potential DoS concerns from large evidence submissions.

alternatives.description: Moving evidence handling to the application.
pros: Avoids redundant management of historical validator set data in Tendermint.
Supports cross-chain validation by processing evidence from other chains as transactions.
Engages application's fee mechanism to mitigate DoS vectors from large evidence submissions.
cons: Applications must implement all evidence verification logic.
Potentially more complex coordination for amnesia attacks.
Mempool and ABCI changes needed to prioritize evidence transactions.

template_adherence.title: Improved Trusted Peering
template_adherence.context:
When `max-num-inbound-peers` or `max-num-outbound-peers` of a node is reached, the node cannot spare more slots to any peer by inbound or outbound. Therefore, after a certain period of disconnection, any important peering can be lost indefinitely because all slots are consumed by other peers, and the node stops trying to dial the peer anymore.

This is happening because of two reasons, exponential backoff and absence of unconditional peering feature for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to maintain important peer connections despite reaching maximum inbound or outbound peer limits, and to overcome issues caused by exponential backoff and lack of unconditional peering for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce two new parameters in `config.toml`: `unconditional-peer-ids` to allow certain peers to connect regardless of max peer limits, and `persistent-peers-max-dial-period` to limit the dial period during exponential backoff for persistent peers. This approach was chosen over modifying persistent-peers due to complexity.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Allows node operators to ensure stable and persistent peering with trusted peers by configuring new parameters.
Negative: Introduces new configuration parameters that require explanation to node operators.
Neutral: None specified.

alternatives.description: Use only persistent-peers for outbound connections and handle id-only items as unconditional peers within persistent-peers.
pros: Simplifies configuration by using existing persistent-peers structure.
cons: Requires complicated structural exceptions due to different item structures in persistent-peers.
Does not cover full utility of unconditional-peer-ids for inbound connections.

template_adherence.title: ADR 051: Double Signing Risk Reduction
template_adherence.context:
To provide a risk reduction method for double signing incidents mistakenly executed by validators
- Validators often mistakenly run duplicated validators to cause double-signing incident
- This proposed feature is to reduce the risk of mistaken double-signing incident by checking recent N blocks before voting begins
- When we think of such serious impact on double-signing incident, it is very reasonable to have multiple risk reduction algorithm built in node daemon
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce risk of double signing incidents caused by validator mistakes
- Desire to have multiple risk reduction algorithms in the node daemon
- Need for configurable parameters to control the checking behavior
- Impact of double signing incidents is serious and justifies additional checks
template_adherence.decision: We would like to suggest a double signing risk reduction method. - Methodology : query recent consensus results to find out whether node's consensus key is used on consensus recently or not - When to check - When the state machine starts `ConsensusReactor` after fully synced - When the node is validator ( with privValidator ) - When `cs.config.DoubleSignCheckHeight > 0` - How to check 1. When a validator is transformed from syncing status to fully synced status, the state machine check recent N blocks (`latest_height - double_sign_check_height`) to find out whether there exists consensus votes using the validator's consensus key 2. If there exists votes from the validator's consensus key, exit state machine program - Configuration - We would like to suggest by introducing `double_sign_check_height` parameter in `config.toml` and cli, how many blocks state machine looks back to check votes - `double_sign_check_height = {{ .Consensus.DoubleSignCheckHeight }}` in `config.toml` - `tendermint node --consensus.double_sign_check_height` in cli - State machine ignore checking procedure when `double_sign_check_height == 0`
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Validators can avoid double signing incident by mistakes. (eg. If another validator node is voting on consensus, starting new validator node with same consensus key will cause panic stop of the state machine because consensus votes with the consensus key are found in recent blocks)
- We expect this method will prevent majority of double signing incident by mistakes.

### Negative

- When the risk reduction method is on, restarting a validator node will panic because the node itself voted on consensus with the same consensus key. So, validators should stop the state machine, wait for some blocks, and then restart the state machine to avoid panic stop.

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 052: Tendermint Mode
template_adherence.context:
- Full mode: full mode does not have the capability to become a validator.
- Validator mode : this mode is exactly same as existing state machine behavior. sync without voting on consensus, and participate consensus when fully synced
- Seed mode : lightweight seed node maintaining an address book, p2p like TenderSeed
template_adherence.decision:
We would like to suggest a simple Tendermint mode abstraction. These modes will live under one binary, and when initializing a node the user will be able to specify which node they would like to create.

- Which reactor, component to include for each node
- full
- switch, transport
- reactors
- mempool
- consensus
- evidence
- blockchain
- p2p/pex
- statesync
- rpc (safe connections only)
- *~~no privValidator(priv_validator_key.json, priv_validator_state.json)~~*
- validator
- switch, transport
- reactors
- mempool
- consensus
- evidence
- blockchain
- p2p/pex
- statesync
- rpc (safe connections only)
- with privValidator(priv_validator_key.json, priv_validator_state.json)
- seed
- switch, transport
- reactor
- p2p/pex
- Configuration, cli command
- We would like to suggest by introducing `mode` parameter in `config.toml` and cli
- `mode = "{{ .BaseConfig.Mode }}"` in `config.toml`
- `tendermint start --mode validator`  in cli
- full | validator | seednode
- There will be no default. Users will need to specify when they run `tendermint init`
- RPC modification
- `host:26657/status`
- return empty `validator_info` when in full mode
- no rpc server in seednode
- Where to modify in codebase
- Add  switch for `config.Mode` on `node/node.go:DefaultNewNode`
- If `config.Mode==validator`, call default `NewNode` (current logic)
- If `config.Mode==full`, call `NewNode` with `nil` `privValidator` (do not load or generation)
- Need to add exception routine for `nil` `privValidator` to related functions
- If `config.Mode==seed`, call `NewSeedNode` (seed node version of `node/node.go:NewNode`)
- Need to add exception routine for `nil` `reactor`, `component` to related functions
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Node operators can choose mode when they run state machine according to the purpose of the node.
- Mode can prevent mistakes because users have to specify which mode they want to run via flag. (eg. If a user want to run a validator node, she/he should explicitly write down validator as mode)
- Different mode needs different reactors, resulting in efficient resource usage.

### Negative

- Users need to study how each mode operate and which capability it has.

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 054: Crypto encoding (part 2)
template_adherence.context:
Amino has been a pain point of many users in the ecosystem. While Tendermint does not suffer greatly from the performance degradation introduced by amino, we are making an effort in moving the encoding format to a widely adopted format, Protocol Buffers. With this migration a new standard is needed for the encoding of keys. This will cause ecosystem wide breaking changes.

Currently amino encodes keys as <PrefixBytes> <Length> <ByteArray>.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to move away from amino encoding due to its pain points and performance degradation, adoption of a widely used encoding format (Protocol Buffers), the requirement to define a new standard for encoding keys, and the impact on ecosystem compatibility and upgrade paths.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to have the Cosmos-SDK define its own protobuf type for keys, allowing Tendermint to define only the keys used in its codebase (ed25519). The approach includes shifting all key encoding to protobuf, with custom marshal and unmarshal functions for amino where backward compatibility is needed. This will require a hardfork upgrade and will be implemented in stages via multiple PRs merged into a proto-breakage branch.
template_adherence.consequences: Keys will move to protobuf encoding, with amino marshal and unmarshal functions used where backward compatibility is necessary. Positive consequences include stable protocol buffer encoding, reduced amino overhead, and a large ecosystem of supported languages. Negative consequence is the requirement of a hardfork to integrate changes into running chains.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implied alternatives include continuing to use amino encoding or postponing the use of 'oneof' protobuf types for keys.
pros: Continuing with amino avoids immediate breaking changes and hardforks.
cons: Continued performance degradation and ecosystem pain points.
Lack of adoption of a widely used encoding format.
Postponing 'oneof' usage delays necessary work and may complicate future transitions.

template_adherence.title: ADR 055: Protobuf Design
template_adherence.context: Currently we use go-amino throughout Tendermint. Amino is not being maintained anymore (April 15, 2020) by the Tendermint team and has been found to have issues. Amino enables quick prototyping and development of features but does not provide the performance and developer convenience that is expected. For Tendermint to see wider adoption as a BFT protocol engine a transition to an adopted encoding format is needed. Several options are considered including Protobuf, FlatBuffers, and CapnProto, with pros and cons discussed.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for better performance, developer convenience, wider adoption, and support for multiple languages. The current solution (Amino) is unmaintained and has known issues. The ecosystem and tooling support of the serialization format are important factors.
template_adherence.decision: Transition Tendermint to Protobuf because of its performance and tooling. The ecosystem behind Protobuf is vast and has outstanding support for many languages. The approach includes keeping current handwritten types and creating a /proto directory for .proto files, with utility functions to transition between handwritten Go types and protobuf generated types, following recommended file structure from buf.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling modular types in the future, less refactoring, ability to pull proto files into the spec repo, improved performance, and tooling support in multiple languages. Negative consequence is the need for developers to update proto types when updating types. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Use Protobuf as the serialization format.
pros: Widely adopted and proven in production for many years.
Supported in many languages.
Good performance and tooling ecosystem.
cons: Requires maintaining proto files alongside handwritten types.
Developers must update proto types when updating types.

alternatives.description: Use FlatBuffers as the serialization format.
pros: More efficient than Protobuf due to no parsing/unpacking step.
Tested and used in production.
cons: Not widely adopted in the industry.

alternatives.description: Use CapnProto as the serialization format.
pros: Very fast data interchange format with no encoding/decoding step.
Supports random access and canonical form useful for determinism.
cons: Not widely adopted in the industry.
Less ecosystem support compared to Protobuf.

template_adherence.title: ADR 058: Event hashing
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses the problem of including events in the `LastResultsHash` in Tendermint. Previously, only certain deterministic fields were included in the hash, and events added to `ResponseBeginBlock`, `ResponseEndBlock`, and `ResponseDeliverTx` were not provable unless included in the state tree. The challenge is that adding or removing events breaks the `LastResultsHash`, requiring hard-forks, which is undesirable for evolving applications.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to prove events as part of the result, avoid hard-forks when events change, allow applications to evolve their event sets, and maintain consensus safety and upgradeability.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen decision is to add a new consensus parameter `Block#LastResultsEvents` which is a list of event types to be hashed into the `LastResultsHash`. This list can be updated via governance proposals, allowing networks to add or remove events without hard-forks. Initially, the list is empty, and applications can specify which events to include by updating this parameter.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to update the event list via parameter changes, avoiding hard-forks, and allowing flexible event additions without breaking consensus. Negative consequences include adding another consensus parameter and increased state tracking complexity in Tendermint.

alternatives.description: Add a `Hash bool` flag to each `Event` to indicate whether it should be hashed into `LastResultsHash`.
pros: Makes event hashing explicit at the event level.
Allows per-event control over hashing.
cons: Logic is implicit and depends on node operator's application code choice.
Less explicit and harder to upgrade via governance.

template_adherence.title: ADR 061: P2P Refactor Scope
template_adherence.context:
The `p2p` package responsible for peer-to-peer networking is rather old and has a number of weaknesses, including tight coupling, leaky abstractions, lack of tests, DoS vulnerabilites, poor performance, custom protocols, and incorrect behavior. A refactor has been discussed for several years ([#2067](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2067)).

Informal Systems are also building a Rust implementation of Tendermint, [Tendermint-rs](https://github.com/informalsystems/tendermint-rs), and plan to implement P2P networking support over the next year. As part of this work, they have requested adopting e.g. [QUIC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-transport/) as a transport protocol instead of implementing the custom application-level `MConnection` stream multiplexing protocol that Tendermint currently uses.

This ADR summarizes recent discussion with stakeholders on the scope of a P2P refactor. Specific designs and implementations will be submitted as separate ADRs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve the existing P2P package due to multiple weaknesses (tight coupling, leaky abstractions, lack of tests, DoS vulnerabilities, poor performance, custom protocols, incorrect behavior).
- Desire to maintain protocol compatibility initially.
- Interest in adopting modern transport protocols like QUIC and Noise.
- Concerns about breaking changes and resource intensity of maintaining own P2P stack.
- Stakeholder input including Informal Systems' plans and requests.
- Incremental approach preferred to reduce disruption and allow experimentation.
- Desire for improved testability, observability, performance, security, QoS, backpressure, and DoS resilience.
template_adherence.decision:
The P2P stack will be refactored and improved iteratively, in several phases:

* Phase 1: code and API refactoring, maintaining protocol compatibility as far as possible.

* Phase 2: additional transports and incremental protocol improvements.

* Phase 3: disruptive protocol changes.

The scope of phases 2 and 3 is still uncertain, and will be revisited once the preceding phases have been completed as we'll have a better sense of requirements and challenges.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:

* Cleaner, simpler architecture that's easier to reason about and test, and thus hopefully less buggy.

* Improved performance and robustness.

* Reduced maintenance burden and increased interoperability by the possible adoption of standardized protocols such as QUIC and Noise.

* Improved usability, with better observability, simpler configuration, and more automation (e.g. peer/service/address discovery, rate-limiting, and backpressure).

Negative:

* Maintaining our own P2P networking stack is resource-intensive.

* Abstracting away the underlying transport may prevent usage of advanced transport features.

* Breaking changes to APIs and protocols are disruptive to users.

alternatives.description: Adopt LibP2P instead of maintaining our own P2P networking stack.
pros: Potentially good idea in principle.
Could leverage a widely used P2P networking stack.
cons: Highly breaking protocol change.
Might require forking and modifying LibP2P.
Concerns about the abstractions used.

alternatives.description: Incremental improvements to the current P2P stack, add support for pluggable transports, and gradually experiment with LibP2P as a transport layer.
pros: Allows gradual improvement without immediate breaking changes.
Enables experimentation with LibP2P as a transport layer first.
Reduces risk by phased approach.
cons: Longer timeline for full adoption of new technologies.
Scope of later phases uncertain.

template_adherence.title: ADR 063: Privval gRPC
template_adherence.context:
Validators use remote signers to help secure their keys. This system is Tendermint's recommended way to secure validators, but the path to integration with Tendermint's private validator client is plagued with custom protocols.

Tendermint uses its own custom secure connection protocol (`SecretConnection`) and a raw tcp/unix socket connection protocol. The secure connection protocol until recently was exposed to man in the middle attacks and can take longer to integrate if not using Golang. The raw tcp connection protocol is less custom, but has been causing minute issues with users.

Migrating Tendermint's private validator client to a widely adopted protocol, gRPC, will ease the current maintenance and integration burden experienced with the current protocol.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve security and integration ease of the private validator client protocol.
- Desire to use a widely adopted, language-agnostic protocol.
- Existing use of protobuf in Tendermint making gRPC a natural fit.
- Need to simplify the protocol and improve maintainability.
- Support for metrics and security features like TLS.
- Consideration of upgrade path to minimize disruption to users.
template_adherence.decision: After discussing with multiple stake holders, gRPC was decided on to replace the current private validator protocol. gRPC is a widely adopted protocol in the micro-service and cloud infrastructure world. gRPC uses protocol-buffers to describe its services, providing a language agnostic implementation. Tendermint uses protobuf for on disk and over the wire encoding already making the integration with gRPC simpler.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include adoption of a standard secure communication protocol (TLS), use of a widely adopted communication protocol (gRPC), multiplexing requests over a single TCP connection (HTTP/2), and language agnostic service definitions.

Negative consequences include the added step for users to generate certificates to use TLS and the need for users to find a supported gRPC key management system.

Neutral consequences are not explicitly detailed.

alternatives.description: JSON-RPC was considered as an alternative but was not chosen because Tendermint extensively uses protobuf, making gRPC a more natural choice.
pros: JSON-RPC is a simpler and widely known protocol.
cons: Not aligned with Tendermint's existing protobuf usage.
Less efficient and less feature rich compared to gRPC.

template_adherence.title: ADR 064: Batch Verification
template_adherence.context:
Tendermint uses public private key cryptography for validator signing. When a block is proposed and voted on validators sign a message representing acceptance of a block, rejection is signaled via a nil vote. These signatures are also used to verify previous blocks are correct if a node is syncing. Currently, Tendermint requires each signature to be verified individually, this leads to a slow down of block times.

Batch Verification is the process of taking many messages, keys, and signatures adding them together and verifying them all at once. The public key can be the same in which case it would mean a single user is signing many messages. In our case each public key is unique, each validator has their own and contribute a unique message. The algorithm can vary from curve to curve but the performance benefit, over single verifying messages, public keys and signatures is shared.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve verification speed for validator signatures to reduce block times.
- Each validator signs a unique message, which affects the choice of verification method.
- Desire to minimize mistakes in verification API usage.
- Compatibility with existing Tendermint consensus and syncing processes.
- Support for curves that allow batch verification (starting with ed25519).
template_adherence.decision: Adopt Batch Verification as the method to verify multiple signatures at once, introducing a new interface with methods to add entries and verify them in batch. This approach is chosen over signature aggregation due to the unique message signing by each validator and potential slowdowns with aggregation.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Faster verification times if the curve supports batch verification.
- Negative: No way to identify which key failed verification in batch mode; failure requires reverting to single signature verification.
- Neutral: No impact on users other than improved verification speed.
- Implementation complexity added with new interface and fallback mechanisms.
- Initial support limited to ed25519 curve.

alternatives.description: Signature aggregation as an alternative to batch verification.
pros: Leads to fast verification and smaller block sizes.
cons: Not suitable currently because every validator signs a unique message, preventing aggregation before verification.
Potential slow down of 10x-100x in verification speeds if implemented with BLS in current context.

template_adherence.title: ADR 66: End-to-End Testing
template_adherence.context:
The current set of end-to-end tests under `test/` are very limited, mostly focusing on P2P testing in a standard configuration. They do not test various configurations (e.g. fast sync reactor versions, state sync, block pruning, genesis vs InitChain setup), nor do they test various network topologies (e.g. sentry node architecture). This leads to poor test coverage, which has caused several serious bugs to go unnoticed.

We need an end-to-end test suite that can run a large number of combinations of configuration options, genesis settings, network topologies, ABCI interactions, and failure scenarios and check that the network is still functional. This ADR outlines the basic requirements and design for such a system.

This ADR will not cover comprehensive chaos testing, only a few simple scenarios (e.g. abrupt process termination and network partitioning). Chaos testing of the core consensus algorithm should be implemented e.g. via Jepsen tests or a similar framework, or alternatively be added to these end-to-end tests at a later time. Similarly, malicious or adversarial behavior is out of scope for the first implementation, but may be added later.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for comprehensive end-to-end test coverage beyond current limited tests.
- Ability to test various configurations, network topologies, and failure scenarios.
- Feasibility constraints due to combinatorial explosion of test cases.
- Desire to have reproducible test environments locally and in CI.
- Limitations on scope (e.g., no comprehensive chaos or adversarial testing initially).
- Engineering resource constraints for building custom test framework.
- Need for integration with existing tools and workflows (Docker Compose, Go test framework).
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a custom end-to-end test suite that covers a broad range of configurations and scenarios by grouping functionality into global, local, and temporal classes to manage combinatorial complexity. The testnets will run in Docker Compose environments, configured via YAML files, and tests will be written using the Go test framework. The approach focuses on black-box testing via RPC interfaces, avoiding internal implementation details. The existing `testnet` command may be extended to support needed topologies. Comprehensive chaos and adversarial testing are out of scope for the initial implementation.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include comprehensive end-to-end test coverage of basic Tendermint functionality, reproducible test environments, and exercising common code paths as users would. Negative consequences include limited coverage of consensus correctness and adversarial behavior, the need to develop a custom test framework requiring engineering effort, potentially slower CI times, and operational overhead. Neutral consequences include lack of support for alternative infrastructure platforms like Kubernetes or VMs.

alternatives.description: Continue with the existing limited end-to-end tests focusing mainly on P2P testing in a standard configuration.
pros: No additional engineering effort required.
Existing tests are already in place and understood.
cons: Poor test coverage leading to serious bugs going unnoticed.
Does not test various configurations, network topologies, or failure scenarios.
Does not improve confidence in network functionality under diverse conditions.

alternatives.description: Use off-the-shelf testing frameworks or tools for end-to-end testing instead of building a custom solution.
pros: Potentially faster to implement if suitable tools exist.
May leverage community support and updates.
cons: No suitable off-the-shelf solutions appear to exist for the required scope.
Less flexibility to tailor tests to specific needs.
May not integrate well with existing infrastructure (Docker Compose, Go test).

template_adherence.title: ADR 067: Mempool Refactor
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the need to refactor the Tendermint Core mempool to support prioritized transaction handling instead of the current FIFO queue. It outlines the challenges with the current design and the desired properties for the new mempool design, including application-determined priority, efficient concurrent access, eviction policies, and extensibility.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for transaction prioritization by applications, efficient concurrent reads and writes, efficient transaction selection by priority for block proposals, fixed mempool capacity with eviction of lower priority transactions, efficient gossiping by priority, operator-configurable TTL for transactions, and extensibility for future features like replace-by-priority and multiple pending transactions per sender.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to introduce new fields 'priority' and 'sender' into the ResponseCheckTx type and implement a new versioned mempool reactor 'v1' that maintains a mapping from senders to transactions and indexes transactions by priority using a thread-safe priority queue (max heap). The design keeps the existing linked list for gossiping and supports eviction of lower priority transactions when the mempool is full.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling transaction prioritization by applications. Negative consequences include increased size of the ResponseCheckTx protobuf, loss of causal ordering, and potential transaction failures due to out-of-order execution. Neutral consequences include possible eviction of transactions that passed CheckTx if higher priority transactions arrive later.

template_adherence.title: ADR 068: Reverse Sync
template_adherence.context:
The advent of state sync and block pruning gave rise to the opportunity for full nodes to participate in consensus without needing complete block history. This also introduced a problem with respect to evidence handling. Nodes that didn't have all the blocks within the evidence age were incapable of validating evidence, thus halting if that evidence was committed on chain.

ADR 068 was published in response to this problem and modified the spec to add a minimum block history invariant. This predominantly sought to extend state sync so that it was capable of fetching and storing the Header, Commit and ValidatorSet (essentially a LightBlock) of the last n heights, where n was calculated based from the evidence age.

This ADR sets out to describe the design of this state sync extension as well as modifications to the light client provider and the merging of tm store.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to allow full nodes to participate in consensus without complete block history, specifically to handle evidence validation properly.
The desire to extend state sync to fetch and store recent light blocks to cover evidence age.
The need to integrate reverse sync into the state sync reactor and provide a P2P light client provider.
Maintainability concerns due to added code complexity.
Performance and UX improvements by using P2P for light client verification.
template_adherence.decision:
The state sync reactor will be extended by introducing two new P2P messages (LightBlockRequest and LightBlockResponse) and a new channel to implement a reverse sync protocol.
This protocol fetches, verifies, and stores prior light blocks so the node can safely participate in consensus.
A new light client provider will be created to use the P2P stack instead of RPC.
Integration involves running reverse sync after state sync and before fast sync or consensus, with state sync given access to StateStore and BlockStore to persist necessary data.
The Dispatcher and BlockQueue components will be used to manage concurrent requests and serialization.
Pruning will be restricted for blocks within the evidence age.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- All nodes have sufficient history to validate all types of evidence.
- State syncing nodes can use the P2P layer for light client verification, potentially improving UX and speed.

Negative:
- Introduces more code, increasing maintenance burden.

Neutral:
- No explicit neutral consequences stated.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative was to not extend state sync with reverse sync, which would leave nodes unable to validate evidence properly if they lack block history.
pros: Simplicity, no additional code or complexity.
cons: Nodes unable to validate evidence properly, leading to halting if evidence is committed on chain.
No improvement in UX or performance for light client verification.

template_adherence.title: ADR 069: Flexible Node Initialization
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to support more flexible node initialization in the Tendermint project, particularly to reduce API surface area and internalize interfaces while still allowing operational patterns such as introspection and component replacement. The current tightly coupled node implementation hinders modularity and maintainability, motivating a redesign of node initialization to be more flexible and less hard-coded.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to reduce coupling between components, improve maintainability, support future extensibility for component replacement, and avoid breaking existing user-facing APIs. Constraints include limited scope and resources, the desire to keep changes opaque to users, and the need to prioritize certain features like p2p-based statesync reactor.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to refactor the node package so that packages handle their own initialization, minimize code in the node package, reduce direct coupling, and iterate on a flexible internal framework for node initialization. Reactors should not expose interfaces within the node implementation. The refactoring should be opaque to users and not require reevaluation of the service.Service or a generic orchestration framework. No proactive system for injecting components is provided, but future retrofit is possible. Priority is given to implementing the p2p-based statesync reactor.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include improved maintainability, easier addition of services, ability to replace default components without vendoring, and thorough testing. Negative consequences include increased reliance on the service.Service interface, which has limitations, and a minimal scope that leaves many features for future work. Neutral consequences are not specified.

template_adherence.title: Migrate Timeout Parameters to Consensus Parameters
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the current situation where Tendermint's consensus timeout parameters are configured locally by each validator, leading to potential inconsistencies across validators. It explains the problem that these parameters should be uniform for proper consensus functioning and outlines the specific timeout parameters involved. The context also includes an overview of the proposed change to consolidate and migrate these parameters to network-global consensus parameters, along with reasons for consolidation and the impact on user experience and network operation.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for uniform timeout parameters across validators, reducing configuration complexity and confusion, maintaining proper consensus operation, and allowing applications to control these parameters via governance proposals. Other drivers include minimizing risk by providing safe defaults and ensuring compatibility with existing chains and applications.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement the migration of timeout parameters from local configuration files to network-wide consensus parameters, consolidating eight parameters into six. The ADR notes that the specific mechanism for introducing these new parameters to chains is still being decided, but the overall approach is accepted.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include uniform timeout parameters across validators and removal of superfluous parameters, improving UX and network consistency. Neutral consequences include that changing timeout parameters will require consensus. Negative consequences are not explicitly listed. The ADR also details the design and migration plan, including new protobuf message definitions and validation rules.

template_adherence.title: 9. Changes extended with task data
template_adherence.context: As a user, I want to get Changes metrics related to tasks defined in a task tracker. A simple usecase example is to get insight of the ratio of changes related to Feature Requests vs Bug fixing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Simple implementation
* No assumption about the tasks tracker
* Support of a set of generic fields related to a task
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "Monocle API provides an interface for external task data crawlers", because it will ease integration between Monocle and the various task trackers available in the market.

A Monocle operator will need to write the crawler for its own task tracker. However, over the time, operators might have written crawlers for most popular systems and released them under a open source license.

From the Monocle side, we provide a clear API for a task tracker crawler to push task related data to Monocle. Each task data sent to Monocle must at least set a predifined set of generic attributes like "severity", "change_url", "title", ... The monocle API is then able to find corresponding Changes in the database that match the "change_url" field.

Each changes get a new attribute called "task_data" that is a list of related task data records. Indeed multiple tasks might be related to a single change.

Also, Monocle keeps track of task data that do not match any Changes in the database. The Monocle change crawlers engine triggers a search for adoption of orphaned task data.
template_adherence.consequences: Not explicitly stated in the ADR text.

pros: Eases integration between Monocle and various task trackers.

cons: Requires operators to write their own crawlers initially.

alternatives.description: Monocle provides crawlers for most popular task trackers
pros: Out-of-the-box support for popular task trackers.
cons: Potentially more complex implementation.
Less flexible for less common or custom task trackers.

template_adherence.title: 1 ADR directory identified by marker file
template_adherence.context: The ADR utility is meant to be run inside a project, and initialize the ADR management in that project's file system. We would like to rely only on the project's file system, and make it versionable in traditional version control tools, e.g. git. To this end, all scripts in this utility must rely solely on the file system to find the correct location of the ADR files and relevant configurations. In order not to rely on some environment setting, we decided to opt for a special marker file, named specifically `.adr`, that will mark the location of the ADRs. Other options include to have an environment variable, rely on a naming convention, or specify it in a configuration in the root. The option of the marker file seems safest and at the same time simplest, with the least number of assumptions or conventions made by the user. The downside is of course that moving the file will potentially lead to malfunctioning scripts. At the same time, moving the marker file, with the ADRs to a new place is easy - just move the files. The only remaining assumption is that the ADR utility with a working directory that is a parent of the ADR. This is usually not a problem if the user is working on a specific project.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to identify the ADR directory reliably within a project's file system.
- Avoid reliance on environment variables or external configuration.
- Keep the solution simple and safe with minimal assumptions.
- Ensure version control compatibility.
- Allow configuration flexibility via the marker file.
- Minimize risk of malfunction due to file movement.

template_adherence.title: 4 Allow Overriding Configuration with Local Configuration
template_adherence.context:
The ADR flow tool is a command line tool for managing ADR files. It is aimed to be used in command line, in MS-Windows primarily, but also other platforms.

As a guiding principle, and in order to preserve simplicity, we don't want to introduce a separate data store. Data is stored and managed in files. This includes configuration, which should be explicit and easily identifiable and editable.

Given this, in [ADR 1](1-ADR_directory_identified_by_marker_file.md), we decided that the ADR directory is identified by a file called `.adr`. This file will also contain configuration of the tool. This is to reduce the number of moving parts; so the marker file (`.adr`) is used also as a configuration file.

Part of the value statement is for these files to be available in source control, and easily shared and collaborated on by a team. This means the marker file needs to be version-controlled as well.

At the same time, the configuration may change on a per-developer basis. For example, the location of the editor used to edit ADRs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to keep configuration explicit and easily editable.
- Avoid introducing a separate data store.
- Configuration should be shareable and version-controlled.
- Allow per-developer local configuration overrides.
- Maintain simplicity and reduce moving parts.
- Cross-platform compatibility (primarily Windows but also others).
template_adherence.decision:
We will keep the `.adr` file, with its current dual role - a marker file, and a *shared* configuration file.

In addition, we'll add the option to supply a `local.adr` file, with the same format as the `.adr` file, and allow a developer to specify properties to override there.

Properties that are specified only in `.adr` will have their values taken from there.
template_adherence.consequences:
Developers will need to specify a separate `local.adr` file for local configuration (overriding `.adr`).

In order to avoid overriding each other's configuration, the `local.adr` will need to be ignored by the version control system used, e.g. added to `.gitignore` if git is used.

alternatives.description: Introduce a separate configuration file, distinct from the marker file `.adr`.
pros: Clear separation of marker and configuration files.
Potentially easier to manage configuration independently.
cons: Always have a separate configuration file, increasing complexity.
Makes sharing configuration slightly harder.
Harder to share some configuration and customize others.

alternatives.description: Use environment variables for configuration.
pros: No need for additional files.
Configuration can be set per environment easily.
cons: OS-dependent, reducing portability.
Configuration is less explicit and harder to track.
Harder to share configuration across a team.

template_adherence.title: 5 Utility Context Lazily Initialized
template_adherence.context: The synchronous utils are intended to be used by commands to work on ADRs, with the given context of the project, e.g. the adr marker file. Since the context is mandatory (the ADR directory, existing ADRs), it is initialized at the beginning, in the object's constructor. Several commands (scripts) already include that script, and initialize the object on the script loading, as part of the require statement. This resulted in loading the context whenever a command is loaded. This might have performance implications, but the more immediate functional lacuna is that this then assumes that the context can be loaded every time. Of course, this assumption breaks - when running the init command, where by definition there is no context to load - the init command creates that. This resulted in trying to run the init command, on an existing directory, in an error.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Performance implications of loading context eagerly; functional issues when context is not available (e.g., during init command); need to avoid errors when context is not present; desire to load context only when needed; memoization to avoid repeated context creation.
template_adherence.decision: The ADR project context will be loaded lazily, only when needed. This assumes the init command doesn't require it, and hence will not invoke any commands that require that context (e.g. the existing files). So any command that is loaded can still create the context object and create an instance of, but the actual context will be loaded lazily. This assumption seems safe enough since init command indeed creates the context (the .adr file). Commands that will require the ADR context will continue to use it as today, and it will be loaded lazily. Memoization will be used to avoid repeated context creation.
template_adherence.consequences: ADR context will be created when necessary, and cached to be used throughout the command execution.

template_adherence.title: 7 Defining Customizations
template_adherence.context:
The need to customize different features in the tool raises the question of how to specify the customization.

On the one hand, there's a need to offer flexibility and expressive power. Assuming the average user is a competent developer, the most obvious way to achieve this  is to enable
some kind of a programming interface/definition.
Given that the tool is written in JS, it's reasonable to assume a definition that will be done in JS as well.
This might be too much power, resulting in potential performance/bugs/security issues.

On the other hand, there's the motivation to keep the tool simple enough, so configuration is minimal, but still expressive.

We can always start with a limited definition, but with an eye for further extensions. In any case, we'd like customizations to happen in a consistent and uniform manner.

This in a sense extends/generalizes the [decision to allow more permissive file names](3-Allow_More_Permissive_File_Names.md) by simply allowing any kind of customized file names, when working with the file name customization.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for flexibility and expressive power in customization.
- Assumption that users are competent developers.
- Desire to keep the tool simple with minimal but expressive configuration.
- Potential risks of too much power (performance, bugs, security).
- Desire for consistent and uniform customization approach.
- Future extensibility of customization methods.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a JS-based customization method by defining a file called `adr_custom.js` in the ADR directory. This file will contain simple JS code with predefined objects as per the tool's API, structured as a module (using `module.export`). This approach assumes users are competent enough to handle simple scripting and leaves limitations to specific features.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Features requiring customization must read the `adr_custom.js` file.
- Documentation is needed for the expected objects in the customization file.
- Enables future extensions through JS-based customization.
- Assumes user competency in scripting.
- Potential complexity in customization is managed by limiting specific features.

alternatives.description:
Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR, but implied alternatives include:
- Using a simpler configuration format instead of JS (e.g., JSON, YAML).
- Not allowing customization or limiting it severely.
- Using a different programming language or interface for customization.
pros: JS-based customization offers high flexibility and expressive power.
Leverages the existing knowledge of users familiar with JS.
Allows future extensions easily.
cons: Potential for performance, bugs, and security issues due to powerful scripting.
Requires users to be competent in JS scripting.
May complicate the tool compared to simpler configuration methods.

template_adherence.title: 8 Remove ADR Util Sync Module
template_adherence.context: The ADR Util module grew as an attempt to centralize a list of utility functions that require the context of the ADR file and directory. The resulting module was very central to the logic of the entire program, but resulted in a module that had too much differing concerns (too many responsibilities/reasons to change). This has eventually resulted in tangled code, and sometimes to (unintentional) circular dependencies, e.g. as when trying to isolate the handling of links. At the same time, the usage of the shared context - ADR files and directory - hasn't proved that useful in most case. In the cases where it should be used, it can be defined and cached.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR Util module had too many responsibilities, causing tangled code and circular dependencies. The shared context usage was not very useful in most cases. There was a need to isolate concerns and improve modularity by dividing utilities into more focused modules.
template_adherence.decision: Divide the utilities defined in this module to other, more focused modules (under `core` directory): 1. `files.js`: handles all file reading and writing 2. `adrobj.js`: handles all ADR logical-level operations. Essentially linking the ID to the file. 3. `links.js`: handles logic around linking ADRs. In cases where caching the ADR files is needed, e.g. in `adrobj.js`, it is done in that module.
template_adherence.consequences: In some cases, the API has to change - instead of the API defined at the logical ADR level (the ADR ID), it is defined at the file level, and client modules (namely commands) need to bridge the gap. In cases we see that this repeats itself, we can add a wrapping in the `adrobj` module to bridge the gap; e.g. as it is done for the `contentOf` function.

template_adherence.title: Do not duplicate validation performed by the server-side.
template_adherence.context:
many APIs impose restrictions on their parameters. Names may have
length limits, or strings may need to conform to specific formats, or ranges
must be non-empty. It is tempting to validate these arguments in the
client-side, since we *know* the API will fail if it is allowed to continue with
the invalid parameters. However, any such validation is redundant, since the
server is going to validate its inputs as well. Furthermore, any such validation
is wasteful: most of the time the application will pass on valid arguments,
checking them twice is just wasting client-side CPU cycles. Moreover, the
server-side is the source of truth, so having the validations performed on the
client side will require extra work if the server restrictions are ever
modified.
template_adherence.decision:
the client libraries do not validate any of the request parameters
beyond what is required to avoid local crashes.
template_adherence.consequences:
the main downsides are:

- The error messages could be better if generated locally.
- The server must validate all inputs correctly.
- Sometimes, we will need to validate inputs to avoid library crashes, and that
will be confusing because it will seem like a violation of this ADR.

template_adherence.title: The GCS Library uses optional fields only for sub-objects.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to handle JSON fields that may be absent, the semantic differences between empty/default values and missing fields, and the usability of the API for client applications. The design should balance ease of use for common cases with correctness and clarity when fields are optional or filtered.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use plain types (e.g., std::string, std::vector, int, bool) for fields where the default value is semantically equivalent to the field being absent, and to use optional<> only for object fields where the distinction matters. Additionally, convenience functions are provided for optional fields to facilitate usage.
template_adherence.consequences: The approach makes most fields easy to use in typical cases but introduces ambiguity when fields are filtered and default values may be indistinguishable from missing fields. It requires more careful design and testing to handle optional fields correctly, potentially leading to crashes during testing or the need for defensive programming.

alternatives.description: Use optional<T> for all fields regardless of type.
pros: Clear semantic distinction between missing and default values for all fields.
Consistent API usage pattern.
cons: More cumbersome to use for simple fields where default values suffice.
Increased complexity in client code.

alternatives.description: Use plain types for all fields, ignoring optional semantics.
pros: Simpler API and usage.
No need for optional handling.
cons: Cannot distinguish between missing and default values.
Potential semantic errors when fields are filtered or missing.

template_adherence.title: Functions should report errors using `StatusOr<T>` instead of throwing exceptions.
template_adherence.context: We know there will be users of these C++ libraries who want to use C++ exceptions as well as those who are not able to. Our C++ libraries must work for all of our users, regardless of their ability to use exceptions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Users have different capabilities and preferences regarding exception handling; the library must support both users who can use exceptions and those who cannot. Consistency and usability across all users are important.
template_adherence.decision: None of our APIs will throw exceptions to indicate errors. Instead, our APIs will typically report errors to callers by returning a `Status` or `StatusOr<T>` object, unless the library we're using has another non-throwing way to report errors (e.g., badbit in the standard I/O library).
template_adherence.consequences: This decision results in a single set of APIs and a consistent vocabulary for all users, whether or not they choose to compile with exceptions. It does not prevent callers from using exceptions in their own code. A downside is that APIs will not be natural or idiomatic for users who prefer exceptions. Changing existing APIs is a breaking change, with plans to change some components immediately and others later, communicated separately.

alternatives.description: Continue throwing exceptions for error reporting in APIs.
pros: Natural and idiomatic for users who prefer exceptions.
Aligns with common C++ practices.
cons: Not all users can or want to use exceptions.
Inconsistent experience for users unable to use exceptions.

alternatives.description: Use other non-throwing error reporting mechanisms (e.g., error codes).
pros: Avoids exceptions, compatible with all users.
Simple error reporting mechanism.
cons: Less expressive than `StatusOr<T>`.
May lead to inconsistent or less informative error handling.

template_adherence.title: We will not distribute/own/maintain binary packages, but we will support others doing so within reason.
template_adherence.context: Compiling google-cloud-cpp from source is not always possible nor desired by all users. Some users may want to install a binary package that contains our public headers and pre-compiled libraries so that they can link against our library. There is no single standard binary package manager in C++, instead there are a variety of others that users might want to use (e.g., dpkg, rpm, vcpkg).
template_adherence.decision: We will not directly support nor provide any binary packages. We will not test binary distributions of our code. And we will not host configs for binary distributions, since that would involve hosting files which we do not test. However, we will do our best to make our code easily packageable by others in a wide variety of formats. For more context, see [#333](https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-cpp/issues/333).
template_adherence.consequences: This decision will shield from endorsing any particular binary package management system. Other individuals who want to build and maintain a binary distribution of our code may do so without our permission or knowledge. If they need small and reasonable tweaks from us to support their binary distributions, they may file an issue and we'll do our best to accommodate them within reason.

template_adherence.title: Credential refresh failures participate in retry loop.
template_adherence.context: many credential types require fetching tokens from a remote service. For example, service account impersonation credentials must obtain an access token (which are time limited) by contacting the [IAM service account credentials] service. Likewise, for services without [self-signed JWT] support (e.g. GCS) the access tokens must be obtained via a separate service. The question arises: should we use a retry loop to refresh the credentials? Or should rely on the retry loop of the RPC that triggers a token refresh?
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to handle token refresh failures properly, deciding whether to have a separate retry loop for credential refresh or to integrate it into the overall retry loop of RPCs. Considerations include complexity for customers, behavior of retry loops, and handling of non-idempotent operations triggering token refreshes.
template_adherence.decision: No separate loop to refresh credentials; the failures participate in the overall retry loop.
template_adherence.consequences: Customers have one less retry loop to consider. Avoids surprising behavior where some RPCs take longer or shorter to fail than configured by the main retry loop. However, token refresh failures triggered by non-idempotent operations can cause issues. Mitigation includes using background threads to refresh tokens before expiry, which can be retried independently.

alternatives.description: Retry the token refresh but only use remaining time.
pros: Uses existing retry strategy for token refresh.
Ensures token refresh respects overall retry policy time and error count.
cons: Requires changing all stubs and decorators to consume a retry policy.
Increases complexity of implementation.

template_adherence.title: 4. In-depth katas are separated from "normal" katas
template_adherence.context:
I (Wolfram) am writing most of the katas and slowly I see a pattern arising in how I write them and also of which depth
I want them to be. Lately some things made me think about in-depth versions of katas.
One was writing the ES10 `Object.fromEntries()` kata. Writing this kata took me more than a week, every evening
figuring out certain details of the spec and how to transport those into a kata. This made me realize that
this kata has become too complex to get just a feeling for how `Object.fromEntries()` works, and it also made
me realize that I want this depth because I don't want to write any kata that states wrong things.
But this kata has simply become too big and too detailed.
Discussing this at #jscc19 and also at the #jslang meetup, I realized that people would appreciate a simple
introductory kata, which allows one to learn the feature (superficially) and have an in-depth or expert kata,
which covers all specifics that might be described in the spec.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to separate katas by depth to cater to different learning needs.
The complexity and length of in-depth katas making them unsuitable as introductory material.
The desire to avoid incorrect or misleading information in katas.
Community feedback indicating a preference for both simple and in-depth katas.
template_adherence.decision:
Katas will be created in two flavors: simple and in-depth.
For example, the `Object.fromEntries()` kata will have two separate files and metadata: one simple and one in-depth.
Simple katas focus on understanding and using the feature.
In-depth katas cover edge cases, type coercion, and detailed behavior.
template_adherence.consequences:
There will be more katas overall.
Simple katas will be easier to solve and less complex, facilitating learning.
In-depth katas will provide detailed, expert-level understanding.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative is to keep all katas as a single version regardless of depth.
pros: Simplicity in managing a single kata per feature.
No need to maintain multiple versions.
cons: Katas may become too complex or too superficial for some learners.
Risk of either overwhelming beginners or not providing enough depth for experts.
