template_adherence.title: 5. Kata naming
template_adherence.context:
The more katas come to life and the more overlap between es6, es7, es8, etc. versions exist the more a structure is needed on how to allow grouping the katas in any other form. One example. ES6 has katas in the group "Array API", "Object API", "String API", etc. ES1, ES7, ES10 and other also have katas that have the same group names and that is logically correct.

In order to make these easy to use and allow grouping, for example all Array-API-katas into one group and present them on the website (or somewhere else), the groups must be used consistently.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a consistent structure to group katas across different ECMAScript versions and other libraries to make them easier to use and understand.
template_adherence.decision:
Many katas can be put into the following X groups and this is done across the board (not only for language katas, also for libraries, etc.) in order to have a coherent structure and make it easier for the user's to understand where to look for katas.

The "Xxx API" katas: group name "Xxx API", directory naming convention, contents including basics and API overview katas.

Syntax katas: katas that help to learn JavaScript syntax.

Consideration of other kata types to be described or standardized.
template_adherence.consequences: Kata groups become easier to identify and understand, potentially leading to better visualization and usefulness of katas/topics across language versions.

template_adherence.title: 001 - Feature Flags
template_adherence.context:
We need to add a mechanism to toggle features in MMW so that we can deploy multiple implementations from the same codebase. For example, in BiG CZ, we'll need to disable Analyze mode and other MMW-specific features such as ITSI integration.

Primary deciding factors:

* How will this impact development?
* How easy will it be to switch from MMW to BiGCZ?
* How will this impact deployments?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Primary deciding factors:

* How will this impact development?
* How easy will it be to switch from MMW to BiGCZ?
* How will this impact deployments?
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided to follow existing conventions to add custom settings to MMW to support BiG CZ instead of adding a feature flipper library.

Because flags will rarely change, and we don't need any advanced features beyond swiching boolean flags, the overhead of adding and maintaining another dependency may not be worthwhile.
By storing custom settings in Python instead of the database, we'll avoid the need to enhance our deployment process to support loading data fixtures. Switching between MMW and BiG CZ will be done by using an environment variable.
template_adherence.consequences: There may be long-running consequences to disabling entire features using flags, no matter which implementation we choose. We'll need to be careful to make sure that the work we do on BiG CZ doesn't negatively impact the functionality of MMW and vice versa.

alternatives.description: Considered several feature flag libraries and a custom code approach.
pros: gargoyle-yplan: Actively maintained fork, can add default values in settings.py, flags stored in database
django-waffle: Popular, good documentation, has JavaScript interface, flags stored in database
Custom code: No database required, existing conventions in place for custom settings
cons: gutter-django: Too complicated, not actively maintained
gargoyle-yplan: Documentation not great
django-waffle: Not very active

template_adherence.title: Switching to Collections API
template_adherence.context: The geoprocessing service currently runs in an Apache Spark container using Spark JobServer with RDDs for layer reading. However, since it runs on a single machine, it does not leverage parallelism effectively, resulting in significant overhead and limited performance benefits.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve geoprocessing performance by reducing overhead and increasing speed, simplify code and deployment by removing Spark and Docker dependencies, and maintain or improve accuracy of results. Also, compatibility with Java 8 and changes in service interaction (synchronous vs asynchronous) are considerations.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt the GeoTrellis 1.0 Collections API for layer reading, which returns a Scala Sequence instead of an RDD, to improve performance by 300-500%, simplify the codebase and deployment, and allow for larger area of interest thresholds. This approach is contingent on the current geoprocessing model continuing to be used rather than switching to a database pre-processing model.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include significant performance improvements, simpler code and deployment, and potential for larger user-selected areas. Negative consequences include the need to upgrade to Java 8, switch to Akka HTTP, synchronous interaction between Celery and geoprocessing service, potential differences in results, and risks associated with deploying an untested API in production.

alternatives.description: Continue using the current Spark JobServer with RDDs for layer reading.
pros: Existing system is stable and well-understood.
Supports a wider range of MapAlgebra operations.
cons: High overhead and limited performance gains on a single machine.
Complex deployment with Spark and Docker dependencies.
Slower response times limiting area of interest size.

alternatives.description: Switch to a database pre-processing model that stores pre-processed information for faster runtime geoprocessing.
pros: Potentially much faster runtime geoprocessing.
Could reduce load on geoprocessing service.
cons: Less precise results.
Requires significant changes to data storage and processing workflows.
Uncertainty if this approach will be adopted, making optimization of current service less beneficial.

template_adherence.title: 004 - Expose Geoprocessing API
template_adherence.context:
The MMW/BigCZ platform performs a number of geospatial processing tasks which can be initiated by submitting tasks to an HTTP endpoint. The web application provides the tools and workflow for assembling and submitting the input, monitoring execution progress, and collecting and visualizing the results of these jobs. The platform provides value by assembling the required national scale data and the infrastructure necessary to perform the processing. In an effort to extend this capability to alternate workflows that don't involve the web platform, the client wants to formalize an externally consumable HTTP API.

MMW/BigCZ already includes and makes limited use of the Django REST Framework (DRF), which supports convenience methods around creating HTTP APIs.

API Objectives and Considerations are also described, detailing requirements and constraints for the API.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to support execution of current and future geoprocessing tasks, authentication mechanisms, rate limiting, avoiding code duplication, validation enforcement, and considerations about security, usage logging, and backward compatibility.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use the existing Django REST Framework to implement new API endpoints, secured by the default Token Authentication provided by the framework. Requests will be throttled to a configurable amount per minute. An account page will list the user's API key and allow it to be invalidated/regenerated. Validation will be encoded into the endpoints. Basic logging of requests will be done within the Django model/database with attributes confirmed by the client.
template_adherence.consequences: Using non-expiring keys balances security and consumer convenience, allowing low barrier to entry. Logging to the database requires an interface for usage data export, initially via a management task exporting CSV files. Swagger will be used to generate documentation. Potential upgrades to DRF and Django may be required to support latest features.

alternatives.description: Reuse existing endpoints `/start/analyze/*` and `/start/rwd` which have needed functionality but lack authentication, proper validation, appropriate paths, and CORS support.
pros: Leverages existing functionality without new development.
No need to create new endpoints.
cons: Endpoints do not require authentication.
Validation is handled mostly on the front end, not robust.
Paths and naming are not designed for public API use.
CORS is not enabled, limiting cross-origin requests.

alternatives.description: Create new DRF based API endpoints using Django REST Framework's support for authentication, throttling, and extensibility.
pros: DRF supports token authentication and pluggable auth systems including JWT.
Supports throttling to limit request rates.
Allows centralized validation and logging.
Familiar technology already used in the application.
cons: No default usage logging; requires manual implementation.
Requires development effort to create new endpoints and features.

alternatives.description: Use AWS API Gateway to proxy API requests, providing robust features like usage plans, rate limiting, logging, and versioning.
pros: Robust feature set for API management.
Built-in usage plans, rate limiting, logging, and versioning.
cons: Team has limited experience with AWS API Gateway tooling and execution.
Requires custom code to authorize requests based on application authentication.
Adds external dependency and complexity.

template_adherence.title: Geoprocessing API: Only Allow Anonymous Requests From The Client App
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the need to secure previously open API endpoints (analyze and RWD) with token authentication to better track users, prevent abuse, and enable future paid tiers. However, the client app requires unauthenticated access to these endpoints, creating a challenge to identify the client app as a special case without overly complex or insecure solutions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to secure the API while allowing the client app to access endpoints without user authentication, balancing security with simplicity, and acknowledging that no fully secure client-side identification is possible. The solution should be maintainable and allow token cycling if misuse occurs.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen decision is to give the client app its own API token, so all users use tokens uniformly. This approach simplifies the mental model, allows token cycling to mitigate misuse, and avoids complex conditional logic. Having the `backend` configured in the module means that consumers can't overwrite the configuration. When building and testing modules it is useful to be able to use a "local" `backend`.
template_adherence.decision: We have not set the `backend` configuration in the `main.tf`.
template_adherence.consequences:
When running locally, such as when using the examples, the consumer can set the `backend`. This enables the `backend` to be decided by the consumer rather than the module.

When running in labelled environments the configuration will need to be set up to use the appropriate backend. In most cases this will be the `s3` backend.

template_adherence.title: Develop v6 and v7 on main simultaneously
template_adherence.context: We have two teams developing the CLI. One (CLI) is building out functionality (such as a better UAA and login experience) for the current, stable v6 releases. One (VAT) is dropping compatibility with CAPI v2 to more quickly integrate with and build out CAPI v3. VAT is doing so in v7 releases of the CLI. For the last three weeks, VAT has been developing on a long-running _vat_ branch based on v6.39. Part of the goals for VAT include incorporating all 7-10 new epics that will be built on _main_, along with sharing any bugfixes back and forth between the two branches. VAT has been tracking which commits should be cherry-picked back and forth each day, resulting in significant overhead and bookkeeping. Rather than continuously merging two long-running branches into each other, the VAT team proposes to develop on _main_ simultaneously with CLI. This would allow the CAPI v3 acceleration work to proceed faster. The CLI team is constrained by needing to continue shipping stable versions of v6. There would be increased risk of shipping unstable versions, given that the VAT team's work involves modifying existing code for which there are no integration tests. The VAT team would bear little of this risk and would reap most of the benefit.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to accelerate CAPI v3 integration and development.
- Reduce overhead and bookkeeping from cherry-picking commits between branches.
- Maintain stable v6 releases while developing v7.
- Manage risk of shipping unstable versions.
- Facilitate sharing of bug fixes and features between versions.
- Avoid long-term branching/forking difficulties.
template_adherence.decision: VAT is proposing to have both teams develop in the _main_ branch simultaneously. One code base would be building two different versions of the binary. The v6 binary would not include any v7 actors or commands. Integration tests will need to split to represent v6 behaviour vs v7 behaviour. We will need two separate command lists. The main.go file can either be copied as two separate packages or as a single file that relies on go build flags to determine the version. Any v6 commands that are already backed by v3 endpoints will need to be carefully dealt with in order to ensure backwards compatibility when working with the v6 CLI. Several packages are differentiated by a v2/v3 prefix, but should be v6/v7 going forward to avoid confusion. Removal of v3 prefix commands from the v6 CLI to reduce overlapping surface area.
template_adherence.consequences: The v7 CLI will automatically gain all new features, bug fixes, etc., from the v6 CLI. When VAT makes fixes to the CLI as a whole (e.g. solving a race condition in a test), the CLI team automatically gains that benefit. There is less risk of dropping commits that should be shared. It will be easier for each team to restructure the code base (or even rename files) and continue to share code. There is an increased risk of blocking each others' pipelines. There is an increased risk of inadvertently shipping breaking changes in the v6 CLI. There is going to be confusion as to which team owns which section of the code. The integration test structure could become difficult to work with, especially as the two products drift apart. The teams can still decide to branch/fork in the future if this proposal becomes untenable, however, branching/forking now will make it nigh-impossible to merge in the future.

alternatives.description: Continue developing on separate long-running branches (v6 and vat branch) and cherry-pick commits back and forth.
pros: Maintains clear separation between v6 and v7 development.
Reduces risk of unstable versions affecting stable releases.
cons: High overhead and bookkeeping to track cherry-picked commits.
Slower integration of new features and bug fixes between branches.
Increased complexity in merging and sharing code.

alternatives.description: Branch/fork now and maintain separate codebases for v6 and v7.
pros: Clear ownership and separation of codebases.
Reduced risk of breaking changes crossing versions.
cons: Difficult to merge changes in the future.
Duplication of effort and code.
Harder to share bug fixes and features between versions.

template_adherence.title: 3. Resource Matching Implementation
template_adherence.context:
When uploading applications to a particular foundation, there may be duplicate files that are shared between apps. In order to reduce the load from uploading duplicate files, the Cloud Controller exposes an endpoint to match existing files prior to uploading application bits. The client then uses this endpoint to determine which files require upload.

During the first stage of push, PushPlans are created to determine what actions need to take place during the remaining push operation. This introduced a unique decision, perform resource match when creating push plans or perform resource matching immediately prior to uploading application bits.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to reduce upload load by avoiding duplicate file uploads, the timing of resource matching (early during push plan creation vs. immediately prior to upload), and the impact on performance and complexity.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was made to perform resource matching immediately prior to uploading application bits. This approach optimizes matching by deferring it until just before app-specific upload, allowing shared files between multiple apps to be matched effectively.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision diverges from the original intention of having a single place (CreatePushPlans) to determine push actions, potentially causing future confusion. However, the performance benefits outweigh the added complexity due to the later positioning of resource matching.

alternatives.description: Perform resource matching when creating push plans (early in the push process).
pros: Centralizes determination of push actions in one place (CreatePushPlans).
Simplifies understanding of push process flow.
cons: Less optimized matching since shared files between apps are not yet uploaded.
Potentially higher upload load due to duplicate file uploads.

alternatives.description: Perform resource matching immediately prior to uploading application bits (chosen option).
pros: More optimized matching by deferring until just before upload.
Reduces upload load by matching shared files across multiple apps effectively.
cons: Diverges from the original design intention of centralized push action determination.
May introduce complexity and potential confusion in the push process.

template_adherence.title: 8. Swap Traffic Controller for Log Cache
template_adherence.context: The Loggregator team decided to move to a "Shared Nothing" architecture that would improve scalability of log egress from the platform. This architecture deprecated the V1 Firehose Traffic Controller, the component from which the cf CLI retrieved application logs. As a result, the Loggregator team proposed modifying the cf CLI to retrieve logs from Log Cache instead.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve scalability of log egress, deprecation of the V1 Firehose Traffic Controller, and the presence of Log Cache in the minimum supported version of cf-deployment after December 2019.
template_adherence.decision: After December 2019, the CLI's minimum supported version of cf-deployment contains Log Cache. Therefore, in 2020, cf CLI v7 will be modified to retrieve application logs from Log Cache; cf CLI v6 will be modified to retrieve application logs from Log Cache with the exception of experimental v3-prefixed commands; and cf CLI v6/v7 legacy command implementations accessible through the Plugin API will be modified to retrieve application logs from Log Cache. There will be no user-facing or breaking changes.
template_adherence.consequences: Cloud Foundry log egress is expected to become more scalable and resource efficient. Limitations on modifying the Log Cache API due to minimum supported version policy. Change from long-lived WebSocket connections to HTTP GET requests for log retrieval. Potential risk of logs being shown for different operations due to grouping by source-id buckets. Authorization must be performed for each request rather than once per connection. Possible caching issues in Log Cache affecting users pushing multiple applications quickly.

alternatives.description: Continue using the V1 Firehose Traffic Controller for log retrieval.
pros: No changes required to the cf CLI.
Existing user experience remains unchanged.
cons: Does not improve scalability of log egress.
Uses deprecated architecture.
May not be supported in future versions.

alternatives.description: Develop a new log retrieval mechanism separate from Log Cache and Traffic Controller.
pros: Potential for a custom solution tailored to specific needs.
Could optimize performance and features independently.
cons: Requires significant development effort.
Increases maintenance burden.
Delays improvements in scalability.

template_adherence.title: 10. Synchronizing V7 and V8 (Main) code
template_adherence.context:
_The issue motivating this decision, and any context that influences or constrains the decision._

**Current**: Changes committed to the [V7
branch](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/cli/tree/v7) need to be cherry-picked
onto the [main (V8) branch](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/cli), a manual
process.

This depends on the pair to remember to cherry-pick. If forgotten, the commit
will not be merged, and we run the risk of bugfixes (and features) not
manifested in both branches.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly labeled or sectioned in the ADR. However, the context and decision sections imply drivers such as the need to synchronize changes between branches, reduce manual errors, and maintain a manageable git history. The drawbacks and notes from Ops Manager also hint at concerns about git history cleanliness, branch divergence, and overhead of merging strategies.
template_adherence.decision:
_The change that we're proposing or have agreed to implement._

Commit changes on the v7 branch then merge to main/v8, e.g.:

```bash
git co v7
git pull -r
# make changes
make
git add -p
git ci
bin/push.sh
```

[`push.sh`](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/cli/blob/main/bin/push.sh) is a
scripts which pushes the v7 commit, rebases against main, checks out main,
pulls, merges v7, pushes, and then checks out v7. It automates some of the more
tedious aspects of the commit cycle.

This is the process that Ops Manager follows to maintain several branches.

It is not without drawbacks, though. Here are the notes from the Ops Mgr anchor:

> We're still using merge forward as the primary method of sharing features / bug fixes across all of our releases. It generally still works well for us, but there are drawbacks.
> * If you care about a "clean", fairly linear git history for each branch. The merge commits can definitely make things difficult to follow sometimes. This isn't much of an issue for us, but I can imagine it being more important for ya'll since it's an open source project
> * It assumes that everything in the earlier branch belongs in the later branch. This makes a lot of sense for common bug fixes, but perhaps there are feature differences that could make it trickier in your case.
> * It somewhat discourages large refactors or cleanups. In 2.7 we did a major refactor of our React code, so anytime we need to do a UI bug fix in 2.6 or below, it becomes a pain to merge forward and we basically have to re-do the work. (Though this probably would apply to a cherry-pick strategy as well!)
> I think for Ops Manager, since we're maintaining so many branches at once, and the fact that most of what we would do on earlier branches is bug fixes for ALL branches, it's slightly less overhead for us to do merge forward. If the CF CLI is diverging in any significant manner between versions, and you're only going to be dealing with 2 versions, cherry-picking from one branch to the other might be cleaner. Merge forward should still work, but maybe you'd be getting less benefit out of it.
template_adherence.consequences:
_What becomes easier or more difficult to do and any risks introduced by the change that will need to be mitigated._

If a pair forgets to merge their commit to main, the subsequent merge to
main will pick up that change (this is a good thing).

Sometimes a merge conflict will occur. This happens with cherry-picks, too.

The first merge will entail duplicate commits (the ones that have been
cherry-picked).

alternatives.description: Cherry-picking commits from V7 branch to main (V8) branch manually.
pros: Allows selective commits to be merged.
Keeps git history linear without merge commits.
cons: Manual process prone to human error (forgetting to cherry-pick).
Risk of missing bugfixes or features in one branch.
Tedious and error-prone.

alternatives.description: Automated merge forward process using a script (push.sh) to merge V7 into main (V8).
pros: Automates tedious aspects of merging.
Reduces risk of forgetting to merge changes.
Used successfully by Ops Manager for multiple branches.
cons: Creates merge commits, making git history less linear and harder to follow.
Assumes all changes in earlier branch belong in later branch, which may not always be true.
Discourages large refactors or cleanups due to merge complexity.

template_adherence.context: Since we do not have the expertise and experience needed to build ui library projects and since we cannot fully anticipate the future needs of such library it's best to follow the path of other libraries and implement it in a similar way.

- We will only copy features that we need, we will not implement features we do not need like the ripple effects or support for bidirectionality.
- We will not copy paste the code as is without understanding it, we will first study it carefully and then borrow what we need from it.
- We will use the CDK as much as possible.

- We learn new things about good Angular design patterns.
- We have components that are generic enough to account for future use cases - The Angular team has much bigger developer audience so most chances are that they've already encountered many use cases.

template_adherence.title: 6. Keep the api surface as minimal as possible
template_adherence.context: Since many developers are going to use this library for many different features, we need to have some rules of thumb for what goes into the component and what does not go.
template_adherence.decision:
- We will choose to keep the api surface as minimal as possible, adding only the most necessary features in.
- We will prefer leaving some features to the user of the library.
- If we are not sure about something, it's better to leave it out and wait before we make the decision to add it.
template_adherence.consequences:
- It's relatively easy to add something later in a non breaking way, but removing something out of the api always means breaking backwards compatibility and is harder.
- Leaving features out also means that it gives us more time to see how the component is actually being used and decided if that feature is actually needed.
- By deferring some features to the user of the library means that the user might need to write more code to use the component. But the user can write higher order components that use the underlying components from this library. These higher order components can then be reused as well in the user's application.
- Code is smaller, less bloated and easier to maintain and test.

template_adherence.title: 2. deployments
template_adherence.context: We need a way of deploying our services to our various hosted environments (dev, staging, prod, etc.). We would prefer these deployments to be automated with minimal to zero human interaction.
template_adherence.decision: The DIT infrastructure already has a lot of tooling and infrastructure around deployments so we will utilise this. We will use Jenkins to automatically deploy from dedicated git branches - these will be: development, staging, uat. We will have 5 Jenkins jobs in total - these will be: trade-access-program-backoffice, trade-access-program-frontend, trade-access-program-polling-dev, trade-access-program-polling-staging, trade-access-program-polling-uat. The role of the "polling" jobs are to watch a related git branch for any commit changes. Once a change is detected then it will trigger the `trade-access-program-backoffice` and `trade-access-program-frontend` jobs with a set of environment parameters triggering the deployment to one of our three environments. This allows us to simply merge or push to one of the three dedicated git branches above and a full automated deployment will occur for that environment.

template_adherence.title: Use of Templates over JavaScript Framework for TAP Project UI Development
template_adherence.context: We need to decide how we want to develop and maintain our service UI. In fact we require 3 different user interfaces for the TAP project: a grant application UI for external companies and individuals to apply for a grant; a grant management UI for internal TAP team members to help them organise the approval/rejection process; and an admin interface to manage the inner workings of the TAP service. As of right now the development team consists of 1 developer with experience in backend development. Therefore we will take the simpler solutions when making decisions about UI development.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The main drivers are the development team constraints (only one developer with backend experience), the need for simplicity and development efficiency, and the requirement to use GDS styling for the public-facing grant application UI. Also, the grant management portal is internal and can use Viewflow frontend library, and the admin interface can use Django's built-in admin panel.
template_adherence.decision: For the grant application UI, use standard HTML template views served from Django with GDS styling. For the grant management UI, use the Viewflow frontend library as decided in a separate ADR. For the admin interface, use the built-in Django admin panel.
template_adherence.consequences: The choices maximize development efficiency and simplicity, allowing quick iteration. However, this restricts flexibility as the UIs will be limited by the libraries, patterns, and HTML components used.

alternatives.description: Use a modern JavaScript framework (e.g., React, Angular, Vue) for all UIs.
pros: Potentially more flexible and dynamic UIs.
Better separation of frontend and backend concerns.
cons: Requires more frontend development expertise.
Longer development time given current team constraints.

alternatives.description: Use only Django templates for all UIs without any frontend libraries.
pros: Simplest approach.
Easiest to maintain with current backend-focused developer.
cons: May lack advanced UI features.
Less user-friendly for complex internal portals.

template_adherence.title: 6. split-service-into-two
template_adherence.context:
The TAP service comprises of 2 distinct responsibilities:

- Provide a public facing grant application form styled using the GOVUK GDS style guide.
- Provide a private portal to manage grant applications in a formal recorded manner.

The private grant management area will need to be secured behind the DIT VPN while the public facing grant application
process will not.

Both areas will require an authentication system but they will not necessarily be required to use the same
authentication system.

These two areas should not share the same user accounts or user types.

A person could feasibly have the need to access both areas for different purposes but this should be done using two
unconnected user accounts.

Grant application data will need to be shared between these two areas.
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided to separate these two systems into services.

These services will be split out in the codebase as separate projects. However, we will leave these within the same git
repository for a few reasons:
- Having these services share a single git repo will remove any need for versioning between the two services. Thus
saving valuable development effort.
- The development environment will be much easier to spin up locally because all services can be managed within a
single docker-compose.yml file
- We do not foresee that the codebase for these services will become very large.

We will name these services `frontend` and `backoffice`.

Due to developer constraints within the team (we are a small team with 1 backend developer) we will use the Django
framework to create both services.

These services will communicate via json REST requests only. They will each have their own database and will not have
read or write access to the other's database.
template_adherence.consequences:
This will require more work on the infrastructure side of the project. However, the DIT ecosystem is already made up of
many small services running through PAAS so the ground work around tooling is already available for us to utilise,
mitigating any additional work this decision will create.

Development and testing will require more effort when building features which require changes to both services.

The separation of data and users will help to manage the data access requirement that a user only has access to what
they need and nothing more.

template_adherence.title: 8. passwordless-magic-link-authentication-for-frontend
template_adherence.context:
We need a authentication system for the frontend service.

The authentication method must be publicly accessed.
template_adherence.decision:
A few authentication options were suggested and discussed:
- username/password
- social authentication (facebook, twitter, etc.)
- passwordless email link authentication (also known as magic link)

It was decided that we would use passwordless email link authentication to authenticate our public users (grant
applicants).

The user will enter their email address into a login page served by the frontend service. The service will then
send a authentication link containing a one time use token in the url. The user can then visit this url to start or
continue their application.

Constraints
- The token will be limited to one time use.
- The token will have a datetime expiry assigned to it.
- On issuing a new token to a user all previous tokens will be invalidated.
template_adherence.consequences:
Users will not need to remember a password.

Users will be able to save and continue incomplete grant applications.

alternatives.description: username/password authentication
pros: Widely understood and implemented.
cons: Users need to remember passwords.
Security risks if passwords are weak or reused.

alternatives.description: social authentication (facebook, twitter, etc.)
pros: Users can login using existing social accounts.
No need to manage passwords.
cons: Dependency on third-party providers.
Privacy concerns for users.

alternatives.description: passwordless email link authentication (magic link)
pros: No password to remember.
Simplifies user experience.
cons: Relies on email delivery and security.
Potential for token interception if not secured.

template_adherence.title: Isolating payment content with third-party widgets from general account management
template_adherence.context: In the implementation of payment features for subscription services, we've decided to use third-party JavaScript for payment widgets. Best practices established by our security team indicate that third-party JS should not be included on the highly-sensitive pages - i.e. such as those used for general account management on Firefox Accounts. So, we need a way to isolate the pages responsible for subscription sign-up and management from the rest of Firefox Accounts.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Security when dealing with financial transactions.
* Security when including with third-party JS code for payment widgets.
* Simplicity in user experience flows.
* Delivering against the subscription services deadline.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "Option A - Payment pages as separate app supplied with pre-generated access token", because

* Further refinements to access token delivery mechanism in Option A do not significantly affect the rest of the payments app.
* Doesn't preclude an upgrade to Option B in the future - i.e. once [Issue #640](https://github.com/mozilla/fxa/issues/640) is resolved.
* Doesn't preclude Option C as a future option - e.g. offering embedded subscription widgets to third-parties.
* Fastest practical option given existing record of reviews by security & UX and work completed so far.
* Fresh start with a more modern web stack (i.e. React).
template_adherence.consequences:
The decision to choose Option A means:

- Payment pages will be a separate standalone web app, isolating third-party widgets effectively.
- The approach aligns with security and UX reviews already conducted.
- It allows future upgrades to other options if needed.
- It requires building a new app with React and standing up another server.

Positive impacts include improved security isolation and modern technology use. Negative impacts include the overhead of maintaining an additional server and adopting new technology for the project.

alternatives.description: Option A - Payment pages as separate app supplied with pre-generated access token
pros: Can effectively isolate third-party widgets by virtue of living on a separate origin and receiving a scoped access token.
Our original plan of record reviewed by security and UX teams - i.e. time already spent.
Allows us to build something from scratch using a more modern framework like React.
cons: Building something with React is novel for the project overall.
We need to stand up yet another server.

alternatives.description: Option B - Payment pages as separate app and normal OAuth Relying Party
pros: Can effectively isolate third-party widgets by virtue of living on a separate origin and receiving a scoped access token.
Allows us to build something from scratch using a more modern framework like React.
cons: There is an open issue to support `?prompt=none` for OpenID Connect login, which if unresolved means redundant login prompts in UX flows.
Building something with React is novel for the project overall.
We need to stand up yet another server.

alternatives.description: Option C - Payment-related content embedded in iframes with pre-generated access token passed via postMessage
pros: This can effectively isolate third-party widgets by virtue of living on a separate origin and receiving a scoped access token.
cons: We need to stand up yet another server - i.e. at least for the separate origin.
Security story around iframes on the same origin as user management pages has not been reviewed - i.e. additional time needed.
Seems an awkward fit with UX flows drafted so far, for both subscription management and sign-up.
Would most likely be more content built using Backbone requiring modernization later.
Unless we combined React & Backbone on fxa-content-server, which is not as clean as a separate app.

alternatives.description: Option D - Payment pages as normal FxA content using iframes to isolate third-party widgets
pros: Requires the fewest novel technology choices.
Can reuse the existing fxa-content-server.
cons: Security story around iframes on the same origin as user management pages has not been reviewed - i.e. additional time needed.
Would most likely be more content built using Backbone requiring modernization later.
Unless we combined React & Backbone on fxa-content-server, which is not as clean as a separate app.

template_adherence.title: Event Broker for Subscription Platform
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to keep external OAuth Relying Parties (RPs) updated about Firefox Account users' subscription status and data deletion events. Existing internal notification mechanisms are unsuitable for external RPs, necessitating a new system (FxA Event Broker) to store and distribute relevant events via webhooks. Challenges include determining where to store RP authentication data, event streams, and how to communicate data efficiently without overloading existing services.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Key drivers include subscription service deadlines, available effort and experience for FxA changes, separation of concerns from existing FxA microservices, difficulty of schema migrations, suitability of existing FxA databases for large-scale event storage, and architectural goals to unify FxA Auth and OAuth.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen decision is option C: Implementing RP notification as a new FxA Event Broker service with webhook and login activity stored in the FxA Event Broker. This choice minimizes timeline risk, addresses database limitations of existing services, and reduces load on FxA Auth databases by centralizing event storage and notification.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision leads to a dedicated service for event storage and delivery, improving scalability and separation of concerns. However, it requires maintaining RP login records in FxA OAuth server separately. The new service can handle event storage at scale without impacting existing FxA Auth/OAuth services.

alternatives.description: Implementing RP notification as a FxA Auth Service feature with webhook and login activity stored in FxA Auth Service.
pros: Auth service has direct access to subscription capability mapping and OAuth webhook URLs.
cons: Event logs for each user are not well suited for existing MySQL database.
Additional database schema migrations needed.
Later features needing to query for user events could impact FxA Auth Service availability.

FxA OAuth server should still have a record of which RPs a user has logged into so a later issue to add this is still needed.

template_adherence.title: Utilizing JSON-Schemas, SemVer, and Tooling for JSON Messaging
template_adherence.context:
Firefox Accounts sends and receives messages in JSON utilizing queues. This ADR addresses this use-case only and does not apply to JSON used in RESTful APIs.

Tracking and minimizing drift between the accuracy of message format documentation and the underlying implementation is an error-prone process. In addition, JSON messages are frequently produced and consumed from multiple systems, and in multiple langauges. Ensuring validity of these messages frequently requires implementing validation logic in each language that consumes these JSON messages to ensure correctness for message handling.

Adding a field to a message format is non-trivial, as every consumer must also update its own validation logic. Currently there are a variety of places where messages are consumed and produced, most producers do not validate the message they send as the consumer code is not always in the same service where the validation code typically resides.

There is currently no versioning for our message formats, which also creates difficulties in knowing when validation logic must change and when existing flexibility is sufficient.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Accurate documentation via JSON-Schema doc generation
- Validation logic generated from JSON-Schema to reduce manually written/maintained code
- [Semantic Versioning][schemaver] to effectively communicate breaking vs. non-breaking message format changes
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "option 3", because our existing messages can be represented without any migration needed and external consumers already work with JSON.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Existing consumers require no changes, validation and documentation can be generated from JSON-Schema, JSON is human readable and widely supported.
- Negative: [SchemaVer] is a draft and not officially part of JSON-Schema specification, some manual logic is required for versioning.

alternatives.description: Keep existing approach
pros: No additional work is needed that we don't already do.
cons: Documentation frequently drifts.
Additional work to maintain accurate joi schemas spread throughout the code-base or consolidate them.
joi schemas can't be used by consumers not written in JS.

alternatives.description: Use protobuf to format/validate/document message formats
pros: High throughput messaging benefits from efficient serialization/deserialization.
Documentation stays in sync with message spec.
Validation is built-in to serialization/deserialization process.
cons: Messages are in binary and not easily introspectable.
Existing message consumers need updates to handle protobuf.
Migration procedure needed to shift from JSON.

alternatives.description: Use JSON-Schemas with SemVer for doc/validation of existing JSON message formats
pros: No changes needed for existing consumers.
Validation can be done based on JSON-Schema without custom code.
Documentation can be generated to stay in sync with message spec.
JSON is human readable and widely used.
JSON-Schema is widely supported in many languages.
cons: [SchemaVer] is a draft and not officially used by JSON-Schema committees.

template_adherence.title: Transition FxA from Backbone to React
template_adherence.context: When Firefox Accounts was created some 6-7 years ago, the front-end Javascript framework and HTML templating options were limited significantly to those available at the time. This ADR details the pros and cons of various FE libraries and frameworks, and why it is desirable for FxA to move to a different technology. It does not cover _how_ we will begin the conversion which can be read about elsewhere. While Backbone and Mustache have served their purposes for FxA thus far, other modern libraries and frameworks not only offer more appealing architecture and developer conveniences, but also offer better data predictability, potential performance boosts, and a strong community of online support.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- The desire for a more modern FE architecture and a more efficient UI
- As Backbone declines in popularity, the desire to move to a library or framework actively being improved with great community support is prevalent
- A modern framework will likely feel more familiar to new engineers to the team as well as open source contributors
template_adherence.decision: The chosen option is "Option B - Move to client-side React" because the team desires the benefits from moving to a more modern library, has experience with React, React is already used in other parts of the ecosystem, FxA does not need server-side rendering, Angular is heavy and opinionated with features not needed, and web components are new and a distant potential shift. React was chosen over Vue due to existing team knowledge, existing use in payments server, prior security review, and considerations of package age, support, popularity, and stability.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to move to client-side React will modernize the front-end stack, improve developer experience, and align with existing ecosystem usage. However, it introduces a large refactor effort, learning curve, and ongoing maintenance of the new technology. It also mitigates risks of future major refactors by choosing a stable and popular framework.

alternatives.description: Continue to use Backbone and Mustache without introducing a new framework.
pros: No tech debt or large refactoring effort would be necessary right now.
cons: Backbone's declining popularity may cause future challenges in support, documentation, features, and developer knowledge.

template_adherence.title: Create a New React Application for the Settings Redesign Project
template_adherence.context:
"Settings" refers widely to the `accounts.firefox.com/settings` page where users can manage their Firefox account. The "Settings Redesign Project" refers to a 2019/2020 project centered around giving this page a fresh user interface. The changes are fairly significant and will require a lot of component shuffling and some functionality refactoring. [See the PRD](https://docs.google.com/document/d/18zu7JCYIsUp8tUMJqb2uErNlzL9f6CQvefLy9HFZ4UY/edit?pli=1#heading=h.cf57dt1i8634).

The FxA Engineering team desires to migrate from [Backbone and Mustache to React](https://github.com/mozilla/fxa/blob/main/docs/adr/0010-transition-fxa-from-backbone-to-react.md). This ADR addresses questions around what level of action we should take regarding this desire and the Settings Redesign Project - should a conversion to React be done at a later time, or are the changes significant enough to justify propelling us into React now?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to decide the level of React adoption for the Settings Redesign Project.
- Desire to migrate from Backbone and Mustache to React.
- Consideration of project scope, future maintainability, and development speed.
- Risk mitigation strategies for deployment and integration.
- Flexibility to expand Settings functionality and support future features.
- Testing, accessibility, and workflow improvements.
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "Option C - Take the 'ground up' approach and create a new settings React application" because it aligns with the overall goal of offering more flexibility, reduces future refactoring, allows for improved testing and accessibility, simplifies workflows, and mitigates risks by incremental deployment alongside the existing system.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include propelling the project into the new framework (React), reducing future refactoring efforts, enabling better testing and accessibility practices, simplifying GitHub workflow and A/B testing, and allowing incremental deployment to mitigate risks.

Negative consequences include the longer rollout time compared to other options and the risk associated with a "ground up remake," which is generally viewed as taboo and involves changing a large chunk of the front-end codebase.

alternatives.description: Use the existing JS framework (Backbone) and templating library (Mustache), and make all changes in these files.
pros: Allows for reuse of the existing `fxa-content-server`.
Many changes can be satisfied with Mustache/CSS updates.
Requires less initial setup and changes will be in production more quickly.
cons: Significant functionality changes will need to be refactored again later with React.
Does not set up well for future feature requests; React conversion backlog would grow.
Integration into `main` must be done carefully; A/B testing may be complicated.

alternatives.description: Take the "100/0" approach by creating all new components with React, but modify existing Backbone/Mustache files or refactor these components as React components.
pros: Can reuse the existing `fxa-content-server`.
Requires less initial setup and upfront refactoring; changes in production more quickly.
Allows piecemeal React integration, reducing future refactoring compared to Option A.
Enables creation of React components usable elsewhere in FxA ecosystem.
cons: Full benefits of React won't be realized until many pieces are converted.
Requires later refactoring to move away from interlinked Backbone-React dependencies.
Additional dependencies like NestedReact add complexity and need removal later.
Integration into `main` must be done carefully; A/B testing may be complicated.

alternatives.description: Take the "ground up" approach and create a new settings React application.
pros: Propels us into the new framework and reduces future refactoring.
Settings is a reasonable place to begin conversion regardless of redesign.
Allows fresh audit of HTML semantics, CSS, and accessibility.
Enables test auditing and potential improvements.
Opportunity to set up and use Storybook in FxA.
Potential to review and extract model and API code into shared modules.
Simplifies GitHub management and A/B testing.
cons: Generally viewed as taboo to do a "ground up remake."
Takes much longer to rollout than other options.

template_adherence.title: Next Two Factor authentication in FxA
template_adherence.context:
Firefox Account originally implemented multi-factor authentication (MFA) support in Q1 of 2018.
This feature used TOTP based codes and was based on RFC 6238.
Additionally, if users lost their MFA device, they could use one time backup authentication codes to regain access to the account.

Having MFA support has helped secure our users' accounts and given them more security flexibility.
However, over time it has become more obvious that users that lose their MFA device (usually phone) are at risk of getting locked out of their account because they don't save their backup authentication codes.
There are a non-trivial amount of users that don’t save or download their backup authentication codes, which is currently the only way they can regain access.
In 2019 Q4, FxA started requiring that users confirm backup authentication codes before enabling MFA.
While this did help reduce lockouts, we still want to reduce it further.

We believe that adding a new MFA method to Firefox Accounts that has the similar security properties as TOTP would allow users to have another method to recover their account.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Improve user's account security
- Reduce the risk of account lockout because of lost device/backup authentication code
- Could be completed in roughly a quarter
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: Option A, because this is more inline with Mozilla's security and privacy principles than option B.
There is less security risk to users if this feature is added.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to implement WebAuthn and FIDO2 authentication as the second factor will enhance security and align with Mozilla's privacy principles. However, it may introduce UX challenges, user unfamiliarity, and potential complexity that could extend development time beyond a quarter.

alternatives.description: Use WebAuthn JS api and FIDO2 based authentication as a second authentication factor for FxA.
pros: WebAuthn and FIDO2 are open standards with good browser support
More secure than SMS
Aligns with Mozilla's security and privacy features
Not dependent on other features and could be worked independently
cons: Some unknowns with UX parts and design
Less familiar to users
Losing authenticator could still potentially lock you out of account
More complex feature that has risk of taking longer than a quarter to complete

alternatives.description: Add the ability to have users send a backup authentication code to a phone number associated to the account, which could then be used to recover the account.
pros: Common account recovery pattern used on many sites
Less UX unknowns
In theory easier to implement
Could be completed over a quarter
cons: Would require additional security reviews
Less secure

template_adherence.title: Authentication in Settings Redesign
template_adherence.context: The Settings Redesign app needs to query & mutate the same protected user data as the existing settings app hosted on content-server. This will require some form of authentication & authorization to manage that data.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Smooth UX
- Security
- Development velocity
- Ease of integration
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "Authenticate via OAuth2 to use auth-server APIs", because:

- It requires minimal changes to existing auth-server implementation and infrastructure.
- It relies on an authentication mechanism with relatively well-known security properties.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive Consequences

- The OAuth2 access token mechanism is better suited to this purpose than a novel scheme to share session token credentials.
- The new Settings Redesign app can use existing auth-server APIs with minimal modifications to accept scoped OAuth2 access tokens. This can constrain most of the novelty in the project to the redesigned & reimplemented settings UX.

### Negative Consequences

- We will need to modify auth strategies in auth-server APIs, taking care not to affect existing usage in the production settings app.
- We don't have an entirely greenfield project, which could be a bit of a drag. But, rediscovering lessons learned in existing code can also be a drag.

alternatives.description: Authenticate via OAuth2 to use auth-server APIs
pros: Security properties of OAuth2 authn / authz are known and not entirely novel
Auth-server APIs can be reused with small changes
cons: APIs on auth-server need auth strategy changes to accept OAuth tokens
May initially require a hack similar to payments-server where a pre-generated access token is passed along

alternatives.description: Authenticate via OAuth2 to use DB directly
pros: Security properties of OAuth2 authn / authz are known and not entirely novel
Can re-use at least the oauth APIs on auth-server to validate token stored in client
cons: Auth UX flow will require user to confirm permissions
Skipping auth-server requires reinventing many things
New implementation will require security reviews of auth-server reimplementations

alternatives.description: Reuse existing sessionToken on content-server with auth-server APIs
pros: Can be done with seamless UX - user visits new settings without confirmation
cons: We use Hawk request signing with the session token credentials for authentication. Passing these credentials from the frontend to a GQL backend essentially defeats the purpose of Hawk, since the scheme is in part meant to minimize the transmission of credentials over the network.

alternatives.description: Implement own login sessions
pros: None?
cons: User must login separately - cannot piggy-back atop existing FxA login
Novel security properties of new login session system
Need to maintain storage for persistent sessions - e.g. a database or redistribution
Skipping auth-server requires reinventing many auth-server things

template_adherence.title: Use CSS Variables, Prefer SCSS over CSS-in-JS
template_adherence.context: The Settings Redesign project offers an ideal opportunity to review CSS conventions and architecture for FxA to not only use while building new components for this project, but also for FxA moving forward. This ADR concerns the use of CSS variables, how they come into play with SCSS (vs using SCSS variables), CSS-in-JS considerations, and CSS modules.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Simplicity and clarity
- DRY and reusable styles
- Easy integration and use
- Current engineering experience and preferences
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen options: "CSS variables" and "SCSS", because:

- While using CSS variables with SASS will prevent using mixins (or SASS functions like `darken`) that rely on variable values, they can be used without impeding core functionality FxA uses SASS for like nested selectors, extends, and functions and mixins that don't rely on variable values like the generation and use of our media queries.
- CSS variables are native to the browser and decision to use them now is a prudent one. They have good browser support and can be used without a preprocessor and changed after preprocessor compilation. They are targetable by JavaScript, easily themed, and can be scoped globally or on an element, providing options for usage.
- Scoped component solutions (CSS-in-JS, CSS modules) encourage self-contained components rather than building the UI as a whole. While one goal of FxA is to reuse components across the ecosystem where possible (e.g. the `fxa-react` package), FxA will likely reap more benefits from a class-based approach. This allows for globally shared styles and a loosely coupled stylesheet rather than a tightly coupled CSS-in-JS solution with conditional styles based on props and how the component is used. Classes promote a DRYer and more consistent approach.
- CSS-in-JS would add one additional layer of tech to learn (like `styled-components` syntax and best practices) while the Settings Redesign project is already introducing other novel tech, and members of the FxA engineering team also as a whole personally prefer not to use CSS-in-JS.
- This decision doesn't preclude the option of implementing CSS modules at a later time if it's determined that we would prefer component scoped styles with SCSS, and CSS variables could still be used if we later switch to CSS-in-JS.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The project will use CSS variables and SCSS for styling, leveraging the benefits of native CSS variables and SCSS features.
- The approach favors global shared styles and class-based styling over component-scoped CSS-in-JS or CSS modules.
- This decision aligns with team preferences and current engineering experience, reducing learning overhead.
- Future adoption of CSS modules remains possible without abandoning CSS variables.
- Some SASS functions relying on variable values will not be usable with CSS variables, but this is acceptable given current usage.
- The approach supports easier theming and JavaScript interaction with styles.

cons: CSS-in-JS can lead to less shared styles, adds dependencies, and is disliked by some team members.
CSS modules can complicate debugging and introduce new concepts.
SCSS requires naming conventions and may obscure per-component styles.

template_adherence.title: Switch from OAuth2 to sharing sessionToken with GraphQL server for settings redesign auth
template_adherence.context:
The Settings Redesign app needs to query & mutate the same protected user data as the existing settings app hosted on content-server. This will require some form of authentication & authorization to manage that data.

In ADR-0014, OAuth2 was decided as the mechanism, but implementation revealed missing context in OAuth2 tokens making it unusable.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Smooth UX
Security
Development velocity
Ease of integration
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "Reuse existing sessionToken on content-server with auth-server APIs", because it's the least novel option requiring fewest changes to auth-server.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
- Easiest path to authenticating on auth-server for API requests, works almost exactly like the settings client does already.

Negative Consequences:
- We defeat the security promises of Hawk, but we're not really relying on them. We'd also like to move away from Hawk in the future anyway.

alternatives.description: Reuse existing sessionToken on content-server with auth-server APIs
pros: Can be done with seamless UX - user visits new settings without confirmation
Requires little to no changes on auth-server since the existing sessionToken auth process will be followed.
cons: sessionTokens are long lived. Problems if one leaked, though this is unlikely.
Passing credentials from client to server defeats the purpose of Hawk.
We don't take advantage of Hawk's security promises
Replay protection is ignored
FxA is served via HTTPS, so we don't need security over unencrypted HTTP.
We'd like to move away from Hawk altogether in the future.

alternatives.description: Authenticate via OAuth2 to use auth-server APIs
pros: Security properties of OAuth2 authn / authz are known and not entirely novel
Auth-server APIs can be reused with small changes
cons: APIs on auth-server need auth strategy changes to accept OAuth tokens
May initially require a hack similar to payments-server where a pre-generated access token is passed along

OAuth2 access token would need reimplementation of many contextual details from sessionToken - i.e. different levels of authentication & verification like ACCOUNT_UNVERIFIED, SESSION_UNVERIFIED, TOTP_REQUIRED that could be implemented in scopes with additional work.

template_adherence.title: Use workspace dependencies in package.json
template_adherence.context: Since becoming a monorepo we haven't found a way to share code across packages that works well in local development, CI, and production without fragile, ad-hoc workarounds.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Simpler code sharing
- Minimal overhead in setup and deployment
- Works well for js and ts packages
- Low maintenance
- Long term viability
template_adherence.decision:
The [workspace:*](https://yarnpkg.com/features/workspaces) dependency type along with typescript [project references](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/project-references.html) provide a good internal dependency solution that addresses the shortcomings of our current situation.

Workspaces are not yet supported by npm but are on the [v7 roadmap](https://blog.npmjs.org/post/617484925547986944/npm-v7-series-introduction) so it's pretty safe to assume that they will be widely supported for the foreseeable future. In order to start using workspaces today we'll need to use yarn. This is a slight risk because although it is well supported it doesn't have the level of backing that npm does, however once workspaces are supported by npm there is nothing locking us in to yarn.
template_adherence.consequences:
Advantages:
- No manual linking of dependencies
- Simpler builds
- Single lock file
- Hoisted dependencies

Disadvantages:
- In the short term this requires us to switch from npm to yarn as our package manager. This will change dev workflows and is another tool to understand.
- Some code changes are required to be compatible with yarn, however they're also backward compatible with npm.
- Yarn doesn't currently support auditing dependencies like npm does.

alternatives.description: Using "long" relative paths
pros: Doesn't require any linking
Doesn't disturb package-locks
Works okay when packages are plain js and have no build steps
cons: Requires careful copying of dependencies in production build steps
Needs orchestration of build order due to implicit relations
Includes additions to package.json scripts that are difficult to maintain

alternatives.description: Using lerna and 'file' dependencies
pros: Lerna works fine as a task runner
File dependency type allows local dependencies to be declared
cons: Lerna primarily designed for published packages, no simple way to depend on unpublished packages
File dependencies cause problems with package-locks
Breaks regular `npm ci` within package directories due to npm bugs
Difficult to maintain package-lock once file dependency added

alternatives.description: Using published dependencies
pros: Some packages were public before monorepo
cons: Leads to versioning confusion
Requires awkward workflow when updating dependent packages
Publishing all packages just to workaround lerna limitations is undesirable and wasteful

template_adherence.title: Use a documented Application Architecture for new back-end services
template_adherence.context: The FxA back-end service stack contains an application architecture that is ad-hoc, not documented, and missing modern features (such as Dependency Injection) which results in several problems including difficulty for new developers to get up to speed, time-consuming setup, mixing of concerns, and inconsistent architectures across services. It is assumed that the four newest FxA back-end services will be switched to the chosen approach for consistency.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Documented application architecture.
- Tooling that reduces boiler-plate and creates consistent code architecture.
- Modern paradigms to ease creation of global objects and their testability, such as DI.
- Training materials so that new developers can understand and work on application features easily.
- Ability to migrate legacy applications to similar conventions/setup.
- Handles situations such as exception handling, validation, service instantiation (DI, etc), authentication, RESTful APIs (Swagger/OpenAPI a bonus), GraphQL, and use of components/services easily in a script.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use an existing framework: NestJS. NestJS was chosen over LoopBack and Adonis due to better GraphQL support, a larger user base, and alignment with existing paradigms. The four newest services will be migrated to NestJS. For legacy services like auth-server, code organization schemes and DI (using typedi) inspired by NestJS will be backported to ease configuration and testing, allowing developers familiar with NestJS to work on legacy packages.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include less documentation to create and close alignment of NestJS GraphQL support with existing paradigms. Negative consequences include the effort required to migrate the four packages to NestJS and the need to document differences between NestJS and legacy services.

alternatives.description: Evolve/improve our ad-hoc application architecture with docs, tools, etc.
pros: Could be easier to convert existing backend services as they will likely be closer in libs/structure to the chosen structure if desired.

template_adherence.title: Deprecate Hawk authentication on fxa-auth-server
template_adherence.context:
The new FxA settings page introduces a new service in the form of a GQL API that will provide account and profile data to the browser. This service needs to make api requests to the auth-server on behalf of logged in users. The auth-server uses hawk authentication so adding another service between the browser and auth-server is not straightforward. In ADR-0017 we decided to allow the browser to share the session token with the GQL server so that it can make hawk authenticated requests. This leads us to question whether we should deprecate our use of hawk altogether.

Long ago, the precursor to onepw had 2-phase signup/login that would establish a secret key that would be used to encrypt/decrypt the sessionToken so that it was never in the clear on the wire. It was secure enough that you could login over HTTP and still be safe. We'd still use TLS, but - defense in depth. Once we had the sessionToken we used Hawk for API requests to maintain that level of security. We implemented this protocol and it worked as designed. The problem at the time was we wanted to support low-end phones on slow networks and the extra round trips meant we were too slow; bad UX. Instead of scrapping the whole thing we modified the protocol to the one we use today. The sessionToken is now sent over TLS in the signup/login response, but the "secure even over HTTP" dream is gone.

Hawk is designed for authentication over HTTP. Quoting from the design goals of Hawk:

- simplify and improve HTTP authentication for services that are unwilling or unable to deploy TLS for all resources,
- secure credentials against leakage (e.g., when the client uses some form of dynamic configuration to determine where to send an authenticated request), and
- avoid the exposure of credentials sent to a malicious server over an unauthenticated secure channel due to client failure to validate the server's identity as part of its TLS handshake.

None of those scenarios apply to auth-server.

Defining the replacement for hawk is out of scope, but let's consider the properties of the interim replacement: using the sessionToken as a bearer token.

The new surface area to which the token is exposed is in the HTTP header of API requests, sent over TLS. Both the client and server storage of the token remains unchanged. A compromised TLS connection would expose the token on more API calls where it would not have been with hawk. The sessionToken is in the body of the login response, so even with hawk that endpoint could leak the token if the TLS connection is compromised.

A leaked sessionToken would allow access to personal information, email addresses and device metadata, but not the FxA password, secret keys, or Firefox Sync data.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: - Security
template_adherence.decision: We will stop using hawk in future work that requires authentication. Selecting a preferred scheme is out of scope of this ADR. Sharing the session token with trusted services is an acceptable interim solution.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to deprecate hawk simplifies cross-service and client integrations but introduces uncertainty about the long-term support of the deprecated authentication scheme. It removes the complexity and maintenance burden associated with hawk, but the interim solution exposes the session token in HTTP headers over TLS, which could be compromised if TLS is breached. Overall, it streamlines future development at the cost of some security considerations that are deemed acceptable in the interim.

pros: simpler cross service integrations
simpler browser / client integrations
cons: unknown duration of long-term support of deprecated auth scheme

alternatives.description: Continue using hawk in future work
pros: none. hawk is a pita
postpones considering better options
cons: more awkward cases like GQL API
higher long-term maintenance burden
more difficult integrations

template_adherence.title: Add PayPal as a supported payment option
template_adherence.context: The Subscription Platform was implemented with Stripe as the payment processor and driver of subscription logic. Stripe is used as the source of truth for whether an account has subscriptions associated with it. We would like to add PayPal as a payment option for subscriptions, and integrate it appropriately with the existing system in a least-effort manner that is ideally flexible enough to support future expansions of payment processors, such as IAP.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Engineering resources
- Future effort needed to integrate IAP
- Code complexity as it relates to existing Subscription Platform infrastructure
template_adherence.decision: Stripe-driven out-of-band invoice processing. This was originally considered to be the slower of the approaches, but using PayPal subscriptions ended up being approximately the same engineering effort. Given additional user experience benefits of the Stripe-driven approach, it is now the recommend implementation path.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Stripe continues to serve as an accurate source of truth regarding a customers subscription.
- All the logic that determines active subscriptions and entitlements using Stripe can be used as-is.
- Multiple product support works as-is.
- Support representatives can see accurate payment history in Stripe for customers paying via PayPal.
- Support can credit a PayPal customer, just as they can for a credit card customer.
- Can extend in a similar manner to track a correlating IAP for a user.
- Can handle switching payment method from credit card to PayPal reference ID, and vice versa.
- PayPal authorization is retained so that additional products can be purchased/credited without requiring the user to return to the PayPal flow.
- Cancel/resubscribe before the subscription expires works as-is.
- Additional metadata in Stripe can start pushing us closer to metadata limits on objects.
- Recreate Stripe's automatic advancement and collection logic that runs PayPal transactions which we need to ensure work correctly (checks to prevent double-charging, retries, and transaction success verification).
- We still could end up storing PayPal reference ID's in a separate db table to ensure we track prior PayPal billing.
- While we could more easily support multiple payment methods on the back end, this would add complexity to the subscription management flow on the front end.

pros: Stripe continues to serve as an accurate source of truth regarding a customers subscription.

Can extend in a similar manner to track a correlating IAP for a user.
Can handle switching payment method from credit card to PayPal reference ID, and vice versa.
PayPal authorization is retained so that additional products can be purchased/credited without requiring the user to return to the PayPal flow.
Cancel/resubscribe before the subscription expires works as-is.
cons: Additional metadata in Stripe can start pushing us closer to metadata limits on objects.

Recreate Stripe's automatic advancement and collection logic that runs PayPal transactions which we need to ensure work correctly (checks to prevent double-charging, retries, and transaction success verification).
We still could end up storing PayPal reference ID's in a separate db table to ensure we track prior PayPal billing.
While we could more easily support multiple payment methods on the back end, this would add complexity to the subscription management flow on the front end.

alternatives.description: PayPal Subscriptions linked/tracked by FxA
pros: PayPal is responsible for charging the customer and managing the subscription lifecycle.
Can extend in a similar manner to track a correlating IAP for a user.
cons: All the logic that determines active subscriptions and entitlements needs additional logic/abstractions to query the database table and map active PayPal subscriptions to the Stripe subscription.
Ability to easily cancel/re-subscribe on management page is lost, as canceled PayPal billing agreements cannot be restored.

To reduce complexity, anyone paying via PayPal would be locked into using PayPal for later subscriptions and users paying via Stripe would not be presented with any PayPal payment options. This could frustrate users that want to switch, as they'd have to cancel, wait till the subscription expires, and then subscribe again with PayPal.
Stripe subscription features can't be used, such as: Crediting a user for a month, Coupons, Consolidating multiple plans into a single subscription for aligned billing.
Every additional subscription requires a full PayPal authorization flow.

PayPal occasionally misses delivery of webhooks, which requires us to build our own script to periodically verify that PayPal subscriptions are still active and have had their latest transaction processed successfully.
PayPal subscriptions can be suspended and resumed. This doesn't map to any equivalent in Stripe subscriptions and would require custom handling in our code logic, entitlements, and UX.

alternatives.description: Recurly
pros: We do not need to implement PayPal logic at all, as Recurly handles it for us.
Ongoing future maintenance should be lower as Stripe/PayPal/etc changes over time are maintained by Recurly, not us.
cons: Recurly does not list the actual cost for the integration, but its estimated to be around an additional 1.5% of total revenue in addition to the payment processing costs.
Substantial work involved to migrate users over and switch all Stripe integration logic to work with Recurly APIs.
Would need a completely custom solution still for IAP.

template_adherence.title: Upgrade the templating toolset of Auth Server emails
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the limitations of the current templating system (Handlebars/Mustache) used in Firefox Accounts (FxA) email templates, which restricts logic and complicates styling. The goal is to evaluate and select a more modern, maintainable, and flexible templating and styling solution for FxA emails, including improvements in CSS handling, email previewing, localization, and deployment processes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Key drivers include improving template logic capabilities, enhancing styling consistency and reusability, simplifying email responsiveness, enabling better email previewing workflows, supporting localization improvements, minimizing build complexity, and ensuring maintainability and QA processes.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt Option C for templating and styling: use EJS and MJML with MJML's CSS options, and Option B for email previewing: use Storybook. Additional decisions include using html-to-text for plaintext generation, transitioning localization to Fluent, and implementing feature-flagged release groups for integration and QA.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include abstracting HTML email quirks via MJML, improved styling consistency, and simpler templating with EJS. Negative consequences include increased complexity in Storybook setup, new dependencies and learning curves, and potential introduction of bugs due to changes in battle-tested templates.
