template_adherence.title: Processing of nested line items
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to handle nested order line items in the checkout cart. Currently, cart processors only consider the first level of line items, while nested line items are added via plugins that implement their own processing logic.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to maintain compatibility with existing core cart processors, avoid collisions in processing nested line items, and allow plugins to implement their own processing logic for nested items.
template_adherence.decision: The core cart processors will continue to work with a flattened list of line items (`getFlat()`) during enrichment, ensuring data fencing and individual item processing. The `process` method will only handle first-level line items, leaving nested line items to be processed by plugins that can call other processors as needed.
template_adherence.consequences: Plugins must implement their own processing logic or extend Shopware's cart processors to handle nested line items. This approach avoids collisions but requires additional plugin development for nested item processing.

pros: Unified processing logic within core processors.
No need for plugins to handle nested items separately.
cons: Increased complexity in core processors.
Potential for processing collisions.
Less flexibility for plugin-specific logic.

alternatives.description: Allow plugins to implement their own processing logic for nested line items.
pros: Flexibility for plugins to handle nested items as needed.
Avoids collisions in processing.
Keeps core processors simpler.
cons: Requires plugin developers to implement additional logic.
Potential inconsistency in processing implementations.

template_adherence.title: When to use plain SQL or the DAL
template_adherence.context: It is often discussed whether to work with plain SQL or with the Data Abstraction Layer.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to decide when to use plain SQL or the Data Abstraction Layer (DAL) in different application layers, considering extensibility by third party developers, security (ACL), data integrity, and performance concerns.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use the DAL in application layers where extensibility, security, and data integrity are critical, such as Store API, Storefront page loader and controller, admin API, and when writing data. Plain SQL should be used in entity indexers and core components where direct database access is more efficient and where extensibility is not required.
template_adherence.consequences: Using DAL in extensible and secure layers ensures data integrity and extensibility but may introduce overhead. Using plain SQL in entity indexers and core components improves performance and avoids unnecessary overhead but limits extensibility and should be used carefully to avoid bypassing validation and security.

alternatives.description: Use only plain SQL for all data access.
pros: Maximum control over SQL queries.
Potentially better performance in all cases.
cons: Lack of extensibility for third party developers.
Bypassing validation, event, and indexing systems.
Security concerns due to lack of ACL enforcement.

alternatives.description: Use only the Data Abstraction Layer (DAL) for all data access.
pros: Consistent use of validation, events, and indexing.
Extensibility for third party developers.
Security enforcement via ACL.
cons: Potential performance overhead in scenarios like entity indexers.
Not suitable for internal processing where direct DB access is more efficient.

template_adherence.title: Vue administration app has ESLint support
template_adherence.context:
We want to support ESLint of the administration vue app to keep and increase code quality.

By adding ESLint to the administration app, every developer will get instant feedback and best practices on his code by writing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need to maintain and increase code quality in the Vue administration app.
Support linting for both JavaScript (*.js) and Twig template (*.html.twig) files.
Ensure developer feedback is immediate and practical.
Handle the special syntax of Twig templates during linting.
Maintain consistency with standard Vue CLI linting where possible.
template_adherence.decision:
For the `*.js` linting, we want to get pretty close to a standard vue2 app linting with some specific rule adjustments.
For the `*.html.twig` linting, we decided to convert all twig syntax to HTML comments within the linting process so the linter can handle twig files like typical vue templates, accepting the tradeoff that twig blocks are not considered for indentation.
Custom eslint plugin (`eslint-twig-vue-plugin`) was created to support this.
Specific linting rules and exceptions were defined for both JS and Twig files.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Improved code quality and consistency.
- Immediate developer feedback during coding.
- Support for linting Twig templates despite their special syntax.
Negative:
- Tradeoff in twig linting where indentation levels do not consider twig blocks.
- Some linting rules are turned off or adjusted to accommodate project specifics.
- Requires developers to follow certain template writing conventions (e.g., whitespace in twig blocks).
- Additional setup steps for IDEs to support Twig linting.

alternatives.description: Do not add ESLint support to the Vue administration app.
pros: No additional setup or maintenance required.
No need to handle Twig syntax in linting.
cons: Code quality may degrade over time.
Developers lack immediate feedback on code issues.
Inconsistent code style and potential bugs.

alternatives.description: Use standard ESLint configuration without custom handling for Twig templates.
pros: Simpler setup.
No need to maintain custom plugins or processes.
cons: Linting will fail or produce many false positives on Twig files.
Developers may ignore linting errors in templates.
Code quality in templates may suffer.

alternatives.description: Use a different linting tool that natively supports Twig templates.
pros: Potentially better support for Twig syntax.
No need for custom conversion to HTML comments.
cons: May require learning and integrating a new tool.
Possible lack of integration with existing Vue linting rules.
Uncertain community support and tooling.

template_adherence.title: Introduce jest-fail-on-console
template_adherence.context: A jest pipeline run produced previously hundreds of errors and warnings, which made it hard to see why a test failed and if a passing test isn’t just a false positive.
template_adherence.decision: To combat this, we decided to introduce the npm package jest-fail-on-console, which causes individual unit tests to fail if they log an error or a warning to the console.
template_adherence.consequences:
Jest-fail-on-console makes unit tests a lot more expressive because it prevents easy mistakes, which would previously lead to an error that is hard to find and notice. Like an incorrect key in a v-for loop, which could potentially lead to vue update errors, but would have not caused the test to fail.

Jest tests might be a little harder to write, because errors cannot simply be ignored anymore. All needed components have to be provided to the component being tested either by being mocked or built, all API requests need to be mocked, and all needed mixins have to be provided. Although it is a little more work, it makes the jest tests, as previously mentioned, more expressive and as a neat side benefit it keeps the console clean.

template_adherence.title: Move storefront script to head with defer
template_adherence.context:
* Currently, our main storefront scripts (inline scripts as well as `all.js`) are located at the bottom of the page near the body end tag.
* The `async` attribute is used for the `all.js` but it isn't really suitable because our own JavaScript plugins depend on DOM elements in order to be initialized, and we have to wait for the document to be finished anyway.
* Additionally, the `DOMContentLoaded` is not compatible with `async` scripts because they might run before this particular event. That's why `document.readystatechange --> complete` is being used at the moment.
* This has the downside, that none of our JavaScript plugins initializes before the entire document is fully loaded including all resources like images.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Improve script loading performance and initialization timing of JavaScript plugins by changing script placement and attributes to better align with DOM readiness events.
template_adherence.decision:
* In order to improve the script loading all default `<script>` tags are moved to the `<head>` and get a `defer` attribute in favor of `async`.
* To initialize the JavaScript plugins, the `DOMContentLoaded` is being used instead of `document.readystatechange --> complete`.
* This ensures that the JavaScript plugins initialization must only wait for the document itself but not for additional resources like images.
* This change allows the browser to download/fetch the scripts right away when the `<head>` is parsed instead of when almost the entire document is already parsed.
* Because of `defer` the script execution will wait until the document is parsed (Just right before the `DOMContentLoaded` event).
* `defer` also ensures that the different `<script>`'s are executed in the order in which they are declared.
template_adherence.consequences: All app/plugin script tags which extended one of the `base_body_script` child blocks must be moved to `Resources/views/storefront/layout/meta.html.twig`

template_adherence.title: 2021-08-10 - Storefront coding standars
template_adherence.context:
* The current coding standards are not put into an ADR yet.
* This ADR is to determine the current standards to have a start from where to enhance the storefront concept further more.
template_adherence.decision:
### Controller
* Each controller action has to be declared with a @Since tag
* Each controller action requires a @Route annotation
* The name of the route should be starting with "frontend"
* Each route should define the corresponding HTTP Method (GET, POST, DELETE, PATCH)
* Routes which renders pages for the storefront (GET calls) are calling a respective pageloader to get the data it needs.
* The function name should be concise
* Each function should define a return type hint
* A route should have a single purpose
* Use Symfony flash bags for error reporting
* Each storefront functionality has to be available inside the store-api too
* A storefront controller should never contain business logic
* The controller class requires the annotation: @RouteScope(scopes={"storefront"})
* Depending services has to be injected over the class constructor
* Depending services has to be defined in the DI-Container service definition
* Depending services has to be assigned to a private class property
* A storefront controller has to extend the \Shopware\Storefront\Controller\StorefrontController
* Using LoginRequired annotation to identify whether the Customer is logged in or not.
* Each storefront functionality needs to make use of a store-api route service. to make sure, this functionality is also available via API

### Operations inside Storefront controllers
A storefront controller should never use a repository directly, It should be injected inside a Route.

Routes which should load a full storefront page, should use a PageLoader class to load all corresponding data that returns a Page-Object.

Pages which contains data which are the same for all customers, should have the @HttpCache annotation

#### Write operations inside Storefront controllers
Write operations should create their response with the createActionResponse function to allow different forwards and redirects.
Each write operation has to call a corresponding store-api route.

### Page-/PageletLoader
* A PageLoader is a class which creates a page-object with the data for the called whole page.
* A PageletLoader is a class which creates a pagelet-object with the data for a part of a page.

The pageLoaders are a specific class to load the data for a given page.
The controller calls the pageloader, which collects the needed data for that page via the Store-api.
The pageloader can call other pageletloaders to get the data for pagelets(subcontent for a page).
The pageloader always returns a page-object.
template_adherence.consequences:
All dependencies in the controllers for routes which render a page have to be moved to the `Loaders` and if still missing, the `Loader` and `Page` has to be created.
All direct DAL-dependencies inside the storefront have to be moved to Store-Api routes and respective calls.
All other dependencies which are not allowed have to be checked for individual alternatives

template_adherence.title: Make shopware/platform stand-alone for development and testing
template_adherence.context: The platform requires some additional config, a console and web entrypoint and additional development tooling for development, tests and running the application. In practice this is provided by one of the templates: `shopware/development` or `shopware/production`. This creates a cyclic dependency, which brings some problems: - `shopware/development` and `shopware/platform` need to be updated in lockstep, which makes updating them individually sometimes impossible - some IDEs have trouble with multi repository projects - updating development tooling breaks everything - auto-detection of git revision and diff is broken, because the development template is the root - for each release branch an additional branch needs to be maintained
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to break cyclic dependency between shopware/platform and development templates
- Simplify development and testing setup
- Avoid issues with IDEs and multi-repository projects
- Maintain compatibility with existing templates
- Provide easy and standard development tooling and environment setup
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use shopware/platform directly in the pipeline and allow development without a template by moving development tooling into platform. The development setup will be advertised as shopware/platform development setup, while projects should still start with shopware/production as a template. shopware/development should continue to work. Testing will be enabled by adding CLI and web entrypoints. Composer scripts will be added to ease common tasks, keeping them small and simple, with essential functionality implemented as npm scripts or symfony commands. Standard conventions for environment files and docker-compose will be used, with defaults that work out of the box and avoid hard-coded ports.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Simplified CI and easier local error reproduction
- Simplified local setup
- No custom scripts unavailable in all setups
- Projects may try to use shopware/platform directly
- Another shopware setup option to choose from

alternatives.description: Continue using shopware/development and shopware/production templates as before, accepting the cyclic dependency and its problems.
pros: No changes to existing workflows
No need to move development tooling into platform
cons: Cyclic dependency remains
Updating templates in lockstep is required
IDE issues with multi-repository projects persist
Development tooling updates can break everything
Git revision auto-detection broken
Additional branches needed for each release

alternatives.description: Create a new unified template that combines development and production setups to avoid cyclic dependencies.

Potentially confusing for users accustomed to existing templates

template_adherence.title: Refactor admin build process to webpack-multi-compiler mode
template_adherence.context:
Previously the plugins are not completely independent from the core and other plugins. This has sometimes caused built plugin files to be incompatible with the core. Unless they were rebuilt again with the core.

The reason for this was that dependencies between plugins and the Core were optimized by Webpack. This was because Webpack saw the combination of Core and plugins as one big program. So using tree-shaking, sometimes dependencies were removed or added depending on which plugins were installed.

Also, a custom Webpack configuration in plugins resulted in it unavoidably being applied in core as well. This could sometimes result in the plugin only being compatible with the core if both were built together. If the plugin was then installed on other systems with only the built files, it could cause it not to work.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to ensure plugins are independent from the core and other plugins to avoid incompatibility.
- Avoid forcing plugin developers to learn a new bundler.
- Maintain backward compatibility.
- Allow plugin developers to customize Webpack configuration without causing incompatibility.
- Use a known and widely used bundler (Webpack).
- Enable isolated compiling and production bundling.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Webpack's multi-compiler mode to build several independent configurations that do not affect each other. This approach allows isolated compiling and production bundling while maintaining the use of Webpack, which is already known and in use. The watch mode also works with this setup, so developers do not need to relearn anything.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Potential errors caused by plugin-core dependencies are eliminated.
- Each plugin is built completely isolated and cannot affect other plugins or the core.
- Plugin developers can customize their Webpack configuration freely without compatibility concerns.
- The refactoring is backward compatible; plugin developers do not need to change anything.
- The build process is more stable, secure, and flexible.

alternatives.description: Switch to another bundler instead of Webpack.
pros: Could potentially solve the problem if the new bundler handles dependencies better.
cons: Requires deep analysis before switching.
Plugin developers need to learn a new bundler, which can be frustrating.
Unnecessary learning curve when current bundler (Webpack) can solve the problem.

template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support headless mode without storefront URLs, scalability concerns with configuration, clarity in URL generation across different mail triggers, and maintainability of URLs as part of the public API.

template_adherence.title: Refactor theme inheritance
template_adherence.context: Currently, the themes can only inherit config fields from the default Storefront theme. template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve theme config inheritance to avoid snapshot issues, allow inheritance from multiple themes, and provide a dynamic inheritance mechanism that reflects changes automatically. template_adherence.decision: Add a new inheritance key `configInheritance` in the `theme.json` allowing a theme to inherit its config from other themes in a given order, enabling dynamic inheritance rather than snapshot copying. template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include dynamic config inheritance reflecting changes automatically, improved admin control over inheritance, and support for multiple theme dependencies. Negative consequences include potential incompatibility errors due to missing subsets in dependent themes and the need to manage dependencies explicitly in composer.json.

alternatives.description: Keep the current inheritance mechanism where themes inherit config fields only from the default Storefront theme as a snapshot at activation time.

No changes required to existing themes or admin.
cons: Inheritance is a snapshot and does not reflect changes after activation.
Limited to inheriting only from the default Storefront theme.

template_adherence.title: Introduce increment pattern
template_adherence.context:
The current `message_queue_stats` table records which messages are in the message queue and how often. This is done by a subscriber, which then writes a record to the database via the mysql connection. If this record already exists, a duplicate key is triggered and the `count` value of the record will be updated. Systems with many write operations generate a lot of traffic on the message queue. This in turn generates a lot of traffic on the `message_queue_stats` table, resulting in bottlenecks and/or deadlocks.

On another issue, we also provide a feature called `Frequently Used modules` to increase the count everytime an admin module is visited which faces a similar issue.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce bottlenecks and deadlocks caused by high traffic on the `message_queue_stats` table.
- Desire to improve performance and scalability of counting operations.
- Requirement to support multiple increment pools with different storage backends.
- Need for configurability and extensibility of increment storage adapters.
- Maintainability and deprecation of legacy components related to `message_queue_stats`.
template_adherence.decision:
We introduce a new table `increment` to store these countable information and deprecated `message_queue_stats` table. We create a possibility to control the access to the `increment` table via Redis or another storage, which is optimized for such scenarios. To do this, however, we need to prevent / extend access via the DAL.

So we implement a new gateway with the following methods:
* `increment(string $cluster, string $key): void`
* `decrement(string $cluster, string $key): void`
* `list(string $cluster, int $limit = 5, int $offset = 0): array`
* `reset(string $cluster, ?string $key = null): array`
* `getPool(): string`
* `getConfig(): array`
* `getDecorated(): self`

This then enables the following functional flow (illustrated in the ADR).

Furthermore, it should also be possible to completely disable the message queue stats or any pool via config file.

You can easily tweak or define new increment pools in config file with your own pool's configuration.

By default, we ship a Redis, MySQL and array adapter for the gateway. It should be possible to easily switch the adapter via config.

If you want to override the default mysql or redis adapter, you need to register your own incrementer gateway in DI container with the id `shopware.increment.<custom_pool>.gateway.<adapter>`.
template_adherence.consequences:
* We deprecate the `message_queue_stats` DAL classes
* We deprecate the current `message_queue_stats` endpoint in the api
* We deprecate the `message_queue_stats` services
* We deprecate the `message_queue_stats` table
* We create a new `increment` table
* We implement new endpoints to work with the new gateway
* We implement a new node for `increment` configuration
* We use the new gateway in the admin for the notifications
* With the next major we remove all deprecations to the `message_queue_stats`.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing `message_queue_stats` table and DAL classes without changes.
pros: No development effort required.
No changes to existing codebase or configuration.
cons: Continued bottlenecks and deadlocks under high traffic.
No scalability improvements.
Legacy issues remain unresolved.

alternatives.description: Use only MySQL with optimized queries and indexing to handle increment counts.
pros: Leverages existing database technology.
No need to introduce new storage systems.
cons: May not fully resolve bottlenecks under very high load.
Less flexible than multi-adapter approach.
Potentially complex query optimization required.

alternatives.description: Use a single Redis-based increment system without fallback or multiple adapters.
pros: High performance and low latency increments.
Simpler implementation than multi-adapter system.
cons: Single point of failure if Redis is down.
Less flexible for different use cases.
No fallback to other storage types.

template_adherence.title: Add feature flag support for Storefront SCSS
template_adherence.context:
* There is no possibility to check for feature flags inside the Storefront SCSS.
* Altering the SCSS depending on a feature flag will require workarounds like e.g. "making up" and additional class in the template and use the feature toggle in twig instead.
* The SCSS of a selector which is hidden behind a feature flag will still be in the compiled CSS.
* It is not easily possible to make breaking changes inside SCSS functions, mixins or variables backward-compatible with the use of feature flags.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support feature flags directly in Storefront SCSS to avoid workarounds.
- Desire to keep SCSS clean and avoid unnecessary CSS for disabled features.
- Compatibility with existing feature flag configuration and tooling.
- Maintainability and ease of use for developers working with SCSS and feature flags.
template_adherence.decision: Add the possibility to check for feature flags inside SCSS, similar to the twig implementation. The feature configuration from `Feature::getAll()` is converted to a SCSS map inside `\Shopware\Storefront\Theme\ThemeCompiler::getFeatureConfigScssMap`. This SCSS map is always added to the SCSS string processed by `\Shopware\Storefront\Theme\ThemeCompiler::compileTheme`. For webpack hot-proxy, the `var/config_js_features.json` is used instead. A globally available function `feature()` is used to read inside the SCSS map if a desired feature is active.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The feature dump file `var/config_js_features.json` is now used by the Storefront webpack configuration `src/Storefront/Resources/app/storefront/webpack.config.js`.
- When the feature dump cannot be found, all features will be disabled/false inside `webpack.config.js` and hot-proxy SCSS.
- A warning is shown in this case with the request to execute `bin/console feature:dump` manually.
- Enables cleaner and more maintainable SCSS code with feature flags.
- Potentially increases build complexity by adding feature flag processing in SCSS compilation.

alternatives.description: Continue using workarounds such as adding additional classes in templates and toggling features in twig templates instead of SCSS.
pros: No changes needed in SCSS compilation process.
No new feature flag integration in SCSS required.
cons: SCSS still contains styles for all features, increasing CSS size.
Workarounds are cumbersome and error-prone.
Cannot make breaking changes in SCSS functions or mixins backward-compatible easily.

template_adherence.title: Fast API as Rest API framework
template_adherence.context:
Python provides several frameworks to develop RESTful APIs. All of them have their pro and cons and fit different scenarios.

In this project we have the following functional requirements:
* we want to build a REST API
* we don't need templating or HTML rendering features
* we need an OpenAPI specification exposed from the API
* we need a validation framework for input data
* we need a serialization framework for output data
* **OPT** we need an automated mechanism to keep in sync the OpenAPI spec with the implementation

In this project we have the following non-functional requirements:
* we need a small memory consumption, in this way we can replicate the api in several containers
* **OPT** we need support for asynchronous handling of HTTP requests, in this way we can reduce the number of replicas in high I/O bound performance scenarios
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Functional requirements such as building a REST API, no need for templating or HTML rendering, need for OpenAPI spec exposure, validation and serialization frameworks, and optionally automated OpenAPI spec sync.
Non-functional requirements include small memory consumption and optionally asynchronous HTTP request handling for performance.
template_adherence.decision: Use FastAPI as a REST framework because it meets all functional and non-functional requirements, supports Python typing and Pydantic models for validation and serialization, and automatically generates OpenAPI specs and documentation.
template_adherence.consequences:
FastAPI is based on ASGI, requiring an ASGI compatible webserver to run FastAPI apps.
It suggests using Pydantic as the Data Transfer Objects framework for natural integration and up-to-date documentation.

template_adherence.title: Implement liveliness, readiness and startup probes
template_adherence.context:
Cloud providers often rely on the usage of Orchestration systems over a containerization technology.

The orchestration system needs to know at least 2 things about any service:

* If the service started correctly after a deployment
* If the service is still healthy at any moment in time
template_adherence.decision:
When implementing an API that has to be deployed on the cloud, implement the following endpoints:

* `/ready` an endpoint that returns a 200 - OK if the service is ready to accept requests after a new deployment
* `/health` an endpoint that returns a 200 - OK if the service is still alive and functioning correctly
template_adherence.consequences:
Thanks to this 2 endpoints is possible to deterministically and automatically detect problems both after a new deployment and during the normal operation of the service directly into the orchestration service.

Check out this page for more info regarding how `kubernetes` can be configured for this https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/#define-a-liveness-http-request

template_adherence.title: Pydantic for Data Transfer Objects, Validation and Serialization
template_adherence.context: Python is a dynamically typed language that has an extremely powerful data structure, the dictionary (a.k.a. `dict`). Whereas the `dict` is a good choice for many scenarios I think that its usage was abused throughout the python projects I encountered in my career. In many cases, data received from a http endpoint through parameters or POST body is represented in the code as a dict. The same can be said for data returned from a Rest API that adopts the JSON format as response. The simplicity of creating new dicts with literals often wins against the creation and the initialization of a dedicated class. This though brings, after some time, to problems related to the validation and the documentation of what a `dict` instance contains throughout the code, problem that gets even worse when passing the same dictionary throughout a deep stack of function calls.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve data validation and documentation when using dictionaries for data transfer in Python projects. The desire to leverage Python's type annotations and dataclasses for better data handling. The requirement to have a clean and maintainable codebase that handles validation errors gracefully.
template_adherence.decision: Use `pydantic` to represent data objects and validate your data. Pydantic leverages Python 3's type annotations, dataclasses automatic constructors, and a validation framework based on reflection, extendable with decorators.
template_adherence.consequences: For each endpoint, define input and output data types using `pydantic.BaseModel`. This results in cleaner code, better validation, and structured error handling. The approach improves maintainability and clarity of data structures passed through the system. Validation errors can be caught and returned in a structured JSON format.

alternatives.description: Continue using plain Python dictionaries for data transfer without additional validation frameworks.
pros: Simplicity and familiarity for Python developers.
No additional dependencies required.
cons: Lack of automatic validation leads to potential runtime errors.
Poor documentation of expected data structures.
Harder to maintain and understand data flow in complex systems.

alternatives.description: Use custom classes with manual validation methods instead of pydantic.
pros: Full control over validation logic.
No dependency on external libraries.
cons: More boilerplate code to write and maintain.
Reinventing features that pydantic already provides.
Less standardized approach, potentially inconsistent validation.

template_adherence.title: 1. Deployment on-prem & as a SaaS
template_adherence.context:
In global health there are two deployment constraints that push against one another:  the desire for iNGO's, government agencies, multi-laterals, etc to lower the barrier to acquiring software solutions by utilizing a SaaS model, and that of many governments to exercise self-reliance and sovereignty of their software and their data by being able to reasonably deploy software on premise in their own data center.

With regards to SaaS, most customers of the software are able and willing to pay reasonable monthly fees, especially if those fees are predictable over a suitable project timeline.  For organizations that want to offer PCMT as a SaaS they likely will expect the number of instances to be quite low:  likely less than 25 in the next 5 years.  Thus the key attributes for those running PCMT as a SaaS and for those consuming PCMT as a SaaS are reasonable fees and lead-times for signing a new instance on.

When a government agency deploys the software in their own data center a principal concern is that of limited resources.  Limited both in hardware and the maturity of the data center, as well as on the technical staff available. There are few organizations within PCMT's user-base that have extensive experience running highly available services or complicated deployment stacks.

We have a number of choices that are available to us:

1. Multi-tenancy development in theory can achieve the greatest cost-per-customer since the same application code on the same hardware can serve more than one customer.  However it can significantly increase the scope and development of each feature as each needs to consider how many customers would share the same resources without impacting one-another. It can also increase deployment cost and complexity as each instance needs to be configured and monitored for many clients.
1. Multi-single-tenancy is really a single tenancy model that utilizes advances in containerization, oftentimes cloud providers, and deployment tools to manage many single instances, one per customer, in such an automated fashion as to make it nearly indistinguishable from multi-tenancy.
1. Serverless is an approach to reduce overhead for developers by shifting resource management to a provider.  It's included here for completeness, and while it may make development practices easier, the deployment of a serverless architecture on-prem in PCMT's context is non-trivial.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly label a 'Decision Drivers' section, but the context and alternatives imply drivers such as balancing SaaS ease and cost, government self-reliance and sovereignty, limited resources and technical staff in on-prem deployments, cost per customer, deployment complexity, and maintainability.
template_adherence.decision:
We will build PCMT to be multi-single-tenant utilizing containers as the basic unit of deployment. Each instance of PCMT will be served by one or more containers, and where each container serves only one function for one PCMT instance.

We will build simple tools, in the category of Infrastructure as Code, that helps provision computing resources both in one cloud provider as well as on-prem, configure the instance of PCMT, and aid in the maintenance life-cycle of that instance: upgrades, backups, archiving, destruction.

We will provide complete IaC deliverables that are able to provision resources outside of PCMT's scope, such as email & DNS.

We will build PCMT so that it runs in as little as 2GB of RAM, 2 cores of a modern CPU and 10GB of storage which is a reasonable requirement of most on-prem data centers.  As of May 2019 this targets a $30 / month per PCMT instance price-point in one cloud provider, with plenty of opportunity for additional per instance and per month reductions in cost.
template_adherence.consequences:
The development team will not need to scope and build each feature to be multi-tenant.

The development team will need to properly scope and build PCMT and its supporting deployment tools to run both in the cloud and on-premise using a basic set of IaC tools that are free and simple to use.

PCMT's scope and performance characteristics will be constrained in-part by what can be reasonable run within 2GB of RAM and 2 CPU cores with 10GB of storage.

Those wishing to deploy PCMT as a SaaS will have a starting point, however they likely will need to invest more in order to run a large number of instances, reduce the deployment lead-time, or reduce the per-instance cost.

alternatives.description: Multi-tenancy development in theory can achieve the greatest cost-per-customer since the same application code on the same hardware can serve more than one customer. However it can significantly increase the scope and development of each feature as each needs to consider how many customers would share the same resources without impacting one-another. template_adherence.title: 3. Cloud Provisioning through Terraform
template_adherence.context:
Deploying to the cloud is a fundamental part of increasing software delivery frequency. However once the frequency is increased, it becomes increasingly needed to manage the provisioning and configuration of those cloud resources lest a step is forgotten, a security vulnerability is found, or an instance is corrupted. Following patterns found in software development, such as managing infrastructure as code (IaC) and tracking changes in source control, are widely regarded as good practice today.

Many cloud providers have bespoke tooling that helps manage the creation of resources on their infrastructure. While this tooling is hugely powerful, the context of PCMT is that our cloud resources should be kept as simple as possible, in part due to our constraint to allow for on-prem deployments. Further an organization that chooses to deploy PCMT as a SaaS may not use the same cloud provider as the one the PCMT project uses.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly list decision drivers in a dedicated section. However, from the context, the drivers include the need for managing cloud provisioning reliably, supporting multiple cloud providers, simplicity for on-prem deployments, and avoiding dependency on a single cloud provider's tooling.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Terraform to provision cloud resources such as compute instances, storage, DNS, etc.
template_adherence.consequences: Terraform is a newer IaC tool that supports multiple cloud providers, but not all cloud providers or all advanced capabilities of supported providers may be available through Terraform.

pros: Powerful and tailored to each cloud provider's capabilities.
cons: May lead to complexity due to multiple tools.

alternatives.description: Use Terraform to provision cloud resources.
pros: Supports multiple cloud providers.

template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for efficient detection of array length and clear identification of array keys; compatibility with existing metadata conventions; ensuring plugins can rely on correct array metadata early; handling of overrides and cascading lookups; validation of array structure.
template_adherence.decision: Store length in metadata 'array' of key, or keep metadata 'array' empty if empty array. Only children with '#'-syntax are allowed in a valid array, with indices starting at '#0'. Both 'keyAddName("#12")' and 'keyAddBaseName("#_12")' are allowed. The 'spec' plugin will add the 'array' marker with correct length early to ensure plugin reliability. Arrays are validated by the 'spec' plugin to ensure correct metadata and structure.
template_adherence.consequences: Requires fixes and adaptations in yajl, metadata library, and spec plugin. Significant work needed to detect misstructured nested arrays. Potential semantic changes if user or dir keys override system arrays. Documentation must note that mixing array and non-array keys is unsupported and suggest moving array parts to separate child keys.

alternatives.description: Metadata arrays simply work by convention as they are not serialized in special ways nor validated.
pros: Simple to implement
No special serialization or validation needed
cons: Inefficient detection of array length
Ambiguity in array identification

alternatives.description: Use '###empty_array' as in yajl.
pros: Existing approach in yajl
cons: Does not allow efficient access of first element

alternatives.description: Store length (and not last element) with prepending of '#_...'.
pros: Explicit length storage
cons: Needs prepending of '#_...' which complicates key naming

alternatives.description: Store element after last element (C++-Style).
pros: Familiar approach from C++
cons: Does not fit nicely with key-value structure

alternatives.description: Use value and not the metadata 'array'.
pros: Simpler metadata
cons: Ambiguous interpretation

alternatives.description: Use metadata on all children.
pros: Explicit metadata per child
cons: Increased metadata overhead

template_adherence.title: Definition of Bool
template_adherence.context: Inconsistent use of booleans in various parts of Elektra.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for consistent boolean representation as strings; ease of implementation; compatibility with storage plugins and applications.
template_adherence.decision: Only the strings '0' and '1' are allowed in the KeySet for type = boolean, for both values and defaults. A spec with type = boolean without a specified default is interpreted as default = 0. Storage plugins may represent these as suitable (e.g., JSON plugin may render '1' as true). The type checker plugin should allow non-presence, '0', and '1'.
template_adherence.consequences: Storage plugins must emit only '0' or '1' as key values. Applications can safely interpret absence or '0' as false and '1' as true. This simplifies implementation and ensures consistency across the system.

alternatives.description: Only check presence or absence (no cascading override of already present key possible).
pros: Simple to implement.
cons: Does not allow explicit true/false values beyond presence.
Less flexible for applications needing explicit boolean values.

alternatives.description: Use booleans as in CMake, which allows on/off, true/false, etc., requiring convenience across the code.
pros: More expressive and flexible boolean representations.
Aligns with familiar boolean conventions in other systems.
cons: More complex to implement and maintain.
Requires additional convenience functions across the codebase.

alternatives.description: Do not accept a specification with type = boolean without a default.
pros: Ensures explicit defaults are always provided.
Avoids ambiguity in boolean interpretation.
cons: Less flexible; may require more specification from users.
Could lead to errors if defaults are omitted.

template_adherence.title: Bootstrap
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses issues with the current default backend (default.ecf) used for bootstrapping in the system. The problems include incompatibility with most plugins due to absolute path storage and inefficiency caused by rereading large data twice during bootstrapping.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for a fast bootstrap process that avoids unnecessary reading of large files and resolves the problems caused by the current default backend approach.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to split the concepts of default (default.ecf) and bootstrap (elektra.ecf) backends. During bootstrap, only elektra.ecf is read, and the default backend reading default.ecf is relevant only when no root backend is mounted. The algorithm involves trying to get system:/elektra using the file elektra.ecf (KDB_DB_INIT) and mounting the init backend to system:/elektra.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision improves bootstrapping efficiency and plugin compatibility by separating bootstrap and default backends. It requires migration steps for existing setups, which are facilitated by added scripts and instructions.

cons: Does not solve the problem of rereading large data twice.
Is considered a hack and confusing.
Does not work well with persistent data with relative key names.

alternatives.description: Split up without compatibility mode, requiring migration of all mount points by exporting with old version and importing with new version.
pros: Could separate concerns effectively.
cons: Considered too error-prone.
Users might forget to export with the old version, leading to loss of mount points.

template_adherence.title: Capabilities
template_adherence.context: Only plugins like `dump` and `quickdump` are able to represent any KeySet (as they are designed to do so). Limitations of other storage plugins are e.g., that not every structure of configuration is allowed. Some of these limitations were documented `infos/status`, others were not.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for tooling to query existing limitations of storage plugins.
- Complexity of implementing plugins to work around limitations.
- Complexity of Capabilities API for application developers who may not know exact requirements of underlying formats.
template_adherence.decision: Add `infos/features/storage` to document limitations of storage plugins. Ideally, storage plugins should throw an error in `kdbSet` for unrepresentable KeySets. Elektra cannot guarantee that any configuration file format can be mounted anywhere. Developers, maintainers and administrators are responsible for what they mount and need to test the setup.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Storage plugins will have documented limitations via `infos/features/storage`.
- Errors will be thrown for unrepresentable KeySets during `kdbSet`.
- Responsibility for configuration mounting lies with developers and administrators.
- Potentially improved clarity and error handling in storage plugin usage.

alternatives.description: Implement plugins that work around the limitations (e.g., escape characters or rewrite directory values).
pros: May allow more flexible handling of configuration structures.
cons: Too complex.
Leads to new problems such as escaping rewritten values and plugin interactions (e.g., renaming and notification).

alternatives.description: Use Capabilities API to handle limitations.
pros: Provides a formal API to query capabilities.
cons: Found too complex for application developers.

template_adherence.title: Deferred Plugin Calls
template_adherence.context: Calling exported functions is a primary way for coordinating plugins in Elektra. Since some plugins encapsulate other plugins, exported functions from encapsulated plugins become unavailable. Encapsulating plugins cannot implement and forward calls for every function exported by encapsulated plugins, so a generic mechanism for function calls to these encapsulated plugins is needed. Additionally, some plugins lazy-load encapsulated plugins, requiring the call mechanism to defer calls until the plugins are loaded.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
1. Plugins encapsulating other plugins shall be able to lazy-load them.
2. Callers shall not be entangled in encapsulating plugin details.
3. The encapsulation of the plugins shall not be broken.
4. The mechanism shall be generic.
template_adherence.decision: Encapsulating plugins export a function called `deferredCall` with the declaration `void elektraDeferredCall (Plugin * plugin, char * name, KeySet * parameters)`. Encapsulating plugins shall save multiple deferred calls and call the exported functions specified by `name` passing the `parameters` KeySet when a plugin is initialized in the same order as received. Plugins that support deferred calls shall have the following declaration for their functions `void somePluginFunction (Plugin * plugin, KeySet * parameters)`. The calling developer is responsible for ensuring that the called functions have a compatible declaration. Encapsulated plugins that do not export a specified function name are omitted.
template_adherence.consequences: The solution allows changing encapsulating plugin implementations without breaking callers. The called functions receive their parameters via a KeySet. While called functions could return data using the `parameters` KeySet (or a separate KeySet), there is no defined moment when the data can be collected, and defining such a moment would break the lazy-loading constraint. It is recommended to use callbacks passed as `parameters`. Functions supporting deferred calls should allow for multiple calls (i.e., they should be idempotent), leaving state at affected plugins and avoiding duplicating state in encapsulating plugins.

alternatives.description: Encapsulating plugins export a function called `getEncapsulatedPlugins`. This would break encapsulation and break lazy-loading since to return the encapsulated plugin handles they have to be loaded.
pros: Simple to implement.
cons: Breaks encapsulation.
Breaks lazy-loading because plugins must be loaded to return handles.

alternatives.description: Compatible plugins export a function called `getInterfaces` that returns a KeySet with well-known interface names and required functions. Encapsulating plugins collect interfaces from their plugins and combine them into a single KeySet.
pros: Makes encapsulating plugins transparent to the caller.
Caller does not need to know if plugin encapsulates others.
cons: Breaks lazy-loading since all plugins have to be loaded to combine interfaces.
Requires calling `getInterfaces` functions of all encapsulated plugins.

template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the problem of implementing error codes in a way that is suitable for cross compilation and maintainability. template_adherence.decision: The decision is to write the few macros manually and also manually write exceptions for the language bindings, including mappings from Elektra's internal errors to language-specific errors. A tutorial on how to write a binding should be created. This approach minimizes effort but requires manual synchronization when error codes change.

pros: Simplifies the data model.

template_adherence.title: Library Split
template_adherence.context: Only libelektra-core is supposed to access private data but this contradicts the goal to keep the library minimal. `kdbprivate.h` was too generic, it contained many other parts next to the struct definitions of Key/KeySet.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- The C99 standard limits external identifiers in one translation unit to 4095.
- Some parts of Elektra, like `mmapstorage`, need access to private data structures.
- Elektra does not support multiple different struct definitions of Key/KeySet; alternative implementations must use the same struct definitions.
template_adherence.decision: Allow `libelektra-operations` library to access private Key/KeySet. Put struct definitions of Key/KeySet in a separate header file, which gets included by parts that need it.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Enables various users (plugins, applications) to link to exactly what they need.
- Allows symbol versioning on different levels for different evolving libraries.
- Supports alternative implementations of parts of Elektra, e.g., a libcore written in Rust.
- Facilitates code reuse between plugins.
- Requires clear communication about which plugins/libraries must match the version of libelektra-core.

template_adherence.title: Logging
template_adherence.context: Both code comments and assertions are unfortunately not very popular. A quite efficient way to still get some documentation about the code are logging statements. In Elektra they are currently inconsistent and unusable. Thus there is an urge for this decision.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Logging must be disabled by default.
- Should completely compile away with ENABLE_LOGGER=OFF.
- Should support minimalistic, compile-time filtering (per modules and verbosity level?) and some sinks (stderr, syslog or files).
- Run-time problems are checked via assertions, not logged.
- Opinions differ about logging to stderr or files.
- Filtering with grep is not enough.
- By default there should be no output.
- With ENABLE_LOGGER=ON only warnings and errors should be shown on stderr.
- Other sinks like syslog and file may log more (not immediately visible and distracting).
- Performance is not so important (logging usually turned off anyway).
template_adherence.decision:
Provide a Macro

```c
ELEKTRA_LOG (int module, const char *msg, ...);
```

that calls

```c
elektraLog ([as above], const char * function, const char * file, const int line, ...);
```

and adds current function, file and line to `elektraLog`'s arguments.

`elektraLog` is implemented in a separate `log.c` file. If someone needs filtering, logging to different sources or similar, he/she simply modifies `log.c`.

Severity levels and module definitions are also specified to support the logging system.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The current VERBOSE logging would be turned off forever.
- Code within VERBOSE needs to be migrated to `ELEKTRA_LOG`.

template_adherence.title: Plugin Variants
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the problem of plugins that cannot fully define their contract statically, requiring enumeration of plugin variants based on configuration. The problem is that there is no current way to enumerate possible plugin variants to list all functionality of Elektra.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include user customizability (ability to add and suppress plugin variants), modularity (plugin code defines variants and can be iterated over), performance optimization (avoid reopening plugins multiple times), bounded number of variants (fully enumerable), and consistency with existing APIs like checkconf.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to delay implementation until after version 1.0. The best candidate implementation involves providing a function `genconf` that returns all variants with essential configuration and contract changes, allowing overrides and disabling of variants via keys, and defining default behaviors for empty configurations. This approach is consistent with the checkconf API and supports extensibility and customizability.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include the need to implement `genconf` for several plugins, extend the PluginDatabase to list all variants, and enhance the `kdb plugin-list` command to show variants. Currently, only configuration overrides are possible, and adding additional information to variants is not yet supported. This approach provides a structured and extensible way to enumerate plugin variants but requires further implementation work.

Could provide a comprehensive specification-based approach.

Elektra's specification language was incomplete and inconsistent at the time.
Does not fit with the existing checkconf approach.

template_adherence.title: Reference Counting
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses issues with reference counting in the Key and KeySet APIs, including problems with locking not resetting when reference count reaches zero and inconsistencies between C++ API behaviors. The problem is to improve reference counting mechanisms to handle these issues effectively.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for thread safety, memory efficiency, API consistency, error handling on overflow/underflow, and maintaining functionality with minimal complexity.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to add a second counter to Key for locking the keyname with a re-entrant lock, introduce reference counters for KeySets, limit reference counts to UINT16_MAX - 1 with error on overflow, no error on underflow, use fixed size types (uint16_t), and increment/decrement references appropriately when passing instances to plugins.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision saves memory by using smaller counters, adds complexity by maintaining two counters, improves thread safety and API consistency, and requires updates to bindings and implementation of the second counter for keyname locking.

cons: May add complexity.
Does not address all issues like locking and API inconsistencies.

alternatives.description: Start with 1 for reference counting and let keyDecRef do keyDel.
pros: Simplifies reference counting logic.

cons: May not handle locking issues.

template_adherence.title: Metadata in Spec Namespace
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the problem of making storage-plugins suitable for the 'spec' namespace by ensuring they can store all metadata as specified in METADATA.ini. It highlights issues with metadata merging across namespaces and the lack of support in most file formats.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to preserve configuration file structure metadata, avoid errors from storing unrelated metadata in wrong namespaces, and support different meanings of metadata like 'array' and 'type' in different namespaces. It also considers the usability of simple storage plugins and the clarity of metadata handling.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to store metadata unrelated to configuration file structure only in the 'spec:/' namespace. Errors will be raised if other namespaces attempt to store such metadata. Metadata designed for storage plugins (e.g., 'comment', 'order') can be stored in any namespace. Different storage plugins or configurations should be used for the 'spec:/' namespace, such as 'ni' or TOML with 'meta' configuration. The 'kdb mount' tool will add the 'meta' plugin configuration when mounting to 'spec:/'.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision requires different default plugins for 'spec:/' compared to other namespaces, which may cause confusion due to differing metadata meanings (e.g., 'array'). The 'spec:/' meaning of 'array=' must be stored explicitly, while other meanings should be inferred. It prevents internal metadata from leaking into configuration files and allows simple storage plugins to be used with realistic specifications.

alternatives.description: Designate metadata only for 'spec:/' or for restoring configuration file formats, renaming metadata types to clarify namespaces.
pros: No merging of metadata needed.

cons: Requires renaming metadata types.

alternatives.description: Do not support 'array' or 'type' if the underlying format does not support it; rely on 'spec-mount' to ensure plugin support.
pros: Avoids unsupported metadata storage.
cons: Limits metadata support based on underlying format.
May reduce flexibility.

template_adherence.title: Validation
template_adherence.context: Validation plugins operate as independent blackboxes. For every backend each mounted validation plugin iterates over the whole keyset, checks every key for its trigger metakey, and validates the key. Currently all needed validation plugins need to be specified at mount-time - if additional validation is required, the backend has to be remounted with the required plugins and plugin configuration. If validation of a key fails, each plugin decides on its own how to handle the issue and proceed in ways that might be different from what is expected or desired.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the need to handle validation failures consistently, support multiple validation plugins per key, and allow different error handling strategies without requiring each plugin to implement them separately.
template_adherence.decision: Use a wrapper plugin to iterate over the keyset and delegate the validation of each key to the corresponding validation plugin.
template_adherence.consequences: Validation plugins have to export their validation routine `static int validateKey(const Key * key, const Key * errorKey)` returning 1 if validation succeeded, 0 on failure.

template_adherence.title: Selection of Identity Management Platform
template_adherence.context: Wellcome Collection wishes to implement an Identity and Access Management platform, to provide authentication and authorisation services. Such a service is required to integrate with Wellcome Library's existing pool of registered library members, and would expose itself through recognised, standards based protocols.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Ease of implementation and ongoing maintenance.
* Low / nil upfront and ongoing subscription costs.
* Ability to integrate with, and maintain, an existing user pool.
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: Auth0, because it offers superior integration with existing user pools.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to use Auth0 means the platform benefits from simple integration with third-party user pools, no requirement for usernames, extensive out-of-the-box integrations, and customizable hosted pages. However, ongoing subscription costs can be significant depending on usage.

alternatives.description: AWS Cognito
pros: Good, because it is effectively free to use for lower usage tiers.
cons: Integration with third-party user pools is complex and limited.
It enforces the existence of an unwanted immutable "username" attribute.
Core configuration options cannot be changed without destroying and recreating the AWS Cognito resource.
The degree of customisation for user interfaces and automatically generated emails is not sufficient for the identified use cases.

alternatives.description: Auth0
pros: Provides simple integration with a third-party user pool via custom scripts that can run any NodeJS code on login / user lookup.
Does not require the use of usernames (i.e. email addresses only).
Ships with a large number of SSO / social / enterprise integrations out-of-the-box.
Offers the ability to extensively customise hosted pages (e.g. login / forgot password).
cons: Depending on usage, ongoing subscription costs can be significant.

template_adherence.title: Logging Approach
template_adherence.context: The Identity platform consists of numerous interconnected components, each responsible for generating their own log outputs. Some of these log outputs will be driven by the implementation of logging within a component, and others will be provided "out-of-the-box" by a managed service. In either case, these logs files must be readily accessible, queryable, and persisted over a long period.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Collation of logs to a single, centralised platform utilised by all platforms in Wellcome Collection's technical estate.
* Minimal infrastructure / configuration required in components to utilise the centralised logging platform.
template_adherence.decision:
- For containers deployed into AWS ECS / AWS Fargate, Wellcome Collection's existing ELK stack will be utilised. Logs will be pushed to the stack via a Firelens sidecar containers.

- For all log generating services (e.g. Lambda Function and API Gateway logs), the default AWS CloudWatch configurations will be used.

alternatives.description: AWS CloudWatch
Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana (ELK)

template_adherence.title: Infrastructure Secrets Approach
template_adherence.context: Any reasonably sized infrastructure deployment requires the creation, management and utilisation of secrets and configuration. Any approach taken to achieve these goals must be sensitive to maintaining not only the secure storage and usage of these secrets and parameters, but should reduce friction in the design, deployment, and maintenance of the infrastructure.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Secure storage of the secrets and parameters.
* Ease of integration with infrastructure tooling (e.g. Terraform, AWS).
* Ease of maintenance of secrets and parameters.
* Low ongoing costs.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: a combination of both AWS Secrets Store and AWS Systems Manager for storing both secrets and configuration parameters respectively.

For secrets and parameters created outside of the scope of the Terraform, AWS Secrets Store and AWS Systems Manager resources will be created in Terraform with placeholder values provided for the initial resource creation. Actual secrets and parameters will then be manually curated by developers and support staff. This approach allows such secrets and configuration to be referenced in the Terraform by other resources, without exposing them.

For secrets and parameters generated by Terraform, these will be fed directly into other Terraform resources that require them.
template_adherence.consequences: The ADR does not explicitly state consequences in a dedicated section. However, some implications can be inferred from the decision outcome and pros and cons sections, such as secure management and integration benefits, but no explicit consequences section is present.

template_adherence.title: Auth Strategy: Passport vs. OpenID Connect
template_adherence.context:
The Identity client app is served from a lightweight Node.js server, which handles OAuth authentication among other things. It achieves this with the Passport auth middleware, and the Auth0 strategy to interact with our auth service.

Auth0 recently launched a new SDK for OpenID Connect, an alternative to Passport. In the launch announcement, they stated that development on their own Passport strategy was being reduced to security patches, recommending new projects to consider using express-openid-connect.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to maintain current functionality and meet customer requirements.
- Compatibility with existing frameworks (Koa vs Express).
- Maintenance and update status of dependencies (Passport vs OpenID Connect SDK).
- Code complexity and amount of code required.
- Security implications of using outdated packages.
- Development effort and risk of losing existing work.
template_adherence.decision: The project will continue to use Passport and no work to integrate the OpenID Connect SDK is currently required.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Continued use of Passport maintains current functionality without additional development effort.
- Potentially missing out on reduced code complexity and newer features of the OpenID Connect SDK.
- Avoids compatibility issues between Koa and Express middleware.
- Relies on a package (koa-passport) that has not been updated since 2019, which may have security implications.
- No immediate migration effort required, but future considerations may be needed as Passport development slows.

alternatives.description: Continue using Passport for authentication.
pros: Current implementation meets customer requirements.
No dependency on Auth0's Passport strategy which is being deprecated.
Compatible with Koa framework via koa-passport.
Supports local development with existing work already done.
cons: koa-passport has not been updated since 2019, potential security risks.
Passport-Auth0 strategy development is stopping, only security patches planned.
May require future migration as Passport support diminishes.

alternatives.description: Drop Passport in favour of OpenID Connect with the Auth0 SDK.
pros: Significantly reduces amount of code needed for user authentication.
Auth0's target for innovation on Node.js platform.
Potentially more up-to-date and maintained SDK.
cons: OpenID Connect SDK is designed for Express, not directly compatible with Koa.
Would require additional work to integrate and possibly lose existing local development setup.
Compatibility solutions exist but add complexity.

template_adherence.title: Do not use Azure Search Service highlighting
template_adherence.context: Azure Search Service has the ability to return results with the search term hits highlighted. The searches submitted by the application add a wildcard character (`*`) to each term to match the beginning of words. However, this causes the highlighting to return full word matches instead of only the exact term entered. There is no option within the search service to have only the exact term highlighted.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The search service's inability to highlight only the exact term entered, due to the use of wildcard characters in search terms, drives the need for an alternative highlighting approach.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to perform highlighting on the application server after receiving results from the search service, rather than using the search service's built-in highlighting feature.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision results in additional code within the application to handle highlighting. However, it also leads to smaller and less involved requests and responses between the application and the search service.

alternatives.description: Use Azure Search Service's built-in highlighting feature despite its limitation of highlighting full words instead of exact terms.
pros: Leverages existing search service capabilities without additional application code.
Simpler implementation as highlighting is handled by the search service.
cons: Highlighting does not meet the requirement of highlighting only the exact term.
Results may highlight more text than desired, potentially confusing users.

alternatives.description: Perform highlighting entirely on the application server after receiving raw search results without any highlighting.
pros: Allows precise control over highlighting to meet exact term requirements.
Reduces complexity in search service requests and responses.
cons: Requires additional application code to implement highlighting logic.
Potentially increases processing load on the application server.

template_adherence.title: Use micro frontends
template_adherence.context:
We designed the API layer (known as the backend) to be a custom set of services. This allows the user to tailor it to their own requirements, and introduce custom code as needed.

The original plan was to make the presentation layer (known as the frontend) a monolith. That is, a single service that generates all the HTML pages.

As a monolith, it is hard, if not impossible, to change or replace parts without having to replace the whole. This would mean a lot of configuration options to support differing requirements. It would also limit adoption of the platform as it can't meet them.

We investigated the use of micro frontends in [#371][Spike].
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to allow customization and flexibility in the frontend layer, avoiding the limitations of a monolithic frontend that is hard to change or replace. Desire to support differing requirements and increase adoption by making the frontend modular.
template_adherence.decision: We will create separate services for individual, and groups of, pages. The user will use a proxy to make them appear as a single service. The frontends are independent of each other, and are always optional.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The frontends will need to share knowledge of authentication.
- Each frontend will have its own assets.
- The user will need to configure each frontend so it knows how to generate links to other frontends.
- The user can choose which frontends to use.
- The user can add their own frontends as needed.

alternatives.description: Keep the frontend as a monolithic service generating all HTML pages.
pros: Simpler deployment as only one frontend service exists.
Easier to manage a single codebase for the frontend.
cons: Hard or impossible to change or replace parts without replacing the whole.
Would require many configuration options to support differing requirements.
Limits adoption as it can't meet diverse user needs.

template_adherence.title: Why Service sign in pages aren't linked to from transaction pages using a content id
template_adherence.context: Currently, when content designers create a transaction page they enter a URL for the service that the start button should link to, and this service is usually an external (to GOV.UK) URL. Service sign in pages however will be GOV.UK content items, and ideally we should not link to specific content item URLs as they could change in future. Instead, the links should reference a content_id, which never changes. However as the field where content designers enter the URL that the start button should link to doesn't support content_ids currently, the only option available to them is to enter the URL for the service sign in page.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid linking directly to URLs that may change, the current limitation of the content designers' URL field not supporting content_ids, and the risk assessment of linking directly to URLs versus content_ids.
template_adherence.decision: After discussion with the publishing platform team, it was decided that the risk of linking directly to a URL is low because if the base_path of the service sign in page changes, the publishing API will automatically create a redirect. Therefore, the current approach of linking directly to URLs is acceptable for now.
template_adherence.consequences: The current approach carries some risk but is mitigated by automatic redirects. Ideally, in the future, the system should support referencing content_ids instead of URLs to fully mitigate risk. This will require changes to the editing interface in Publisher to support content_ids.

template_adherence.title: Why "Service sign in" is its own format
template_adherence.context: The Q3 Start Pages mission goal was to make it easier for users to choose a sign in option in order to access a service. It was decided that a page should sit in between the transaction/guide page and the service which allows users to select a sign in option such as GOV.UK Verify or Government Gateway, or to register for a new account (henceforth known as the service sign in page). We initially looked at whether we could use an existing format to house this page. At first glance, it felt that transaction pages might be a suitable place for it, as it would be tailored to the transaction. Alternatively we could create a new format for this page.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for flexibility to link service sign in pages from more than one format (transactions and guides), the scope limitations of the mission (not including consolidating product debt around transactions or building UI support), and the desire to deliver a decent user experience for content designers without altering the transaction UI.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to create a new `service_sign_in` format to house the service sign in pages, including a required `choose_sign_in` page and an optional `create_new_account` page, rather than incorporating these pages into the existing transaction format.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequence is that while this new format provides flexibility and better handles additional pages related to service sign in, it may lead to a less flexible format or extension to transactions in the future if user needs are met by abusing the guide format or consolidating hacky usage of other formats into transactions. This could potentially simplify the publisher workflow and allow consistent iterations to start pages as a product.

alternatives.description: Incorporate service sign in pages into the existing transaction format.
pros: Tailored to the transaction, potentially more integrated experience.
cons: Not suitable for guides which also link to service sign pages.
Requires consolidating product debt around transactions, which is out of scope.
Would require altering the transaction UI, which is not in scope.

alternatives.description: Create a separate format for the `create_new_account` page.
pros: Clear separation of concerns.
Potentially easier to manage individual pages.
cons: Currently no need for a standalone page for this.
Adds complexity without immediate benefit.

template_adherence.title: Why "Service sign in" pages are created using rake tasks
template_adherence.context: For the Q3 Start Pages mission, we descoped creating a UI in Publisher to handle the workflow of managing Service sign in pages due to time constraints. As such we needed to find a way for developers to easily create and update service sign in pages.
template_adherence.decision:
One of the options was to hardcode the content within their own views, which would require a developer to manually update content when needed. While this is a simple approach, it isn't very scalable and is prone to error. With this approach we would not be sending the content to the Publishing API. As such we would have to remember to register routes ourselves, and wouldn't have other benefits of the Publishing API such as maintaining content history.

We knew that Smart Answers made use of rake tasks to import content, so we considered following a similar approach. This would involve a content designer providing a YAML file containing the content, which would be imported using a rake task and then presented in a data format that could be sent to the Publishing API. The downside of this approach is that we assume that content designers have some level of familiarity with YAML and would be able to provide the file to us via Git. However we felt that this would be the best approach as a developer tasked with publishing a service sign in page in future would only need to invoke a simple rake task instead of manually updating content themselves. We've also provided an example YAML file so that content designers are able follow a template and ensure that all the data is supplied in a suitable format.
template_adherence.consequences: Due to no UI being provided to create a Service sign in page, the workflow is unusual for content designers and as previously mentioned it does assume familiarity with YAML and Git. While we expect most content designers will have access to a developer who may be able to assist, we should acknowledge some potential risk here.
