template_adherence.title: Implement our own indexing and artifacts search
template_adherence.context:
We need to be able to search (documented) projects, whether they come from Clojars or Maven Central.

See https://github.com/cljdoc/cljdoc/issues/85
template_adherence.decision:
Implement our own search, using direct integration with Lucene. Download and index artifact list from Clojars and "org.clojure" artifacts from Maven Central.

We will use Lucene as that is the absolutely prevailing solution for search in Java. Direct Java interop is quite idiomatic in Clojure; it isn't too much work as we only need to implement the parts relevant for us and not a generic Lucene wrapper.
We avoid the risk of depending on incomplete and potentially abandoned library (as happend to Clojars with clucy). And to be able to use Lucene efficiently we need to understand it sufficiently anyway.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Our search results will be different from those you get from Clojars, we won't benefit from any improvements on Clojars' side
* We will be able to search also for non-Clojars projects (and thus also make their docset available in Dash)
* Cljdoc will become slightly more complex and possibly expensive to operate (due to downloading the ~10MB index from Clojars regularly)
* New projects will not appear immediately in the search until the next scheduled indexing (unless we mitigate that somehow)
* We can fine-tune the search to prioritize the results we want

template_adherence.title: 20. Support links from docs to SCM when testing locally
template_adherence.context:
Background

Cljdoc imports documentation from clojars artifacts and SCM (Source Code Management) repositories.
The SCM is a git repository and usually one hosted on GitHub.

Documentation is imported to cljdoc from 2 distinct sources:

1. API docstrings from sources in a clojars artifact
2. Stand-alone articles such as `README.md` and documentation under `doc/**` from an SCM repository.

It is not uncommon for documentation to contain links to other files under in the SCM repository.
In these cases, cljdoc automatically rewrites these links to target the correct resource.
If the SCM document is an article that has been imported to cljdoc, the link will target the imported article hosted by cljdoc,
otherwise the link will target the hosted SCM, which in most cases, is GitHub.

Issues with Testing Locally

Before a project is released to clojars and automatically imported to cljdoc, an author will often want to preview their
documentation by running cljdoc locally.

Because cljdoc works from the published artifact, when testing locally, authors will first publish their project to their local maven repository.
This will remain true for whatever solution we choose here.

A current limitation of running cljdoc locally, as directed by current guidance, is that direct links to SCM files cannot be previewed.
Concrete examples of non-functioning links are images, source code and articles.

These broken links make it difficult to get a real sense of how docs will appear and behave on cljdoc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to preview documentation locally before official release
- Broken SCM links when testing locally reduce preview quality
- Desire to avoid complex local setup for authors
- Want preview to reflect production behavior
- Minimize maintenance burden
- Security and technical feasibility constraints (e.g., browser restrictions on file:// links)
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to complement the existing guidance for running cljdoc locally by recommending a workflow where authors import documentation from a hosted SCM repository (e.g., GitHub) rather than the local file system.

Authors would commit and push changes to a branch on their hosted SCM and ingest docs from this branch.
This approach ensures that links to SCM files work correctly during preview, reflecting production behavior without extra local setup.

The minor downside is that authors must push changes to a hosted SCM to preview.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Authors gain guidance to preview documentation more accurately before release
- No additional local setup is required for authors
- Preview reflects production environment more closely
- Authors must push changes to hosted SCM, which may be seen as a minor inconvenience
- Maintenance burden is limited to documentation updates and minor fixes

alternatives.description: Update docs to recommend importing from hosted SCM rather than local file system.
pros: No extra local setup required
Preview reflects production environment accurately
cons: Authors must push changes to hosted SCM

alternatives.description: Rewrite SCM links to target the file system using file:// URLs.
pros: No extra setup for tester
cons: Not technically feasible due to browser security restrictions

alternatives.description: Rewrite SCM links to target a local static web server.
pros: Easy setup for tester
cons: Fetches are unversioned
MIME type issues may cause downloads instead of rendering
Links to source lack line number navigation

alternatives.description: Rewrite SCM links to target a local git instaweb server.
pros: Easy setup
Versioned fetches
Support for raw and formatted fetches with line navigation
cons: UI not GitHub-like
Dependency on instaweb implementation stability

alternatives.description: Rewrite SCM links to target a local GitHub URL compatible server (e.g., gitea, gogs).
pros: GitHub-like URLs and UI
cons: Difficult setup
More moving parts
Maintenance burden for external component

alternatives.description: Rewrite SCM links to target a local custom GitHub compatible server.
pros: Potentially feasible
cons: Maintenance burden
Not desired to maintain

alternatives.description: Add preview support to cljdoc production server.
pros: Could provide integrated preview
cons: Larger project
Many concerns to address
Rejected for now

template_adherence.title: Transformation of results to arrays
template_adherence.context:
Developers from BioConductors pointed out that the current format of data returned as hashes e.g.
```
results:[
{id:"123", "name":"xyz", genome:"homo_sapiens"},
{id:"456", "name":"abc", genome:"homo_sapiens"},
{id:"890", "name":"def", genome:"homo_sapiens"}
]
```
would be better returned as:
```
results:[
["123", "xyz", "homo_sapiens"],
["456", "abc", "homo_sapiens"],
["890", "def", "homo_sapiens"]
]
```
This would be better for several reasons:
* smaller payload
* client would probably need to do this (esp for R) so why not do it already
* might work better with tabular views (CSV, web interfaces)

However, this is not a universally desirable result - the gene documents are inherently nested so we would want to support both approaches.

This might be applied at a variety of levels, but is best done as far away from the interactions with ES etc as possible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support returning results as 2d arrays instead of arrays of hashes
- Smaller payload size
- Client convenience, especially for R users
- Compatibility with tabular views like CSV and web interfaces
- Support both formats since gene documents are nested
- Implementation should be unobtrusive and away from ES interactions
- Performance impact considerations
template_adherence.decision: We will implement this as an option for `FetchService` and `QueryService` endpoints with a defined toggle parameter array=true/false. The services will then reformat the data accordingly, but the underlying searches will return data in the same format.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Implementation will be relatively unobtrusive
- Potential performance impact due to on-the-fly re-mapping
- Column headers are essential and already implemented via `fields` returned by endpoints
- If widely used, this might become the default
- Will not work with subfields unless target is used to flatten

template_adherence.title: ADR 002: Improved support of field specification
template_adherence.context:
As we start pulling back data from multiple searches, we run the risk of ending up with multiple parameters (fields, targetFields, targetFields2 etc. etc.)

A better approach is to pass in specifications using a nested hash or similar so fields can be targeted to individual searches e.g.
```
{
"genes":["id","name","description"],
"variations":[""]
}
```

However, for simplicity, this needs to support simple field specifications too e.g.
```
["id","name","description"]
```
or even
```
"id","name","description"
```
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need to improve how output fields are specified when combining data from multiple searches.
Avoid mixing arbitrary arrays and hashes in Java due to poor support and casting issues.
Support both nested and simple field specifications for flexibility and simplicity.
template_adherence.decision:
Create a specific class, `org.ensembl.genesearch.QueryOutput`, capable of representing nested structures for field specifications.
Provide `build()` methods to support parsing various specifications.
Switch `Search` and implementing classes to use this object instead of strings for field specification.
template_adherence.consequences:
`Search` and all implementing classes will need to switch from specifying fields as strings to supplying one of these objects.
This change may require refactoring existing code to accommodate the new class.
Improves clarity and robustness in field specification when combining multiple searches.

alternatives.description: Continue using multiple parameters (fields, targetFields, targetFields2, etc.) for specifying output fields.
pros: Simple to implement initially.
No new classes or structures needed.
cons: Leads to messy and hard-to-maintain code as the number of parameters grows.
Does not scale well when combining multiple searches.
Increases risk of errors and confusion.

alternatives.description: Use nested hashes or similar data structures directly without a dedicated class.
pros: Supports targeting fields to individual searches.
Flexible and expressive.
cons: Mixing arbitrary arrays and hashes in Java is not well supported.
Requires casting and complex parsing logic.
Can lead to runtime errors and less type safety.

template_adherence.title: ADR 003: Search interface refactor
template_adherence.context:
Query and QueryOutput example for simple query:
```
q={"name":"BRCA2"}
fields=["id","name","genome"]
```

Query and QueryOutput example for transcript join:
```
q={"name":"BRCA2"}
fields=["id","name","genome",{"transcripts":["id","seq_region_start"]}]
```

Query and QueryOutput example for sequence join:
```
q={"name":"BRCA2","sequences":{"type":"protein"}}
fields=[{"sequences":["id","desc","seq"]}]
```

One consideration is whether searches should need to have the default search type specified in the queries and fields e.g.
```
q={"genes":{{"name":"BRCA2"}}
fields={"genes":["id","name","genome"]}
```

The best idea here is to use different endpoints for different searches e.g. `/api/genes` to get genes, `/api/variations` to get variations etc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need to support targets in both Query and QueryOutput.
Avoid unsustainable complexity as the range of joined queries increases.
Maintain clarity and simplicity in the search interface.
Consideration of default search types and endpoint design.
template_adherence.decision: We have decided to remove target and targetQueries from the interface as they will rapidly become unsustainable as the range of joined queries increases. At present, the "default" search will not require a separate section.
template_adherence.consequences: `Search` and all implementing classes will need be be refactored to use QueryOutput and Query instead of targetFields and target. JoinAwareSearch will need a comprehensive overhaul.

alternatives.description: Keep target and targetQueries in the interface to handle joined queries.
pros: Maintains backward compatibility with existing interface.
No immediate refactoring needed.
cons: Will become unsustainable as the range of joined queries increases.
Increases complexity and maintenance burden.

alternatives.description: Use different endpoints for different searches (e.g., `/api/genes`, `/api/variations`).
pros: Simplifies query and field arguments by segregating search types.
Avoids need for default search type specification in queries and fields.
cons: Requires multiple endpoints to be maintained.
May complicate client usage with multiple endpoints.

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: Merge/join architecture
template_adherence.context:
We need to be able to specify a target and have that target be the focus
e.g.
genes, with variations mapped to them
variations, with genes mapped to them
transcripts, with genes mapped to them
genes, with transcripts mapped to them
sequences, with genes mapped to them
genes, with sequences mapped to them

Ultimately, we may also need 3-stage joins as well (expression->genes->variations). The current implementation is too restrictive.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to support joins between different data stores and data types, and merging data from two searches.
The current implementation is too restrictive for complex join scenarios.
Desire to have one endpoint per data type to simplify queries.
Need for a flexible merge/join search mechanism that can handle batching and restructuring.
Handling of flattening results to desired levels automatically per endpoint.
Consideration of performance issues when "from" side is larger than "to" side.
template_adherence.decision:
Rather than overloading a search with complex behaviour, the decision is to have one endpoint per data type (e.g., /api/genes/query, /api/variations/query).
Implement a new base search mechanism (e.g., JoinMergeSearch) that decomposes queries, queries primary and secondary databases, hashes results, and merges them accordingly.
Replace the previous JoinAwareSearch with JoinMergeSearch.
Implement new search classes for each data type (GeneSearch, GenomeSearch, TranscriptSearch, etc.) that handle flattening and merging appropriately.
template_adherence.consequences:
Dataset info may need more work to set correctly.
Flattening is no longer controlled by endpoints but handled automatically by specific search implementations.
New search implementations are required for each data type.
Some situations may require flipping the query logic when the "from" side is larger than the "to" side.
Improved flexibility and scalability for complex join scenarios.
Potential increased complexity in managing multiple search implementations.

alternatives.description: Continue using the current implementation with overloaded searches handling complex join behaviour.
pros: No need to implement new search endpoints or mechanisms.
Leverages existing code and infrastructure.
cons: Current implementation is too restrictive for complex join scenarios.
Harder to maintain and extend due to overloaded behaviour.
Less flexible and scalable for future requirements.

alternatives.description: Implement a single generic search endpoint that dynamically handles all join and merge scenarios without separate endpoints per data type.
pros: Single endpoint simplifies API surface.
Potentially more flexible if implemented correctly.
cons: Increased complexity in the search implementation.
Harder to optimize for specific data types.
May lead to performance issues and complicated query logic.

template_adherence.title: ADR 005: Search flattening
template_adherence.context:
We need to be able to turn this structure:
```
[{name:"ID", description:"Bob", transcripts:[{ID:"t1",start:10},{ID:"t2",start:20}]}]
```
into:
```
[
{ID:"t1", start:10, gene.name:"ID", gene.description:"Bob"},
{ID:"t2", start:20, gene.name:"ID", gene.description:"Bob"}
]
```

The search should also be capable of handling query and output targetted at this level e.g.
```
{"name":"bob", "genes":{"genome":"eric"}} # query
["biotype","id",{"genes":["name","description"]} # output
```
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support flattening to a specified level in search results, to handle nested data structures effectively, and to maintain minimal code duplication while increasing flexibility in search implementations.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to override the ESSearch implementation to include a target for flattening by implementing ESSearchFlatten, removing flattening code from ESSearch, and extending ResultsRemodeller.flatten with a 'toplevel' key to support promoting targeted fields. ESSearchFlatten uses specified targets in consumeHits and processResults, and ESSearch overrides query and fetch to transform output and query specifications.
template_adherence.consequences: The approach increases complexity but allows the use of a single repository for genes, transcripts, and translations. Dataset info may need more work to set correctly. Sorting needs adjustment to handle nested fields with filters, which is non-trivial. Consideration is needed on whether a completely flat form is sensible or if a hash should be used. Translations may require additional work or may be restricted.

alternatives.description: Continue using the magic 'target' parameter in Search to invoke flattening.
pros: Simple to implement initially.
No need to change existing Search interface.
cons: Leads to code duplication.
Less explicit and harder to maintain.
Does not align with the new design in adr-004.md.

alternatives.description: Implement a completely flat form for all nested data without promoting targeted fields.
pros: Simplifies data structure to a flat form.
Potentially easier to query.
cons: May lose semantic clarity of nested relationships.
Could complicate sorting and filtering.
Not currently chosen; needs further investigation.

template_adherence.title: ADR 010: Inner joins
template_adherence.decision:
The simplest approach is to create a new query to use in "from" instead e.g.
```
search a:
x:1, b:{c:2}
where b is a separate dataset joined by a.n to b.m
step 1:
find all a.n where a.x=1 -> list[a.n]
step 2:
query b for b.n=list[a.n] and b.c=2 and retrieve b.m -> list[b.m]
step 3:
query is now n:list[b.m], b:{c.2}
```
However, since there may be n-m relationships between the joined objects, you still need to retain the original "from" query (`x:1` in this case).

This has been implemented in `JoinMergeSearch.innerJoinQuery` which creates a new query and inserts into into a new instance of `SubSearchParams` which is then passed to the standard join query mechanism (now abstracted out into ).

These new methods are now used by `query` and `fetch`, and are triggered by `isInnerJoin` which returns true if the request is for an inner join. Currently, this is triggered with the magic field `inner` in the "to" query e.g. `{variants:{inner:1, annot:banana}}`. This magic field is stripped from the query before execution.
template_adherence.consequences:
`inner` cannot be a field in a joined query. Perhaps some other form of encoding is needed here.

Note that `count` is an output field, but `inner` is a query field. Logically, this makes sense, but there may be a better way of doing this.

template_adherence.title: Multiple location support
template_adherence.context:
An important use-case is to search for genes found in multiple regions of the genome e.g 1:1000-1500,1:3000-3600,5:2000-3330 etc. This needs to be supported for searching genes and variants.

Currently, location is dealt with using `QueryType.RANGE` that `DefaultQueryHandler` processes a single location string to start, end etc. but this approach will not work with multiple values. It is also likely that different search engines need to search in different ways.

In addition, there is a separate need for general range and numeric queries.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to support multiple genomic locations in queries; current single location handling is insufficient; different search engines may require different handling; need to support general range and numeric queries.
template_adherence.decision:
We will do the following:
* `LOCATION` will become a new `QueryType` which will be handled separately by each search implementation and accept one or more strings of the format `seq_region:start-end:[strand]`
* `DefaultQueryHandler` will no longer deal with locations.
* `QueryType.RANGE` will be removed
* `QueryType.NUMBER` will be added and processed by each search implementation, supporting numbers of the form `([<>]=)?[0-9.-]+(-[-0-9.]+)?`
template_adherence.consequences: Original examples will not work though `{"seq_region_name":1, "start":>45000, "end":<96000}` should work fine.

template_adherence.title: ADR 013: Query language enhancements
template_adherence.context:
The following minor language improvements need to be made:
* querying by number explicitly for a field
* querying by text match vs an exact term match
* generic NOT support
template_adherence.decision:
To support these, `QueryHandler` needs to have a `DataTypeInfo` instance to figure out what type each field is. This has some knock-on effects in parsing a string into a query.

In order to make testing simpler, `DefaultQueryHandler` will remain `DataTypeInfo` agnostic and a new sub-class `DataTypeAwareQueryHandler` created which uses an internal `DataTypeInfo` to figure out the type.

The main place where this comes in is in `FetchParams` which transforms a string into a list of `Query` objects. This functionality will be shifted out of the `FetchParams` object and into a generic `SearchBasedService` method.

In addition, `FieldType` and `QueryType` have now converged so that `QueryType` can be retired. This means that some of the query builders will need updating to deal with things like `GENOME`, `ID` and `ONTOLOGY`.

`Query` now also has a `not` property so that a query handler can decide if a query is "not" or not. The search implementation should deal with this.

template_adherence.title: ADR 014: Range based join
template_adherence.context: The current model for joining between genes and variants is via the annotation field, matching on gene IDs. This is not sustainable in future for two main reasons: 1. EVA have expressed their opinion that range based querying is the only efficient way to do this with the current MongoDB schema 2. Restricted data for EBiSC/HipSci is only available via a HTSlib based endpoint which responds solely to range queries To this end, we need to support range based joins as well as term based joins
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to support efficient range based querying for joining genes to variants due to limitations of current annotation field joins and external data access constraints.
template_adherence.decision: The main changes can be made fairly easily in `JoinMergeSearch`, but require the following changes to `JoinStrategy`: 1. A `JoinType` enum to trigger RANGE vs TERM 2. Changing the key fields from single strings to arrays. The latter is a simple way to encode the fields required (seq region, min, max) though note that species/assembly may also be required. In an ideal world, `JoinStrategy` would have a defined generic type with these fields explicitly declared, but this is the simplest approach for now. This change has triggered matching changes in all objects that use including `SubSearchParams`. The implementation provided currently has separate query and fetch methods for range-based joins, which are separate to the term-based methods. `RangeBasedJoinGeneSearch` provides a range-based join from gene to variation.
template_adherence.consequences: Inner join is not currently supported. More work is needed to consider how best to do this. Grouping is not supported as this is not appropriate for variation searches. Different code for range and term searches could be abstracted out into separate classes. MongoSearchBuilder is currently hardcoded for EVA, this needs generalising.

template_adherence.context:

template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid direct use of the unstable and complex MongoDB schema, and to comply with EVA's request to use the REST API instead, drives the decision to implement a new search using the REST endpoints.
template_adherence.decision: A new `Search` implementation named `EVARestSearch` has been developed. It handles querying by splitting query fields into mandatory and optional filters, applies them correctly to the endpoints, looks up species_assembly strings from Ensembl style genome names, and manages filtering mostly on the server side. Faceting and sorting are not supported.

template_adherence.context:
We need to be able to run the application using different search backends in different scenarios. Rather than using a complicated if-else switch in EndpointSearchProvider, there are now multiple instances that extend from a common EndpointSearchProvider class.
These are
* EnsemblVariationEndpointProvider - profile `default`
* EnsemblRESTVariationEndpointProvider - profile `ensembl_rest`
* EVAMongoEndpointProvider - profile `eva_mongo`
* EVAEndpointProvider - profile `eva_rest`
* EbiscEndpointProvider - profile `ebisc`

Profiles are set at runtime via the property `spring.profiles.active`. If not set, the default profile will be used. This allows rapid switching of implementations at startup.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the need to support multiple search backends in different scenarios, avoid complicated conditional logic in the code, enable rapid switching of implementations at startup, and ensure tests can be run with the appropriate profile set.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement profile-based search implementations using Spring profiles. Multiple EndpointSearchProvider instances are created, each associated with a specific Spring profile. The active profile is set at runtime via the `spring.profiles.active` property, defaulting to the `default` profile if not set.
template_adherence.consequences: The profile needs to be set if a non-default profile is required. Tests must have the profile set appropriately, for example using annotations like `@WebIntegrationTest({"spring.profiles.active=eva_mongo"})` and `@ActiveProfiles("eva_mongo")`.

alternatives.description: Use a complicated if-else switch in EndpointSearchProvider to select the search backend implementation at runtime.
pros: Simple to implement initially.
All logic centralized in one class.
cons: Code becomes complicated and hard to maintain as more backends are added.
Less flexible and harder to extend.
Does not leverage Spring profiles for configuration management.

alternatives.description: Use environment variables or external configuration files to select the backend implementation without Spring profiles.
pros: Decouples configuration from code.
Can be changed without code changes.
cons: Requires manual parsing and management of configuration.
Less integrated with Spring's native profile management.
Potentially more error-prone and less standardized.

template_adherence.title: File system folder structure using type-namespace-id structure
template_adherence.context: Winery's data is stored in a file system as per ADR-0001. The repository contents should be human readable and machine processable.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for a folder structure that supports human readability and machine processability, handling naming conflicts via namespaces, and compatibility with Windows filesystem constraints.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen alternative is to use folders subdivided in type-namespace-id structure, documented in RepositoryLayout. template_adherence.consequences: The file system layout is organized and documented, improving human navigation and machine processing. However, folder names require encoding to be compatible with Windows, adding complexity.

cons: Requires encoding folder names for Windows compatibility.

template_adherence.title: Use logback for logging
template_adherence.context: Each application should log.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "Logback", because it
1) natively implements SLF4J and
2) SLF4J offers bridging legacy APIs and thus allows to unify logging.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:

* Single point for logging configuration
* Logging over SLF4J API

Negative consequences:

* Developers have to include following dependencies in their `pom.xml`, because the concrete logging framework should be chosen at the project executed by a user (or on a server).
Tests still require logging and thus the concrete logging framework has to be included for tests.

* For easy logging, it is enough to include logback libraries at `WEB-INF/lib`.

* Any logging wrapper has also has to be included at "user-facing" ends (CLI or WAR).
Note that it cannot be included at libraries, because it leads to an infinite loop.

* Legacy/old libraries depending on a certain logging framework have to be loaded with an exclusion of the logging framework.

* The documentation of Winery has to state that slf4j was chosen and that the logging has to be configured accordingly.

alternatives.description: Logback
pros: Natively implements SLF4J
SLF4J offers bridging legacy APIs allowing unified logging

template_adherence.title: tosca.model is more relaxed than the XSD
template_adherence.context: There is a data model for a) serializing/deserializing the XML contents, b) internal backend handling, c) working with algorithms, d) communicating with the REST service. Currently, this is the same model. The UI might generate non-valid XML files (in the sense of not passing the XSD validation). For instance, if a user creates a service template, that service template does not contain a topology template. Furthermore, a topology template needs to have at least one node template.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to handle a data model that serves multiple purposes (serialization, backend handling, algorithms, REST communication) and the issue that the UI might generate XML files that do not pass XSD validation. Also, the complexity and effort involved in maintaining multiple models.
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "Keep one model and allow non-XSD validating models in `org.eclipse.winery.model.tosca`", because XSD is meant for "executable" TOSCA definitions, not for intermediate modeling results, and currently too much effort to develop two models.
template_adherence.consequences: By keeping one model that allows non-XSD validating models, the system can handle intermediate modeling results without strict XSD validation, simplifying development and maintenance. However, this may allow some invalid XML states temporarily, which must be managed appropriately.

alternatives.description: Keep one model and allow non-XSD validating models in `org.eclipse.winery.model.tosca`.
pros: Simplifies the model by having only one representation.
Allows flexibility for intermediate modeling results that do not conform to XSD.
Reduces development effort compared to maintaining multiple models.
cons: May allow invalid XML states that do not pass XSD validation.
Potentially less strict validation could lead to errors downstream.

alternatives.description: Only allow (XSD-) validating models.
pros: Ensures all models conform strictly to XSD validation.
Reduces risk of invalid XML data.
Improves data integrity and consistency.
cons: May be too restrictive for intermediate modeling states.
Could complicate UI and backend handling.
Might require more complex validation logic.

alternatives.description: Develop two models.
pros: Separates concerns between intermediate and executable models.
Allows strict validation on executable models while permitting flexibility on intermediate ones.
Clear distinction between different model purposes.
cons: Increases development and maintenance effort.
Requires synchronization between two models.
Adds complexity to the system architecture.

For instance `com.sun.jersey` is configured in all projects, but is only used in the REST API project.

cons: May include log level configurations for unused classes in some sub projects.

alternatives.description: Different, individually configured `logback-test.xml` files for each sub project
pros: Allows tailored logging configurations per sub project.
cons: Increases maintenance effort as each sub project requires separate configuration management.

template_adherence.title: Build Nimbus Console As Part Of The Experimenter Code Base
template_adherence.context: Experimenter is a web application developed solely for the purpose of managing product experiments at Mozilla.  It was originally designed to manage the Shield experimentation workflow, and has expanded to include a comprehensive workflow for managing Normandy experiments.  Project Nimbus is being developed with very different core assumptions than the previous experimentation platforms, and it is unclear whether building on top of the existing Experimenter infrastructure or creating a new purpose specific application will best suit the project's needs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Meeting Project Nimbus' needs in a rapid, continuous fashion with minimal downtime
* the impact to (a) near-term goals of launching our first real set of feature experiments (b) mid-term goals of deprecating and replacing existing experimentation channels (Normandy pref-flips, leanplum) (c) long-term developer productivity and maintenance costs.
* Contributability by a large, distributed group of people with different backgrounds (web engineers, data engineers, data scientists)
* Fitting cohesively into the FXA engineering pipeline/culture
* Continuing to support the existing experimentation (Normandy) workflow until Normandy experiments can be deprecated and transitioned to Nimbus
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: After careful consideration of both options, we have decided to adopt the proposal to build on top of Experimenter and invest in improvements. This includes work to create new models, improve and document a development workflow that can be used by all members of the team, and write a new front end in React. While we carefully considered the proposal to start a new application in Node/Typescript, we determined that the risk around the time to bring a new application up to parity and the operations overhead of maintaining parallel systems was too significant to adopt the proposal.

We already have a list of improvements we’d like to make – over the next few days we will work on clarifying any details, breaking things down, and getting everyone up to speed on running the existing code base.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to build on top of Experimenter leverages existing infrastructure, enabling reuse of components, APIs, and deployment workflows, which accelerates development and maintains a single source of truth for experiments. However, it requires addressing challenges such as adapting the existing workflow/UI to new needs, refactoring database schemas, and managing complexity from supporting both Normandy and Nimbus experiments. This approach balances rapid delivery with maintainability but may impose constraints due to legacy design decisions.

Nimbus is intended to manage the whole process from experiment design to launch to monitoring, with a lighter-weight peer review process, in which individuals creating experiments are more responsible for the entire life cycle and viability of their own experiments.

template_adherence.title: Monitoring Data Import
template_adherence.context:
Currently, Jetstream is responsible for daily processing experiment data for analysis after enrollment has completed. We're also interested in processing experiment data for monitoring purposes. Monitoring data is a little different from analysis data in that it is live (updated every few minutes) and needs to be available immediately when an experiment starts collecting data. Also, unlike analysis data, monitoring data sacrifices absolute accuracy for timeliness in order to detect big problems early. Jetstream is only responsible for generating analysis data and we need an alternative approach to access monitoring data from Experimenter.

Currently, Grafana is used to display monitoring data. It works by querying live tables from BigQuery on-demand and does not have any caching. We would like to eventually replace Grafana capabilities with custom visualizations inside of Experimenter. The goal is to have more flexibility than Grafana gives for how to display the data as well as less overhead for users when context switching from one visualization platform to another.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Data needs to be displayed "live", updating within minutes
* Cost needs to stay low
* Have flexibility with how the data is visualized
* Data loading speed
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "(2) Query Data On-Demand from Experimenter short term and (4) Optimize the ETL long term"

Option (3) has too many cons compared to (1), (2) and (4) so it can be dismissed.
Option (1) is fast but will be quite expensive compared to Option (2) and (4) so it can also be dismissed.
Option (2) would be slower than (1) and (4) but it is cheaper than (1) and (3). Although Option (2) is slow, it would not be any slower than Grafana currently is for loading data. In some cases when the cache is hit, it would be faster than Grafana.
Option (4) has the potential to be the cheapest but it cannot be implemented immediately as it needs some further breakdown.

It would be ideal to implement option (2) immediately to get some basic user-friendly monitoring in experimenter as soon as possible while continuing work on option (4). Once (4) ETL optimizations are complete, the Experimenter backend can switch to pulling data from this new source.

For this first pass at adding monitoring data, only basic user counts per branch and experiment health metrics will be added.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to query data on-demand from Experimenter in the short term and optimize ETL in the long term allows for immediate implementation of monitoring capabilities with acceptable performance and cost, while planning for a more efficient and cheaper solution later. This approach balances timeliness, cost, and flexibility but requires building and maintaining complex data fetching and caching logic in Experimenter. The long-term ETL optimization is not yet fully detailed and will require further work.

template_adherence.title: Location for the new Experiment "Docs Hub" codebase + docs
template_adherence.context:
ADR #5, ["Use Docusaurus + GH Pages for the Nimbus User Doc Hub"](https://github.com/mozilla/experimenter/blob/main/experimenter/experimenter/docs/adrs/0005-doc-hub.md), determined that our approach to setting up a new central location for Experimenter/Nimbus and related project documentation would use [Docusaurus](https://v2.docusaurus.io/), a static site generator, with the static files being served from [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com/). While we knew we would be introducing a new set of code we didn't explicitly decide where it would live and what the process for deploying would look like, beyond suggesting it could live in the existing Experimenter repository.

In investigating how to set all of this up we realized there would be certain caveats to hosting and deploying this code from the Experimenter repository, and this lead to the consideration of using a dedicated repository. This ADR outlines our options and end decision.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- How much setup work is involved, both for the code _and_ for integrations or other non-code processes?
- How much overhead and complexity is involved in maintaining this setup, as well as keeping our processes and tools in sync with Experimenter?
- Not everyone who contributes to these docs is a programmer; how much of a learning curve does this present?
template_adherence.decision:
Set up a new, dedicated repository

Editor's note, 2021-03-12 - This ADR was written after a separate repository was already set up, worked on, and put into use. We've decided to, for approximately one month, use it and see if there is any major fallout. This ADR should be amended with the result of that experiment.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Allows greater initial and long-term flexibility in code setup, organization, and deployment.
- Positive: Simplifies deployment processes, potentially using GitHub Actions or a simpler CircleCI config.
- Positive: Provides a neutral spot for documentation across all projects associated with Experimenter.
- Negative: Adds cultural overhead with a new repository to learn and manage.
- Negative: Technical overhead for permissions, integrations, and contributor setup.
- Negative: Cannot merge changes to both documentation and Experimenter codebase in the same Pull Request.

template_adherence.title: Front-end web development with HTMX
template_adherence.context: Nimbus UI uses GraphQL to fetch data from the backend and it highly depends on the three packages i.e. graphene-django, graphene and apollo-client. These packages have not had new releases for a while. Using GraphQL significantly hinders the performance of the Experimenter as it adds extra overhead while making the call and the benefit of using GraphQL is not fully utilized. Maintaining both DRF and GraphQL APIs adds significant maintenance burden and testing requirements. As the application grows, steps are needed to improve performance and maintainability.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Improve performance which leads to better UX Experience
- Reduce dependency on extra packages
- Better easier development tooling
- Better maintainability of the application
template_adherence.decision: After careful consideration, the chosen option is to design new pages with HTMX, keep the existing UI (React and GraphQL), and eventually move to HTMX. This approach is simpler in terms of backend compatibility as existing code can be reused without major modifications. Work includes creating new pages using HTMX, setting up test cases for HTMX pages, and evaluating success on the Experimenter platform. If successful, a full transition from React to HTMX can begin. The alternative of switching to REST APIs requires active work on both backend and frontend and full conversion before benefits are realized. HTMX can coexist with React/GraphQL, allowing gradual transition and dependency updates.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include all web pages using HTMX, better performance, and learning a new tool HTMX. Negative consequences include the need to evaluate success and potentially rewrite pages in Typescript/React with REST API if HTMX pages are unsuccessful.

template_adherence.title: Nimbus Web SDK Architecture
template_adherence.context: This is part of a body of work necessary to support the use of Nimbus within web applications. The current Nimbus SDK is written in such a way that it supports client-oriented experimentation — experiments are downloaded, evaluated, and stored on the client, and a feature store is exposed with the experiment branches applied. In previous decisions (not in this repository), we've already decided that in order to support web experimentation the Nimbus SDK will need to be updated to be stateless, to support a more statically defined set of helper methods, and to have additional support for Python. Ultimately, the problem we're trying to solve can be boiled down to one question — how can we update the Nimbus SDK to support web applications while continuing to support the existing clients? As an example of what the Cirrus API might look like, we can likely expect endpoints to perform the following: Enroll a user into available experiment(s), This would return the enrolled experiments as well as the feature values given the enrollments, Fetch the default feature values, Fetch the feature manifest, Fetch a specific feature value given enrolled experiments.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Architecture decisions for Nimbus on the web; The core logic of the existing SDK (Rust) will be re-used for the Nimbus web service (Cirrus); The SDK needs to support Python via UniFFI; The SDK needs to be stateless.
template_adherence.decision: We have decided to move forward with option number 2, "Cargo features, one library". This option, like the others mentioned, meets the key decision drivers. We believe using this option will be the most maintainable long-term, despite the added complexity of using cargo features. In addition, implementing this option has a similarly short timeline and amount of work necessary as compared to the "Cargo features, separate library" option, without the additional overhead of more complex typing.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive Consequences: Meets all decision drivers. Small amount of work necessary with a very limited amount of code churn. Negative Consequences: It will be difficult to draw boundaries between Cirrus and Nimbus code. We could run into unexpected issues with UniFFI, as multiple UDL files in a single crate has not yet been tested.

alternatives.description: Separate `nimbus-core`, `nimbus-sdk`, and `cirrus-sdk` libraries
pros: Separate libraries allow for strong separation of concerns.
Changes in the `cirrus-sdk` library will not require changes the `nimbus-sdk` library.
Certain Nimbus-only features (such as the event store) will not available in the Cirrus library.
Dependencies can be excluded based on enabled features.
As an example, RKV will only be needed for Nimbus, so the RKV dependency will only be included in compilation when the `nimbus` feature is enabled.
It will not increase the size of the existing Nimbus SDK binary.
All code relating to core Nimbus business logic remains in one place.
cons: Defining and using types becomes more difficult.
Traits will be needed to extend functionality in the Nimbus Core library. While dynamic typing with traits is supported, it is quite complex.
Would result in a significant amount of code churn.
Many methods, structs, and other sections of code would need to move to the new `nimbus-core` library.
Additionally, a number of methods would need to have their call signatures updated.

alternatives.description: Cargo features, one library
pros: The use of feature configurations is familiar to Rust developers.
All code relating to Nimbus business logic remains in one place.
UniFFI bindings can be conditionally generated for each feature with different UDLs.
Dependencies can be excluded based on enabled features.
It will not increase the size of the existing Nimbus SDK binary.
cons: Onboarding developers learning Rust would likely have a more difficult time understanding Cargo features.
Cirrus and Nimbus logic within the same crate could make it harder to draw boundaries between the logic for each feature.
This will be the first time we have included more than one UniFFI UDL in a single crate, and could run into unexpected issues.

alternatives.description: Cargo features, separate library
pros: All the good things in the "Cargo features, one library" option above.
The changes required will require minimal churn.
Better separation of concerns between Nimbus and Cirrus.
Defining and using types and traits across the libraries could prove difficult.
Dependencies can be excluded based on enabled features.
It will not increase the size of the existing Nimbus SDK binary.
cons: Onboarding developers learning Rust would likely have a more difficult time understanding Cargo features.
Cirrus calling methods within Nimbus could make it harder to draw boundaries between the logic for each feature.
Changes to method signatures in Nimbus could result in unexpected/unnecessary changes being required for Cirrus.

alternatives.description: Expose a stateless API alongside the stateful API (Do nothing)
pros: It's simple and _mostly_ additive.
cons: It makes Nimbus more prone to developer error.
This is a "someone finds the function in the Nimbus internals and starts using it incorrectly" concern.

The existing Nimbus SDK UDL includes a NimbusClient that compiles into direct FFI bindings into the Rust code. It does not include any utilities for threading methods that require persistence or object builders. This class shouldn't ever actually be used by iOS/Android directly, but it is there and _can_ be used.
By adding the stateless methods for experiment evaluation (and others), they would be available in Python, Kotlin, and Swift, even though they should only be used within the context of Cirrus.
It increases the size of the binary both for Cirrus and Nimbus.

template_adherence.title: Jetstream/Nimbus Shared Schema Architecture
template_adherence.context: Experiment analysis for the Nimbus experimentation platform occurs in a separate project called Jetstream. Jetstream delivers results to Experimenter, which must parse these results based on the expected format of Jetstream’s output. However, Experimenter is forced to make assumptions about what it expects in the results, increasing the potential for buggy behavior during both ingestion and on the Results UI for Experimenter. Currently, various schemas are defined in a few different places for different purposes, but one schema definition shared between Experimenter and Jetstream would allow for validation of outputs from Jetstream while removing the need for Experimenter to make assumptions about the data it is receiving from Jetstream. This document describes the decisions around how and where that schema will be defined.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Single schema definition shared by Experimenter and Jetstream
* No functional changes to Jetstream workflow
* Jetstream can (and should) use the schema definition in forming/validating outputs
* Process for making schema changes
* Simplify Experimenter ingestion of analysis results
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: **Option 1B**: define the schema using Pydantic, and put this definition in the `experimenter` repository. **Option 1** Pydantic was chosen because it meets the needs of the solution, and fits best with the language and approaches in use by the relevant systems. **Option B** `experimenter` repo was chosen as the location for the schema because it represents the closest thing to a monorepo (or at least somewhat consolidated location for shared content), and any schemas shared among Nimbus systems will likely be used in the `experimenter` repo.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Ability to generate and ingest analysis results in a structured way
* Nimbus repository as central source of truth
* Nimbus repository may become home to Jetstream in the future
* Other Nimbus schemas can live in the same place
* Aligns with FastAPI approach used for ongoing Cirrus work
* Easily generate schema definitions for different scenarios
* Pydantic allows us to automatically generate bindings and publish new versions to external repositories (e.g., PyPi for use by Jetstream)
* Django, Typescript, JSON
* Publishing the schema as a library handles concerns about schema changes and synchronization
* Schema versioning is basically free via the published library
* Ability to reference older versions of the schema and tag results with the relevant version

Negative Consequences:
* Could be confusing to have the schema definition not live where the data it defines is generated
* And the definition does not live with the data
* Need to consume a new dependency in order to use the schema

alternatives.description: Schema Definition Options
pros:
Option 1: Pydantic
* Aligns with FastAPI approach used for ongoing Cirrus work
* Easily generate schema definitions for different scenarios
* Django, Typescript, JSON
cons: Setup and maintenance required to publish bindings to, e.g., PyPi
Refactor needed to truly make use of advantages
Refactor ingest using schema for serialization/deserialization
Refactor test cases using serializers
Adding versioning to schema definition adds complexity
Sync schema versions between consuming applications

alternatives.description: Schema Definition Options
pros:
Option 2: Typescript
* Typescript is a well-known language for defining types and schemas
* Frontend of Experimenter uses Typescript
* Jetstream analysis results are JSON
cons: Not as straightforward to convert for use with Python
Jetstream is Python
Jetstream client in Experimenter is Python
Experimenter backend is Django / Python
Verbose
Harder to read (subjective)

alternatives.description: Schema Location Options

* Schema defined in the place where the data originates
cons: No single source of truth for Nimbus schemas

alternatives.description: Schema Location Options
pros:
Option B: `experimenter` (Nimbus) repository
* Single source of truth for Nimbus schemas
* Can re-use the process for generating bindings/libraries from schema definitions for future schemas
* Fits with desired approach to consolidate repositories where applicable
* Including the likelihood of Experimenter repo being renamed Nimbus as its scope expands (with, e.g., Cirrus)

template_adherence.title: Nimbus Web: Glean Application Structure
template_adherence.context: Within the context of the Nimbus Web project, a single Cirrus container will need to support experimentation and data collection for multiple individual applications within the same product domain. As an example, a single Cirrus container could be used to support experimentation for Pocket web, Pocket iOS, and Pocket Android. All apps supported by a single Cirrus container, as best we can estimate at this time, will all be a part of the same product domain. The problem this ADR addresses is as follows: with Cirrus, how should we structure Glean applications for cross-platform apps integrating Cirrus?
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Ease of data collation; How easy is it to collate data for an application?; How easy is it to collate data across applications?; Glean Python SDK architecture
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "One Glean app ID per product domain", because it has the most advantages and fewest disadvantages. Option "One Glean app ID" is also viable, but it could come with additional disadvantages in the form of conflicting data retention policies across product domains. Option "One glean app ID per application"'s disadvantages are simply too detrimental to the project for the option to be viable.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive Consequences: Its usage will work with the existing Glean Python SDK architecture; Collating data for one app and across apps is straightforward; Probe-scraper repository list will have overall fewer listings for Nimbus web applications than the current model; Sidecar deployment model remains viable within Pocket's architecture; Data retention can be set differently for each product domain. Negative Consequences: Jetstream will require changes in order to support this choice; We are breaking away from our historical standard of Glean practices; We may have to make more intensive changes to Experimenter.

alternatives.description: One Glean app ID: One Glean application ID shared across all instances of Cirrus, allowing lower maintenance burden and easier data collation but with data retention and practice drawbacks.

cons: Data retention cannot be handled separately for each application or product domain.

Could require more changes to Experimenter than expected.

pros: Smaller footprint in the probe-scraper repository.

cons: Breaks away from existing Glean usage practices.

template_adherence.title: Nimbus Metrics Guardrail Versioning
template_adherence.context:
- We want to change some Guardrail definitions
- Guardrails are hard-corded in Experimenter, so changing the identifier will mean they are not treated as Guardrails in Experimenter
- There is a task on the Roadmap to make guardrails configurable, but it is not currently prioritized high enough that we expect to do it this half
- There is a possibility to make minimal changes in Experimenter to change the hard-coding of guardrails as a short-term solution
- Other tools may be affected by our decisions (e.g., OpMon, Looker)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Speed of implementation
- this capability is wanted as soon as possible so that already-accepted guardrail metric changes can be made
- Fit with current/future plans
- solution should fit with the planned future task to make guardrails configurable
- solution should minimally disrupt current work (i.e., lower effort short-term is better)
- Complexity of maintenance
- From perspective of both metric maintainers and developers of the system/tools
- Things to consider: uses existing paradigms, affects (or not) other tools, ability to trace historical definitions, etc.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to choose Option 2: Add the new definition as a new metric. This option fits best with the planned future task to make guardrails configurable, aligns with the current practice of using `_v#` suffix to version metric definitions, minimally disrupts existing near-term plans, and presents fewer or no more negatives or risks than other solutions.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Preserves history of definitions in an obvious lineage
- No chance of other tools erroneously adopting new definition
- Precedent for this with other metric definition changes
- Jetstream automatically manages metric versions based on timestamps and metric-hub commits, so each experiment can decide whether or not to adopt the new definition
- Requires Experimenter update in order for new metric to be shown as a guardrail
- Other tools may require updates to adopt new definition

alternatives.description: Modify the existing metric in place
pros: No changes needed to Experimenter
Jetstream automatically manages metric versions based on timestamps and metric-hub commits, so each experiment can decide whether or not to adopt the new definition
cons: Harder for users to keep track of old definitions, which would still be used in older experiments
Would need to reference git history
Non-Jetstream tools that use metric-hub (e.g., OpMon) do not have automatic version management for metric definitions, so they would adopt the new definition without option to decide
No easy way to compare results of old and new definitions
Probably not the best solution for other metrics or for when we have configurable guardrails

alternatives.description: Add the new definition as a new metric
pros: Preserves history of definitions in an obvious lineage
No chance of other tools erroneously adopting new definition
Precedent for this with other metric definition changes
Jetstream automatically manages metric versions based on timestamps and metric-hub commits, so each experiment can decide whether or not to adopt the new definition
cons: Requires Experimenter update in order for new metric to be shown as a guardrail
Other tools may require updates to adopt new definition

alternatives.description: Rename existing metric and create new definition under current name
pros: No changes needed to Experimenter
Jetstream automatically manages metric versions based on timestamps and metric-hub commits, so each experiment can decide whether or not to adopt the new definition
cons: Harder for users to keep track of old definitions, which would still be used in older experiments
Would need to know that the metric name changed
Non-Jetstream tools that use metric-hub (e.g., OpMon) would adopt the new definition without option to decide
Not very intuitive to change an existing metric name

template_adherence.title: 3. Run kubernetes locally
template_adherence.context:
There are many cloud kubernetes offerings (Amazon, Microsoft, and Google all offer it), and part of the appeal in general is to not have to think about where the servers are and what kind of maintenance they need.

However, we already operate servers in three datacenters, and we fully manage one of those. We may prefer this not to be the case, but as of writing this, we deal with bare-metal servers regardless of what we'd prefer. Adding ec2 instances costs extra money, where running additional software on servers (with an electric bill we're already paying) costs the labor of setting it up.

The attitude of the field so far appears to be "definitely just run it in AKS," but the field is largely made up of people whose primary interests are reliability and profits. As a digital academic library, we also have those interests, but we have an additional responsibility to always have our own copy of everything.

template_adherence.consequences: By providing a service that mirrors a cloud service, we can use the same code and configuration to deploy locally and remotely. We'll need to figure out how we want to manage applications and how we'll want them to scale depending on where they live. template_adherence.title: 4. Roll our own kubernetes profiles
template_adherence.context: Puppetlabs maintains a kubernetes module in the forge, and Rancher maintains software for managing multiple clusters running anywhere. template_adherence.title: Stack kubernetes controllers with etcd
template_adherence.context:
There are three basic ways to lay out controller nodes in a kubernetes cluster:

1.  A single master is the easiest way to do it, but if that node is ever unavailable, then the entire cluster is unavailable.

2.  A highly-available group of at least three controller nodes that also run etcd.

3.  Two highly-available groups: one of at least three controller nodes, and the other of at least three etcd nodes.

The kubernetes website has [a detailed rundown][1], but it boils down to this: high availability complicates the set-up significantly, and separating etcd from the control plane complicates it yet more.

However, if we want to allocate a lot of resources to high availability in our kubernetes clusters, then etcd is a nice seam to further divide responsibility as we scale up the count of control nodes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers are not explicitly titled or separated, but can be inferred from the context section where the trade-offs between availability, complexity, and resource allocation are discussed. The drivers include the need for high availability, resource constraints, and complexity of setup.
template_adherence.decision: We will start with the middle path of minimal (but extant) high availability. Low availability would fail to grant us a lot of what makes kubernetes worthwhile, but we're just not in a place where we're ready to commit the extra resources to get the highest availability possible.
template_adherence.consequences: If we start growing our pool of stacked controller nodes beyond 5, then we should consider revisiting this decision.

cons: More resource usage than single master

template_adherence.title: 6. Use calico for kubernetes networking
template_adherence.context:
Kubernetes requires an internal private network, just for its pods and services (i.e. not for physical/virtual nodes). It has specific expectations, but it doesn't actually provide networking itself. There are a few options for internal networking: flannel, calico, canal, and weave.

Of these, Flannel is the most popular. It's known for being easy to set up and then never having problems ever. The network it creates is a layer 3 IPv4 overlay network that spans across every node in the cluster. Each node gets its own subnet for allocating internal IP addresses for docker containers.

Project Calico is also popular, but is less simple and (allegedly) more performant. The network it creates isn't an overlay but rather a layer 3 network using the BGP protocol to route packets between hosts.

Canal is a combination of flannel and calico. It's not a project anymore because it collaborated itself out of existence by making pull requests to flannel and calico until they worked well enough together that there was nothing extra for canal to do. People still use the word "canal" to refer to using a combination of flannel and calico.

Weave Net creates a mesh overlay network between each of the nodes in the cluster. Each host becomes a router, and they're always exchanging topology information with each other. One of weave's unique features is that it can (with some network overhead) encrypt all routed traffic.

The rancher project wrote [a pretty informative comparison][1] if you're interested in more details.

[1]: https://rancher.com/blog/2019/2019-03-21-comparing-kubernetes-cni-providers-flannel-calico-canal-and-weave/
template_adherence.decision: We will use calico because it's rancher's default. It's easy enough to set up.
template_adherence.consequences: As of yet unknown.

alternatives.description: Flannel: the most popular, easy to set up, creates a layer 3 IPv4 overlay network with subnets per node.
pros: Easy to set up
Stable and reliable network
cons: Overlay network may have performance overhead

alternatives.description: Calico: less simple but allegedly more performant, uses BGP protocol for routing, not an overlay network.
pros: More performant
Uses BGP routing, which can be more efficient
cons: Less simple to set up

alternatives.description: Canal: combination of flannel and calico, no longer a separate project, integrates features of both.
pros: Combines benefits of flannel and calico
cons: No longer maintained as a separate project

alternatives.description: Weave Net: creates a mesh overlay network, each host is a router, supports encrypted traffic.
pros: Mesh network topology
Supports encrypted traffic
cons: Network overhead due to encryption and mesh maintenance

template_adherence.title: 7. Only manage certain netfilter chains in kubernetes machines
template_adherence.context: When using the puppetlabs firewall module, one of the recommended settings is to purge all rules not managed by puppet. Since kubernetes and calico perform networking and load balancing at the kernel level, this means puppet finds itself with hundreds of rules to purge every 30 minutes. The firewall module also has an undocumented feature that lets you manage individual netfilter chains. This doesn't work in conjunction with `purge => true` for all firewall resources. If we use `firewallchain` resources instead, then any chains we don't explicitly define will be ignored by puppet.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid purging hundreds of kernel-level networking rules managed by kubernetes and calico, and the limitation that managing individual netfilter chains does not work with global purge settings.
template_adherence.decision: We will only manage INPUT, OUTPUT, and FORWARD chains on kubernetes machines. We will specifically whitelist particular lines known to be used in those chains by kubernetes and calico.
template_adherence.consequences: We now have two firewall profiles (`networking::firewall` and `kubernetes::firewall`) sharing most of their code. The purge setting should be split out of the central firewall profile to work more broadly. Docker performs its own networking, so a similar approach is needed for the docker profile with different exceptions. Security consequences are unknown.

alternatives.description: Continue using the puppetlabs firewall module with `purge => true` for all firewall resources, purging all unmanaged rules.
pros: Ensures all unmanaged firewall rules are purged, maintaining strict control.
cons: Causes puppet to purge hundreds of rules every 30 minutes due to kubernetes and calico kernel-level networking, leading to performance issues.

alternatives.description: Use `firewallchain` resources to manage individual netfilter chains, ignoring chains not explicitly defined.
pros: Avoids purging chains not explicitly managed, reducing unnecessary purges.
cons: Does not work in conjunction with `purge => true` for all firewall resources, leading to inconsistent management.

template_adherence.title: 8. Dedicate separate HAProxy machines for load-balancing kubernetes
template_adherence.context:
With three controller nodes all listening on 6443, they need a single IP address they can use to represent "the kubernetes master." Additionally, each worker node listens on 30000-32767 in order to expose NodePort services to the outside world. Rather than choose a particular worker node to talk to, it makes sense to load-balance these requests as well to whichever worker nodes are currently online.

What's written above is straightforward enough to add to our current HAProxy config.

However, kubernetes doesn't provide any support for claiming IP addresses outside its internal network. Rather, kubernetes merely indicates that it wants an IP address for a service.

For example, let's say we have a web service that is listening on ports 80 and 443. If we set its exposure to LoadBalancer, then kubernetes will indicate that and set some NodePort mappings. So, for example, it might map 80:32689 and 443:31268.

It's then our job to do the following, outside kubernetes:

1.  Notice a new service requesting to be type LoadBalancer.
2.  Choose an IP address that isn't already in use.
3.  Configure our load balancers to claim that floating IP address.
4.  Configure our load balancers to round robin 80 and 443 requests for that IP address to the kubernetes worker nodes over 32689 and 31268, respectively.

It would be good if we didn't have to do that by hand. If we do automate it, that means our HAProxy config could be changing routinely, which could have an affect on other production services.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to represent the kubernetes master with a single IP address.
- Need to load-balance NodePort services exposed on worker nodes.
- Kubernetes does not support claiming IP addresses outside its internal network.
- Desire to automate load balancer configuration to avoid manual errors and routine changes.
- Avoid impacting existing production services when changing HAProxy configurations.
template_adherence.decision: Kubernetes gets its own HAProxy servers, separate from the ones currently configured by puppet. For the time being, puppet will configure them, but it also provides a simple list of peer IP addresses so that they will one day be capable of configuring themselves.
template_adherence.consequences: We can make changes to the load balancers for kubernetes without worrying about breaking access to our first-class services already in production. Even though the details of these servers are very similar, this separation lets us view these HAProxy machines not as load balancers but rather as highly available gateways to kubernetes.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing HAProxy configuration for both kubernetes and other services without separation.
pros: No need to manage additional HAProxy servers.
Simpler infrastructure with fewer components.
cons: Risk of impacting existing production services when changing HAProxy config for kubernetes.
Less isolation and flexibility for kubernetes load balancing.

alternatives.description: Manually configure load balancers for each new LoadBalancer service in kubernetes.
pros: Full control over load balancer configuration.
No need to add new HAProxy servers.
cons: Manual process is error-prone and time-consuming.
Frequent changes could affect production stability.

template_adherence.title: Manage Prometheus node exporter package ourselves
template_adherence.context:
The Prometheus model is that nodes, applications, and services expose metrics, and a Prometheus server scrapes them every 10 seconds. It's up to the Prometheus server to organize metrics, track them over time, and store them long-term.

However, it's up to each node to decide exactly what metrics it exposes. For example, the node exporter (which exports general system metrics) has changed the names of its metrics as it's changed versions. It's in the apt repos for Debian and Ubuntu, but with different versions for different releases.

So if we stick with Debian/Ubuntu-maintained packages, we might end up with jessie machines running v0.11.2, stretch running v0.13.1, buster running v0.16.0, and bionic running v0.18.1. In this case, we'd be using one aggregation server to scrape four different types of metrics all baring the same name.

Not only would this be cumbersome to aggregate, but also if someone at Debian or Ubuntu did upgrade the exporter in a repo, then all time serieses for computers using that repo would essentially be reset.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for consistent Prometheus node exporter versions across different Debian/Ubuntu releases.
- Avoiding inconsistent metric names due to different exporter versions.
- Avoiding reset of time series data caused by repo upgrades.

template_adherence.title: 10. Use nginx for simple HTTPS proxies
template_adherence.context:
We currently use Apache on all our web hosts. While writing a profile for forwarding HTTPS to a local HTTP port, I found that the puppet Apache module didn't provide a simple approach to this. I would have had to use `mod_proxy` and then add custom fragments.

On the other hand, if I went with nginx instead of Apache, such a proxy could be configured with a single line:

proxy => "http://localhost:${port}",

This carries with it a cost however. If we use nginx in this one case, then we can no longer claim to use a single web server, as we'll be using Apache on some servers and nginx on others.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for a simple approach to forwarding HTTPS to a local HTTP port, which the current Apache setup does not provide easily. The desire to maintain a single web server type across servers is a concern but is weighed against configuration simplicity.
template_adherence.decision: We will use nginx for simple cases where all we need is to forward to a local port.
template_adherence.consequences: Forwarding https traffic to a local port is very easy. We now use both nginx and Apache.

alternatives.description: Continue using Apache with mod_proxy and custom fragments to handle HTTPS forwarding.
pros: Maintain a single web server type across all servers (Apache).
No need to introduce a new technology (nginx).
cons: Configuration is more complex and less straightforward.
Requires additional custom fragments and setup.

alternatives.description: Use nginx for simple HTTPS proxy forwarding cases.
pros: Simple configuration with a single line for proxying.
Easier to manage HTTPS forwarding in these cases.
cons: Introduce a second web server type, losing uniformity.
Potentially more complexity in managing two different web servers.

template_adherence.title: 11. Prefer APT to CPAN for Perl libraries
template_adherence.context:
We have a number of applications and servers that need numerous Perl libraries installed. We have historically managed the libraries at a system level and coordinated versions with application teams. While there are now compelling options like Carton, which allow an application to manage and isolate its dependencies, most of our apps would require changes to be ready to use something like this.

To aid in keeping the versions stable and ensuring that underlying system libraries like OpenSSL are in sync, Debian packages many CPAN libraries at specific versions for a release. These are still at a system level, but we have an already-running process that would catch updates in the case of a major bug fix or security release.

In service of completing OS and hardware upgrades, we are seeking primarily to identify the dependencies and to be able to reproduce our application environments. In the long term, applications are likely to be containerized or otherwise placed under PSGI/Plack, where many of these concerns could be isolated more readily. This decision is a record of current realities, rather than a long-term position.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage numerous Perl libraries across applications and servers.
- Desire to keep versions stable and in sync with system libraries like OpenSSL.
- Existing process for Debian packaging and updates.
- Long-term plans for containerization and isolation of dependencies.
- Minimizing changes required in existing applications.
- Balancing maintenance overhead and version consistency.
template_adherence.decision: Where possible, when installing Perl libraries at the system level, we will use the Debian-released package. Where practical, we will use dh-make-perl to create local .deb packages from those in CPAN, but not released by Debian. We will use nebula::cpan as a last resort.
template_adherence.consequences: Using Debian-released libraries means that we are limited to the versions selected in their process. This could be a stabilizing or limiting force. Producing our own packages requires additional maintenance and monitoring. Using bare CPAN installs could result in different versions on different systems, depending on when the installation happens.

alternatives.description: Use Carton or similar tools to manage and isolate Perl dependencies at the application level.
pros: Allows application-level dependency isolation.
Enables more precise control over library versions per application.
cons: Requires changes to existing applications.
May increase complexity in deployment and management.

alternatives.description: Use bare CPAN installs for Perl libraries.
pros: Direct access to latest CPAN modules.
No need to rely on Debian packaging process.
cons: Potential for inconsistent versions across systems.
Lack of centralized version control and updates.

alternatives.description: Use Debian-released packages for Perl libraries.
pros: Stable versions vetted by Debian.
Integration with system-level package management.
Existing processes for updates and security fixes.
cons: Limited to versions provided by Debian.
May lag behind latest CPAN releases.

template_adherence.title: 8. Support IndexedDB as a data store
template_adherence.context:
We need to persist the user data to the backend. Rather than building our frontend to be tightly coupled to an API, we want a layer that can sit between the application and the API.

We know that we will need to support offline use of these forms. We also want users to be able to recover unsubmitted forms if they haven't gone online between sessions.

We also know that some forms will require the upload of images.

IndexedDB is a [well supported](https://caniuse.com/#feat=indexeddb) browser database that persists data across sessions. It supports storing blob data (such as images), and has decent storage limits.

template_adherence.decision: We will support IndexedDB as a data store layer, sitting between the application and the API.
template_adherence.consequences:
IndexedDB has a fairly complicated interface. There is some overhead in understanding and using it, but hopefully we can insulate the user for most of it by using libraries and wrapping the implementation.

If a consumer of this library doesn't need to support offline use, they may not need IndexedDB, and may be able to use a plain object. We should make sure we continue to support that use case.

IndexedDB has good support in modern browsers, except Edge and IE. Those browsers support a subset of features, so we should make sure we're testing on those browsers when we need to support them, and that we polyfill any missing features we need.
