template_adherence.title: Decision record: dropping kafka
template_adherence.context: When we first started to model a register as two separate apps (mint and presentation), we explored Kafka as a means of storing the append-only datastore, and streaming it from the mint to the presentation database. Kafka was initially chosen because its append-only journal model seemed a good fit for the way we model registers as an append-only list of entries. Kafka also offers the ability to replay the journal from the start, which allows you to create new ways of presenting data and retrofit them to existing datasets. However, as we used kafka more and more, we found certain pain points: kafka is not offered as a service in the computing platforms we were targeting, such as Amazon or Heroku; kafka has zookeeper as a dependency, which further increases operational complexity; kafka and zookeeper consume a lot of memory, requiring us to deploy larger machines and costing more; one of kafka's main selling points is sheer throughput performance, which isn't really a need we have; kafka is a new technology and our team did not understand it as well as older technologies. In particular, we did not have a good understanding of its failure modes. This last point is key. Because kafka is such a new technology, we did not have confidence to rely on it as a primary data source, so we ended up running Postgres as a primary source of truth (which is a well-understood technology, where we have confidence we can back it up and replicate it to mitigate risks of data loss), and using Kafka as a means of communicating between mint and presentation. Running both postgres and kafka to store the same data seemed wasteful. We ended up needing to administer both postgres and kafka, and having all the operational complexities of both. We considered choosing only one of these technologies to play both roles -- being the mint's primary data store, and communicating the stream of entries from the mint to the presentation. We therefore thought about what it would mean to choose either postgres alone or kafka alone. Using kafka as a primary data store had a few downsides. Already mentioned is our lack of confidence for being a primary data store. We also did not understand its failure modes well. In particular, if a message is sent to Kafka and the connection times out, was it successful? Can we safely retry? Will we get duplicates? Furthermore, a key part of our domain model is an incrementing serial number, used to identify each entry in a register. Kafka does not have a message-level serial number; instead it uses an index into a stream of bytes. If we want to assign a serial number to each entry as it's entered into the register, we need some sort of coordination mechanism to ensure we add these serial numbers in a strictly serial order. When we were using postgres and kafka together, postgres provided this coordination mechanism. If we removed postgres, we'd have to add something else to meet this need. On the presentation side of the equation, we also discovered a need for a separate process for consuming the register stream and inserting it into the presentation database. Our original design had the presentation app consume the kafka stream directly; however, this didn't fit well with the presentation being a stateless appserver which could be horizontally scaled, because each app instance would independently try to consume the kafka stream, but only one would actually be successful. We also looked at Amazon Kinesis which is similar to Kafka. However as it discards all messages after 24 hours it did not fit our needs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce operational complexity and resource consumption.
- Lack of confidence and understanding of Kafka's failure modes.
- Requirement for a reliable primary data store with coordination for serial numbers.
- Need for a scalable presentation app architecture.
- Unsuitability of alternatives like Amazon Kinesis due to message retention policies.
template_adherence.decision: We will use postgres alone, as the mint's primary data store, and also as a means of communicating from the mint to the presentation app. We will remove kafka and zookeeper from the architecture. Postgres will be the tool which assigns serial numbers, through the use of a `SERIAL` column type. In order to replicate the data from the mint to the presentation databases, an indexer app will be created.
template_adherence.consequences: We will remove kafka and zookeeper from the system, and all the administrative effort associated with them. The indexer will at first be directly consuming the mint's primary data store. If there are security or performance concerns about this, the indexer can always be configured to consume a postgres read replica instead. Our architecture will now depend heavily on heterogeneous apps integrating on a common database: firstly, the indexer will be consuming the mint's primary postgres data store; and secondly, the indexer will be injecting data into the presentation's indexed data store. There is quite a bit written on the problems of integration databases, and we should keep these problems in mind. That said, we can be reasonably confident that the schema won't change for the mint (because it is so simple - a serial number and a json entry), and that the schema can change for the presentation (because we can create a new indexer and presentation instance, have the indexer replay the entire stream from the start, migrate users to use the new presentation, and turn off the original services).

alternatives.description: Continue using Kafka as the primary data store and communication mechanism.
pros: Kafka's append-only journal model fits the register model well.
Ability to replay the journal from the start.
cons: Kafka is not offered as a service on targeted platforms like Amazon or Heroku.
Kafka depends on Zookeeper, increasing operational complexity.
Kafka and Zookeeper consume a lot of memory, increasing costs.
Kafka's high throughput is unnecessary for our needs.
Lack of team understanding and confidence in Kafka's failure modes.
No native message-level serial number, requiring additional coordination mechanisms.

alternatives.description: Use Amazon Kinesis as an alternative to Kafka.
pros: Similar to Kafka in streaming capabilities.
cons: Discards all messages after 24 hours, which does not fit our needs.

template_adherence.title: Not using xjson-server as a primary data store
template_adherence.context:
We have been experimenting with the [`xjson-server`][xjson] binary available from google's certificate-transparency repository. This server is, as the name suggests, experimental. It is like a certificate transparency log server, except that it accepts JSON documents rather than X.509 certificates.

Our current model of a register includes a total ordering of entries, and we want to have a cryptographic certification of those entries. Therefore, the natural way to approach this was to submit entries to the xjson-server and accept that the ordering of those entries is simply the order in which they appear in the log.

However, this has caused us some problems. In particular, it doesn't feel right that the ordering, which is a key concept within the register domain, is entirely within the control of the xjson-server. Because of the asynchronous nature of the `/add-json` endpoint, the documents added within a given update interval are merged in to the log in an arbitrary order.

For extensibility, we want to support multiple methods of proof on a given register. An example might be one proof based on simple sha256-of-canonical-JSON, with another based on [objecthash][]. Both could be supported by xjson-server. However both would then impose their own ordering, and they wouldn't necessarily agree with one another.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for cryptographic certification of entries with a total ordering.
- Concern that xjson-server controls ordering, which is critical in the domain.
- Desire to support multiple methods of proof on a register.
- Asynchronous nature of xjson-server's `/add-json` endpoint causing arbitrary ordering.
- Extensibility and correctness of ordering and proofs.
template_adherence.decision:
We will not use xjson-server as a primary data store.

Specifically, we will not treat its ordering of documents as the primary order of entries in a register; and we will not use it as the primary data store for all data about entries.
template_adherence.consequences:
We will need to review the way in which we handle proofs, given that the mint is now maintaining ownership of the order of entries.

There are a number of options: we could implement our own Merkle tree based on the ideas in certificate-transparency; or we could submit documents to xjson-server that contain our own ordering (and accept that our ordering and xjson-server's ordering will not be the same, though they should broadly agree). When doing this, we should also refer to data items by hash rather than storing the complete item within xjson-server.

alternatives.description: Use xjson-server as the primary data store and accept its ordering as the primary order of entries.
pros: Leverages existing server capabilities.
Simplifies ordering by relying on server's order.
cons: Ordering is controlled externally and may be arbitrary due to asynchronous merging.
Does not support multiple proof methods well.
Ordering may not align with domain requirements.

alternatives.description: Implement own ordering and proofs, using xjson-server only as a secondary store or for additional proofs.
pros: Maintains control over ordering, critical for domain.
Supports multiple proof methods.
Allows flexibility in proof implementation.
cons: Requires additional implementation effort.
Potentially more complex system architecture.

template_adherence.title: TSV does not support escaping
template_adherence.context:
Registers support multiple different formats for data. One of them is TSV or tab-separated values. Superficially, TSV is similar to CSV (comma-separated values) but they fit different use cases.

TSV is useful because it can be munged by simple command-line tools such as `grep`, `awk`, or `cut`.

CSV is useful because it can be used by programs such as Excel.

As a result, they often have different rules for escaping. CSV often allows data which includes commas or newlines by quoting: as long as a newline or a comma is within double quotes, it does not terminate the current value or record.

If we took this approach with TSV, then tools like `awk` and `cut` would become dramatically less useful because they would not be able to distinguish between quoted and unquoted tabs and newlines.

There is prior art for this approach. The original [IANA TSV][] assignment document says:

> Note that fields that contain tabs are not allowable in this encoding.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to maintain compatibility with simple command-line tools like `grep`, `awk`, and `cut` that rely on TSV's simple format, the difference in escaping rules between CSV and TSV, and the prior art from the IANA TSV assignment document which disallows fields containing tabs.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to not support any rules for escaping in TSV formats. It is not possible to express a tab or a newline character in TSV, since a tab always ends the current field, and a newline always ends the current row.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences are that there is no way to express data containing newlines or tabs when loading in through the loader. Also, no checks are performed if a register contains newlines or tabs, so invalid TSV values may be generated if such data exists.

template_adherence.title: Items resource implementation ordering and pagination
template_adherence.context: The Items resource imposes an implementation challenge regarding how to order items in a pagination scenario. This ADR defines a way to create a deterministic order for this implementation.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to define a deterministic order for items that have no natural order, identified by their hash, and to implement pagination effectively using a cursor-based approach.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to assign an index or timestamp based on order of arrival to the database, using a serial number 'n' as an index, and implement keyset pagination (seek method) using this index as a cursor. The API endpoint /items will use this cursor for pagination.

template_adherence.title: Trailing slash in HTTP resources
template_adherence.context: Currently, HTTP resources have many URLs representing the same thing. This is not an ideal scenario for search engine indexing or caching. For example, the record `GB` resource can be accessed via multiple URLs with and without trailing slashes and different extensions. This ADR proposes a canonical URL and a way to consolidate around it.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have a canonical URL to improve search engine indexing and caching effectiveness, and to avoid multiple URLs representing the same resource.
template_adherence.decision: The canonical path for a resource MUST NOT have a trailing slash. Aliases MUST redirect (301) to the canonical path. The `Link` header for aliases should add the canonical URL using the `rel="canonical"` as per RFC6596. Paginated resources follow similar rules, with trailing slashes as aliases to the equivalent without trailing slashes. The decision about the canonical path for the first page is postponed.
template_adherence.consequences: This change is expected to make caching and caching invalidation easier without disrupting any user.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative is to allow multiple URLs with and without trailing slashes to coexist without canonicalization or redirects.
pros: No need to implement redirects or canonical headers.
cons: Multiple URLs represent the same resource, causing issues with search engine indexing and caching.

template_adherence.title: Remove indexes
template_adherence.context:
Currently, it is possible to configure an "index" for a particular register. An index is a transformation of a register entry log to create a new entry log against a different key value. The appropriate API structure for accessing an index is (after a very long time) still unconfirmed and therefore indexes are not used.

Because it is not used, the code that exists for indexes is therefore technical debt. To solve this technical debt we had two options:

* Decide and implement an API structure for accessing indexes as well and it's impact on the current data model and specification.
* Remove indexes as a feature (and code).

Note that although current users cannot access indexes, they are affected by some changes we made to the existing API (see [decision record](adr-007-read-api-changes.md).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- The feature (indexes) is currently unused and unconfirmed in API structure.
- The existing code for indexes is technical debt.
- Implementing the feature would require significant work.
- No evidence of user need for the feature.
- Desire to minimize disruption to existing users.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to remove the indexes feature and any corresponding code. This is because we do not have evidence of the need for this feature from our users. To decide and implement the API structure and resulting changes to the specification would be a significant amount of work which we cannot currently prioritise. We will have the opportunity to implement indexes again later, if we decide there is a need for it.
template_adherence.consequences: Remove all code related to indexes and remove `/index/*` endpoints. We will plan to revert the changes made to the registers API in a way that minimises disruption to existing users.

alternatives.description: Decide and implement an API structure for accessing indexes and its impact on the current data model and specification.
pros: Potentially useful feature if user need is confirmed.
Keeps the feature available for users.
cons: Significant amount of work to decide and implement.
No current evidence of user need.
Maintains technical debt until fully implemented.

alternatives.description: Remove indexes as a feature (and code).
pros: Removes unused code and technical debt.
Simplifies the codebase.
Avoids investing effort in unneeded feature.
cons: Feature is no longer available unless reimplemented later.
Potential disruption if users expected the feature.

template_adherence.title: Root path handling
template_adherence.context: As part of the work to release the next major version, there are three routes that need special handling: `/`, `/v1` and `/v2`. This ADR proposes a behaviour for each one of them.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to handle the root path and version roots as follows:
- Root (`/`): Return the same HTML as currently when HTML is requested; otherwise redirect (301) to the Register resource (`/{version}/register`) in JSON.
- Version root (`/v1`): Redirect (301) to `/` when HTML is requested; otherwise redirect (301) to the Register resource (`/{version}/register`) in JSON.

template_adherence.title: Prefer arrays for collection resources
template_adherence.context:
V1 of the registers specification represented collections of entries, items (now called blobs), and records using different data structures, including nested arrays and associative arrays. This decision was influenced by the concept of indexes, an experimental feature which we later removed (see [ADR 10: remove indexes](doc/arch/adr-010-remove-indexes.md)).

For a long time openregister-java was also out of sync with the registers specification in various ways. One manifestation of this was that the specification described an `/items` endpoint which was not actually available. Although [ADR 8](doc/arch/adr-008-items-resource.md) outlined an approach for this, we never fully implemented it.

We currently have an undocumented, incomplete version of this endpoint at `/next/blobs`.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to unify the JSON representation of collection resources for consistency and ease of client processing. The desire to follow established RFC patterns for records and blobs. The requirement to maintain compatibility with existing API behaviors, such as ordering blobs by arrival order and the use of "entry-number" for entries identifiers.
template_adherence.decision:
1. The JSON representation for any collection resource should be an array of objects, unless there is a good reason to break this rule.
2. The special value `_id` should be used to include identifiers in the objects.

This decision aligns with RFC 25 for records and RFC 27 for blobs. The ordering of blobs by arrival order will continue as per ADR 8. The entries resource will keep using "entry-number" for identifiers and will not change in V2 of the API.
template_adherence.consequences:
The JSON representation of a collection resource will not contain additional structure that is not present in the CSV representation.

The core collections provided by the API (entries, items, records) can be processed the same way by API clients.

alternatives.description: Continue using different data structures for collections, such as nested arrays and associative arrays, as in V1 of the registers specification.
pros: Allows flexibility in data representation for different collection types.
May support legacy clients expecting previous formats.
cons: Leads to inconsistency across collection resources.
Increases complexity for API clients processing collections.
Does not align with updated RFCs and internal decisions.

alternatives.description: Use associative arrays with custom keys for identifiers instead of arrays of objects with `_id`.
pros: May provide clearer key-based access to items.
Could align with some existing internal data structures.
cons: Breaks consistency with RFC 25 and RFC 27.
Increases complexity for clients expecting arrays.
Not aligned with the decision to unify JSON representation.

template_adherence.title: Artifacts Deployment
template_adherence.context: Deploying artifacts to nexus was done with this plugin before, but a bug was reported. When reading a child pom without `version`, for example, it does not retrieve the information inherited from the parent pom. We have to investigate alternatives.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to deploy artifacts to Nexus reliably, handle credentials securely, avoid bugs related to missing version information in child poms, and adhere to the build-once principle.
template_adherence.decision: `Nexus Artifact Uploader` is chosen, because: - `Maven lifecycle phase: deploy` does not meet our build-once principle. - `Nexus Artifact Uploader` has the same situation regarding parameters as `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin`, but can handle credentials as a Jenkins plugin.
template_adherence.consequences: Using `Nexus Artifact Uploader` allows handling credentials securely as a Jenkins plugin and avoids the build-once principle violation present in the Maven lifecycle deploy phase. However, it still requires preparing a list of parameters similar to the Apache Maven Deploy Plugin.

alternatives.description: Apache Maven Deploy Plugin (deploy:deploy-file)
pros: Official maven plugin for deployment, which is perfect for any maven projects if you only care whether your artifacts are deployed correctly.
cons: A list of parameters has to be generated before using the plugin, including `artifactId` and `version`, which is the same case as the `Nexus Artifact Uploader`.
Credential info has to be stored in the `settings.xml`, which introduces additional implementation.

alternatives.description: Maven lifecycle phase : deploy
pros: Same as the `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin`.

You don't have to pass the parameters as `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin` and `Nexus Artifact Uploader`, because `package` phase is executed implicitly and makes the parameters ready before `deploy` phase.
cons: Same case as the `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin` for handling credentials.

A list of phases is triggered implicitly before this phase, including `compile`, `test` and `package`. To follow the build-once principle, all these phases have to be skipped, but it's not possible to skip some of the maven goals binding to certain phases.
For example, `Apache Maven JAR Plugin` does not provide an option to skip the `jar:jar` goal, which is the main reason why this option cannot be used.

alternatives.description: Nexus Artifact Uploader
pros: Without the pain of handling the credentials, which was mentioned above in `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin` section.
It's promising, when the plugin is used properly.
cons: Same as the `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin`. A list of parameters has to be prepared.

template_adherence.title: Automatic Versioning and Release of Cloud Applications
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the context of providing a Continuous Delivery (CD) pipeline for SAP Cloud Platform applications that adheres to the "build once" principle. It explains the problem with using Maven's default versioning (SNAPSHOT suffix) which does not uniquely identify builds and the need for auditability and automation in versioning and releasing software.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for auditability (unique and identifiable versioning), automation (to handle multiple releases per day), compatibility with existing build tools (Maven), and avoiding manual release processes. The requirements emphasize that SNAPSHOT versions are insufficient due to their non-uniqueness and potential deletion by artifact repositories.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement an automated versioning schema where each commit to the productive branch (master) is treated as a new release. The version number includes a human-readable build timestamp (ISO 8601 format, UTC, without colons) and the git commit id, e.g., "2.7.3-2018-03-02T114757UTC_ff46bb0f00a663018f3efea697b2fb5e86fe6d41". Automatic versioning is enabled by default but can be disabled. Git tags are not created automatically to avoid clutter, but can be created manually.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include improved auditability by having unique version identifiers tied to commits and build times, enabling automated releases on each commit to master, and avoiding clutter in git tags. It also means that multiple builds of the same commit have distinct versions, preventing conflicts in artifact repositories. However, it requires adherence to the new versioning scheme and may require disabling the feature for legacy builds.

alternatives.description: Use Maven Release Plugin for versioning and releasing.
pros: Standard Maven approach, well supported and documented.
Integrates with existing Maven workflows.
cons: Does not satisfy auditability requirements as SNAPSHOT versions are ambiguous.
Manual release steps may be required, reducing automation.
SNAPSHOT versions can be deleted by artifact repositories, causing audit issues.

alternatives.description: Manual versioning and tagging by developers.
pros: Full control over versioning and tagging.
Can use semantic versioning as desired.
cons: Manual process is error-prone and not scalable for multiple releases per day.
Lacks automation, increasing overhead.
Potential for inconsistent versioning and auditability issues.

template_adherence.title: Move Cx Server Script in Container
template_adherence.context: We have a bash script (`cx-server`), which orchestrates the Docker containers used by our Cx Server. Using bash is inconvenient for Windows users, as Windows does not include bash by default. There is options for running bash on Windows, such as the Windows Subsystem for Linux, but this is not trivial to setup and requires switching Windows to Developer Mode. Other options include running a virtual machine locally, or connecting to a remove Linux system, but both are not always possible and have too much overhead. Recently, we added a "companion" Docker image which is used by `cx-server` to run scripts. Unrelated, the idea was born to move `cx-server` into this image, so the remaining `cx-server` is a very thin wrapper which can also be added as a Windows compatible script file.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support Windows users who do not have bash by default.
- Avoid complex setup like Windows Subsystem for Linux or virtual machines.
- Maintain compatibility and smooth upgrade path for existing users.

template_adherence.title: Treatment of application with a frontend that don't have a package lock file
template_adherence.context:
The node package manager (npm) creates a so called ["lock file"](https://docs.npmjs.com/files/package-locks) when running `npm install`. The recommended action is to commit this file to version control, as stated by the command itself:

```
$ npm install
npm notice created a lockfile as package-lock.json. You should commit this file.
```

Some npm commands, which are part of the pipeline, such as `ci` and `audit` require that a package lock file exists.

Thus, if a project lacks the package lock file, there are tree options:

* Refuse to build the project, which enforces the recommended practice of committing the lock file
* Silently create a package lock file as part of the pipeline
* Avoid npm commands which require a package lock
* Would disable the npm audit stage
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle projects that lack a package lock file in the build pipeline.
- Ensure npm commands that require a package lock file can run without failure.
- Balance between enforcing best practices and developer convenience.
- Maintain reliability of builds and audit stages.
template_adherence.decision: If a project has a `package.json` file, but no package lock, we create a package lock file as part of the pipeline and warn the user about this. The created package lock file is not archived as part of the pipeline build artifacts.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Jenkins builds don't fail when developers forget to commit the package lock.
- If the developers chose not to commit the package lock long term, the build is less reliable.
- npm audit can run always on projects with a frontend component.

alternatives.description: Refuse to build the project if the package lock file is missing, enforcing the recommended practice of committing the lock file.
pros: Enforces best practice strictly.
Ensures build consistency and reliability.
cons: Builds fail if developers forget to commit the lock file.
May cause frustration or delays in development.

alternatives.description: Silently create a package lock file as part of the pipeline.
pros: Builds do not fail due to missing lock file.
Allows npm commands requiring lock file to run.
Less disruption to developers.
cons: May reduce build reliability if developers do not commit lock file long term.
Created lock file is not archived, so may differ between builds.

alternatives.description: Avoid npm commands which require a package lock, disabling npm audit stage.
pros: Simplifies pipeline by skipping problematic commands.
Avoids build failures related to missing lock file.
cons: Disables npm audit stage, reducing security checks.
May allow issues to go undetected.

template_adherence.title: Structure of SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Maven Projects
template_adherence.context:
SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK encompasses components such as Java libraries, Maven archetypes, a Virtual Data Model and a Continuous Delivery Toolkit.
The Continuous Delivery Toolkit must be able to build, test and deploy arbitrary SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Maven projects developed by teams within and outside of SAP.

Based on best practices gained when developing cloud-native applications, we learned that it should be possible to separate unit- and integration tests to run them in isolation.
Reasoning for requiring running them in isolation are:

* Dependencies for unit tests might not be required for integration tests and vice versa, or even conflict with them
* Unit- and integration test can be run independently and parallel, locally and on CI/CD

Alternative options to separate unit- and integration tests:

* Use [Maven profiles](https://maven.apache.org/guides/introduction/introduction-to-profiles.html)
* Use [Maven multi-module](https://maven.apache.org/guides/mini/guide-multiple-modules.html) projects

Archetypes for generating valid projects are provided.
[Example projects](https://github.com/sap/cloud-s4-sdk-examples) are available.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to build, test, and deploy SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Maven projects reliably.
- Best practices for cloud-native applications suggest separating unit and integration tests.
- Desire to run unit and integration tests independently and in isolation.
- Avoid conflicts and unnecessary dependencies between unit and integration tests.
- Simplify usage for users, including inexperienced Maven users.
- Enforce conventions and structure for projects to ease pipeline processing.
- Support build once principle and efficient CI/CD pipelines.
template_adherence.decision:
Projects built by SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Pipeline need to be Maven multi-module projects.
Required modules are `application`, `integration-tests` and `unit-tests`.
Additional modules are **not** allowed.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Users don't need to select Maven profiles for running tests.
- For inexperienced Maven users, selecting profiles for running tests might be more confusing compared to choosing the right module.
- There would need to be a common convention which profiles need to exist with fixed names if profiles were used.
- Fine grained dependency selection for each module is possible.
- Possible to use different versions of a dependency in productive and test code.
- Less likely that test dependencies leak into production code.
- Forces separation of unit- and integration tests.
- Easier to check adherence to the testing pyramid.
- Enforce that typical integration test dependencies are not used in unit tests.
- Allows easier implementation of the build once principle.
- Avoids rebuilding application artifact unnecessarily in CI/CD.
- Existing projects need to adapt to this structure.
- Tests in the application module are ignored by the Pipeline.
- Developers must put tests into the correct module.
- Pipeline can assume which Maven modules exist, simplifying scanning.
- Avoids fragile module discovery methods in the pipeline.

alternatives.description: Use Maven profiles to separate unit and integration tests.
pros: Allows separation of tests without multi-module projects.
Maven profiles are a built-in feature and widely used.
cons: Users need to select profiles to run tests, which can be confusing.
Requires common conventions for profile names.
Potential conflicts or dependency issues between profiles.
Less fine-grained dependency management compared to modules.

alternatives.description: Use Maven multi-module projects to separate unit and integration tests.
pros: Clear separation of tests into modules.
Fine-grained dependency management per module.
Simplifies pipeline assumptions and scanning.
Supports build once principle effectively.
Reduces risk of test dependencies leaking into production code.
cons: Existing projects need to adapt to this structure.
Developers must correctly place tests into modules.
Additional complexity in project structure.

template_adherence.title: Unify the "build" Stage
template_adherence.context:
Our CI/CD Pipeline has a build stage, which contains a `buildBackend` and a `buildFrontend` component.
`buildFrontend` is optional, and only run if the project has a frontend, which is determined by the existence of a `package.json` file.
If both are run, they are executed in parallel.
`buildFrontend` actually does not build anything, it only downloads dependencies.
"Building" the frontend is facilitated via maven, which is run in `buildBackend`.
template_adherence.decision: Both `buildBackend` and `buildFrontend` are unified into one `build` stage.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Execution of maven and npm is not parallel anymore, which might delay the build process a little.
* The configuration format of `pipeline_config.yml` needs to be updated to reflect the new stage.
Our existing legacy configuration layer could be used to mitigate this.
* We reduce the number of stashes, which makes the pipeline execute a little faster
* Existing documentation needs to be updated, if possible.
Non-updatable documentation exists (such as the "Extending SAP S/4HANA" book for example).

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: Formatting of response values
template_adherence.context:
As we introduce new and more complex response types, we need to come up with a consistent, homogeneous solution for serializing all the values.

The historical solution for this issue has been to separate multiple values with pipes, and in some scenarios, creating a JSON-encoded response (i.e. geoshapes).

We currently need to add a new `code` property to some responses, namely to cascade and option types, but we also want to avoid introducing new properties as the response content grows.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a consistent and homogeneous serialization format for all response values.
- Increasing complexity of response types.
- Avoiding scalability issues by not adding new properties as response content grows.
- Ensuring backward compatibility with existing responses.
- Need to support various response types like barcodes, option questions, cascades, etc.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to extend the JSON-based schema and encode complex answers in a packed string format. The meaning of each response type will be reviewed to determine the encoding format (JSON, string, array, etc). Multiple responses will be encoded using a JSON array.
template_adherence.consequences:
- All response types will contain a single value property whose format depends on the question type.
- Response values will need to be processed in different components (dashboard, reports, etc) to visualize a human-readable version.
- Existing responses must be considered to ensure backward compatibility.
- GAE test harnesses might need adaptation to support the new format.

alternatives.description: Continue using the historical solution of separating multiple values with pipes and JSON-encoded responses for complex types.
pros: Familiarity with existing approach.
No immediate need to change existing systems.
cons: Not consistent or homogeneous across all response types.
Does not scale well with increasing complexity.
Adding new properties like `code` is problematic.

alternatives.description: Introduce new properties for each new requirement in response values.
pros: Explicit representation of new data.
Potentially easier to understand individual properties.
cons: Does not scale well as response content grows.
Increases complexity and maintenance overhead.
Not aligned with the goal to avoid adding new properties.

template_adherence.title: ADR 006: App datapoint sync and display architecture improvement
template_adherence.context: Currently, when user requests data point sync from either DataPointsMapFragment or SurveyedLocaleListFragment and a service, SurveyedDataPointSyncService is started and for each batch of datapoints both fragments get notified of new data available via local Broadcast which both subscribe too. While data is being loaded a non-blocking "loading" ui is shown. Once the loading is finished that loading needs to be dismissed. We also display a snackBar with the number of updated datapoints or some eventual errors.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The current implementation causes unnecessary broadcasts to fragments even when UI is not present, leading to inefficiencies. There is a need to decouple UI from data sync notifications and improve separation of concerns to enable better testability and maintainability. Desired qualities include reducing unnecessary broadcasts, improving UI notification mechanisms, modularizing the project into layers (app, domain, data), and enabling unit testing with single responsibility components.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to refactor the current implementation to have the UI subscribe to database changes instead of broadcasts, using RX Java (e.g., sqlbrite). The project will be separated into three modules: app, domain, and data. View logic will be moved to presenters, fragments will only display and collect user input, and presenters will subscribe to database changes. Use cases will be created for retrieving datapoints from network and database, along with network and database data sources. Broadcast sending and receivers will be removed, and an error management system will be implemented in the use case logic to notify UI via subscribers.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include affecting only the data points sync and display functionality. The project will be modularized into app, domain, and data modules. View logic will be moved to presenters, and fragments will be simplified. Presenters will subscribe to database changes. Use cases and data sources will be created for network and database operations. Broadcast mechanisms will be removed. An error management system will be introduced to handle different error types and notify the UI accordingly.

alternatives.description: Continue using local broadcasts to notify UI fragments of data updates.
pros: Simple to implement with existing code.
UI fragments receive updates directly.
cons: Broadcasts are sent even when UI is not present, causing unnecessary processing.
Both fragments must subscribe even if only one displays notifications.
Tight coupling between service and UI via broadcasts.
Harder to test and maintain due to mixed concerns.

alternatives.description: Use a polling mechanism where UI periodically checks for data updates.
pros: Decouples service from UI broadcasts.
Simpler to implement than reactive subscriptions.
cons: Inefficient due to constant polling.
Delayed UI updates depending on polling interval.
Increased resource consumption.

template_adherence.title: Use json for scratch to local server communication
template_adherence.context:
We are using POST HTTP requests to communicate with the local server.
To pass multiple parameters we would use requests with `multipart/form-data` or `text/plain` type.
Creating correctly encoded multipart requests is tricky.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use json for scratch to local server communication.
I.e. responses from server to scratch will be json objects similar to this:

````json
{
"status" : "", | "SUCCESS" or "FAILED"
"errorMessage" : "", | null when no error happened, otherwise an error message
"result" : "" | null when there is no output (e.g. in case of an error), otherwise the result
}
````
template_adherence.consequences:
Values will have to be converted from json to java objects and vice versa.
Conversion could theoretically fail.

template_adherence.title: 2. Sidekiq Queues
template_adherence.context: We have background jobs that are processed by Sidekiq workers on several dedicated background processing machines. The background jobs include a variety of different tasks from different sources: processing user requests (e.g., ingesting files, (re)generating derivatives), cleaning up after user actions (e.g., propagating state and visibility, removing files before deleting their parent resource), refreshing metadata from Voyager/PULFA, bulk-ingesting content, routine cleanup (cleaning out guest users), fixity checking.
template_adherence.decision: We will have three queues for processing background jobs: 1. `default` for processing user-initiated requests needed for ingesting and displaying objects 2. `low` for bulk processing, validation, cleanup, etc. 3. `super_low` for fixity checking and other long-term preservation actions
template_adherence.consequences: Fixity checking from user-initiated ingest will be lower priority than bulk ingest or processing, and may be significantly delayed when there are large volumes of materials being ingested.

template_adherence.title: 6. Preservation Tombstones
template_adherence.context: After an item is deleted from the database all traces of it are gone, but if it's been preserved then it's possible to restore it. However, finding the particular ID of the item to restore is difficult if all that's known are pieces of its metadata (title, source metadata ID, etc.) We will remedy this by storing a "tombstone" of deleted items as a small record of what was deleted.
template_adherence.decision:
1. When a preserved item is deleted it will create a "tombstone" containing the following metadata:
1. ID of deleted resource
1. Title of deleted resource
1. Original Filename of deleted resource (if a FileSet)
1. Embedded PreservationObject that existed at time of deletion
1. ID of Parent at time of deletion.
2. These tombstones will be displayed in the Figgy UI and used as a way to discover material that can be recovered.
template_adherence.consequences: 1. The database will likely have many tombstones. If it turns out to be too many to reliably sift through, we may have to change our strategy.

template_adherence.title: 7. Pyramidal Tiffs & AWS Serverless Delivery
template_adherence.context:
We have several TB of images to deliver through a IIIF service, more than any of our physical boxes can currently hold all in one place. We have to pay Kakadu a licensing fee in order to get acceptable tile delivery, and the Cantaloupe server we use has been proven to be easily Denial-of-Service'd to the point of freezing and no images being able to be served.

We will remedy this problem of scale by storing Pyramidal Tiffs in the cloud which an AWS Lambda service (scale-able to at least a thousand simultaneous request) will use to respond to IIIF image server requests, using Northwestern's serverless-iiif project.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to handle several terabytes of images beyond local storage capacity, the cost and limitations of current solutions (Kakadu licensing fee, Cantaloupe server instability), and the requirement for scalable, reliable image delivery through IIIF service.
template_adherence.decision:
1. Generate Pyramidal tiffs using VIPS and upload them to an AWS bucket using valkyrie-shrine, downsizing images greater than 15k pixels on the long side by half.
2. Configure and deploy serverless-iiif to serve IIIF Image API requests using those pyramidal tiffs.
3. Configure an Amazon CloudFront cache in front of the lambda to automatically cache tiles and info.jsons for one year.
template_adherence.consequences:
1. Cost per request, estimated at roughly $0.01/thousand requests/month, which is affordable.
2. Slightly reduced zoom-ability for scrolls due to downsizing, but testing shows minimal impact and sufficient quality.
3. Need to regenerate pyramidals for all FileSets, with fallback to Cantaloupe if not yet generated.
4. Improved tile accuracy compared to previous servers, avoiding issues like high saturation.

alternatives.description: Continue using the current Cantaloupe server despite its limitations and risk of Denial-of-Service.
pros: No additional cost or infrastructure changes.
Familiarity with existing system.
cons: Server is easily Denial-of-Service'd and freezes.
Cannot handle scale of several TB of images.
Poor tile delivery quality requiring Kakadu licensing.

alternatives.description: Use Kakadu for tile delivery despite licensing fees.
pros: Acceptable tile delivery quality.
Established solution.
cons: Requires paying licensing fees.
May not scale well with large image volumes.

alternatives.description: Store images locally on physical boxes.
pros: No cloud costs.
Full control over hardware.
cons: Insufficient storage capacity for several TB of images.
Scalability issues.

template_adherence.title: 8. Unlinked Files
template_adherence.context:
When an ingest fails in the middle of a transaction which is adding files, the FileSets will not get persisted. However, the files will have already been copied to the repository via `FileAppender`. This results in files in the repository which have no corresponding database record.

Fixing this will require development of a transactional disk StorageAdapter which moves files at the end of a metadata transaction.
template_adherence.decision:
1. We don't have time to implement a transactional disk StorageAdapter at this time.
2. Accept this situation, document it here, and know we can free up space in the future by looking for unlinked files and deleting them.
template_adherence.consequences:
1. Extra disk space will be used for files which aren't accessible. If we need space in the future we can find and delete them.
2. If we migrate disk storage to the cloud, we would end up paying for these files, and should implement transactional storage. This might also have implications for our migration strategy - rather than a straight RSync we may want to migrate database-first.

I decided to learn some more web technologies. For browser apps that means React and Redux, which is commonly used with Node, NPM, and Webpack. Learning the common stuff is a good way to get my bearings in the field.

template_adherence.context:

I like the principles in the book Infrastructure as Code. It suggests avoiding making changes to services except in an automated, configured manner.

I've had some exposure to the infrastructure provisioning tool [Serverless](https://serverless.com), so I'd like to try using it on this project. Serverless abstracts AWS CloudFormation and similar tools from other cloud vendors.
template_adherence.decision: I will use Serverless to describe and provision my AWS components.
template_adherence.consequences:
I was able to create and update an AWS stack with no consequential components. I was able to do all AWS changes in code that was committed to the repository and versioned.

Terraform, however, is a less magical and more generic tool. I switched to it.

template_adherence.title: 007. Terraform
template_adherence.context:
Serverless has the problem of narrowing available functionality from CloudFormation, which itself narrows functionality from AWS. For instance, CloudFormation can create stacks no larger than 200 resources, and Serverless wants to put everything in one CloudFormation stack. In short, Serverless is good for a basic API, but it's not very appropriate for other cloud resources.

In my research I kept running across Terraform. It is a less magical, more granular tool. It's open source and has very broad support for provisioning AWS resources and other services. It was called out in the book Infrastructure as Code several years ago, and it has had all that time to mature.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the context section implies some drivers: limitations of Serverless and CloudFormation (e.g., stack size limit, limited functionality), the maturity and broad support of Terraform, and the desire for more granular control over infrastructure provisioning.
template_adherence.decision: I will use Terraform for infrastructure definition and deployment, not Serverless.
template_adherence.consequences:
I was able to reprovision the whole Serverless stack in Terraform and separate that from the API definition and build process.

It's tedious to write these definitions, at least at first, but no more tedious than manually building CloudFormation templates would be, and it's a lot of fun. I've also learned a lot about how API Gateway and Lambda and IAM roles work, just from having to address each piece of their schemas.

I had to discard the serverless-offline debugging plugin, so now I don't have a local API debugging solution.

I also found that API Gateway's deployments are not regular cloud resources like practically everything else Terraform expects to manage. When you mutate some resource it depends on, it doesn't get recreated like AWS expects you to do. So I created a post-apply script step that specifically redeploys the API. This is not necessarily Terraform's fault, but it is a challenge, and I'm wary of what else might have unique behavior at deployment time.

template_adherence.title: 008. Artifact-based deployment
template_adherence.context: At work we've been talking about ideal continuous delivery setups, and a goal we have is to separate our build and deployment processes into discrete steps. Now that I'm using Terraform and I'm looking carefully at how Lambda functions get their code, it's obvious that pointing Lambda at build artifacts in S3 is a good way to do that. So, I should have a build-package-archive process for the API (and in the future for other components), and a plan-verify-deploy process for Terraform.
template_adherence.decision: I will archive artifacts as a build step, and refer to them in deployment configuration.
template_adherence.consequences:
In the API, I changed from deploying with Serverless to packaging an artifact and archiving it to S3, keyed by the GitHub commit sha. In Terraform, I referred to the artifact in such a way that you just need to know which commit's artifacts you are provisioning.

The S3 bucket for artifacts is shared among all stages, so you package a build once and deploy it to all environments. The environment itself is not considered during the build process.

template_adherence.title: 8. Provide an End To End Stub
template_adherence.context:
We wish to run regular user research and testing against the prototype Service Provider.

To support user research we need to provide a user journey that resembles a typical Verify journey.

The area we are most interested in is the interface between the Service and the Hub.
template_adherence.decision:
We will create a Stub Verify Hub that will allow for end-to-end testing of the prototype.

It will not provide a SAML implementation.

It will expect a form submission on a web resource that mimics the behaviour of receiving an AuthnRequest.

If the form post is successful then a browser redirect will be issued to a page explaining where the user is in their
journey.  Continuing from this page will take the user to a page containing a series of possible response scenarios that
can be selected.

Any information that needs to be stored from the original request or between pages will be stored in a session
cookie. The session cookie does not need to be signed or encrypted initially.

Some scenarios will require additional user input such as a providing a pid value or user account creation attributes.
These will be provided on subsequent pages. In every case the user will need to provide the URL that the stub-hub should
send its responses to.

Each response will mimic the shape of a Hub SAML Response form that can be submitted back to the Service and SP
prototype.

The details of each canned response will be encoded as base64 encoded JSON in the SAMLResponse parameter of the form.

The prototype service provider will be able to understand each canned response and produce a specific response to the
Service/client.

Using these responses it will be possible able to test different scenarios in the client, Service, and browser.

The Stub Verify Hub will provide the following responses:

| Response Scenario     | Message                                                                                                                   |
| --                    | --                                                                                                                         |
| Successful Match      | scenario: SUCCESS_MATCH, levelOfAssurance: ${specified loa}, pid: ${specified PID}                                         |
| Account Creation      | scenario: ACCOUNT_CREATION, levelOfAssurance: ${specified loa}, pid: ${specified PID}, attributes: [${user attributes}]  |
| No Match              | scenario: NO_MATCH                                                                                                         |
| Cancellation          | scenario: CANCELLATION                                                                                                     |
| Authentication failed | scenario: AUTHENTICATION_FAILED                                                                                           |
| Requestor Error       | scenario: REQUEST_ERROR                                                                                                 |
| Internal Server Error | scenario: INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR

template_adherence.title: We will use a secure token to validate InResponseTo
template_adherence.context:
A SAML relying party must check that responses it receives have an InResponseTo attribute that matches the ID of a request that the relying party sent for this user.

Since we're trying to keep the verify service provider as stateless as possible we don't want it to have to remember which IDs belong to which users. Instead we'd like to delegate this behaviour to the client of the service provider (i.e. the service itself), which will have its own session store.

If a relying party's session store was insecure (for example and unsigned session cookie) then an attacker could circumvent the InResponseTo check by setting the value in session to something else. To mitigate against this attack the verify service provider could pass the service back a HMAC of the ID (either alongside the ID or instead of it).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to validate the InResponseTo attribute securely.
- Desire to keep the verify service provider stateless.
- Concern about insecure session stores allowing attackers to circumvent checks.
- Consideration of implementing HMAC as an additional security measure.
template_adherence.decision: We won't implement this for now because initially we're happy that our relying parties will store the session securely. We may want to implement it later as an extra level of security.
template_adherence.consequences: We will defer implementing the "secure token" until later in the project.

alternatives.description: Implement the secure token (HMAC) mechanism immediately to ensure stronger security.
pros: Provides an extra level of security against session store attacks.
Ensures the InResponseTo attribute is validated with a secure token.
cons: Increases complexity of the system.
May require changes to relying parties and their session management.
Contradicts the goal of keeping the verify service provider stateless.

alternatives.description: Do not implement the secure token mechanism and rely on secure session stores of relying parties.
pros: Keeps the verify service provider stateless.
Simpler implementation.
Faster initial development.
cons: Relies on the assumption that relying parties store sessions securely.
Potential security risk if relying parties have insecure session stores.

template_adherence.title: Use of the "full" SAML profile for signing Responses and Assertions
template_adherence.context: Verify's SAML profile specifies that Responses and Assertions should be signed. As a workaround, Verify introduced a "simple" profile where we do not sign Responses.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to comply with Verify's SAML profile requirements for signing Responses and Assertions; compatibility issues with some SAML service providers; security considerations favoring the "full" profile.

template_adherence.consequences: The verify-service-provider will need to request metadata from hub, so it will need a bit more configuration. We'll have to do a bit more work to handle responses correctly. Relying parties using the verify-service-provider will be more secure.

alternatives.description: Use the "simple" profile where Responses are not signed to avoid compatibility issues with some SAML service providers.
pros: Avoids problems with off-the-shelf SAML service providers that can't handle multiple signatures.
cons: Less secure because Responses are not signed.
Does not comply fully with Verify's SAML profile requirements.

template_adherence.title: 17. We will pass the request ID to the client
template_adherence.context:
Verify will send the same request ID that it sees in the AuthnRequest to the MSA when it does matching. If the service is able to see the request ID in a convenient form then they are able to correlate MSA attribute query requests with AuthnRequests they've sent.

We also need to be able to validate that the InResponseTo attribute on the Response matches the ID we sent in the AuthnRequest. So long as the service is able to store the ID in a secure way (i.e. without the possibility of a malicious user changing it in their session) it should be fine for them to send this back to the service to validate directly.

There was also discussion about sending an HMAC of the ID back to the client be stored in session - this would mitigate against attacks due a relying party storing the ID insecurely.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to correlate MSA attribute query requests with AuthnRequests, the requirement to validate the InResponseTo attribute on the Response, and the security concern of storing the request ID securely to prevent malicious tampering.
template_adherence.decision: We'll return the request ID alongside the AuthnRequest when we generate it and ask for it when translating Responses.
template_adherence.consequences: Relying parties will need to store the request ID in session securely and send it back to the verify-service-provider when handling responses.

template_adherence.title: We will have hubSSOLocation as a configuration option
template_adherence.context:
Verify Service Provider needs to know the SSO location for Verify Hub in order to generate a valid AuthnRequest.

Hub Metadata does not provide SSOLocation because if it would, it would have to describe Hub as an IDP and therefore provide signing certificates. Having signing certificates in the Hub metadata makes Relying Parties trust assertions signed by hub, which would break the security contract between the Matching Service Adapter and the Hub.

Matching Service Adapter does provide Hub SSOLocation in its metadata. However, the value is directly copied in from the Matching Service Adapter configuration. Matching Service Adapter itself does not use the value, therefore we do not trust this feature to remain as part of the Matching Service Adapter.
template_adherence.decision: We will provide the hub sso-location as a configuration option instead of parsing it from the msa-metadata.
template_adherence.consequences: Relying parties will need to spend extra effort to configure the hubSSOLocation.

template_adherence.title: We will not validate the recipient
template_adherence.context:
The subject confirmation data on assertions has a recipient attribute, which the MSA sets to the assertion consumer service url. The assertions also have an audience restriction, which is set to the service entity id.

The verify service provider, conceptually, should not need to know the assertion consumer service url - as this ties somewhat to the relying party's infrastructure, and makes it difficult to change. Knowing it would also lead to more complicated configuration for relying parties as we introduce multi tenancy to the verify service provider.

In usual usages of SAML, the recipient should be validated, as should the audience restriction (if present), and these might be different and have slightly different meanings. However, since we control the production of this SAML (via the MSA), we know that the audience restriction will always be present and set to the service entity id, so validating this will mitigate any potential issues from not validating the recipient.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid tight coupling to the relying party's infrastructure and to simplify configuration in a multi-tenant environment. The assurance that audience restriction validation covers the security concerns that would otherwise require recipient validation.
template_adherence.decision: The verify service provider will not validate the assertion consumer service url.
template_adherence.consequences:
We will not be performing a check that the SAML specification says should be performed (however, as above, we believe this is covered by the audience restriction check).
We will have to revert some commits already merged.

alternatives.description: Validate the recipient attribute as per usual SAML usage.
pros: Adheres strictly to SAML specification.
Potentially more secure by validating recipient explicitly.
cons: Ties the verify service provider to the relying party's infrastructure.
Complicates configuration in multi-tenant scenarios.

alternatives.description: Validate only the audience restriction and not the recipient attribute.
pros: Simplifies configuration for relying parties.
Avoids tight coupling to relying party infrastructure.
Leverages control over SAML production to ensure security.
cons: Deviates from usual SAML validation practices.
May require reverting some commits if previously validated recipient.

template_adherence.title: We will report the version in a saml extension
template_adherence.context: The verify-service-provider will be deployed to a number of relying parties. Which relying party is using which version could potentially become difficult to keep track of. To make it as easy as possible for us to manage this we'd like the verify-service-provider to report its version in some way. Because the verify-service-provider is not intended to be accessible to the internet we can't simply expose an endpoint that reports the version number. Also, since the SAML messages go via the browser we can't use a custom HTTP header. There's also a concern about the security implications of reporting a version number in cleartext. We considered a couple of options: - Requesting metadata from Verify with a custom user-agent string - Sending the version in an unencrypted saml extension - Sending the version in an encrypted saml extension
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to track which relying party is using which version; security concerns about exposing version number in cleartext; constraints due to deployment and communication methods (no internet access, no custom HTTP headers).
template_adherence.decision: We decided to send the version number in the SAML AuthnRequests as an encrypted SAML extension. This approach balances the need to report version information with security concerns by encrypting the version data within the SAML message extensions.
template_adherence.consequences: Verify will be able to monitor the versions of connected instances of the verify-service-provider. AuthnRequests will be approximately 2,500 bytes longer but still within acceptable limits. Version numbers will not be visible to malicious third parties due to encryption with Verify's public key.

alternatives.description: Requesting metadata from Verify with a custom user-agent string
pros: Potentially straightforward to implement.
cons: May not be feasible due to deployment constraints.
Does not address security concerns about exposing version information.

alternatives.description: Sending the version in an unencrypted saml extension
pros: Simple to implement.
cons: Version number exposed in cleartext, raising security concerns.

alternatives.description: Sending the version in an encrypted saml extension
pros: Secures version information by encrypting it.
Allows version tracking without exposing sensitive data.
cons: Increases AuthnRequest size by approximately 2,500 bytes.

template_adherence.title: 25. We will only release one configuration file
template_adherence.context:
Historically we have had "two ways" of configuring Verify Service Provider:

- Using environment variables
- Using a YAML file

When using environment variables the application used the verify-service-provider-env.yml
file from the resources directory (so inside the jar). When using the YAML file you would
pass the path to a different file as a command line parameter - usually people
would use the example one that's contained in the repo.

There were a couple of reasons for the extra complexity of managing two files, both due to
restrictions with the java buildpack used by cloudfoundry:

- It's not possible to specify command line arguments through the java buildpack,
so you can't specify a path to your config file
- We weren't confident in the way cloudfoundry manages static files, so we didn't want
to rely on one.

There was also a philosophical point that 12 factor applications should be configured through
their environment. This made the "hide the configuration in the .jar and do everything through
env vars" way appealing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to simplify configuration management by reducing complexity of having two configuration methods.
- Limitations of the java buildpack on cloudfoundry preventing command line argument specification.
- Uncertainty about cloudfoundry's static file management.
- Philosophical alignment with 12 factor app principles favoring environment variable configuration.
- Desire to maintain compatibility with existing environment variable based configuration.
- Improve user experience by removing confusion between two configuration methods.
template_adherence.decision:
We will remove the verify-service-provider-env.yml file from src/main/resources.

The application will default to the verify-service-provider.yml file that's included in the .zip if no command line arguments are provided.

If the application is started without command line arguments specifying a yml file AND no environment variables have been set, startup should error gracefully and tell the user that the configuration fields have not been specified.

We will establish the path to verify-service-provider.yml by asking java for the path to the .jar file containing the Application class and looking in the parent folder.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to implement a story to make the default configuration file work compatibly with the current environment variable based solution.
- Only one configuration file will need to be maintained going forward.
- Users will not have to learn about the dichotomy between "configure with env vars" and "configure with files".
- The application will still run on PaaS using the default java buildpack.

template_adherence.title: 26. Development mode for the Verify Service Provider
template_adherence.context: Interacting with the Compliance Tool (CT) is not a straightforward process and the API could be better. When a user is using the VSP for the first time it can be frustrating having to make sense of the CT API in order to make progress. In order to get the VSP running with the CT so that can start development they need to: 1. Create a set of private keys and certificates 2. Configure the VSP to interact with the CT and use the newly generated keys and certificates 3. Create a script that can initiate a session with the CT 4. Create a client that can interact with the VSP 5. Test the interaction between the client, VSP, and CT
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to simplify the initial development experience with the Verify Service Provider (VSP) and Compliance Tool (CT) integration, reducing complexity for first-time users. The desire to provide a development mode that automates key and certificate creation, session initialization, and configuration to facilitate easier development and testing. Compatibility with different operating systems (e.g., Windows). Limiting the scope to the 'non-matching' journey to simplify implementation.
template_adherence.decision: The VSP will provide a development mode initialized by a Dropwizard command. This mode will create in-memory keys and self-signed certificates, use a random UUID for an entity ID, configure itself to read the CT's metadata, run in non-matching mode, and initialize a new session with the compliance tool. Users can start this mode via a shell command with options to control host, port, SAML response location, and matching dataset contents. The mode will be available only for the 'non-matching' journey.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision supersedes ADR-0008, which was never implemented. The VSP will have a dependency on bouncycastle to create in-memory certificates. The development mode simplifies the developer experience but is limited to the non-matching journey. It provides a clear command interface for starting development mode with configurable options.

template_adherence.title: Use Swagger annotations to generate and maintain konduit-serving clients
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the current state of konduit-serving clients with two endpoints for inference inputs and the challenges in maintaining and documenting clients across multiple languages. It highlights the need for a better approach to generate and maintain client APIs consistently.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need for easier maintenance and documentation of client APIs across multiple languages, the desire to generate clients automatically from source code, and the need to reduce manual effort and inconsistencies in client API generation and documentation.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Swagger annotations in the source code to generate OpenAPI specifications automatically, which can then be used with openapi-generator to produce client libraries in multiple languages. This involves refactoring the source code to use Swagger annotations and generating clients from the resulting OpenAPI YAML specification.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include easier documentation and maintenance, ability to generate clients for any language supported by openapi-generator, and elimination of custom code generation for python clients. Negative consequences include the time required for code refactoring, some loss of API flexibility due to OpenAPI constraints, and the need to write wrapper layers on top of generated clients to handle features not supported by OpenAPI (e.g., numpy/INDArray types).

alternatives.description: Continue maintaining client APIs manually for each language without using Swagger annotations or automatic generation.
pros: No need for initial refactoring effort.
Full flexibility in API design without OpenAPI constraints.
cons: High maintenance overhead.
Inconsistent documentation and client APIs across languages.
Difficult to keep clients up to date with server changes.

alternatives.description: Use a different API specification or code generation tool other than Swagger/OpenAPI annotations.
pros: Potentially more flexibility depending on the tool.
May better fit specific project needs.
cons: Less community support and tooling compared to Swagger/OpenAPI.
May require additional learning and integration effort.
Uncertain compatibility with existing codebase.

template_adherence.title: CLI Dependencies and Launching
template_adherence.context: There are multiple ways a user might want to use Konduit Serving to serve a model. For the sake of this ADR, I'll refer to two use cases as: 1. Immediate deployment case: "Deploy a server for this pipeline right now on this machine via the CLI" 2. Deployment artifact case: "Create an artifact (JAR, docker image, etc) for deployment somewhere else" The ADR 0005-Packaging_System_Design.md dealt with the "create deployment artifact" (2) case above. However, the build system in its current form it does well not serve the needs of the immediate deployment use case particularly well, mainly due to its uber-jar design. This causes a few usability problems: 1. Deploying a pipeline with different modules (dl4j vs. samediff vs. TF, or CPU vs. GPU) requires building an uber-jar 2. Uber-jar builds can take a long time (30-120+ seconds, plus download time) 3. Either we always rebuild (slow launches) or we have an uber-JAR cache (potentially lots of unnecessary disk space used) The old API CLI dependency/launching approach for this use case also had/has the following problems: 1. Requiring the user to build a JAR ahead of time and manually include the modules they need 2. Not being able to launch (for example) both CPU and GPU servers simultaneously without rebuilding the whole Konduit Serving uber-jar in between launching the different servers For the CLI-based "deploy right now" use case, an alternative is proposed.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support immediate deployment use case efficiently via CLI
- Avoid slow uber-jar builds and large disk usage
- Support multiple device profiles (CPU, GPU) and simultaneous launches
- Workaround command line length limits on Windows
- Provide a user-friendly, fast, and flexible deployment experience
- Compatibility with existing build tools (Gradle)
- Consider offline/no network deployment scenarios
template_adherence.decision: For the "immediate deployment via CLI" scenario, we will not create an uber-jar; instead, we will use the Konduit Serving build tool to work out the dependencies we need, download them, and return a list of all dependencies (i.e., a list of JAR file paths) that the Konduit Serving server will be launched with. Due to command line length constraints on Windows, we will use a small manifest JAR containing the absolute paths of all dependencies, passed via the `-classpath` argument during launch. This approach is similar to how IntelliJ handles launching with many dependencies. We will have a static CLI JAR without modules, and introduce "device profiles" to allow users to select CPU, CUDA, or other targets. On first run, device profiles are auto-created based on hardware detection, with a default profile set. Users can override the profile at launch time. This design avoids rebuilding uber-jars, supports multiple device profiles, and improves launch speed and usability.
template_adherence.consequences:
Advantages:
- Simple two-command workflow from no installation to server launch
- Faster launches without uber-jar builds
- Reduced disk space usage
- Supports mixing CPU and GPU deployments on one system
- No need to distribute pre-built binaries
- Potential adaptability to OSGi in future

Disadvantages:
- Reliance on JARs in Gradle/Maven caches, which might cause issues if server runs during install
- Dependency on build tool and Gradle, which may be problematic for offline or space-restricted deployments
- Offline deployments may require bundling Gradle and using offline mode
- Uber-jar style deployments remain an option for offline scenarios

alternatives.description: Continue using uber-jar builds for immediate deployment.
pros: Simple and well-understood approach
Single JAR file for deployment
cons: Slow build times (30-120+ seconds)
Large disk space usage due to redundant dependencies
Inflexible for multiple device profiles
Not user-friendly for immediate deployment

alternatives.description: Require users to build JARs manually with needed modules.
pros: Gives users control over dependencies
No changes to build system needed
cons: User burden is high
Error-prone and inconvenient
Does not support simultaneous CPU/GPU launches without rebuilds

alternatives.description: Use assembly-JAR style embedding original dependency JARs instead of uber-jar.
pros: Potentially smaller than uber-jar
May allow more flexible dependency management
cons: Not currently implemented
Uncertain compatibility with deployment scenarios
May add complexity
