template_adherence.title: [ADR-0002] P3 Archive elastic search integration
template_adherence.context: The previous Greenpeace website application (P3) will be decommissioned soon (~end of March 2020). There is a need to enable access to this content by archiving it and allowing searching that archive from the P4 websites. The content has already been archived to http://web.archive.org/, which has search functionality, but the archive API returns only 100 results per search request and takes almost 10 seconds. Also, it has one collection for all NROs, while the P3 data is under one archive collection. Searching archive content returns results for all P3 NRO data with only 100 records at a time.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Tight timeline: P3 will be decommissioned at the end of March (Akamai) and the Datacenter will be closed at the end of May.
- Ensuring data is indexed in a persistent way.
- Ensuring it doesn’t slow down P4 search.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use ElasticSearch to index the minimum dataset to have results displayed on P4 search, linking results to the Internet Archive for actual content. Exporting P3 data into XML files by crawling P3 sites and scraping required data (third option) is chosen as the easiest option compared to fetching data from the P3 database or getting post index from the Archive team.
template_adherence.consequences: By choosing to crawl and scrape P3 data for export, the team can meet the tight timeline and have a persistent, performant search index for P4 without relying on slow or limited archive API responses. However, this approach may require maintenance of the scraping process and handling potential data inconsistencies from scraping.

alternatives.description: Get post index from Archive team.
pros: Potentially direct access to indexed data.
cons: No response from archive team, so uncertain availability.

alternatives.description: Retrieve data from P3 database.
pros: Direct access to original data source.
cons: P3 database structure is unclear.
Database access is restricted (VPN only).

pros: Easiest option compared to fetching from database.
Does not rely on archive team response.
cons: Requires building and maintaining a scraper.
Potential issues with data completeness or accuracy.

template_adherence.title: [ADR-0004] Switch to Monorepo
template_adherence.context:
The top-level choice is to organize the code as a "monorepo" or leave as we currently have it (polyrepo). Monorepo means we put all pieces into one big repo. Polyrepo means we put each piece in its own repo.

All the code that we're developing is for one organization's offerings, and not for the general public. Our theme and plugins are highly opinionated in terms of UI, but also functionality, to meet the needs of the organization. We also don’t depend on external stakeholders or end users when we do releases or make breaking changes.

Planet4 is considered a single "project" because currently the main 5 repositories are quite dependent on each other: Master Theme, Blocks Plugin, EN Forms plugin, Medialibrary plugin, Styleguide. We even disable native blocks for the editors, so actually it's a quite opinionated Wordpress setup.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to organize application code repositories effectively.
- Desire to unify versioning and reduce build times.
- Consideration of dependencies and usage by other organizations.
- The current high dependency among repositories.
- The impact on external usage and modularity.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: Deprecate EN block & Media library plugins. Instead integrate those into the main blocks plugin and master theme respectively. For the time being we will continue with these two main repositories.

This decision balances the benefits of a monorepo approach (unified versioning, reduced build time, deduplication) with the current organizational needs and dependencies.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Unified versioning.
- Reduced build times due to fewer composer/npm calls and git checkouts.
- Deduplication of shared code and configuration.

Negative:
- More difficult for other organizations to use individual plugins or blocks.
- Potential mitigation needed (e.g., via composer) to address external usage concerns.

alternatives.description: Switch to one repo for theme and plugins (Monorepo)
pros: Versioning would be unified.
Merging repos would reduce build time: less composer calls, less npm calls, git checkouts, etc.
Could deduplicate shared code and configuration.
cons: Makes it more difficult for other organizations to use our plugins, blocks, etc.

alternatives.description: Keep using different repos for each one of them (Polyrepo)
pros: Maintains modularity and separation of concerns.
Easier for external organizations to use individual plugins or blocks.
cons: Versioning is not unified.
Build times may be longer due to multiple repos.
Potential duplication of shared code and configuration.

template_adherence.title: Define scope for deployment environments
template_adherence.context:
Currently it’s not clear what’s the difference between Develop and Staging environment. Both are part of a new version deployment cycle to production.

Before Continuous Delivery (CD) these 3 environments were semantically used to represent the 3 different branches. Production > master, Staging > release/vx.x, Develop > develop. Now this distinction no longer makes sense, since we only have one branch (master). We use the test instances (in practice these are Develop environments) to deploy the feature branches, for testing and UAT.

The NROs that have dev teams also use their Develop environments for testing new plugin versions or specific branches. In order to deploy to Production they need to commit to the develop branch first (or trigger the Develop pipeline), although this branch has different versions of dependencies from master. This can be confusing. There is also no branch that reflects the Staging environment, since the release branches in the deployment repos are ephemeral and deleted during the deployment cycle.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to clarify the distinction and scope of deployment environments (Develop, Staging, Production).
- Simplify and speed up the Continuous Delivery (CD) process.
- Reduce confusion caused by branching and environment mismatches.
- Maintain testing quality and environment stability.
- Consider impact on NRO Develop sites and deployment pipelines.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to implement option one: re-define the scope and exclude the Develop environment from the release deployment pipelines. This redefinition clarifies the roles of Develop, Staging, and Production environments and adapts the CI/CD pipelines accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include lifting confusion on NRO-level deployments, significantly faster full version deployment to Production on over 40 NROs, simplification of the CD process, and alignment of branching models across repositories.

Negative consequences include the risk that some NRO Develop sites may lag if not regularly updated, which can be mitigated by triggering updates regularly.

alternatives.description: Re-define the three environments and adapt CI/CD pipelines to reflect that: Develop as sandboxes for unmerged code, Staging as pre-production matching Production, and Production as live environment.
pros: Lifts confusion on NRO-level deployments.
Speeds up full version deployment to Production.
Simplifies the CD process.
Aligns branching model with application repositories.
cons: Some NRO Develop sites may lag if not updated regularly.

alternatives.description: Keep things as they are, maintaining the current environment definitions and deployment process.
pros: Provides an extra layer of testing if properly considered.
cons: Complicates management when Develop sites need to point to different branches.

template_adherence.title: [ADR-0020] Form Builder data retention policy
template_adherence.context: Most of the Form types (as identified) are already integrating into external systems. But not all of them do (eg. Quiz). For the ones that don’t we need to identify what’s a reasonable policy for NRO admins to have the time to decide the extent of data they want to keep but also have the time to export them. But even for the forms that send data to other systems (eg. Petitions) we need a failsafe to make sure data is actually sent over before deletion. At the same time we should aim for respecting GDPR requirements for the period of time these data remain on websites’ databases.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Avoid storing supporters’ personal data into the websites’ databases; ensure data is stored in relevant external systems where applicable; respect GDPR requirements; provide NRO admins time to export data; ensure failsafe for data sent to external systems before deletion.
template_adherence.decision: Enforce a 90 days retention policy where all submission entries will be automatically deleted after this period. NRO admins are responsible for exporting any submission data not synced to external systems. Integrate with Wordpress export/delete tools to handle supporter requests for data deletion or export. Minimize personal data footprint by not storing IP addresses on form submissions.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Ensures compliance with GDPR, reduces personal data stored on websites, provides clear retention policy, and supports data export/deletion requests. Negative: Requires NRO admins to manage exports for unsynced data; potential risk if data is not properly synced before deletion.

Potential legal and reputational risks.

alternatives.description: Shorter or longer retention periods (e.g., 30 days or 1 year).
pros: Flexibility to adjust retention based on organizational needs.

template_adherence.title: 2. Use aws-eks terraform module
template_adherence.context: A fully configured EKS cluster requires many AWS resources and a lot of configuration. Defining each resource in our own Terraform module maximises flexibility but also requires a significant level of effort. We could instead make use of the existing Terraform registry EKS module to optimise for speed of delivery.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but can be inferred from the context and decision sections: need for speed of delivery, flexibility, ease of configuration, and potential future maintainability concerns.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt the existing Terraform registry EKS module.
template_adherence.consequences:
A fully configured EKS cluster can be defined quickly and easily, as many module defaults will be fine for our purposes for the foreseeable future.

The EKS module has comprehensive support for many of the options for EKS cluster config (e.g. worker node types). This will allow us to make changes more easily, and to experiment with different options quickly.

It is possible that we will in future discover some areas of the module that don't work for our needs. Potential options in that instance include contributing to the module, forking it, or moving to our own module (likely with large chunks of code taken from the EKS module).

We must be careful to avoid errors and issues that may be caused by the module's default use of a terraform `kubernetes` provider that is configured by AWS resource outputs. The behaviour of providers derived from other providers' resources is non-deterministic and can lead to intermittent and unpredictable issues - see the warning callout in the Kubernetes provider docs. The approach for handling this limitation will be covered in a subsequent ADR.

alternatives.description: Define each AWS resource in our own Terraform module to maximize flexibility.
pros: Maximizes flexibility and control over configuration.
cons: Requires significant effort and time to configure all resources.
Slower delivery compared to using an existing module.

alternatives.description: Use the existing Terraform registry EKS module.
pros: Optimizes for speed of delivery.
Provides comprehensive support for many EKS cluster configuration options.
Allows easier changes and experimentation.
cons: Potential future limitations if the module does not meet all needs.
Risk of issues due to module's default use of terraform `kubernetes` provider configured by AWS resource outputs.

template_adherence.title: 3. Split terraform state into separate AWS cluster and Kubernetes resource phases
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to handle Terraform providers (`aws` and `kubernetes`) correctly given their dependencies and the limitations of Terraform's plan graph.
The requirement to avoid non-deterministic behavior and race conditions when configuring the `kubernetes` provider.
The desire to separate concerns between cluster infrastructure and in-cluster resources.
The need to prevent issues during cluster teardown related to AWS load balancers not managed by Terraform.
The goal to maintain flexibility for future changes in cluster provisioning.
template_adherence.decision:
Split Terraform resources into two separate states and phases:

1. cluster-infrastructure - EKS cluster and associated AWS resources. No `kubernetes` provider should be defined.
2. cluster-services - Kubernetes resources and in-cluster configuration, with the `kubernetes` provider configured via TF remote state after `cluster-infrastructure` has been applied. No `aws` provider should be defined unless needed for AWS data sources in k8s resources.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The EKS module's `manage_aws_auth` input variable must be set to `false` to prevent the module from creating aws auth `ConfigMap` objects.
- Prevents potential issues when tearing down an EKS cluster with deployed workloads due to Terraform not managing AWS load balancers created by k8s resources.
- Introduces a clear boundary and separation of concerns between k8s cluster provisioning and in-cluster resources and configuration.
- Provides a path to switch from an EKS cluster to any other Kubernetes cluster and supports future use cases beyond GOV.UK-specific configurations.

template_adherence.title: 4. Use AWS Load Balancer Controller for edge traffic services
template_adherence.context: We require a method of managing and directing external internet traffic into the cluster. Kubernetes provides several options for handling inbound traffic. We do not want to expose the cluster directly to the internet, and so require an AWS load balancer in front of the cluster. The load balancer must support TLS termination and integration with our DNS provider (AWS Route 53). Historically Kubernetes has supported provisioning of ALBs and NLBs for Service resources of type=LoadBalancer via the in-tree (built-in) AWS cloud provider, with out-of-tree controllers required for Ingress resources. Built-in cloud providers are now considered deprecated overall, in favour of out-of-tree providers, so an Ingress Controller with support for Service resources is required. The primary and recommended ingress controller for AWS/EKS is the AWS Load Balancer Controller, which can provision and manage ALBs for Ingress resources and NLBs for Service resources. We must also consider how Kubernetes edge services and AWS load balancers will interact with the existing GOV.UK Router service, as there is significant overlap in their functionality and responsibilities. This will require further investigation and likely experimentation, and so that end we should ensure that we're able to use both Ingress and Service Kubernetes resources so that we have the flexibility to support a wide range of use cases in the immediate term - L4 & L7 traffic, name-based routing, HTTP->HTTPS redirection, etc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage and direct external internet traffic into the cluster securely.
- Avoid exposing the cluster directly to the internet.
- Requirement for AWS load balancer with TLS termination and DNS integration.
- Deprecation of built-in AWS cloud provider in Kubernetes, favoring out-of-tree providers.
- Need for flexibility to support various use cases (L4 & L7 traffic, name-based routing, HTTP->HTTPS redirection).
- Integration considerations with existing GOV.UK Router service.

template_adherence.title: 5. Use EKS managed node groups
template_adherence.context: EKS supports three different types of EKS worker node groups: managed, self-managed, and Fargate. These options can be combined within a single cluster. Managed and self-managed node groups are EC2 instances within autoscaling groups, while Fargate is a managed service with fewer configuration options but less management overhead. Cluster upgrades are frequent due to Kubernetes' 4-month release cycle, requiring a robust node upgrade process. Requirements for worker nodes are not fully known, so flexibility is important. Managed and self-managed node groups have equivalent functional capabilities, but Fargate has limitations. The main difference between managed and self-managed node groups is the upgrade process, with managed node groups handling upgrades automatically.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for a robust and mature node upgrade process due to frequent Kubernetes upgrades, the importance of maintaining flexibility given unknown requirements, and the functional equivalence of managed and self-managed node groups versus the limitations of Fargate. Also, the desire to avoid handling low-level details and complexity of rolling out node updates manually.
template_adherence.decision: Use managed node groups for EKS worker nodes.
template_adherence.consequences: Retain maximum flexibility over node configuration without managing the complexity of rolling out node updates. Choosing managed node groups does not preclude future use of self-managed node groups or Fargate, which can be added later without discarding work on managed node groups.

alternatives.description: Use self-managed node groups.
pros: Full control over node configuration and upgrade process.
cons: Requires manual orchestration of node upgrades, increasing complexity and risk.

alternatives.description: Use Fargate for worker nodes.
pros: Less management overhead due to being a managed service.
cons: Limited configuration options and functional limitations such as inability to run DaemonSets, specify alternative CNI providers, or attach persistent EBS volumes.

template_adherence.title: 6. Use Helm for application package management
template_adherence.context:
We require something more sophisticated than handcrafted YAML when defining an application's Kubernetes resources, to ensure that applications can be defined once, and deployed to multiple targets with differing configurations. At a high level, we require a means to define an application's Kubernetes resources as an installable package, with configuration options passed in at deploy time.

There are many options for packaging Kubernetes applictions, including but not limited to:

- [Helm](https://helm.sh)
- [Terraform](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/kubernetes/latest/docs)
- [Kustomize](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/kustomization/)
- [Pulumi](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/intro/cloud-providers/kubernetes/#pulumi-kubernetes-provider)
- [Skaffold](https://skaffold.dev)

While we are currently using Terraform for AWS infrastructure management, we should maintain a strict separation of concerns between managing cloud infrastructure and the software applications that run on top; using a single tool for both will inevitably lead to blurred lines between the two. In addition, [Terraform's kubernetes support is still quite new](https://www.hashicorp.com/blog/beta-support-for-crds-in-the-terraform-provider-for-kubernetes), and can lag behind Kubernetes itself.

While Kustomize has been adopted into the main Kubernetes project, that decision has [not been without controversy](https://goteleport.com/blog/kubernetes-kustomize-kep-kerfuffle/). Kustomize has also not yet seen wide adoption within the industry, and offers little beyond the basic functions of interpolating values into YAML files.

Helm by comparison has widespread industry adoption, a [large number of existing packages](https://artifacthub.io/packages/search), and widespread support in the wider devops and development ecosystem (e.g. [Github Actions](https://github.com/helm/chart-releaser-action), [CircleCI Orb](https://circleci.com/developer/orbs/orb/circleci/helm), [VS Code extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-kubernetes-tools.vscode-kubernetes-tools), [Terraform provider](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/helm/latest/docs)).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a sophisticated, reusable, and configurable packaging solution for Kubernetes applications.
- Desire to separate concerns between infrastructure management and application deployment.
- Consideration of maturity and adoption of tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem.
- Industry adoption and ecosystem support for the packaging tool.
- Avoiding blurred lines between infrastructure and application management.
- Awareness of limitations and controversies around alternative tools.
template_adherence.decision: Use Helm v3+ for application package management.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Ability to leverage existing Helm charts for supporting tools and services such as AWS Load Balancer Controller, Prometheus + Grafana, and Fluentd.
- Potential future introduction of a Helm chart repository.
- Helm provides release history and rollback capabilities, with caution advised when rolling back applications dependent on database migrations.
- Helm charts are versioned separately from application versions, requiring clear communication to avoid confusion.
- Helm uses Go templates in YAML, which requires awareness of YAML idiosyncrasies when authoring charts.
- Adoption of Helm does not preclude the use of other tools like Kustomize or Skaffold by development teams.

template_adherence.title: 7. Use fluentbit, elasticsearch and kibana for application logs
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses the need for application containers to output logs as stdout/stderr streams, which are then forwarded to a centralized log store. It outlines two approaches for log collection in Kubernetes: sidecar containers or DaemonSet agents. It emphasizes the need for logging as a service enabled by default, requiring metadata annotation for logs. Fluentbit and fluentd are identified as common logging agents, with fluentbit preferred for its lightweight and performance benefits. For log storage and UI, Elasticsearch and Kibana are chosen due to their ecosystem support. The ADR also notes the possibility of future integration with a central log store and the need for authentication and authorization for Kibana access.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for a logging service enabled by default for all containers, the requirement for logs to be searchable and annotated with Kubernetes metadata, the performance and plugin ecosystem trade-offs between fluentbit and fluentd, and the need for a browser-based UI for log searching and filtering. Additionally, considerations include ease of deployment, integration with AWS services, and security for Kibana access.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a fluentbit DaemonSet with AWS Elasticsearch Service for application logs.
template_adherence.consequences: Using fluentbit provides a lightweight and fast logging agent with Kubernetes support, though with a smaller plugin ecosystem. Fluentbit and fluentd are largely interchangeable, allowing flexibility. Deployment is simplified via the official Helm chart. AWS Elasticsearch Service offers both Elasticsearch and Kibana. Kibana access requires secure authentication and authorization, potentially using AWS SSO or Cognito. This ADR focuses on application-level logging, excluding cluster control plane or node logs, which will be addressed separately.

template_adherence.title: 10. Use Dex IdP for user web auth
template_adherence.context:
We want to implement user authentication on the monitoring stack's web applications (Grafana, Prometheus, Alertmanager).

We also want to use Github as the identity provider (IdP), as that provides a means for us to control access based on GDS Github organisation and team membership; the alternative option, GSuite, does not currently have the granular role/group structure that we would require to effectively control access, and introducing that group structure would be out of scope for this project, and would likely replicate the Github group/team structure that currently exists.

Grafana supports many authentication methods, including [Github OAuth2](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/auth/github/) and [OIDC (via generic OAuth2)](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/auth/generic-oauth/).

Prometheus and Alertmanager do not support any form of web-based user authentication, so this must be handled via a proxy or load balancer in front of the application.

We are currently using ALBs in front of Prometheus and Alertmanager, via the [AWS Load Balancer Controller](0004-use-aws-load-balancer-controller-for-edge-traffic-services.md), which supports [authentication via AWS Cognito or OIDC-compliant identity providers](https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/aws-load-balancer-controller/v2.3/guide/ingress/annotations/#authentication).

Github as an IdP does not support OIDC, only OAuth2, so cannot be used with ALB auth. AWS Cognito [does not support OAuth2, only OIDC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html), so cannot be used with Github as an IdP.

ArgoCD, our current CD tool, also [implements authentication via OIDC](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/user-management/#existing-oidc-provider), and [includes an OIDC-compliant identity broker](https://argoproj.github.io/argo-workflows/argo-server-sso-argocd/), [Dex](https://dexidp.io).

In summary, OIDC is the only auth protocol supported universally by both our current web-based UIs that support authentication internally, and by ALBs for apps that do not. Github however does not provide an OIDC-compliant IdP.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for user authentication on monitoring stack web applications.
- Desire to use Github as the identity provider for access control based on organisation and team membership.
- Limitations of alternative IdPs like GSuite lacking granular group structures.
- Compatibility requirements: Grafana supports Github OAuth2 and OIDC; Prometheus and Alertmanager require proxy-based auth.
- AWS ALB supports authentication via AWS Cognito or OIDC-compliant IdPs.
- Github supports OAuth2 but not OIDC; AWS Cognito supports OIDC but not OAuth2.
- ArgoCD uses OIDC and includes Dex as an OIDC-compliant identity broker.
- Need for a universal auth protocol supported by all components (OIDC).
- Security and availability considerations for the chosen solution.
template_adherence.decision: Use Dex as an SSO service and identity provider for all web-based user authentication for user-facing web-based cluster services such as monitoring and CI/CD tools. Dex will act as a bridge to the underlying identity provider (Github) and should not be used for other purposes like AWS or Kubernetes authentication.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Establishes a single signon (SSO) service and consistent identity provider for all user-facing platform UIs.
- Provides a single point of integration with the underlying identity provider, simplifying future changes.
- Dex is currently deployed as part of Argo; it should be deployed as a standalone Helm chart for shared platform service use.
- Dex becomes a single point of failure and a potential attack target, requiring high availability, security, and penetration testing coverage.

alternatives.description: Use Github OAuth2 directly for authentication where supported.
pros: Direct integration with Github, the chosen identity provider.
Simpler setup for components supporting Github OAuth2.
cons: Not supported by all components (e.g., Prometheus, Alertmanager).
Incompatible with AWS ALB authentication which requires OIDC.
Lacks a unified authentication approach across all services.

alternatives.description: Use AWS Cognito as the identity provider.
pros: Supported by AWS ALB for authentication.
Provides OIDC-compliant identity provider capabilities.
cons: Does not support OAuth2, incompatible with Github OAuth2.
Would require migration or duplication of user identities from Github.
Adds complexity and potential duplication of identity management.

alternatives.description: Use GSuite as the identity provider.
pros: Potentially supports OIDC.
May integrate with existing Google accounts.
cons: Lacks granular group/role structures needed for access control.
Out of scope to introduce required group structures.
Would replicate existing Github team structures, adding complexity.

template_adherence.title: use event sourcing
template_adherence.context: The aim of the publishing platform project is to simplify GOV.UK's technical architecture and make it easier to iterate quickly. We plan to build new features to support a write api and shared workflow features. One of the sources of complexity in the current architecture is that state is distributed across many microservices and there's no way to verify whether the overall system is in a valid state. This leads to insidious bugs such as this one which are hard to debug. We built a prototype to investigate whether an event sourcing approach might work for us, and felt that the pattern provides a number of benefits. Firstly it gives us an audit trail out of the box, a feature which we've hoped to have for some time. Secondly, it will make it easier to respond to changing requirements because we can use the event log to modify or build new derived representations at any point in time. Lastly it addresses the issue of data consistency across the platform by providing a single point of truth against which other systems can be validated or potentially rebuilt from scratch. We also have a requirement that some data is updated synchronously when making calls to the publishing API. This synchronously updated data will need to be held within the same database as the publishing API so that we can guarantee consistency. Other data (for example rummager, content store) can be held in a separate systems and updated asynchronously.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need to simplify the technical architecture, enable quick iteration, support new features like a write API and shared workflow, address complexity from distributed state, provide an audit trail, enable easier response to changing requirements, ensure data consistency with a single point of truth, and balance synchronous and asynchronous data updates for consistency and performance.
template_adherence.decision: We'll adopt the event sourcing pattern for the publishing api. All operations which may mutate the state of the publishing platform should be logged as an event in the publishing API. The publishing API will store some derived representations locally in its own database and update them synchronously with the logging of the event, within a database transaction. Other derived representations will be updated asynchronously, e.g., content store and rummager.
template_adherence.consequences: Since this is a pattern which we don't have much experience of, we'll need to be open to learning and reviewing our approach as we go forward. In particular the choices around what data is updated synchronously/asynchronously should be considered carefully to balance the trade-off between speed of api calls and the value of consistent reads to api clients. There's some ideas around replaying of the event log to rebuild derived systems but until we have a concrete use-case for this there's no point in speculating about the implementation.

template_adherence.title: Resolve consistency and uniqueness in content
template_adherence.context: Publishing API has adopted the open/closed principle where the domain model is based around a central ContentItem model, where there are numerous entities that store data related to the ContentItem - however the ContentItem does not have knowledge about them. Over time this data structure revealed a number of problems to developers and users of the Publishing API, such as difficulty in maintaining uniqueness constraints, long verbose queries, slow performing queries, and large amounts of code to resolve these problems.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need to maintain uniqueness constraints effectively, improve query performance and simplicity, reduce code complexity, and adhere to or reconsider the open/closed principle in the domain model design.
template_adherence.decision: Among several options considered, Option 2 (merging user_facing_version, locale, base_path, and state into ContentItem table) was accepted despite breaking from the open/closed principle, due to the complexity cost of maintaining the principle. Option 3 (splitting ContentItems into Document and Edition models) and Option 5 (specifying ContentStore directly in the database) were also accepted. Other options were rejected or delayed.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision leads to a more complex ContentItem model but aims to keep models thin by avoiding logic in the model layer. It simplifies uniqueness constraints and query interfaces but may risk creating a 'god' model. Some options were rejected to avoid unnecessary complexity or because they were not current concerns.

alternatives.description: Merge user_facing_version and locale into ContentItem table to set a single uniqueness constraint.
pros: Allows setting a single uniqueness constraint.
Simplifies concurrency error handling.
cons: Rejected in favor of Option 2 which supersedes it.

alternatives.description: Merge user_facing_version, locale, base_path, and state into ContentItem table.
pros: Allows multiple uniqueness constraints.
Simplifies uniqueness management.
cons: Breaks from open/closed principle.
May lead to a 'god' model.

alternatives.description: Split ContentItems into Document and Edition models.
pros: Simple means to lock requests for concurrency.
Simpler interface to look up draft or live content.
Clarifies distinctions between translations.
cons: Uncertainty about naming.
Not all content fits 'document' concept.

alternatives.description: Split ContentItem model into two separate models focusing on uniqueness and content respectively.
pros: Potential separation of concerns.
cons: Rejected due to unclear responsibility division.
Challenging abstraction to explain.

alternatives.description: Specify ContentStore directly in the database rather than as a byproduct of state value.
pros: Needed for unique index between base_path and state in PostgreSQL.
cons: Initially delayed for further investigation.

alternatives.description: Store state history as a collection rather than a single field.
pros: Could support workflow history and more states.
cons: Rejected as not a current concern.

alternatives.description: Take a location centric approach to storing base_path values for ContentItems.
pros: Could support storing other items like redirects requiring base_path.
cons: Rejected due to added complexity without clear benefits.
Not currently a concern.

template_adherence.title: 3. New annotation removal stage present in all webapi pipelines
template_adherence.context:
When referencing external files there are certain cases where AMF inlines the parsed content without creating a links (this is because the targeted elements are not present in the references of the base unit).
For these cases, when a emitting an unresolved model these references are being emitted inlined.
template_adherence.decision:
In order to avoid emitting these references inlined for an unresolved model, we must make use of annotation to save the original reference.
When saving this reference, we must make sure that if the model is resolved this annotation is no longer present so that the emitter does not render references for a flattened model.
This leads to the creation of a new resolution stage that removes specific annotations from the model that must not be present in a resolved base unit.
template_adherence.consequences:
References can be emitted when receiving an unresolved model with inlined content.
This stage iterates over the whole model removing specific annotations which can lead to more processing, however performance tests have been made showing that this processing is insignificant.

template_adherence.title: 6. Message headers schema
template_adherence.context:
Async Api 2.0 spec details that message headers property must be a Schema Object in which his properties will be the headers for that message.
AMF currently is parsing that object as the schema of a parameter object. This is confusing and semantically incorrect, because that property represents a set of parameters, not just one
template_adherence.decision:
Create a new field to the Message model, similar to the query string property of Raml 1.0 operations, that will contains the Schema Object. Any user looking at the model, will be able to read that schema as a list of headers based on the field in which is contained:
####ApiContract:HeaderSchema

The header example property of the message will be validated against that schema.
template_adherence.consequences:
We will start to model the headers as properties of the Schema Object. Eventually, those properties should be transformed into headers (maybe in resolution time). The problem is that the spec does not clarify any other restriction over the Schema, regarding the object type, so technically a user could write complex constraints like allOf, anyOf, oneOf, etc
The spec should detail that the schema can only have properties and not only complex constraint, or specify how the transduction should be done in those cases.

template_adherence.title: 8. Included JSON Schemas domain element merging
template_adherence.context: APIMF-2622 reports a StackOverflowError in Domain Element Merging when merging the same included recursive JSON Schema in a trait/resource type and an operation/endpoint. The problem arises because JSON Schemas are inlined, producing different in-memory Shape objects for the same included schema, and the resolution step ordering causes recursion detection to happen after merging, leading to errors.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to prevent StackOverflowError caused by recursive merging of JSON Schemas, the inlining nature of JSON Schemas producing different in-memory objects, and the resolution step ordering that delays recursion detection until after merging.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to skip merging not only equal in-memory objects but also objects that have the `SchemaIsJsonSchema` annotation and the same `ExternalSourceElementModel.ReferenceId` field. This involves creating a new annotation `ReferenceId` for Data Nodes, maintaining a map from emitted YNodes to ReferenceIds, and passing this information to the JSON Schema parser via the WebApiContext to create the necessary fields and annotations for merging checks.
template_adherence.consequences: The fix addresses the specific corner case causing the StackOverflowError but introduces technical debt. Other corner cases involving inlined schemas or nested recursive nodes require additional ad-hoc fixes, potentially increasing debt. A more robust refactoring of Domain Element Merging might be preferable in the future.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative is to not implement the ReferenceId annotation and mapping, which would leave the StackOverflowError unresolved.
pros: No additional technical debt introduced.
Simpler implementation without added complexity.
cons: StackOverflowError persists in recursive JSON Schema merging.
No solution to the problem described.

template_adherence.title: 10. Annotation types
template_adherence.context:
When AMF builds a model from a content, it must justify from where each node and property came from, so the users can track and know for sure the origin of the values. This source map information is fundamental for editing features.

In a parsed API, the elements declared in the source document have their corresponding annotations (think of `LexicalInformation` or `SourceNode`) in the final model, but some elements in the AMF model are not explicitly declared. Moreover, some of this not-declared elements are fields we can easily infer from the source document (like the name of an operation) while others have no real counterpart in the source document.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need to track the origin of each node and property in the AMF model to support source mapping and editing features.
Some elements are explicitly declared in the source document, others are inferred or generated.
The model must distinguish between inferred, virtual, and synthesized elements to properly represent their origin and traversal behavior.
template_adherence.decision:
Add three annotation types to make every object or field traceable to its origin:
- `Annotations.inferred()` for fields inferred from the source document but not explicitly declared.
- `Annotations.virtual()` for objects generated based on document elements but without specific declarations.
- `Annotations.synthesized()` for fields and values entirely generated, with no counterpart in the source document.
This classification supports accurate source mapping and model traversal behavior.
template_adherence.consequences:
The decision has no immediate impact.
It clarifies the traceability of model elements to their source or generation status.
It enables better editing and tracking features by distinguishing element origins.

pros: N/A
cons: N/A

template_adherence.title: Array Datatypes Design
template_adherence.context:
The current data model does not directly provide for devices which provide array data. Small fixed-length arrays may be handled by defining multiple device resources - one for each element - and aggregating them via a resource command. Other array data may be passed using the Binary type. Neither of these approaches is ideal: the binary data is opaque and any service processing it would need specific knowledge to do so, and aggregation presents the device service implementation with a multiple-read request that could in many cases be better handled by a single request.

This design adds arrays of primitives to the range of supported types in EdgeX. It comprises an extension of the DeviceProfile model, and an update to the definition of Reading.
template_adherence.decision:
The permitted values of the `Type` field in `PropertyValue` are extended to include:
"BoolArray", "Uint8Array", "Uint16Array", "Uint32Array", "Uint64Array", "Int8Array", Int16Array", "Int32Array", "Int64Array", "Float32Array", "Float64Array"

In the API (v1 and v2), `Reading.Value` is a string representation of the data. If this is maintained, the representation for Array types will follow the JSON array syntax, ie `["value1", "value2", ...]`
template_adherence.consequences:
Any service which processes Readings will need to be reworked to account for the new Reading type.

Device Service considerations

The API used for interfacing between device SDKs and devices service implementations contains a local representation of reading values. This will need to be updated in line with the changes outlined here. For C, this will involve an extension of the existing union type. For Go, additional fields may be added to the `CommandValue` structure.

Processing of numeric data in the device service, ie `offset`, `scale` etc will not be applied to the values in an array.

template_adherence.title: Service Self Config Init & Config Seed Removal
template_adherence.context:
Since its debut, EdgeX has had a configuration seed service (config-seed) that, on start of EdgeX, deposits configuration for all the services into Consul (our configuration/registry service). For development purposes, or on resource constrained platforms, EdgeX can be run without Consul with services simply reading configuration from the filesystem.

While this process has nominally worked for several releases of EdgeX, there have always been some issues with this extra initialization process (config-seed), including race conditions during bootstrap, handling of overrides, and the presence of an additional service only for initialization.

The design/architectural proposal is to remove the config-seed service and have each EdgeX microservice self-seed its own configuration on bootstrap.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to remove the config-seed service due to issues like race conditions and complexity.
- Desire for each microservice to self-seed its configuration to simplify startup and reduce confusion.
- Support for environment variable overrides.
- Maintain backward compatibility where possible.
- Minimize impact on development cycles and release schedule.
- Address configuration initialization and command line options handling.
- Consideration of high availability concerns (not addressed in this ADR).
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to remove the config-seed service and have each EdgeX microservice self-seed its own configuration on bootstrap. This includes reading local configuration files and populating the configuration provider (Consul) if needed, supporting environment variable overrides, and adjusting command line options accordingly. The implementation has been done in code branches and partially in SDKs, with plans to remove the config-seed code from the repository.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Docker compose files and main Snap need changes to remove config-seed.
- Config-seed code will be removed from the repository.
- Service-specific environment overrides must be moved to respective services.
- Docker configuration files used for config-seed can be eliminated.
- Documentation must be updated to reflect removal and self-seeding process.
- Removes race condition issues related to config-seed.
- Reduces user confusion about config-seed service behavior.
- Minimal impact on development and release schedules.
- Configuration endpoints must reflect environment variable overrides.
- Docker files and compose files need modification to remove docker profiles and add environment overrides.
- High availability concerns remain unaddressed in this ADR.

alternatives.description: Keep the existing config-seed service as is.
pros: No immediate changes required.
Existing process is familiar to users and developers.
cons: Continued race conditions during service bootstrap.
Additional service adds complexity and confusion.
Overrides handling remains problematic.

alternatives.description: Modify config-seed service to handle overrides and race conditions better.
pros: Retains centralized configuration seeding.
Potentially reduces race conditions with improvements.
cons: Still requires maintaining an extra service.
Complexity remains.
May not fully resolve override issues.

template_adherence.title: Creation and Distribution of Secrets
template_adherence.context: This ADR seeks to clarify and prioritize the secret handling approach taken by EdgeX. EdgeX microservices need a number of secrets to be created and distributed in order to create a functional, secure system. Among these secrets are privileged administrator passwords, service account passwords, and PKI private keys. There is a lack of consistency on how secrets are created and distributed to EdgeX microservices, and when developers need to add new components to the system, it is unclear on what the preferred approach should be. The document assumes a threat model wherein EdgeX services are sandboxed and the host system is trusted, with all services sharing a trust boundary. It also defines terms such as _SECRETSLOC_ and surveys current practices for system-managed and user-managed secrets.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for a consistent and secure approach to secret creation and distribution, avoidance of hard-coded secrets, preference for cryptographic keys over plain-text secrets, support for various runtime environments (Docker, snaps), and the need to align with best practices and threat models. The drivers also consider the limitations of existing implementations and the desire to improve compliance and security posture.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to designate the EdgeX secret store as the system of reference for secrets, preferring creation of secrets inside the secret store when possible. Cryptographic keys are preferred over plain-text secrets when alternatives exist. Hard-coded secrets are prohibited. Four recommended practices for secret distribution are identified: direct consumption from secret store, dynamic injection into environment variables, dynamic injection into container-scoped tmpfs volumes, and distribution via _SECRETSLOC_. The ADR also outlines prohibited practices and platform-specific considerations for Docker, snaps, Docker Swarm, and Kubernetes.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include significant scope added to current and future EdgeX releases to bring implementations into compliance with the ADR. Specific improvements are listed for PKI private keys, Kong certificates, secret store master password, Postgres superuser password, Redis authentication passwords, and Kong authentication tokens. Some components require no changes. The ADR also highlights the need for hardware protection hooks and improved secret management mechanisms.

alternatives.description: Continue with the current inconsistent and partially non-compliant secret management practices.
pros: No immediate development effort required.
Maintains status quo without disruption.
cons: Security risks due to hard-coded secrets and inconsistent handling.
Lack of clarity for developers adding new components.
Non-compliance with best practices and potential vulnerabilities.

alternatives.description: Adopt the recommended practices outlined in the ADR, including using the EdgeX secret store as the system of reference, prohibiting hard-coded secrets, and using the four recommended distribution methods.

Alignment with best practices and threat models.
Facilitates future enhancements and hardware protection integration.

Need for ongoing maintenance and compliance monitoring.

template_adherence.title: Secure Bootstrapping of EdgeX
template_adherence.context: Docker-compose, the tool used by EdgeX to manage its Docker-based stack, lacks support for initialization logic, which is critical for secure microservice communication. The ADR addresses the need for a Docker-based initialization framework to enable secure startup and removal of hard-coded secrets.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a portable, reliable initialization mechanism compatible with docker-compose across multiple OS platforms; requirement to secure microservice communication by bootstrapping secrets and configurations; limitations of existing docker-compose features; desire to avoid fragile sentinel files and complex health check parsing; need for a standardized startup sequencing mechanism.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a stage-gate mechanism using entrypoint scripts and TCP socket semaphores to coordinate startup sequencing and initialization across containers. Introduce a new bootstrap container to inject scripts, manage semaphores, and coordinate initialization. This approach works across Linux, Windows, and MacOS with docker-compose and avoids reliance on removed or unsupported docker-compose features.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive impacts include standardized initialization, reduced fragility, improved security by removing hard-coded secrets, and simplified container management. Drawbacks include added complexity with a new container and expanded responsibilities for entrypoint scripts.

template_adherence.title: Securing access to Consul
template_adherence.context:
This ADR defines the motiviation and approach used to secure access to the Consul component in the EdgeX architecture for security-enabled configurations only. Non-secure configurations continue to use Consul in anonymous read-write mode. As this Consul security feature requires Vault to function, if EDGEX_SECURITY_SECRET_STORE=false and Vault is not present, the legacy behavior (unauthenticated Consul access) will be preserved.

Consul provides several services for the EdgeX architecture including service registry, service health monitoring, and mutable configuration data. Use of these services is optional on a service-by-service basis. Configuration data can affect runtime behavior, so compensating controls must be introduced to mitigate risks from moving configuration to an HTTP-accessible service with mutable state.

Currently, Consul is exposed via unencrypted HTTP in anonymous read/write mode to all processes and EdgeX services on the host machine.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to secure Consul access in security-enabled configurations, the requirement to integrate with Vault for token management, the desire to avoid introducing additional bootstrapping secrets, and the need to maintain compatibility and phased deployment to limit breaking changes.
template_adherence.decision: Consul will be configured with ACL functionality enabled, and each EdgeX service will use a Consul access token to authenticate. Tokens will be requested from the Vault Consul secrets engine. DNS will be disabled as it is unused. The API gateway will proxy Consul service requests, adding the global management token via the X-Consul-Token header. Proxying the Consul UI is problematic and currently unresolved.
template_adherence.consequences: The implementation will deny access to all existing Consul clients initially, requiring phased deployment to limit impact. Phase 1 establishes plumbing with permissive mode; Phase 2 introduces breaking changes with default deny policy and API changes; Phase 3 refines access control with per-service roles and scoped tokens. There are also considerations for token lifetime tied to Vault token lifetime and mitigations for token revocation issues.

alternatives.description: Continue using Consul in anonymous read-write mode without ACLs or Vault integration.
pros: Simpler setup with no additional configuration.
No breaking changes to existing clients.
cons: No security for Consul access, exposing configuration and service registry to unauthorized access.
Does not meet security requirements for security-enabled configurations.

alternatives.description: Use Consul ACLs but manage tokens manually without Vault integration.
pros: Provides access control to Consul.
Avoids dependency on Vault for token management.
cons: Manual token management increases operational complexity and risk.
Does not leverage existing Vault infrastructure for secret management.

template_adherence.title: Use an id and data attributes on the SCRIPT tag for configuration
template_adherence.context: In the context of the need to inject configuration into the tracking consent snippet (PLATUI-775 and PLATUI-649) while not wanting to duplicate knowledge of the platform and tracking consent url structure, delivering a simple, easily testable solution and delivering a solution that works on IE. - delivering a simple, easily testable solution and

- Very small risk that if an insufficiently unique id is chosen, service code that relies on other elements with the same id may break.

id attribute to the SCRIPT tag
data-id attribute on the SCRIPT tag
document.currentScript (not supported on IE)

* The need to improve the operability of tracking consent

Negative Consequences:
* Service developers need to add id="tracking-consent-script-tag" to the SCRIPT tag when integrating.

template_adherence.title: Namespace the gtm.container attribute for tracking consent
template_adherence.context: Our existing guidance for service developers implementing tracking consent asks developers to set the `gtm.container` key in `application.conf` to configure the GTM container used by tracking consent. This configuration key was already used by play-ui in its GTMSnippet component and the intent was by re-using this key, it would be simpler for service developers to integrate if they are already using play-ui to provide their GTM integration. Unfortunately, setting this key in application.conf can break services using play-ui because gtm.container is an implicit feature toggle for GTMSnippet and GTMSnippet is not designed to work locally. It requires configuration keys like gtm.<CONTAINER>.url that are only defined on the MDTP platform environments (via app-config-common). Should tracking-consent-frontend, therefore, use its own gtm.container attribute namespaced inside the tracking-consent-frontend configuration block? For example, `tracking-consent-frontend { gtm.container = "a" }`
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* The need to keep things simple for service developers
* The desire not be constrained by the design decisions made for the existing GTMSnippet
* The need to be able to test the GTM integration and tracking consent banner locally
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "Move", because we want to support testing tracking consent locally.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Service developers do not receive an error when integrating with tracking consent
* Tracking consent can be tested locally
* This decision can be implemented by a simple update to the existing guidance with no further code changes to tracking consent
* No changes are needed for the proposed helpers for play-ui and play-frontend-hmrc
* Tracking consent is not constrained by the design choices made for GTMSnippet

Negative Consequences:
* Services uplifting from GTMSnippet will need to move the gtm.container key into the tracking-consent-frontend configuration block.

pros: No need to change existing configuration keys for services already using gtm.container
cons: Testing tracking consent locally is not supported
Potential for errors when integrating with tracking consent

template_adherence.title: Use data attribute for specifying tracking consent banner language
template_adherence.context:
Tracking consent reads the PLAY_LANG cookie to determine whether to render the banner in Welsh. PLAY_LANG is the cookie used by the Play Framework to persist a user's language preferences. It will be set to 'cy' when a user has selected Welsh using the language toggle in MDTP services using the Play Framework.

Teams are increasingly setting PLAY_LANG to HttpOnly in an attempt to get green ZAP tests, even though there are no known security concerns around keeping PLAY_LANG as a normal cookie. Setting a cookie to HttpOnly makes it unreadable within the client-side Javascript code that renders the tracking consent banner. The result of this is that the banner will not be translated into Welsh for these services.

A related issue is that PLAY_LANG is not set for classic services written in Java, which means a Welsh version of the banner is not currently available for classic services.

It is worth noting that the only other known instance of our reading PLAY_LANG using Javascript is in the assets-frontend timeout dialog. All the new govuk-frontend and hmrc-frontend components use data attributes instead.

Should we remove the reading of PLAY_LANG in tracking consent and accept a data-language attribute instead?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* The need to support classic services
* The time-sensitive nature of this issue. The need to deploy quickly before too many services have integrated, to avoid services having to upgrade a second time.
* The preference for avoiding further changes to tracking consent. This is a non-breaking change.
* The preference for not advising teams to add exemptions to ZAP tests across MDTP
* The preference for consistency in language settings across our frontend components
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "Re-work" because we need to act now and in the medium term we are not in a position to uncouple services' dependency on PLAY_LANG nor add a global exemption for PLAY_LANG into Zap tests. We also agreed that our frontend components should be consistent in their treatment of language until such time as we are able to provide an alternative approach that works for all components.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Classic services or services using other non-Scala or non-Play frameworks can get Welsh translations for the banner
* Services do not need to set any HttpOnly exemptions in their ZAP tests, which may mask other legitimate warnings/errors
* Language setting is consistent with other components e.g. hmrcTimeoutDialog, hmrcReportATechnicalProblem etc

Negative Consequences:
* We will need to make a small change to tracking consent and communicate this change to teams
* Teams will need to upgrade to the latest version of play-ui/play-frontend-hmrc to get language translations
* Teams not using the tracking consent helpers will need to add a data-attribute for the language

alternatives.description: Do nothing
Re-work to use data-language instead of PLAY_LANG

template_adherence.title: Use eslint for linting and formatting javascript
template_adherence.context: We found that without a standardised format our javascript files ended up with different formats in different files or even multiple formats in the same file. We also found that our IDEs had different configurations which meant that using an autoformat tool would give different results when each of us do it.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* We wanted to spend less time doing manual formatting
* We wanted to spend less time undoing autoformatting which had been applied to unchanged lines
* We wanted to see easily which lines had actually changed when reviewing PRs
* We wanted to avoid discussions about individual's preferences for particular
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: ESLint + Airbnb

We decided to use ESLint with Airbnb because the Airbnb approach is [well documented](https://github.com/airbnb/javascript) and adopting this meant we wouldn't have to make each decision ourselves. We decided not to use Prettier as well, there was a discussion about the possibility of conflicting format changes between the two tools - we encountered one of these, it was overcome with config updates.

ESLint is compatible with both Javascript and Typescript projects which made it seem particularly suitable for us as we chose to use Typescript for Tracking Consent but we usually use Javascript.

Each of the current team members use JetBrains IDEs and that has a built-in plugin which supports auto formatting on save, this is also a common feature which most IDEs have.

We decided to add pre-commit and pre-push hooks which ensure that the style rules have been met but do not mutate code. We discussed the option of formatting the code on commit but we felt that this introduced an uncertainty about what we were committing.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive Consequences

* Code style within a file will be consistent
* Files within a project will be consistent with each other
* When widely applied this Javascript/Typescript files between projects will be consistent
* IDE will reformat for us which takes away the need for us to do it ourselves
* Code reviews will focus less on code format and more on the details of the changes made
* Builds will fail if format isn't followed which guarentees consistency

### Negative Consequences

* Builds will fail if format isn't followed which can disrupt focus/workflow (mitigated by pre-commit hooks)

alternatives.description: StandardJS - this is the tool GDS use and we've historically used that on some repos
Prettier - an opinionated code formatter
ESLint - a tool we haven't used before in this team but is widely used and widely supported and is highly customisable
ESLint + Airbnb - using Airbnb's style as a rule set would mean we don't have to decide between the many different configuration options available
ESLint + Prettier + Airbnb - Both ESLint and Prettier have Airbnb setups and can be used simultaniously

template_adherence.title: Make visual regression tests reproducible on jenkins
template_adherence.context:
Jenkins's builds would fail if our visual regression test reference images for classic services were updated from images generated on our local machines. We identified that the issue was because of different available fonts between systems. So we needed a way for our tests for classic services to always have the same fonts available during visual regression tests.

Technical details: Classic Services are not built on top of our libraries, and instead of the GDS Transport font that the tracking consent banner relies on they use a font called Open Sans. A copy of the Open Sans font is provided by classic services, but the Open Sans font is not listed as one of the tracking consent banners preferred fallback fonts. So when someone views a classic service, their browser will attempt to display the banner using Arial, or, if that's unavailable, the browsers default sans-serif font.

On jenkins we've found the browsers used during visual regression tests do not have Arial available, whereas, on our local machines, we will normally either have Arial available or we will have a different default sans-serif font. Which means that jenkins isn't able to recreate the results of reference images created on our local machines, and we aren't able to recreate locally the results of reference images created on jenkins.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have reproducible visual regression tests across different environments (local machines and Jenkins). The problem caused by different fonts available on Jenkins and local machines leading to inconsistent test results. The desire to avoid disabling tests or introducing impractical solutions. Consideration of impact on other tests and practical limitations of Jenkins environment.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen option is option 3: update our classic services fixture to include a copy of the GDS Transport font. This decision was made because option 1 (disabling tests) was undesirable, option 2 (installing Arial font on Jenkins) could impact other tests, option 4 (using the same docker image on Jenkins) was impractical due to Jenkins limitations, and option 5 (adding Open Sans as a fallback font) was outside the scope of current work.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include that visual regression tests will be reproducible regardless of where they are run, as the font used will be consistent. Negative consequences include that test images may not exactly match what a user would see (since users might see Arial or default sans-serif), and that OS or browser text rendering differences could still affect reproducibility, though this is mitigated by using Docker locally.

alternatives.description: Disable visual regression tests to avoid overhead of working around this problem.
pros: Simplifies the testing process by removing problematic tests.
cons: Loses the benefits of visual regression testing, potentially allowing visual bugs to go unnoticed.

alternatives.description: Install the Arial font for browsers used by Jenkins.
pros: Could make Jenkins environment match local machines more closely.
Potentially resolves font mismatch issue directly.
cons: Might impact other tests relying on current browser behavior on Jenkins.
Requires changes to Jenkins environment which may be complex.

alternatives.description: Update our classic services fixture to include a copy of the GDS Transport font.
pros: Ensures consistent font availability across environments.
Does not require changes to Jenkins environment.
Maintains visual regression tests active and reliable.
cons: Test images may not exactly match user experience.
Requires maintenance of font copies in fixtures.

alternatives.description: Get Jenkins to use the same docker image we use locally to run visual regression tests.
pros: Ensures environment parity between local and Jenkins.
Potentially most correct and robust solution.
cons: Impractical due to limitations in how Docker can be used on Jenkins.
May require significant infrastructure changes.

alternatives.description: Add Open Sans as a fallback font for the cookie consent banner.
pros: Could align fonts used in classic services with tracking consent banner.
Might reduce font mismatch issues.
cons: Outside the scope of current work.
Does not directly address Jenkins vs local environment differences.

template_adherence.title: 2. DynamoDB composite primary key design
template_adherence.context:
"[In DynamoDB, tables, items, and attributes are the core components that you work with. A table is a collection of items, and each item is a collection of attributes. DynamoDB uses primary keys to uniquely identify each item in a table and secondary indexes to provide more querying flexibility.](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.CoreComponents.html)"

There are two types of primary key in dynamodb.

The first kind is having just a partition key. The partition key is a hash and determines where on physical storage the item is placed. The partition key must be unique.

The second kind is a composite primary key. It consists of a partition key and a sort key. The partition key stays the same but doesn't need to be unique in isolation. Rather the sort key/ partition key pair must be unique.

In a real system this would probably push towards StreamName as the partition key: so that events that logically live together physically live together. And Event Number in the stream as the sort key. So that the order of items as they are stored on physical media matches the order they are likely to be read.

This introduces unwanted complexity at this time in the code for tracking event numbers.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated in the ADR. However, from the context and decision, the drivers can be inferred as: need for unique identification of items, desire to keep related events physically together, and avoidance of complexity in tracking event numbers.
template_adherence.decision: For now instead of an Event Number as the sort key we will introduce a UUID EventId. And use StreamName as the HASH key. StreamNames will need to be unique anyway.
template_adherence.consequences: This will need performance testing to check that there is no significant impact of the items being effectively randomly sorted.

alternatives.description: Use Event Number in the stream as the sort key with StreamName as the partition key.
pros: Events that logically live together physically live together.
Order of items stored matches the order they are likely to be read.
cons: Introduces unwanted complexity in the code for tracking event numbers.

alternatives.description: Use UUID EventId as the sort key with StreamName as the partition key.
pros: Simplifies code by avoiding tracking event numbers.
StreamNames are unique, ensuring uniqueness of the composite key.
cons: Potential performance impact due to effectively random sorting of items, requiring performance testing.

```
{
type: "decisionMade",
decision: "the provided decision"
}
```

Further development might lead to a decision that supercedes this one as it has been made in the context of fewer than five events in the domain.

template_adherence.title: 5. read model tables

template_adherence.title: Dependencies with a native component
template_adherence.context: A number of NPM dependencies (including `react-native` and `react-native-maps`) contain native components. The JS dependency acts as a bridge between JS and the native code. If we specify such a dependency as a direct dependency of our library then consumers are forced to use the dependency we specify, which in turn makes it our responsibility to update such dependencies in the consuming codebases. If the consumer deviates from the version we specify, then it's possible that they would end up with multiple versions installed, which could lead to mismatches between the native and JS libraries.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid forcing consumers to use specific versions of native component dependencies.
- Responsibility for updating dependencies should not fall on the library.
- Avoid multiple versions of native components installed leading to mismatches.
- Desire for safer and easier dependency management for native components.
template_adherence.decision: When an NPM dependency has a native component, we use a peer dependency instead of a direct dependency.
template_adherence.consequences: Using peer dependencies means the library relies on the consuming codebase to provide the native component dependencies, reducing the risk of version mismatches and easing maintenance. However, it requires consumers to manage these dependencies correctly.

alternatives.description: Use direct dependencies for native components.
pros: Ensures the library controls the exact version of the dependency used.
Simplifies dependency management within the library.
cons: Forces consumers to use the specified version, potentially causing conflicts.
Increases maintenance burden on the library to keep dependencies updated.
Risk of multiple versions installed leading to mismatches between native and JS libraries.

alternatives.description: Use peer dependencies for native components.
pros: Allows consumers to manage the versions, reducing conflicts.
Simplifies library maintenance by not managing native dependencies directly.
Reduces risk of multiple versions and mismatches.
cons: Requires consumers to correctly manage and provide dependencies.
Potential for consumers to have incompatible versions if not managed properly.

template_adherence.title: When to use `$FlowFixMe` comments
template_adherence.context: When upgrading to Flow 0.112, components using `...rest` started showing errors due to a known long-standing problem with Flow. Attempts to fix this failed, necessitating a workaround.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to suppress Flow errors caused by spreading inexact types; desire to have a consistent comment format to easily find and remove suppressions later; intention to revisit and remove suppressions when a fix is available; avoid opting out of Flow except for legitimate bugs with proper documentation.
template_adherence.decision: Use a standardized comment format `// $FlowFixMe[cannot-spread-inexact] - inexact rest. See 'decisions/flowfixme.md'.` to suppress these errors. Future suppressions should use the same format to facilitate tracking and removal. Revisit periodically to remove suppressions when Flow fixes the issue.
template_adherence.consequences: Suppressing errors allows continued development without Flow errors blocking progress. Using a consistent comment format aids in maintenance and cleanup. However, suppressing errors may hide real issues if overused. Encouraging minimal use and documentation mitigates this risk.

alternatives.description: Do not suppress errors and wait for Flow to fix the issue.
pros: Avoids suppressing errors and potentially hiding real problems.
Maintains strict type checking without exceptions.
cons: Blocks development due to persistent Flow errors.
No workaround available currently, causing delays.

alternatives.description: Use ad-hoc or inconsistent suppression comments.
pros: Quick to implement without standardization.
Flexible for different cases.
cons: Harder to track and remove suppressions later.
Leads to inconsistent codebase and maintenance challenges.

template_adherence.title: Replace Gitflow with Simple Git Workflow
template_adherence.context:
We want to move to a continuous delivery (CD) model, which would allow us to release new features and fixes as quickly as we write them and put them through our QA process. This ambition is hampered by having an intermediate `development` branch that is intended to isolate 'new development from finished work'. We should not fear releasing unfinished work, but instead should control it via application level routing and/or feature flags. This would enable us to be much more reactive to feature requests from our users and findings made during our user research.

Changing our git workflow is straightforward. All we need is agreement between the devs on changing to a different approach. However, complexity arises owing to the setup of our AWS Codebuild environment and multiple build projects and pipelines tied to branches that we intend to stop using. There are cost and maintenance implications to leaving orphaned resources in AWS.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Desire to increase release velocity and reduce irregular maintenance tasks.
- Need to support continuous delivery model.
- Complexity and cost of maintaining multiple long-lived branches and associated AWS build and pipeline resources.
- Requirement to maintain code quality and stability via protected branches and CI.
- Need for team understanding and responsibility regarding testing and feature flagging.
- Monitoring defect rates as release velocity increases.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to remove all long-lived branches and their supporting pipelines and build integrations except for `main`. The `main` branch will remain protected requiring PRs and passing CI tests. The team will be briefed on responsibilities including testing, feature flagging, and monitoring. The staging pipeline will be adapted to allow on-demand builds triggered by tags. This simplifies the git workflow to a simple git workflow model, supporting continuous delivery and reducing maintenance overhead.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include increased release velocity, simplified branch management, and better alignment with continuous delivery practices. Negative consequences include an initial increase in defects reaching production, though defect rates are expected to decrease as the team adapts. There is also a need for increased discipline in testing and feature flagging to mitigate risks.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing gitflow model with long-lived branches and associated AWS build and pipeline resources.
pros: Familiar workflow for the team.
Clear separation of development and production code.
cons: Complexity in keeping branches in sync.
Slower release velocity due to manual merges and maintenance.
Higher maintenance cost and potential orphaned AWS resources.

alternatives.description: Adopt a different branching strategy such as GitHub Flow or Trunk Based Development.
pros: Potentially simpler workflows than gitflow.
Supports continuous delivery and rapid releases.
cons: May require significant changes to team practices and tooling.
Risk of instability if not managed properly.
