template_adherence.title: Environments after GOV.UK PaaS migration
template_adherence.context:
We're migrating the Teacher Vacancy application to GOV.UK PaaS and we want to rethink and simplify our delivery process and what environments we're using to aid development, testing and deployment.

This is especially relevant as we are moving away from Gitflow toward a simple usage of Git (refer to ADR003). Not having long-living branches we can utilise a simpler environments setup.

The current setup is this:

* testing - user researchers to conduct usability testing sessions
* edge - devs to test or debug features, code and integrations in isolation
* staging - final quality assurance step and demos
* production - the live service
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to simplify delivery process and environment usage
- Moving away from Gitflow to simpler Git usage
- Desire to reduce maintenance overhead
- GOV.UK PaaS allows easy creation and teardown of environments
template_adherence.decision:
We will reduce the number of environment to:

* staging - used for User Acceptance testing, quality assurance testing and demos
* production - the live service, runs the latest version of the main branch

Developers will use local environments to test or debug features, code and integrations.
The same applies to user researchers when conducting usability testing sessions.

Having a staging environment is also handy to test builds and deployments before going to production. Keeping a staging environment close to production reduces the risk of having unexpected issues when deploying a release.
template_adherence.consequences:
Reducing the number of environments results in less maintenance overhead.
It's also worth mentioning that GOV.UK PaaS makes the process to spin up a new environment fairly trivial.
In case there's a need for an extra environment for a short amount of time we're able to spin a new one, deploy to it and tear it down reasonably quickly.

Teaching Vacancies conducted a review into which search engine option to take forward in April 2020 and Algolia was compared to Elastic Search. template_adherence.title: Migrate from Algolia to Postgres-based search
template_adherence.context: Given the user needs we want to meet with our search functionality, and the cost and complexity involved in our integration with Algolia, would we be better off with a simpler solution of leveraging our existing database for search?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Financial cost of Algolia (and risk of eventually losing our cheap grandfathered legacy plan)
* Technical complexity and brittleness of Algolia integration
* Lack of customisability and lack of configuration-as-code on Algolia
* Simplicity of underlying search requirements means enterprise-grade search engine is overkill
* Lack of ability to integration test search results when using SaaS search engine
* Availability of constantly improving full-text search functionality in our database (PostgreSQL)
* Potential for richer geographical querying using PostGIS
template_adherence.decision: Decided to migrate away from Algolia and move to using our database for search functionality.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Simplified infrastructure and one fewer third-party service integration
* Significant complexity savings in search code
* Ability to integration test search results and keep search configuration in code (versioned and auditable)
* End of reliance on Algolia's goodwill in keeping us grandfathered on their legacy plan
* Minor cost savings in the short term (and we no longer need to avoid potential increases in queries in the long term)
* Improved performance and reliability due to not having to interact with a third-party service
* Ability to completely control and debug all aspects of how search works
* Richer geographical querying through use of PostGIS

Negative Consequences:
* Some implementation effort (estimated at 2x developers for ~3-4 sprints)
* Synonym logic will need custom implementation (but at the same time, this allows us to make it significantly "smarter" than on Algolia)
* Typo tolerance/fuzzy search will need custom implementation (but this is an edge-case for us because the majority of queries are straightforward)

template_adherence.title: Encourage use of devcontainers for local development
template_adherence.context: Setting up the Teaching Vacancies app for local development is a frustrating process involving many steps and multiple dependencies driven by manually updated setup documentation. A workflow based on devcontainers would alleviate much of this setup pain, and provide a trivially reproducible environment for local development, benefitting both developers and non-developers on the team.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Complex and time-consuming onboarding and "re-boarding" experience of the application
- Difficulties experiences by non-developers in getting the app set up locally, and getting it running again after major dependency changes (e.g. our recent addition of PostGIS)
- Increasing adoption of devcontainers as a de-facto standard in the wider development community including Ruby on Rails
- Possible use of cloud-based development environments such as Github Codespaces in the future to enable users on restricted organisation-managed devices to contribute to the application
template_adherence.decision: Add devcontainers as an option for now, with a view to iterate on it and improve it to the point where we can consider it the "official" default way of running Teaching Vacancies (while still allowing other development workflows for developers who prefer different ways of working).
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
- Drastically easier onboarding and "re-boarding" (e.g. on a new device or after an OS upgrade causing developer tooling issues)
- Dependencies reduced to just Git, Docker, and VS Code
- A fully functioning development environment is ready in 10 minutes from scratch, with no user interaction beyond opening the repository in VS Code and selecting "Reopen in container"
- Moving entirety of development experience into a container fixes past Docker development workflow issues experienced on the team (where tasks and services where executed from the host instead of interacting with a shell and an editor from inside the container itself)
- Developers and other team members can develop on any host OS (macOS/Linux/Windows) but we only need to support one single consistent environment
- Does away with all the Mac vs Linux vs WSL setup steps in our current documentation
- Reduces likelihood of "works on my machine" development environment issues
- "Leave no trace" on the host machine and complete isolation from other projects
- Removes possibility of "dependency hell" when working on multiple projects
- Removes need to clutter local environment with applications and dependencies that need to be kept up to date and in sync (e.g. Google Chrome and `chromedriver`)
- Removes need for language version managers (`rbenv`, `nvm`)
- Provides executable documentation of project setup and dependencies
- Removes need for manually updated setup documentation that can become stale
- Experienced developers who have a different preferred workflow can get a clear, in-code view of setup steps and dependencies
- Good workflow for everyone, but excellent additional integration with Visual Studio Code
- Automatic passthrough of SSH and GPG keys
- Language extensions run within the container itself, and can be specified in the devcontainer configuration file for instant setup of useful extensions for new users
- Automatic bootstrapping of personal dotfiles
- Ability to easily move to cloud-based workflows in the future
- Ability to easily propagate new tools and improved configuration to all developers on the team
- Trivial rebuilds to a known good state when performing "dangerous" operations in the container

Negative Consequences:
- Slightly reduced performance on some host OSs (non-Linux) due to Docker being Linux-native technology (overhead of containers running in an intermediate VM)
- Somewhat mitigated by use of volumes for IO-intensive cache directories
- Can be worked around entirely by moving workspace root into the container, and we will continue to investigate before we fully agree on devcontainers as our default workflow
- Container layers need occasional pruning on the host as Docker can fill up disk space quickly
- Some duplication of Docker configuration between production and development configuration (but that is to be expected given that use cases are very different)

alternatives.description: Provide devcontainer-based setup for Teaching Vacancies
pros: Easier onboarding and setup
Consistent development environment
cons: Requires maintenance of devcontainer configuration

alternatives.description: Do nothing and continue current local-based workflow
pros: No additional setup required
cons: Continued onboarding difficulties
Manual setup prone to errors and inconsistencies

template_adherence.title: ADR 1: Bootstrap Sentinel
template_adherence.context:
Connaisseur's main components are a MutatingWebhookConfiguration and the Connaisseur Pods. The MutatingWebhookConfiguration intercepts requests to create or update Kubernetes resources and forwards them to the Connaisseur Pods tasked, on a high level, with verifying trust data. The order of deploying both components matters, since a blocking MutatingWebhookConfiguration without the Connaisseur Pods to answer its requests would also block the deployment of said Pods.

In [#3](https://github.com/sse-secure-systems/connaisseur/issues/3) it was noted that prior to version 1.1.5 of Connaisseur when looking at the `Ready` status of Connaisseur Pods, they could report `Ready` while being non-functional due to the MutatingWebhookConfiguration missing. However, as stated above the MutatingWebhookConfiguration can only be deployed _after_ the Connaisseur Pods, which was solved by checking the `Ready` state of said Pods. If one were to add a dependency to this `Ready` state, such that it only shows `Ready` when the MutatingWebhookConfiguration exists, we run into a deadlock, where the MutatingWebhookConfiguration waits for the Pods and the Pods wait for the MutatingWebhookConfiguration.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid deployment deadlock between MutatingWebhookConfiguration and Connaisseur Pods.
- Desire for Connaisseur Pods' `Ready` status to accurately reflect functionality.
- Avoid non-Kubernetes-like solutions.
- Ease of monitoring and deployment status visibility.
template_adherence.decision: Option 1 was chosen: At the start of the Helm deployment, create a Pod named `connaisseur-bootstrap-sentinel` that runs for 5 minutes (Helm installation timeout). Connaisseur Pods report `Ready` if they can access notary and either the MutatingWebhookConfiguration exists or the sentinel Pod is still running. If both access and MutatingWebhookConfiguration exist, the sentinel is killed early. This approach avoids deadlock and allows readiness status to reflect functionality.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Consistent deployment failures if the sentinel Pod ends without readiness.
- Monitoring Connaisseur Pods is sufficient to ensure proper operation.

Negative consequences:
- Potential for adversary to spoof sentinel Pod name and cause false readiness.
- Deployment fails if notary healthcheck fails during sentinel lifetime.
- Sentinel Pod might be left behind but can be cleaned up during deployment.
- Adds minimal deployment complexity.

alternatives.description: Create a sentinel Pod during Helm deployment to manage readiness and avoid deadlock.
pros: Avoids deployment deadlock.
Readiness status reflects actual functionality.
Allows Helm deployment to fail consistently if deployment issues occur.
cons: Potential security risk if adversary can deploy sentinel Pod.
Adds complexity to deployment process.
Sentinel Pod might be left behind if not cleaned up.

alternatives.description: Let Connaisseur Pod readiness be non-indicative and require manual monitoring of MutatingWebhookConfiguration.
pros: Simpler deployment without sentinel Pod.
No additional Pods needed.
cons: Readiness status does not reflect actual functionality.
Requires manual monitoring, increasing operational burden.

alternatives.description: Deploy MutatingWebhookConfiguration when Pods are healthy instead of ready, using health status for readiness.
pros: More accurate readiness based on health.
Avoids sentinel Pod complexity.
cons: Health status requires querying each Pod individually.
Not aligned with Kubernetes conventions.
Considered an ugly solution by authors.

template_adherence.title: ADR 2: Release Management
template_adherence.context:
During its initial development Connaisseur was more or less maintained by a single person and not released frequently. Hence, the easiest option was to just have the maintainer build and push at certain stages of development. With the influx of more team members, the number of contributions and hence the number of needed/reasonable releases went up. Also since publication, it is more important that the uploaded Connaisseur image corresponds to the most recent version referenced in the Helm chart.

A single person having to build, sign and push the images whenever a new pull request is accepted is hence unpractical for both development and agility.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the need to handle increased contributions and releases, the importance of matching the uploaded image to the Helm chart version, avoiding exposing credentials to GitHub Actions due to security concerns, and balancing automation with human intervention to maintain security and process integrity.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to maintain two branches: 'master' for the latest release code and tagged releases, and 'develop' for ongoing development merged into 'master' for releases. For signing images, the process requires the person merging the PR to build, sign, and push the release manually, avoiding exposing credentials in the pipeline. Automation is partially achieved via shell scripts to ease manual steps.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to develop without immediate shipping, avoiding credential exposure in GitHub Actions, and having Git tags for releases. Negative consequences include a more cumbersome release process per change and the need for human intervention in the release process.

pros: Automates the release process.

template_adherence.title: ADR 4: Modular Validation
template_adherence.context: With the upcoming of notaryv2 and similar projects like Cosign the opportunity for Connaisseur arises to support multiple signing mechanisms, and combine all into a single validation tool. For that to work, the internal validation mechanism of connaisseur needs to be more modular, so we can easily swap in and out different methods.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support multiple signing mechanisms and combine them into a single validation tool. The internal validation mechanism must be modular to allow easy swapping of different methods. Configuration changes must accommodate multiple validators with sensitive data handled properly. The validator interface must decide on the return type (JSON patch or digest) for flexibility and core functionality.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to adopt a modular validation approach with the following key points:
- Configuration changes: Use a 'validators' section replacing 'notaries' with each validator having a name and type, supporting multiple validation methods (option 1.1.1.1).
- Sensitive values: Hard-code sensitive fields based on validator type to prevent misconfiguration (option 1.1.2.2).
- Image policy: Use a 'validator' field referencing validators by name, support 'allow' and 'deny' validators for explicit allow/deny options (option 1.2.1.1).
- Default behavior: When no validator is given, default to deny validator to reduce configuration effort (option 1.2.2.1).
- Allow 'allow' and 'deny' validators as explicit static types in default configuration to avoid obscurity (option 1.2.3.2).
- Validator interface: Validator.validate returns a digest, and Connaisseur creates JSON patch, maintaining core functionality and avoiding code duplication (option 2.1.2).
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include increased modularity and flexibility in supporting multiple signing mechanisms, clearer and more powerful configuration options with explicit allow/deny validators, and a standardized validator interface returning digests. Negative consequences include potential larger configuration files due to explicit allow/deny validators and less flexibility in validator interface for future additional changes beyond digest return.

alternatives.description: Configuration changes with different structures and handling of sensitive data.
pros: Provides flexibility to support multiple validation methods.
Allows generic configuration handling for sensitive data.
cons: Some options may allow sensitive data in configmaps accidentally.
Hard-coding sensitive fields may require Helm chart updates for new validators.

alternatives.description: Image policy options with different validator referencing and allow/deny mechanisms.
pros: Explicit deny option provides more powerful configuration.
Maintains known configuration for current users.
cons: More configuration changes required for users.
No explicit deny option in some options.

alternatives.description: Validator interface returning JSON patch vs digest.
pros: Returning JSON patch offers more flexibility for future changes.
Returning digest avoids code duplication and focuses on core functionality.
cons: Returning JSON patch may allow non-core changes.
Returning digest may require additional work for future extensions.

template_adherence.title: Use Cheroot as the WSGI Server for Production Deployment
template_adherence.context: The project was initially running a Flask WSGI application using the built-in Flask server, which is not suitable for production due to issues like potential debug shell exposure and single-threaded operation. Despite mitigations, the warning about using a development server caused concern among users, prompting the need to select a proper production WSGI server.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision was influenced by the need for a stable, efficient, and secure WSGI server suitable for production. Key drivers included performance under complex and high load conditions, resource consumption (CPU and memory), stability (error rates and pod restarts), community recognition, and ease of configuration.
template_adherence.decision: After testing several WSGI servers (Bjoern, Cheroot, Flask, Gunicorn, uWSGI), the team chose Cheroot as the WSGI server. Cheroot showed better performance than Flask for complex requests and better stability than uWSGI under strong load. Although uWSGI performed best under massive load with scaling, its higher memory footprint and poorer performance under strong load made Cheroot the preferred choice. Flask was rejected due to poor performance and security concerns. Bjoern and Gunicorn were dropped due to compatibility and performance issues.
template_adherence.consequences: Adopting Cheroot as the WSGI server improves production stability and performance, especially under complex and strong load scenarios. It balances resource consumption effectively and avoids the security and performance pitfalls of the Flask development server. However, Cheroot is less known and not officially listed by Flask, which may affect community support. The decision may require monitoring and future reassessment if load patterns change significantly.

template_adherence.title: 4. Define Project Structure
template_adherence.context: How should the folders and files in this repo be organized and named?
template_adherence.decision:
1. Add a folder in /src/components.
- Name the folder the same as the component name, in title case without any spaces.
- Beneath that, add a `v1` folder. Each new version of the component that changes its appearance will get a new version folder.
- Do not create any additional layers of subfolders
1. In the folder, add a .js file, a .md file, and a .test.js file, all of them named the same as the component name. If the component needs any component-specific utility functions (to keep the code in the .js file clean), add a folder named `utils` and put them in there. Here is an example folder structure:
```text
/src
/components
/Button
/v1
Button.js
Button.test.js
Button.md
utils
myUtilFunction.js
myUtilFunction.test.js
myOtherUtilFunction.js
myOtherUtilFunction.test.js
```
1. Define a single React component in the .js file. Export it as default. (Refer to "Component Guidelines" section.)
1. Write tests in the .test.js file, using Jest. (Refer to "Writing and Running Tests" section.)
1. Write style guide documentation and examples for the component in the .md file.
1. Add your component to an appropriate style guide section in `styleguide.config.js`
1. If any utility functions used by your component can be helpful to other components, too, put them in a `/src/utils/[functionName].js` file instead of the component-specific `utils` folder

template_adherence.title: 7. Publish Components
template_adherence.context:
We need to be able to pull in these components to other apps as one or more NPM packages. There are pros and cons to a single-package approach versus one package per component.

### One Package Per Component

Pros:

- Minimum dependencies pulled in with each component used. You don't download or package anything you aren't using.
- When you need to pull in a fix to one component, you aren't unintentionally changing the behavior of a hundred other components.

Cons:

- How do we track dependencies per component but also install them so that the whole Style Guide app can run as one?
- Each component package has to be installed by developers as it is needed
- Publishing them will be tricky, especially if there are any interdependencies. Lerna + semantic-release may help, but the typical Lerna repo structure may not be ideal with the context of the Style Guide app we have here.

### A Single Package Exporting All Components

Pros:

- Install a single package and you get access to them all in your app
- Much simpler to publish vs multiple packages
- Easier for people working on the style guide repo to understand.

Cons:

- Every time you bump the dependency version of the component package, you'll pull in potentially changed versions of every component in your app.
- Extra work will be required to ensure that bundled JavaScript does not include any components that an app does not use.

### What about the style guide

There is a further complication here, which is "how does the style guide release cycle relate to the release cycle of the components within it, and how does the style guide represent multiple versions of components as they change?"
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the complexity of maintaining multiple packages versus a single package, the need to minimize unintended changes when updating components, ease of publishing and understanding the package structure, and handling the style guide's release cycle and versioning of components.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to use a single package exporting all components, mitigating its cons by:

- Exporting every component change that affects appearance as a new component version in a versioned folder (e.g., `v2`).
- Avoiding React components importing each other; instead, passing needed components as props or children.
- Using Jest snapshot testing to detect visual changes and decide on version splits.
- Allowing the style guide to naturally show all versions since they remain in versioned folders.
- Recommending apps using the package implement tree shaking to avoid bundling unused components.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include simpler publishing and understanding of the package, clear versioning of components to avoid unintended changes, and natural representation of multiple component versions in the style guide. Negative consequences include the need for developers to manage versioned imports and set up tree shaking in consuming apps to avoid bundling unused components.

template_adherence.title: 8. Keep Styles With Components
template_adherence.context:
So that developers do not have to think too hard, we want a simple rule about where the styles related to a React component should live. The options are "always in a separate styles.js file in the same folder" or "always in the same file as the React component, above the component". (This is referring to JSX or styled-components styles, and not CSS/SASS styles.)

### Separate File

Pros:

- Smaller files, easier to read

Cons:

- Overkill for a single style
- More files for Babel to transform and watchers to watch
- Extra work for dev (minimal)

### Same File

Pros:

- Simple and less work for dev
- Fewer files for Babel to transform and watchers to watch

Cons:

- Larger files, harder to read (but you can code fold in IDE)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR implicitly considers developer simplicity, file size, readability, build performance (Babel transformation and watchers), and developer workload as decision drivers. These are inferred from the pros and cons listed under each alternative.
template_adherence.decision: All styles always live in the same file as the React component, above the component.
template_adherence.consequences: Not explicitly stated in a separate section, but implied consequences include simpler development process, fewer files to manage and transform, and potentially larger files that might be harder to read but can be mitigated by IDE code folding.

alternatives.description: Keep styles in a separate styles.js file in the same folder as the React component.
pros: Smaller files, easier to read
cons: Overkill for a single style

template_adherence.title: 7. Use roles to authorise users to use certain data
template_adherence.context:
We need a way to authorise users in the MOLGENIS "Armadillo" service to use data. We want this to be as straightforward as possible.

Other techniques are ACL's for fine grained permissions on resources and ID-based.

**ACL's**
It is more time consuming to implement ACL's. With roles the you are less flexible, but we believe this is sufficient to use DataSHIELD.

**ID-based**
The ID-based approach was suggested as a first solution to make the service secure. A big disadvantage is that anyone with the link can
share the data. That means that there has to be a lot of trust between the data manager and the researcher. In practices, this is not feasible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a straightforward authorization method in MOLGENIS "Armadillo" service; consideration of alternatives like ACLs and ID-based approaches; trade-offs between flexibility, implementation effort, and security.
template_adherence.decision: Use roles as a basic principle to give users permission on the data they need to have access to. Define at least two types of roles: Researcher and Data manager, each with implicit permissions as described.
template_adherence.consequences:
- File storage must be aware that roles are used as the authorization mechanism.
- Fine-grained permissions within a role are not possible.

alternatives.description: Use ACLs (Access Control Lists) for fine-grained permissions on resources.
pros: More flexible and fine-grained control over permissions.
cons: More time consuming to implement.
More complex to manage.

alternatives.description: Use ID-based authorization where access is granted based on possession of a link or ID.
pros: Simple to implement initially.
cons: Anyone with the link can share the data, leading to security risks.
Requires high trust between data manager and researcher, which is not feasible in practice.

template_adherence.title: 001 - Application Technology Stack
template_adherence.context:
A need has been identified for the development of an API to enable UEC service providers and DoS Leads to change the RAG status (also known as the Capacity Status) of their services in DoS. The API will need to authenticate users via a modern authentication approach, and will need to establish whether the user is authorised to be able to update the state of the service. The API will need full API documentation and will need to have fully automated testing and deployment into our cloud platform.

This ADR is concerned with the technology stack in which the API is to be written in. The following three python web application frameworks were considered and evaluated:

- Flask
- Django
- Tornado
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a modern authentication approach
- Authorization requirements for updating service state
- Requirement for full API documentation
- Need for fully automated testing and deployment
- Limited implementation time
- Size of the API
- Flexibility of the framework
- Suitability for the expected request load
template_adherence.decision:
Due to the size of the API and the limited implementation time, Python and Flask were deemed the most appropriate technologies. It was decided that the Django framework was far too heavy weight and may not offer the flexibility we need. While Tornado seemed inappropriate because we are not dealing with long running queries or processes; neither are we dealing with hundreds of thousands of requests.

The technology stack is therefore:

- Python v3.7
- Flask framework v1.1, with extensions of:
- Flask-Restplus
- Flask-SQLAlchemy (and psycopg2-binary)
- pytest
template_adherence.consequences:
Very light touch framework with available extensions to only bring in exactly what the solution requires. Will need flask extensions to complete the solution, but these are well known about and documented. Identified extensions so far are:

- Flask-Restplus - provides REST functionality and API documentation that Swagger can plug into.
- Flask-SQLAlchemy (and psycopg2-binary) - both required to enable connectivity to a Postgres RDS database. Also provides ORM modelling.
- pytest - pythons automated unit test framework for writing and running unit tests.

Easy to work with. The documentation that comes with Flask is very good. Flask debug mode is concise and understandable.

alternatives.description: Flask framework
pros: Lightweight and flexible
Good documentation
Concise and understandable debug mode
cons: Requires additional extensions to complete the solution

alternatives.description: Django framework
pros: Comprehensive framework with many built-in features
cons: Too heavy weight for the size of the API
May not offer the needed flexibility

alternatives.description: Tornado framework
pros: Suitable for long running queries or high request volumes
cons: Inappropriate for this use case as the API does not deal with long running queries or hundreds of thousands of requests

template_adherence.title: 004 - Authentication and Authorisation
template_adherence.context:
The Capacity Status API will enable UEC service providers and DoS Leads to change the RAG status (also known as the Capacity Status) of their services in DoS.

To protect from unauthenticated users and to prevent authenticated users from being able to update capacity status information for services that they do not have permissions for, the Capacity Status API will need to authenticate users via a modern authentication approach, and will need to establish whether the user is authorised to be able to update the capacity status information of the service.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to protect the API from unauthenticated users.
- Need to prevent authenticated users from updating capacity status information for services they are not authorized for.
- Simplicity of implementation for the private Beta phase.
- Dependency management and alignment with Core DoS permissions.
- Security considerations for authentication mechanisms.
- Future re-evaluation for public beta phase.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use API Key authentication for the private Beta phase due to its simplicity and the limited user base, with a plan to re-evaluate if moving to public beta. For authorisation, the decision is to leverage the existing permissions managed by Core DoS rather than maintaining a separate set within the API, accepting the dependency on Core DoS to ensure alignment and single source of truth for permissions.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Simple implementation of authentication on both API and client side.
- Single core store of user service permissions maintained in Core DoS, avoiding synchronization issues.
- Slightly more complex implementation to link Core DoS users with API Keys, but manageable with Django's extensibility.
- API Key authentication is less secure than OAUTH2 but sufficient for the private Beta use case.
- Decision subject to re-evaluation if the API moves to the next development phase.

template_adherence.title: 005 - Domain Model and REST Interface
template_adherence.context:
The Capacity Status API will be built using the Django web framework. The framework offers a number of modules and features that can be utilised when building an API. This ADR discusses these concepts and the decisions made in determining which Django features to use, and how we can use them. Essentially, this comes down to three distinct parts:

- Rest Interface (views and controllers)
- Serialization (the broker between the request and the domain model; and the domain model and the response)
- Domain Model (where and how the information is kept)

The Capacity Status API is required to:

- Take in capacity status information to update a specific service, containing the following information:
- Capacity Status (the capacity status to put the service into in readable format: Red, Amber, Green)
- Reset Status In Minutes (when setting the capacity status to either a Red or Amber state, this is the number of minutes the service will persist in this state. After this time, the service will be automatically set back to the Green capacity status)
- Notes (a free text field that the requester can set)

- Update the capacity status information in Core DoS with the following information:
- Capacity Status (in enumerated format: 1, 2, 3)
- Reset Date Time (a timestamp specifying when the service should revert back to a Green capacity status)
- Notes
- Modified By (the user who has updated the capacity information)
- Modified Date (a timestamp specifying when the capacity information was last updated)

- Respond with the capacity information for a requested service, containing the following information:
- Service UID (the UID identifying the service)
- Service Name (the human readable name of the service)
- Capacity Status (Red, Amber, Green)
- Reset Date Time
- Notes
- Modified By
- Modified Date
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to build the Capacity Status API using Django framework.
- Desire to leverage Django Rest Framework (DRF) for RESTful API endpoints.
- Need for clear separation of concerns in serialization and data handling.
- Requirement to handle capacity status data and user permissions.
- Minimize boilerplate code and maintenance overhead.
- Manage coupling between API and Core DoS database carefully.
- Use Django's built-in tools for database migrations and management.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Django Rest Framework (DRF) for the REST interface, leveraging its built-in views such as RetrieveUpdateAPIView to provide GET and PUT endpoints. For serialization, a three-serializer approach is adopted: Payload Serializer, Data Model Serializer, and Response Serializer, each handling specific data streams and validation. The domain model is split into Capacity Status and User Management models, with the Capacity Status model tightly coupled to the Core DoS database and the User Management model maintained separately by the API using Django's database migration tools. A dedicated 'DoS' module will handle user permissions data retrieval to reduce coupling concerns.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The framework reduces boilerplate code significantly.
- API documentation is automatically generated from endpoints and serializers, reducing maintenance overhead.
- Clear separation of concerns in data flow handling.
- Separation between service data handling and user permissions/authentication.
- Tight coupling exists between the API and Core DoS database for capacity status data, considered an acceptable risk.
- No need for manual database scripting or maintenance for the User Management model due to Django's migration tools.

alternatives.description: Use a custom-built REST interface without Django Rest Framework, manually handling endpoints and serialization.
pros: Full control over API implementation.
No dependency on external frameworks.
cons: Increased development time and complexity.
More boilerplate code to maintain.
Higher risk of bugs and inconsistencies.
Manual API documentation generation required.

pros: Simpler serializer management.

cons: Less clear separation of concerns.
Harder to manage validation rules specific to each data stream.
Potentially more complex serializer logic.

alternatives.description: Couple both Capacity Status and User Management models tightly to Core DoS database.
pros: Unified data model and storage.
Potentially simpler data access.
cons: Increased coupling risk.
Harder to maintain API independence.
Changes in Core DoS could impact API stability.

template_adherence.title: 006 - SQL Stored Procedures
template_adherence.context: In order to protect DoS services from having capacity status information updated by users of the Capacity Status API that do not have the required permissions to do so. Core DoS maintains user services permissions, therefore the API requires an interface to Core DoS to be able to validate that an API user is able to update capacity status information of the requested service.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to protect DoS services from unauthorized updates, the existing Core DoS APIs being complex and inefficient for the required permission checks, the desire to avoid dependencies on Core DoS team during private Beta, and the need for efficient and fast permission validation.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a simple query within the Capacity Status API's 'DoS' module during the private Beta phase instead of using existing Core DoS APIs or creating a stored procedure in the Core DoS database. This allows for faster development, tuning, and reduces dependencies on Core DoS team. Later, the decision to lodge the query in the Core DoS database may be revisited once stable.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include faster and more efficient permission checks, reduced processing time and complexity, and flexibility to adjust the query during private Beta. Negative consequences include coupling with the Core DoS user services permission data model, though mitigated by isolating this in a separate module and the low likelihood of changes in Core DoS in this area.

template_adherence.title: 008 - Authentication and Authorisation (revisited)
template_adherence.context:
The Capacity Status API will enable UEC service providers and DoS Leads to change the RAG status (also known as the Capacity Status) of their services in DoS.

To protect from unauthenticated users and to prevent authenticated users from being able to update capacity status information for services that they do not have permissions for, the Capacity Status API will need to authenticate users via a modern authentication approach, and will need to establish whether the user is authorised to be able to update the capacity status information of the service.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to protect the API from unauthenticated users, ensure proper authorization so users cannot update services they lack permission for, usability concerns (correct HTTP response codes), security concerns, and maintainability by leveraging existing permission management in Core DoS.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement token-based authentication hooked into Django Rest Framework's authentication classes to ensure proper HTTP 401 responses and security, instead of the initially proposed API Key authentication which was more of an authorization mechanism and hooked into permission classes. For authorization, the decision is to leverage Core DoS's existing permission management rather than maintaining a separate set within the API, accepting the dependency on Core DoS to ensure alignment.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include simple implementation of the chosen authentication mechanism on both API and client side, maintaining a single core store of user service permissions in Core DoS, and ensuring alignment between Core DoS and the API. Negative or cautionary consequences include slightly more complex implementation due to the need to link Core DoS users with tokens, and that token authentication is less secure than mechanisms like OAUTH2, but sufficient for the private Beta phase. The decision will be re-evaluated if the API moves to the next development phase.

alternatives.description: API Key authentication using a Django authentication extension application hooked into DRF's permission classes.
pros: Simple initial implementation.
Familiar approach for private Beta with known user base.
cons: Actually an authorization mechanism, not authentication.
Returns HTTP 403 Forbidden instead of desired HTTP 401 Unauthorized.
Security concerns due to hooking into permission classes rather than authentication classes.

alternatives.description: OAUTH2 authentication.
pros: More secure authentication mechanism.
Industry standard for authentication and authorization.
cons: Not chosen for private Beta phase.
Potentially more complex to implement initially.

template_adherence.title: 0003 - Asynchronous Task Queue
template_adherence.context:
The key component of this project is a 'Bicycle Network Analysis' task which is run on an arbitrary, user-provided neighborhood boundary. This task performs the following actions:
- Import neighborhood boundary into a PostgreSQL database
- Download OSM extract for the provided neighborhood boundary + a buffer and import to PostgreSQL
- Download related census block and job data for the boundary and import to PostgreSQL
- Generate a network graph from the imported data
- Run a series of client-provided analyses on the graph and imported data
- Export relevant data to an external file store for archival
- Generate a tile set of the network graph for display on a web map

The application will be configured with multiple organizations, and each organization can only run one analysis job at a time. A new analysis job triggered by a user of the organization will supersede any existing older analysis, which can be thrown away.

Since the analysis workflow is already a self-contained process, there are a few ways to trigger this job, and a few options for an asynchronous task queue. One option is to use Celery, a tool we are familiar with, to provide a known interface to trigger these analysis jobs. Another is to configure the analysis as an AWS ECS task, and have the application use the ECS API or Boto to start a new analysis.

Celery has multiple options for brokers:

| Broker | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| ------ | ---------- | ------------- |
| SQS | Cheap, easy to set up, now stable, provides configuration options to isolate environments | No result backend, [potential issues with result timeouts](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/getting-started/brokers/sqs.html#caveats) |
| Redis | Trivial to configure, can additionally be used as a results backend without further architecting | Key eviction issues, additional cost to run dedicated instance |

Running the analysis via AWS Lambda was briefly considered, but the project dependencies and resources required are not conducive to that environment.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage asynchronous analysis jobs triggered by users.
- Desire to use a known interface/tool for triggering and managing tasks.
- Consideration of cost and simplicity of the application stack.
- Familiarity of the team with Celery and SQS broker.
- Need for integration with Django and Python peripheral task logic.
- Limitations and trade-offs of different brokers (SQS vs Redis).
- Constraints of project dependencies ruling out AWS Lambda.
template_adherence.decision: The team will use Celery with the SQS broker to manage the asynchronous analysis jobs. Celery provides a useful abstraction layer for triggering tasks, managing jobs, and reporting errors, with out-of-the-box support for Django and Python. The SQS broker was chosen to keep the managed application architecture simple and reduce ongoing costs. The team has prior experience with an older version of the SQS broker.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Potential overhead of Celery might be unnecessary and could be removed later.
- If the chosen Celery broker proves inadequate, the decision will need to be revisited.
- The exact method of triggering analysis tasks is still unknown; likely ECS tasks triggered via Celery using Boto or docker-py.
- Autoscaling task capacity is an open question requiring further investigation as the project matures.

alternatives.description: Use Celery with SQS broker to manage asynchronous tasks.
pros: Provides a known interface to trigger analysis jobs.
Offers abstraction for task triggering, job management, and error reporting.
Out-of-the-box support for Django and Python task logic.
Keeps application architecture simple and reduces ongoing costs.
Team has prior experience with SQS broker.
cons: No result backend with SQS broker.
Potential issues with result timeouts when using SQS broker.

alternatives.description: Use Celery with Redis broker.
pros: Trivial to configure.
Can be used as a results backend without additional architecture.
cons: Key eviction issues with Redis.
Additional cost to run a dedicated Redis instance.

alternatives.description: Configure analysis as AWS ECS tasks and trigger via ECS API or Boto.
pros: Direct integration with AWS ECS.
Potentially simpler architecture without Celery overhead.
cons: Less abstraction and management features compared to Celery.
Uncertainty about triggering and autoscaling mechanisms.

alternatives.description: Run analysis via AWS Lambda.
pros: Serverless, potentially scalable and cost-effective.
cons: Project dependencies and resource requirements not conducive to Lambda environment.

template_adherence.title: ADR-0003 - CQRS and Event Sourcing (ES) for Applications
template_adherence.context:
When building monoliths or microservices that contain non-trivial business logic, we want to have a high-level component architecture pattern that natively leverages a strategic Domain Driven Design (DDD) concepts like ubiquitous language and bounded context. It should also support or allow, at least, the usage of application design architecture patterns like hexagonal architecture.

At the lower technical level, component architecture pattern should provide native support for tactical DDD concepts like aggregates, entities, value objects, and events.

When building microservices, the chosen component architecture pattern should natively support asynchronous communication through events.

It would be ideal to have all of these in a single coherent open-source framework and platform.

For anemic CRUD style applications, more traditional approaches, like layered architecture, would be just fine.

Architectural Context
* System (`klokwrk-project`)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a high-level component architecture pattern leveraging strategic DDD concepts.
- Support for tactical DDD concepts at a technical level.
- Native support for asynchronous communication through events in microservices.
- Desire for a single coherent open-source framework and platform.
- Suitability for anemic CRUD style applications to use traditional layered architecture.
template_adherence.decision: We will use the Axon framework and Axon Server as a mature open-source implementation of the CQRS/ES component architecture pattern. This aligns with the goal of demonstrating complex CQRS/ES microservice applications, while allowing traditional approaches for simpler CRUD applications.
template_adherence.consequences:

- Supports asynchronous communication through events.
- Axon platform is mature and provides necessary building blocks for CQRS/ES, DDD, testing, distribution, and scaling.

Negative:

template_adherence.title: ADR-0004 - Hexagonal Architecture for Applications
template_adherence.context:
We want improved application design architecture that supports and promotes the following characteristics:
* An explicit promotion of application features as first-class citizens, instead of promoting technical aspects or database design.
* Explicit support for DDD tactical patterns.
* Is domain-centric with clear separation of the domain from infrastructure.
* Improves testability, maintainability, flexibility, extensibility, and adaptability.
* Discourages the use of any non-supported shortcuts.
* Is explicit enough to allow testing of architecture constraints and rules.
* Has sound structure and aesthetics where it is easy to find concrete artifacts.
* Allows parallel work on features.
* Is well-known and battle-tested already in the wild.

It is proven that traditional layer-centric designs fail on almost every characteristic above. Layer-centric application design architecture can work for simpler cases but often fails when the
feature set grows, and the domain becomes more complicated. We want architecture that can scale cleanly in terms of design and development.

Architectural Context:

template_adherence.context:
We would like to have a language or language extension that is very close, very similar, and 100% compatible with Java, but that offers significant productivity boosters at the same time.

Java syntax is often verbose, and it is common to use various IDE tricks (folding/unfolding) or 3rd party libraries (e.g., Lombok) to deal with some of that clutter. It would be much better to have

practice implementations of various programming patterns.

template_adherence.title: ADR-0008 - Testing Architecture
template_adherence.context:
Application architecture is commonly expressed as a set of guidelines (written or not) that the development team needs to follow. Although essential, architectural guidelines are rarely reviewed or enforced appropriately. The typical result is that architecture degrades through time.

In some cases, application use component ([ADR-0003 - CQRS and Event Sourcing (ES) for Applications](0003-cqrs-and-event-sourcing-for-applications.md)) and design ([ADR-0004 - Hexagonal Architecture for Applications](0004-hexagonal-architecture-for-applications.md)) architectural patterns that promote architectural guidelines, but usually there is nothing to verify them.

The hexagonal architecture provides a well-defined placeholder for every significant application artifact. But there are also some rules regarding dependencies between those artifacts. It is not allowed that each class or interface access anything that it wants. When you add additional CQRS/ES aspects, there are even more rules to follow.

We want to ensure that rules will not be broken and that developers new to the hexagonal architecture and CQRS/ES can comfortably work with them without breaking anything. It will help if we have in place tests that verify all architectural invariants.

### Architectural Context
* System (`klokwrk-project`)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the context and problem statement imply the drivers: the need to enforce architectural guidelines, prevent architecture degradation, and support developers in following architectural rules, especially in hexagonal architecture and CQRS/ES contexts.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use architectural testing for verifying architectural constraints.

Building on top of the [ArchUnit](https://www.archunit.org/) library, Klokwrk provides DSL for specifying hexagonal architecture layers for CQRS/ES applications. There is support for several subtypes of CQRS/ES flavored hexagonal architecture corresponding to the commandside, projections, and queryside aspects.

For more insight and details, take a look at ["Behavior and architectural testing"](../../article/modules-and-packages/modulesAndPackages.md#behavior-and-architectural-testing). There is also a video ["Project Klokwrk: how it helps defining software architecture and solves integration"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=35oUxjXWNYU) that, besides other things, talks about architectural testing in `klokwrk-project`.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive
* Architectural constraints are verified and enforced by unit tests.
* The architecture will not degrade over time.
* Architectural requirements are expresses in code, not only in the documentation.

### Neutral
* Learning ArchUnit and Klokwrk Architectural Testing DSL take some time.

alternatives.description: Not to test architectural constraints.
pros: No additional learning curve or tooling required.
cons: Architectural constraints may be violated over time.
Architecture may degrade without enforcement.

template_adherence.title: ADR-0009 - Testing Inter-Module Dependencies
template_adherence.context:
Although architectural testing ([ADR-0008 - Testing Architecture](0008-testing-architecture.md)) verifies some application dependencies, there are still dependencies that might be overlooked.
In general, we are not talking about 3rd party dependencies but rather about in-project modules at the lower level of abstraction compared to applications.

Those project modules represent various pieces of functionality developed to streamline and simplify application development. The majority of lower-level modules will typically deal with
infrastructure concerns, but some of them might deal with the domain itself. If we have many of those modules, we might accidentally end up in situations where applications use something they should
not use. This might be just plain error, or it might be a suggestion that the lower-level module needs refactoring or splitting into more modules.

To avoid accidental inter-module dependencies, we should have in place a mechanism for verifying them. Also, as project modules grow, we should have some capable visual tooling that quickly can show

template_adherence.title: ADR-0010 - Integration Testing with Containerized Infrastructure
template_adherence.context:
Integration testing is commonly used in contemporary development. Frameworks like Spring and Spring Boot makes integration testing seamless, and it often looks like plain unit testing in terms of simplicity and speed of execution.

However, the way that integration tests are used today commonly exercises only integration between internal application components (e.g., integration between controllers and services, integration between services and domain objects, configuration correctness, etc.). If the tests require some external infrastructure, it is usually mocked out or replaced by alternative in-memory variants. Internal application integration tests are important, but they do not cover integration with realistic external infrastructure.

As containerized solutions (e.g., Docker) are a norm today, there is an obvious opportunity to use containerized infrastructure in our integration tests. There is a lot of value in such tests since the infrastructure is (almost) the same as it will be in the production.

The most obvious examples are databases. A typical pattern in integration tests is to use an in-memory database, for example, H2. Although very convenient, it is not a real database as it will be in production. It will not behave like an actual database either in a functional (SQL dialect) or non-functional (security, performance) way. If our production uses, say, the PostgreSQL database, it will be much better to use that same database in integration tests.

If we look at other non-database examples of infrastructure components, say some modern messaging system, we will probably encounter no in-memory equivalent exists. In these cases, infrastructure in integration tests is usually mocked at something like the repository layer, and we end up with tests that do not exercise infrastructure at all. Not even inadequate in-memory replacement.

### Architectural Context
* System (`klokwrk-project`)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for realistic integration testing with external infrastructure.
- Limitations of current integration tests that mock or use in-memory infrastructure.
- Availability and norm of containerized solutions like Docker.
- Performance considerations due to container startup time.
- Desire to reuse containerized infrastructure to optimize test execution time.
- Separation of unit/internal integration tests from containerized integration tests for execution control.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use the [Testcontainers](https://www.testcontainers.org/) library and Docker for implementing realistic integration tests whenever it makes sense.

Testcontainers relies on Docker for spawning required infrastructure during integration testing. Therefore, Docker must be available on a system where tests execute. Depending on the concrete external component, starting up the container can require non-negligible time, which can prolong test execution time.

For those reasons, we will use Testcontainers library only in scenarios when a realistic external structure is really required or when having it significantly simplifies tests (e.g., when mocking external infrastructure is complex).

We must reuse containerized infrastructure whenever we can and run as much as possible test suites on the same container instances. It would be inefficient to start new containers, say, for each related test class. We can achieve it with the Testcontainers library by creating abstract parent test classes that start up containers via static initializers.

Of course, when we already have Testcontainers based tests that spawn relevant infrastructure components, we can reuse it for tests that otherwise will be simple internal application integration tests. Test execution time should not extend significantly.

Running unit tests and internal application component integration tests must be separate from running containerized integration tests. Each category of tests needs to have a different execution command. That way, we can trigger containerized tests only when appropriate.

As an example, take a look at `AbstractCommandSideIntegrationSpecification` abstract class, and related test classes `BookingOfferCommandWebControllerIntegrationSpecification` and `AbstractBookingOfferCommandApplicationServiceIntegrationSpecification`.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive
* Integration tests use realistic infrastructure components.

### Negative
* Integration tests execution time is extended.

### Neutral
* Have to use containerized tests selectively, taking into account test execution time.

alternatives.description: Mocked infrastructure.
pros: Simple and fast tests.
cons: Does not test real infrastructure integration.

alternatives.description: Alternative in-memory replacements of infrastructure components.
pros: Convenient and fast.
cons: May not behave like real infrastructure, leading to less reliable tests.

template_adherence.title: ADR-0011 - Component Testing
template_adherence.context:
When developing application monoliths, it is common to have a relatively small number of end-to-end tests (a.k.a. broad-stack tests or system tests). They are usually run on a full system, including necessary infrastructure, either by exercising UI or public system API.

When developing a microservices based system, instead of a single, we have many runnable components. They are usually grouped into corresponding bounded contexts, where each bounded context contains a group of closely related microservices. Further, depending on technology choices, each logical microservice might be split into multiple runnable components.

In an environment like that, spawning a whole system for testing might be challenging to set up and time-consuming to execute. Also, broad-stack tests are not focused on a single logical microservice, which can bring in a whole range of issues, from responsibility for development and maintenance to the expected but not yet developed system features.

For testing microservices, we need tests that have a very different focus than broad-stack tests.

Architectural Context
* System (`klokwrk-project`)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to test microservices in a microservices-based system where spawning the whole system for testing is challenging and time-consuming.
- Broad-stack tests are not focused on single logical microservices and have maintenance and responsibility issues.
- Desire to have tests focused on bounded contexts and logical microservices.
- Technical feasibility of implementing component tests using Testcontainers library.
- Need for realistic testing through public APIs of microservices.
template_adherence.decision: We will use component tests for exercising running instances of a single or multiple logical microservices inside a single bounded context. Component tests will be implemented using the Testcontainers library, containerizing both infrastructure and logical microservices under test, and exercised through the public API of the microservices.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Testing a realistic running microservice through external API as it will be used in production.
- All realistic integrations of a microservice are exercised.

Negative:
- More tests to write and maintain.
- Component tests are usually slower than focused, realistic integration tests.

Neutral:
- Only the main successful and exceptional scenarios are tested.

cons: Challenging to set up and time-consuming to execute in microservices environment.

template_adherence.title: ADR-0012 - Response Format
template_adherence.context:
Every server-side application sends some kind of responses to its clients. Unfortunately, the exact structure of these responses is rarely defined.

The most probable cause is that each **successful** response has a different content and structure as it communicates various domain data depending on the requested endpoint. Consequently, it is
impossible to prescribe a predefined structure for such responses carrying only "concrete" data in its payload.

However, there is often a need to communicate some kind of metadata with every response in more elaborate systems. While metadata can be useful for successful responses, they are almost unavoidable
for responses communicating failures. No matter if the failure cause originates from the client or the server.

The standard way for sharing metadata is through means of a concrete protocol. For example, HTTP uses statuses and headers. Messaging systems also employ headers but of different format, etc.
However, if there is a need for more detailed metadata, headers are often combined with payloads.

Such a situation brings fragmentation and inconsistency in metadata transfers, especially when multiple protocols and channels have to be supported. While standard protocol features must be obeyed,
from the application perspective, it might be helpful having all necessary data and metadata in one place.

To enable generalized creation on the server-side and generalized processing on the client-side, metadata should follow some kind of prescribed shape and format.

### Architectural Context
* System (`klokwrk-project`)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for consistent response metadata communication across different protocols and channels.
- Desire to have a prescribed shape and format for metadata to enable generalized processing.
- Avoid fragmentation and inconsistency in metadata transfer.
- Support for both successful and failure responses with metadata.
- Flexibility in implementation details to suit different protocols.
template_adherence.decision:
We will render responses following the prescribed format.

Format structure is independent of concrete protocol or channel and should be used for all generated responses.

Concrete details of the prescribed format are given in the "[The format of rendered responses](../../article/response-format/responseFormat.md)" article. Although the article presents prescribed
structures in JSON, concrete format implementation is not essential. It can be anything else that is more suitable for some chosen protocol, as long as defined structures are followed.

Implementations of response renderers are specific for each supported channel. At the moment, we have an implementation for the Spring MVC channel that can be found in `cargotracking-lib-web` module
in `org.klokwrk.cargotracking.lib.web.spring.mvc` package.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Improved consistency for response rendering on the server-side.
- Improved consistency for response handling on the client-side.
- Enablement for creating generalized implementations for both rendering and handling of response metadata.

Negative:
- The prescribed format is not defined by any standard.
- We are not using any standard metadata formats.
- We might have missed some vital metadata.
- It is quite possible that the format may be changed and evolved as we apply it in practice.

Neutral:
- The custom format might require some time to accustom and accept.

alternatives.description: No custom response format.
pros: Simplicity, no additional format to maintain.
cons: Lack of consistency in response metadata.
Harder to generalize client and server processing.

alternatives.description: Standard formats for presenting failures like "RFC 7807" or "JSON:API Error Objects".
pros: Use of established standards.
Better interoperability with other systems.
cons: May not cover all metadata needs.
Less flexibility for custom metadata.

template_adherence.title: ADR-0013 - Validation taxonomy
template_adherence.context:
With today's technologies and frameworks, validation of input data looks like a solved problem. You just add few annotations on DTOs (Data Transfer Objects), hook up the validation service with the app, and move on.

However, there are much more under the cover. When digging into the details, various questions pop up. Where exactly is the best place for input data validation? Are there multiple levels or phases of validation? What if we need a system state for validation? What happens when numerous inbound channels are in play?

After trying to answer these, it turns out that validation is more involved than what is commonly shown in basic examples. Solutions are not too complex but require establishing some principles and rules.

Architectural Context:
* System (`klokwrk-project`)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the need for consistent validation handling across multiple inbound channels, the distinction between syntactic and semantic validation phases, the requirement to validate input data both at the application facade and possibly at the adapter layer for UI-specific needs, and the necessity to organize validation to optimize performance and correctness (e.g., syntactic validations first to avoid unnecessary semantic validations).
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to execute syntactic validation at the application facade layer, with optional execution at the adapter layer for UI requirements. Validation is organized into syntactic and semantic phases, with semantic validation executed inside the domain layer either in the aggregate or application facade. Syntactic validations are stateless and executed first; semantic validations require system state and are executed after syntactic validations pass. Syntactic validation is further divided into subphases: existence, size, lexical content, and syntax format. Syntactic validation failures are reported via the validation framework (JSR 380), and semantic validation failures as domain exceptions.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include consistency and predictability in validation handling and processing. Negative consequences are noted as none.

template_adherence.title: ADR-0014 - Commit Message Format
template_adherence.context:
Using commit messages without any structure looks convenient for developers as they do not have to think about messages too much. Unfortunately, that freedom and lack of thinking can impose some additional burden on long-term project maintenance.

Quite often, we can find incomprehensible commit messages that do not communicate anything useful. Hopefully, imposing some lightweight rules and guidance will help developers create commit messages that are helpful for their colleagues.

In addition, with unstructured commit messages, there is much less opportunity to introduce any tools on top of commit history. For example, we would like to employ an automated changelog generator based on extracting some semantical meaning from commits, but this will not work if commit messages lack any structure. Without the commit message structure, we can just dump the commit log in the changelog, which does not make the changelog more helpful than looking at the history of commits in the first place.

template_adherence.title: ADR-0015 - Handling Exceptions in Distributed CQRS System
template_adherence.context:
Developers consider dealing with local (runtime) exceptions in JVM quite convenient and easy. As a consequence, exceptions are often used as a means for an alternative execution flow. One typical example is reporting structural and business validation violations.

In the local JVM environment, expected execution flow exceptions are usually created with a full stack trace included. However, as these exceptions represent "normal" conditions, creating a full stack trace is wasteful in terms of performance and resources.

The full stack trace problem is additionally emphasized in a distributed JVM environment. Not only the stack trace creation is wasteful, but it will take much more bandwidth to transfer it on the other side.

And finally, in a distributed JVM environment, we cannot safely assume that our custom exception classes are present in the classpath of both JVMs. Therefore, we can not assume the exception created on the server-side can be deserialized on the client.

To remedy the situation, we can use a small number of stack-less exception classes shared between JVMs included in the communication. They belong to the boundary layer and are part of the API used for distributed communication. To read more about boundary layer, take a look near the end of "Domain libraries" section in "[Organizing modules and packages](../../article/modules-and-packages/modulesAndPackages.md#domain-libraries)" article.

For communicating various custom exceptions, we can use violation (or error) codes. The violation code defines its severity and contains several additional properties for describing violation details.

### Architectural Context
* System (`klokwrk-project`)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to efficiently handle exceptions in a distributed JVM environment.
- Avoid performance and bandwidth overhead caused by full stack traces.
- Ensure compatibility between JVMs that may not share custom exception classes.
- Provide a consistent way to communicate error codes and details.
- Support internationalization and detailed violation information.
- Differentiate handling of expected business exceptions and unexpected exceptions.
- Maintain developer-friendly exception handling experience.
template_adherence.decision:
For distributed error reporting, we will use stack-less exceptions for communicating custom error codes between JVMs in a distributed Axon environment.

We will use the `DomainException` class and its descendants as stack-less exception DTOs carrying `ViolationInfo` with severity and violation codes. This approach leverages Axon framework's existing infrastructure for exception details.

Business exceptions will be handled without stack traces to optimize performance, while unexpected exceptions will have stack traces logged locally and use error codes for communication, with correlation identifiers for tracking.

This decision ensures consistent and optimal handling of remote business and unexpected exceptions, and identical handling of local and remote business exceptions for developers.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Consistent and optimal handling of remote business exceptions.
- Consistent and optimal handling of remote unexpected exceptions.
- Identical handling of local and remote business exceptions for developers.
- Correlation of remote unexpected exceptions.

Neutral:
- A bit unusual way of constructing exceptions.

Negative:

template_adherence.title: 0002 - API Design Framework/Documentation
template_adherence.context:
Planning and documenting an API is critical to its success. Poorly planned and undocumented APIs are difficult for end-users to build against and make building a front-end application that uses the API more difficult as well. Choosing a good API modeling should not impose a heavy burden on development, but ideally provide a strong set of tools that can be used to produce documentation, testing, and producing scaffolding for software development kits (SDKs)

There are primarily two options for a framework that are worth evaluating:
- Swagger
- RESTful API Modeling Language (RAML)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly label a 'Decision Drivers' section, but the context and decision sections imply drivers such as ease of use, community support, tooling quality, and prior experience.
template_adherence.decision:
Raster Foundry will use Swagger to design and document its API instead of using RAML for a few reasons.
- Azavea has used Swagger successfully on a few projects already and has experience using it
- The community around Swagger is larger and rooted in open source (Swagger has been donated to the Open API Initiative) and is currently at version 2.0
- The tooling around Swagger is better documented and supports a more diverse set of languages compared to RAML
template_adherence.consequences: As a consequence to choosing Swagger for documenting the API we will need to develop a Swagger specification for Raster Foundry. Ideally, we should design the API first and build it second to ensure that it is easy to use and intuitive. Additionally, we should deploy a version of the Swagger UI alongside the application to serve as documentation for end-users and to help with testing.

template_adherence.title: ADR 0004 - Static Asset Pipeline
template_adherence.context:
In selecting a static asset pipeline, there are several factors that are important to us. We don’t want to lose features that speed up developer feedback, such as a dev server with linting, auto-gen, and browser reload. The solution needs to support tests run with a single command similar to what we’ve had in previous projects. The solution needs to be fast. Some team members have expressed dissatisfaction with the stability of the NPM ecosystem, but pretty much everything relies on it to some extent, so the issue is probably best addressed elsewhere (possibly using a lazy NPM cache).

In the past, our team has used Grunt to manage and build static assets. Various team members / designers have expressed discontent with the idea of going forward using Grunt, primarily due to inherent factors such as long compile times and configuration complexity.

Other teams in Azavea have had good experiences with Webpack. Webpack is not a complete replacement for Grunt, but of the difference in functionality, it is highly likely that NPM tasks will cover it if used in conjunction. Despite scattered complaints of complexity and poor documentation found while researching, I was able to set up pipeline using npm and webpack overnight without too many issues. Significant features which are built in include a dev server capable of supporting hot reloading, very fast feedback on changes, and support for all the tools we commonly use in our applications. In addition to quality of life features, Webpack also gives us a dependency graph which includes static assets and bundle splitting. Combined with NPM, it appears to be a good solution.

A final option that we have to consider is Gulp, which has been used on a couple of projects by the Urban Apps team. Where grunt uses configuration files, Gulp uses code. Gulp’s main advantage is speed: streaming operations mean that files never touch disk between chained tasks. Other than the method of configuration and speed of operating, the basic functionality of Gulp and Grunt seem to be fairly aligned.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to maintain developer feedback speed (dev server with linting, auto-gen, browser reload).
- Support for running tests with a single command.
- Performance and speed of the solution.
- Stability concerns with NPM ecosystem.
- Past experiences with Grunt and its drawbacks.
- Positive experiences of other teams with Webpack.
- Consideration of alternatives like Gulp and their characteristics.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a combination of npm and webpack for the static asset pipeline. Npm will manage dependencies and initiate tasks, while webpack will run the dev server and build static assets. This choice is based on positive experiences within the company and the features webpack offers that align with the team's needs.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The team has no prior experience with webpack, so there will be a learning curve.
- Any required functionality not offered by webpack will be implemented using scripts through NPM or Bash, which may increase workload depending on the needs.
