template_adherence.title: Web Backend Language and Framework
template_adherence.context: A backend web framework is needed to handle web requests and coordinate with other backend components such as the database and batch processing workflows. The team has experience with Django (Python), but there are reasons to consider Scala frameworks like Play and Akka HTTP, especially due to integration with a Scala tile server and GeoTrellis. The choice involves trade-offs between Python's dynamic typing and Scala's static typing, as well as framework features and team experience.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Key drivers include the need for integration with a Scala tile server, minimizing inter-server communication complexity, language typing benefits (static vs dynamic), team experience, framework features relevant to the project (API creation, ORM availability), and risk considerations such as framework maturity and development speed.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Scala as the backend language with Akka HTTP as the framework. This choice is driven by the benefits of a unified backend language, compile-time error checking, easier refactoring, and alignment with the Scala tile server. Despite less team experience with Scala, the advantages outweigh the cons.
template_adherence.consequences: Team members must invest effort to gain Scala expertise through training, best practices, and collaboration with the GeoTrellis team. Akka HTTP's relative youth may pose risks of bugs, but fallback to Spray is possible. Unlike Django, Akka HTTP lacks built-in ORM and migration support, so additional libraries like Slick and migration tools (Scala Forklift, slick-migration-api, Flyway) will be needed.

template_adherence.title: 0006 - Workflow/Task Manager
template_adherence.context:
This ADR has been superseded by `ADR-0019`.

Some actions and features of Raster Foundry require a way to manage asynchronous tasks and workflows.
For instance, user uploads of imagery or tools may start workflows in an ad hoc manner, while in
contrast imports of imagery from NASA or partners may need to happen on a schedule. The nature of
these tasks could vary from bash scripts and python functions to spark jobs and ECS tasks.

The ideal tool will provide some means to monitor task progress, retry on some failures, and
notify personnel if necessary. There are a few options of tools we can use: celery, SWF, Luigi, and Airflow.
Azavea has experience working with both celery and SWF; however, due to our past experience with these
tools it seemed prudent to explore additional options as well.

| Workflow Tool   | Pros | Cons |
|-----------------|------|------|
| Celery          | Familiar, written in python, flexible | Provides poor primitives for workflows, many open issues, difficult to monitor workflows |
| SWF (botoflow)) | Familiar, now written in python, maintaining state is not our responsibility (HA by default), great primitives for workflows and tasks | Difficult to monitor, relatively immature tools and projects, not many others using it |
| Luigi           | Mature, seems to be stable, written in python | Unfamiliar execution model, primarily designed for scheduled, recurring task |
| Airflow         | Mature, stable, fits into our execution model, written in python, excellent UI | Requires celery (for what we want to do)), requires managing the scheduler and a cache
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage asynchronous tasks and workflows with varying nature (bash scripts, python functions, spark jobs, ECS tasks).
- Requirement for monitoring task progress, retry on failures, and notification.
- Familiarity and past experience with some tools (celery, SWF).
- Desire to explore additional options.
- Consideration of tool maturity, stability, UI, and fit with existing infrastructure.
template_adherence.decision: Raster Foundry will use Airflow as a task manager due to its large, active user base, Apache incubator status, excellent UI for monitoring tasks and workflows, support for both scheduled and ad hoc tasks, and architectural fit with existing infrastructure components like Postgres and Redis.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to become more familiar with Airflow.
- Potential need to extend Airflow's functionality if lacking in some areas.
- Challenges with task/workflow versioning as Airflow does not provide a best practice out of the box.
- Requirement to manage dependencies inside worker containers or develop custom Airflow operators.
- Need to manage worker queues for job assignment.

cons: Provides poor primitives for workflows.

template_adherence.title: Operating System and Containers
template_adherence.context:
We have used Docker containers, in various ways, on previous projects and our experience has been mixed but overall positive. Containers help to speed up CI builds and deployments, at the cost of added complexity and usage frustrations, especially for non-Linux users (most notably designers). We've decided that the best way to use Docker containers for local development is inside of a Vagrant VM, which lessens some of their benefits for local development but also improves the experience for non-Linux users.

For the past three years or so, we have used Ubuntu as the basis for every new project which required an operating system.

There are other container specifications, such as Rocket, and obviously, other Linux distributions. However, we do not have major complaints about either Docker containers or Ubuntu.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers are not explicitly titled or separated in the ADR, but can be inferred from the context and decision sections. They include: prior experience with Docker and Ubuntu, the benefits of containers for CI and deployment speed, the complexity and frustrations for non-Linux users, the desire to maintain a positive development experience for all users, and the flexibility to change container or OS technologies if needed.
template_adherence.decision: We will continue to use Docker containers to encapsulate running applications, and to use Ubuntu as our host operating system. We have developed quite a bit of experience with both Ubuntu and Docker, and we're generally satisfied with both of them, so there are not compelling reasons to make changes to such foundational components of our software stack at this point. The decision is also flexible to allow changes if necessary, and acknowledges possible use of other Linux distributions or base images in deployment on a case-by-case basis.
template_adherence.consequences: We will need to develop a Docker-centric system architecture and development environment, and determine how best to integrate Docker and Spark. We will need to continue to be vigilant about maintaining a positive development experience for non-Linux users.

alternatives.description: Use other container specifications such as Rocket, or other Linux distributions instead of Docker and Ubuntu.
pros: Potentially smaller base images for containers.
Possibility to optimize for specific deployment environments like AWS ECS.
cons: Lack of major complaints about current technologies suggests limited benefit.
Switching foundational components could introduce unforeseen issues.
Less experience with alternatives may increase risk.

template_adherence.title: 0011 - Framework for Tool UI
template_adherence.context:
Within the Tools section, Raster Foundry needs to provide an interface that allows for the linking of the user's resources with Raster Foundry's various processing tools to easily create an imagery processing pipeline from their browser. Through dragging-and-dropping components into the diagramming interface, the user will be able to specify which sources are fed into which processing tools and whether the output from these tools will be routed into another processing tool or used as a new source of imagery.

Using an already existing robust and well-maintained open-source framework will allow us to focus efforts on building the interface built around the diagramming framework rather than re-invent the wheel.

Previous research from phase 1 of ModelLab evaluated several frameworks and recommended JointJS. This ADR builds on that research, re-evaluates the recommended library to ensure it remains the best choice given the current architecture of Raster Foundry, and finalizes the decision.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a robust, well-maintained open-source diagramming framework

template_adherence.title: Map component ADR
template_adherence.context:
The current leaflet map implementation was intentionally made as a very thin wrapper. We've developed enough code around it to quantify what we need leaflet to do in raster foundry, as well as the shortcomings of our current approach.

The initial approach tries to control the leaflet map exclusively thorugh bindings to callbacks and properties. We've found that this creates a lot of complexity in the components and controllers due to the way that data must flow through components.

Ideally, components should use one-way data bindings where possible, and call bound functions in order to change data in a parent. The current way we have things set up requires all of the important state to be centralized in a parent controller, and modified through two-way bindings in child components.

Adding layers which need to be controlled by a child attribute has necessitated creating a separate binding for each type of interaction, and this has resulted in a bloated leaflet map component.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce complexity in components and controllers caused by two-way bindings and multiple bindings for interactions.
- Desire to use one-way data bindings and callbacks for state changes.
- Requirement to support multiple use cases with different map interaction needs.
- Need for efficient map layer management and event handling.
- Desire to centralize map state and utility functions in a service and wrapper.
- Avoid forcing Leaflet to fit Angular paradigms where it doesn't fit well.
template_adherence.decision:
Adopt a new architecture where the leaflet map component consolidates toggles into an 'options' attribute and uses a MapService and MapWrapper classes to manage map interactions and state.

The MapWrapper provides an API to add, update, delete geojson layers, manage layers, and handle map events with callback registration.

The MapService manages multiple MapWrapper instances, allowing components to register and deregister maps and obtain promises to interact with them.

This approach limits Angular attribute bindings and moves most map interaction to service and wrapper calls, reducing complexity and improving efficiency.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Reduced complexity in Angular components by limiting map interaction to service and wrapper calls.
- Centralized management of map state and utility functions.
- Easier to manage multiple maps on the page.
- More efficient updates to geojson layers and event handling.

Negative consequences:
- Additional manual management of how map interactions affect Angular data lifecycle.
- Potential risk of bloating the MapWrapper with too many convenience functions if not carefully managed.
- Need to carefully decide where to place utility functions (MapWrapper vs MapService).

alternatives.description: Continue using two-way bindings and multiple bindings for each map interaction in Angular components.
pros: Fits Angular's data binding paradigm directly.
No need to introduce new service or wrapper abstractions.
cons: Leads to complex components and controllers.
Bloated leaflet map component with many bindings.
Difficult to manage state and interactions efficiently.
Not scalable for multiple maps or complex interactions.

alternatives.description: Use only one-way bindings and callbacks without a centralized map service or wrapper.
pros: Simplifies data flow compared to two-way bindings.
Allows components to control map via callbacks.
cons: Still requires complex bindings for each interaction.
No centralized state management.
Potential duplication of logic across components.
Less efficient updates to map layers.

template_adherence.title: API documentation ADR
template_adherence.context:
The goal isn't to make this super complicated, but give us a basis for building out more full-fledged documentation as the project goes -- beyond just listing API endpoints (see Auth0's docs section as inspiration https://auth0.com/docs). There are javascript libraries that can assist us with parsing the swagger spec, so a good amount of the work will be purely presentational.

Of significant import is that the framework that we choose here gives us an opportunity to test out design practices and frameworks before we apply them to our primary applications. Choosing a framework here that we don't plan on using elsewhere would have significant opportunity costs. We also need to consider that Raster Foundry is almost certainly going to be transitioned over to Angular 2, and this is the only chance we will have to learn about Angular 2 before we do so. Additionally, other projects at Azavea that the Raster Foundry team work on, such as Hunchlab, are considering moving from Angular 1.X to Angular 2.X
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to choose a framework that supports building more full-fledged documentation beyond just listing API endpoints.
- Opportunity to test design practices and frameworks before applying them to primary applications.
- Consideration that Raster Foundry will transition to Angular 2, so this is a chance to learn Angular 2.
- Other projects are also considering moving from Angular 1.X to Angular 2.X.
- Need for a CMS-lite type system where code and API documentation can live side by side.
- Maintenance and ecosystem considerations of frameworks.
- Performance and future-proofing concerns.
template_adherence.decision: We will write the API documentation as a traditional SPA using Angular 2, using either Webpack or Angular CLI as a build tool. This approach allows us to accomplish our flexibility goals while also allowing us to test Angular 2 before transitioning the main Raster Foundry app over to it.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Maintaining a second application is a cost.
- Static site generators do not meet our needs, so maintaining a standalone website is preferred over maintaining a fork of a static generator.
- Angular 2 solves many issues of Angular 1.X, offering higher performance and more maintainable code.
- Angular 2 is a younger framework; some Angular 1.X libraries may not exist or be less stable.
- Component frameworks for Angular 2 are less mature, but custom components are feasible.
- Team goal to test new frameworks on smaller projects before committing to larger ones.
- Spin-up cost incurred for this application that wouldn't otherwise exist.
- Angular design practices learned will carry forward due to backporting from Angular 2 to 1 over the last 6 months.

template_adherence.title: 0016 - Initial Uploads/Imports Support

The ADR addresses how to support user uploads for initial scene creation, outlining the need to handle imagery data placement, scene metadata creation, and determining the level of ingest. template_adherence.decision: Raster Foundry will implement a two-step process where users upload data to an S3 bucket folder and then submit scene metadata via the API specifying the ingest level. template_adherence.title: 0019 - Workflow/Task Manager
template_adherence.context:
This ADR supersedes `ADR-006`.

Back in August of 2016, we went through an extensive evaluation process for a workflow manager. After looking at a number of open source and hosted solutions, we settled on Apache Airflow. Since then, we've had some success with Airflow, but also a number of setbacks.

First, we've encountered a number of deeply rooted issues with Airflow's scheduler. At times it would lock up and cease scheduling queued jobs, emitting cryptic error messages in the process. Other times, it would consume a large percentage of an instance's CPU while emitting many valueless log messages.

Second, Airflow's UI was a big differentiator in our initial decision making process. In practice, the UI proved confusing to use, and hasn't lended itself well to running in a distributed environment (e.g., task log centralization, real-time log reporting).

Lastly, our troubleshooting processes often led us to community supported help resources, like the Airflow mailing lists and issues. The more time we spent reading through these entries, the lower our confidence in Airflow became. Leadership was in a constant state of turmoil around releases, and a presence of production grade users became less and less visible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to replace Airflow due to scheduler issues and UI limitations.
- Desire for a more reliable, hosted solution.
- Concerns about community support and production readiness of Airflow.
- Need for a solution that integrates well with existing AWS infrastructure.
template_adherence.decision:
We are replacing all of the following Airflow components with AWS Batch:

- Scheduler
- Web server
- Worker
- Executor (Celery)

AWS Batch is a hosted service produced by Amazon Web Services (AWS). When used in `MANAGED` mode, it assists in scheduling, executing, and reporting status on submitted jobs. In addition, it provides a minimal UI for visually tracking job status. Under the covers, its execution environment is Amazon ECS.
template_adherence.consequences:
- By running Airflow in production for almost a year, we've gained a signifiant amount of expertise in troubleshooting issues associated with it, and the tasks it executes for us. A portion of this expertise will be lost, and will need to be rebuilt for AWS Batch.
- AWS Batch aggregates its logs in CloudWatch Logs. The is a departure from our approach of centralizing logs in Papertrail.
- The Airflow migration to AWS Batch has consumed, and will continue to consume engineering resources. Those resources could have been spent in other areas of the product.
- Because AWS Batch is a hosted service, depending on it makes it harder to make Raster Foundry a platform that can be deployed on-premise.
- We will also have to engineering a solution for enabling local development because no mechanisms exist to simulate AWS Batch locally.
- AWS Batch has no support for scheduling jobs on a recurring schedule (e.g., nightly jobs). This support will have to be engineered outside of the hosted service.

template_adherence.title: Handling Anti-meridian Artifacts in Polygon Display
template_adherence.context: Polygons crossing the anti-meridian present ambiguity in display. Various heuristics exist to address this, but none are universally correct. The problem involves determining which polygons need fixing and how to fix them.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for a practical, implementable solution that handles most cases encountered, especially for imagery sources that do not cover wide global areas. The solution should balance correctness and complexity, and be applicable to current data constraints.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a hybrid approach combining the smallest area and degree difference threshold heuristics, applied only to scene footprints. This approach is a compromise that improves upon individual heuristics and suits current imagery sources.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision provides a temporary, practical solution that handles most polygons correctly, especially for current imagery sources. However, it may still have issues with very large polygons and does not address all edge cases. It avoids complexity and is suitable until more comprehensive solutions or data sources are available.

alternatives.description: Smallest area heuristic: Calculate polygon area in two ways and choose the smaller one.
pros: Relatively simple to implement
Likely correct for most imagery
cons: Fails for polygons covering more than half the world horizontally
Imagery providers usually chop imagery to avoid this

alternatives.description: Degree difference threshold: Use coordinate difference threshold to detect crossing polygons.
pros: Only affects polygons close to the meridian
cons: Doesn't fix polygons outside threshold
False positives on small polygons near anti-meridian
Threshold tuning required

alternatives.description: Assume no polygons cross the anti-meridian.
pros: Easy to implement
Assumes polygon sources split multipolygons

template_adherence.title: 0023 - Object ACRs in text array
template_adherence.context: This ADR supersedes ADR-0020 concerning the implementation of Access Control Rules (ACRs) in Raster Foundry. The existing ACR mechanism stores access control rules in a large table, which has grown significantly, causing slow and timed-out queries, especially for scenes. Despite some optimizations, a more sustainable and faster approach is needed to handle access control queries efficiently as the data grows.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The main drivers are the need to improve query performance on access control rules, especially for scenes, to handle the growing size of the ACR table, and to maintain or improve maintainability and correctness of access control management. The solution should reduce expensive JOINs and UNIONs on large tables and support existing access control semantics.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to add text[] fields to all first-class objects to store ACRs at the object level, migrate ACRs from the centralized access_control_rules table to these object-level text arrays, create GIN indices on these fields, drop the original ACR table, and adapt all related endpoints, data models, SQL commands, and tests to use this new structure. This approach has been experimentally shown to improve query performance significantly.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include a new format for ACR strings stored in the text arrays, dropping object information from the strings and encoding subject type, optional subject id, and action type. Serialization and deserialization will be handled via doobie mappings and custom data models. CRUD operations will be adapted accordingly, leveraging PostgreSQL array functions for querying. Migration will require careful handling, possibly involving temporary tables and data copying. Access control endpoints will be adapted to restrict ACR visibility appropriately. Examples and code snippets illustrate the new data models, CRUD operations, and queries. Potential risks include migration complexity and ensuring all access control semantics are preserved.

alternatives.description: Continue using the centralized access_control_rules table with query optimizations and hardware scaling.
pros: No major schema changes required.
Existing code and queries mostly remain unchanged.
cons: Query performance issues persist as data grows.
Scaling hardware is costly and may not fully solve performance problems.
Complex queries with JOINs and UNIONs remain a bottleneck.

alternatives.description: Use a NoSQL or specialized access control system to manage ACRs separately from the main database.
pros: Potentially better scalability and performance for access control queries.
Decouples access control from main data storage.
cons: Significant architectural changes required.
Increased system complexity and maintenance overhead.
Data consistency and transactional integrity challenges.

template_adherence.title: 0025 - User Access Scopes
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to control user permissions on a different axis for the Raster Foundry API, beyond specific object instance permissions. It highlights the current limitation where access control rules are tied to specific object IDs and do not support access control across object types, such as restricting creation or deletion of certain objects. The ADR aims to develop a solution to this problem.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include minimizing performance overhead when evaluating user scopes per request, preventing certain users from creating new objects, and ideally developing a flexible approach to handle unforeseen access control scenarios.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt 'The More Granular Variation' solution. This approach treats scopes as positive permissions (presence of a scope grants access) rather than access reductions, supports granular scoping per domain (e.g., project, scenes), and promotes consistency by narrowing scope types. It is considered more flexible and intuitive at the endpoint level compared to other alternatives.
template_adherence.consequences: The chosen solution will require either multiple columns or a complex encoding/decoding process to represent scopes per domain. It promotes a granular and intuitive access control mechanism but may increase implementation complexity. It also encourages consistency in scope definitions and better aligns with future access control needs.

alternatives.description: The Basic Solution treats scopes as access reduction mechanisms with a single list of read-only scopes per user, preventing certain actions by presence of scopes.
pros: No possible conflicts as it only handles read-only restrictions
Minimal effect on current data-models, requiring only one additional field on User
cons: Only supports read-only scoping
Requires machinery to encode/decode scopes to/from the database

alternatives.description: The Wild West Solution allows a list of scopes per user with minimal constraints, e.g., ProjectReadOnly or ProjectNoDelete.
pros: Easy to add new scopes as needed

cons: Lack of constraints can cause conflicting rules requiring programmatic resolution

Requires machinery to map ObjectTypes to columns

template_adherence.title: ADR 0026 - Post-hoc Metrics Scripting
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to track metrics for events and non-events in Raster Foundry servers, including third-party services and ongoing usage data, to enable querying and visualization. template_adherence.decision: For external events, the decision is to use scheduled metric event aggregation with Lambda and Step Functions, abandoning the webhook approach due to feasibility issues. template_adherence.consequences: For external events, the consequences include the need to implement multiple Lambda functions, Step Functions, and API endpoints, as well as mechanisms to prevent duplicate metric entries. For non-events, consequences include creating a new usage_data table, asynchronous backfill jobs, and Lambda functions to respond to S3 SNS events to maintain accurate usage data.

template_adherence.title: 0027 Annotate Project STAC Export
template_adherence.context:
This is an ADR documenting decisions made on MVP features of exporting Raster Foundry/Annotate label data and scenes in STAC-compliant catalogs. This aims to make us one step closer towards integrating STAC to the path of interoperability among Azavea’s Machine Learning workflow.

In Raster Foundry, we support creating geospatial labels based on images and scenes added to project layers. This feature is further extended in Annotate App, which is an application backed by Raster Foundry APIs, so that teams can work on an image labeling projects simultaneously within status-tracked tasks. To enable downstream Machine Learning work better in interoperating these ground truth labels, we have decided to implement a feature for exporting images and labels in STAC catalogs in an asynchronous manner. The following sections will go into details about the export process, the structure of the exported catalog, and where they are stored.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to export Raster Foundry/Annotate label data and scenes in STAC-compliant catalogs.
- Support asynchronous export process.
- Ensure access control and permissions for export operations.
- Structure exported catalogs to reflect project layers, scenes, and labels.
- Store exported catalogs on S3 for environment-specific access.
- Facilitate interoperability with Machine Learning workflows.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement CRUD endpoints for STAC exports under `api/stac`, create a STAC catalog builder that structures exports into Layer, Scene, and Label collections, and use AWS batch jobs to build exports asynchronously. Exported catalogs are stored on environment-specific S3 buckets with links between resources, initially using absolute links except for root links which are relative. Access control is enforced for export operations, and the export process includes filtering labels by task statuses.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Provides a standardized way to export label and scene data in STAC format.
- Enables asynchronous export processing via AWS batch jobs.
- Ensures exports are stored and accessible on S3 buckets.
- Access control restricts export operations to authorized users.
- Initial use of absolute links may require future updates to relative links for better interoperability.
- Sets foundation for future enhancements such as notifications and export masks.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly discussed in the ADR, but alternatives could include synchronous export processing, different storage mechanisms, or different API designs.
pros: Synchronous processing might simplify implementation.
cons: Synchronous processing could lead to long wait times and poor user experience.
Different storage mechanisms might not integrate well with existing infrastructure.

template_adherence.title: Use scala-opentracing for tracing implementation
template_adherence.context: Our tile servers are under constant load, making it difficult to analyze logs and gather useful metrics for request-response transformations. template_adherence.decision_drivers: We need a tracing library that is maintainable, easy to start with, integrates well with our stack, and supports exporting traces to external services. The library should have reasonable community support and be practical for production use.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to use scala-opentracing for our initial tracing implementation because it is easier to get started with, has a maintainer responsible for a production system, and supports logging and exporting traces to Jaeger. template_adherence.consequences: We will add scala-opentracing to our codebase and start with a logging tracer. We will need to set up infrastructure for trace storage, possibly using AWS X-Ray or Jaeger. We must decide what to trace and configure sampling appropriately to balance observability and performance impact.

template_adherence.title: 3. Redux architecture pattern
template_adherence.context:
We are doing a rewrite.

Holochain Go code shows many implicit dependencies between different modules and stateful objects. In conjunction with the complexity of a p2p network of agents, this leads to a level of overall complexity that feels too much to manage. A clean and fitting architecture for this Rust rebuild is needed.

Having a single global state within the agent feels appropriate and even balancing the distributed nature of the network of agents.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly titled as 'Decision Drivers', but the context section implies drivers such as managing complexity, reducing implicit dependencies, and fitting a clean architecture for the Rust rebuild.
template_adherence.decision:
The new holochain architecture will follow a redux architecture in order for an agent to have one global state.

We will apply nested state objects which represent a state tree, with sub states for each module.

We use reference counting smart pointers for the sub states such that it is possible for each module's reducer to decide if the sub state is to be mutated or reused.
template_adherence.consequences:
Holochain refactor must fit this new model of having State objects and Actions objects.

Each module of the Holochain agent only needs to depend on the state and not on other modules, which helps decoupling and thus reduces code dependencies.

This will also make it easy to have time-machine debugging capabilities (by storing old states), and easy logging and (remote) monitoring of agents (by sending serialized state objects to monitor client).

The processing of redux-like actions through each modules reducer might cause a constant performance overhead.

template_adherence.title: 7. Abstraction for network layer
template_adherence.context:
In switching to Rust, we can no longer use libp2p directly, and we want our own Kademlia implementation anyways (see ADR: 0010)
What we want from a network library:
* Public Key cryptography for end-to-end encryption.
* Hash of public key as network address which wraps the transport layer for use by DHT.
* Possibility of multiple transport layers.
* Built in support for NAT/firewall traversal for case of IP transport.

Updated 7/20 context:

* Conversations with the IPFS folks about libp2p as well as its wider adoption by hyperledger and parity/polkadot as a P2P transport layer, along with the progress of libp2p-rust, and thinking about strategic alignment with other efforts and stewarding of our dev resources make it a more interesting candidate to use as a transport layer to handle the above requirements.
* ZeroMQ looks very interesting.
* neonphog has written lib3 as a prototyping transport.
* Promether questions.
template_adherence.decision:
1. Write our own abstraction layer for the networking library with an API that allows us to build against our needs, and thus makes it easier to choose/switch a networking stack.
2. Assume that this allows connection to a directly compiled-in p2p layer or connection via thin layer to a p2p transport system service (see ADR #14)
3. Assume transport layer handles all multiplexing across different physical transports as well as topological problems (NAT relay etc)
template_adherence.consequences:
* This abstraction is to allow us to switch between transport solutions, and is not explicitly designed for bridging between them, i.e. assumes that routing is handled.
* The kademlia re-implementation we will do (ADR #10) is about updating an maintaining app world model for data resiliency, not routing.

template_adherence.title: 12. Generalized Randomness for Holochain applications
template_adherence.context: Distributed applications, like centralized ones, often need a source of randomness. Having confidence and verifiability of that randomness poses particular challenges in the distributed context. Specifically, we need a source of randomness with some of the following properties: 1. It is outside their control or influence so it can be used for a dice roll, card deck shuffle, or something where they may have an interest in skewing the results. 2. It is predictably reproducable, so that other nodes, whether players in a game, or validating nodes later, can reproduce the SAME random seed to reach the same random output for purposes of validation. 3. It is generalizable. Ideally, every application won't have to build their own approach to randomness, but can take advantage of a useful underlying convention. There are pitfalls we want to help them avoid in a distributed, eventually consistent system. 4. It doesn't require specific parties to be online to access the randomness data, so that later validators can confirm it even if parties with private entries are not online or no longer part of the network. In the case of multiple parties wanting to generate randomness together, cointoss provides an example of sharing of the hash of a secret which when later revealed can be combined to create a random number seed. This method can be generalized into storing a bunch of private secrets, and publishing the hashes of those secrets, and then later revealing the secret to be combined with another party doing the same. In cointoss this revelation happens via node-to-node communication, but in the general case it doesn't have to work that way. Our application environment includes interactions (gossip and validation) the combination of which are highly unpredictable (they include things like network latency, and timestamps) but verifiable after the fact. So for example, using the "first" four validation signatures on your opponent's last move as a random seed, could be one approach.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a source of randomness that is outside control or influence, reproducible for validation, generalizable for multiple applications, and accessible without requiring specific parties to be online. Also, the desire to leverage existing methods like cointoss and unpredictable gossip/validation events for randomness generation.
template_adherence.decision: We will: 1. Implement mixins to provide randomness generation for some usecases using the cointoss combined secret method (both n2n for single events, and dht pushed for multiple events) 2. Provide app level access to unpredictable gossip/validation events for explicit use as seeds for random number generators.
template_adherence.consequences: - Our approach will need to be reviewed as proof of the validity of these approaches (included in security reviews). - We need to add protocol/calls/callbacks in the network abstraction layer (See ADR 7) to gain access to this randomness.

template_adherence.title: 13. Signal/Listener model and API
template_adherence.context:
In the go code we used polling from the UI to discover local state changes, be they in the source-chain or in the DHT.  We want to change this to an event based model where UI (or other clients, like bridged apps) can become listeners to signals.  Additionally there are system level signals (like warrants) as well as other app level definable signals that we want consumers of exposed holochain app APIs to be able to access on a push (i.e. listening) basis.

Note that this is only about signals that can be listened to by conductor context, i.e. by the client of the core_api, NOT by the app nodes themselves.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to move from a polling model to an event-based model for UI and other clients.
The requirement to support system level and app level signals accessible via push.
Clarification that signals are for conductor context clients, not app nodes.
Desire to follow a known pattern (Signal-slot) for API design.
template_adherence.decision:
We will extend the API in a way roughly equivalent to the Signal-slot pattern, including:
- Declaring observable signals in the DNA similar to function declarations.
- Allowing app developers to emit signals via a new emit() function.
- Providing core_api methods to register and unregister listeners (listen() and unlisten()).
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to clarify when emit() calls are valid (e.g., during validations and genesis).
- Ensure app developers understand signals are client-specific, not global.
- Consider which system signals to emit.
- Create a separate ADR for signals between nodes at the DHT level.
- Enforce capability-based permissions for listeners.
- Decide between full pub/sub model or direct signal/slot pattern for producer-subscriber interaction.

template_adherence.title: 14. P2P - IPC Abstraction
template_adherence.context:
Rust as a language, in my opinion, does not lend itself to rapid prototyping. Writing efficient Rust code, while absolutely possible, is a problem domain unto itself, and takes time. E.g. Is it worth returning borrowed references in this case to save memory? Am I able to craft the lifetimes appropriately given all the other api usages of my struct? What about synchronization? These questions are implementation details, not architectural. If we are still working out the details with the underlying architecture, we don't want to be spending brainpower on * how * we accomplish our experiments.

In this prototyping / proof-of-concept phase, I don't want to take the time to write efficient rust code, but I don't want to leave us with a bunch of unmaintainable inefficient spaghetti if we *do* decide to go forward with the prototype.
template_adherence.decision:
Abstract the p2p library at the process level.

- The P2P process will host a [ZeroMQ](http://zeromq.org/) ROUTER socket. This process can be in any language that supports zmq, and using any of the transports it supports. (Likely start with unix domain sockets for their high throughput).
- The holochain rust code will connect to the P2P process with a ROUTER socket using the [zmq](https://crates.io/crates/zmq) crate.
- The holochain rust code will access this ipc abstraction through the [network-abstraction](0007-abstraction-for-network-layer.md) framework allowing the option to implement, for example, the rust version of libp2p both internally, and as a separate process.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Pros
* Ability to prototype and experiment with p2p solutions in other languages (including the more mature nodejs version of [libp2p](https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p)).
* Separation of concerns in terms of security and stability.
* Multiple Holochain processes can share the overhead (cpu, memory, bandwidth) of a single p2p network connection.

### Cons
* Work overhead for creation of additional abstraction layer.
* Additional complexity for system setup / maintanence for both developers and end-users. That is, they will have to start up / configure two processes instead of one.

template_adherence.title: Capabilities & Security ADR
template_adherence.context:
A unified security model for Holochain applications:
* Each zome must be able to represent and enforce its own security modeling because that is the appropriate place to do so. (Push the intelligence to the edges.)
* Developers must be able to build in granualar specificity and revokability of access to functions and entries.
* We must be able to distinguish between application security model, and architectural and code security model.  I.e. what is the security model application developers build into their apps, and the security model of Conductor/Core, etc.  E.g. we have to ensure that zome calls aren't subject to replay attacks in general, and also allow zome developers to declare and create security policies in specific.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a unified security model that allows granular and revokable access control.
- Distinction between application-level security and architectural/code security.
- Requirement to prevent replay attacks and allow developers to specify security policies.
- Desire to push security intelligence to the edges (each zome).
- Support for various call types: end-user UI, cross-zome, bridging, and querying private entries.
template_adherence.decision: Holochain will use a variant of the capabilities security model. DNA instances will grant revokable, cryptographic capability tokens shared as access credentials. Access to functions and private data requires appropriate credentials. Capability grants are recorded as private entries on the grantor's chain and validated on every zome function call. This model supports multiple call types and enforces security consistently.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Provides a unified, flexible, and revokable security model.
- Enables secure access control for various call types including cross-zome and bridging.
- Allows fine-grained control and prevention of replay attacks.
- Negative: Requires implementation of capability token management and validation.
- May add complexity in managing grants and requests.
- Necessitates conventions for public tokens and zome mix-in security.

alternatives.description: Use a traditional role-based access control (RBAC) model instead of capability-based security.
pros: Well-understood and widely used model.
Simpler to implement in some contexts.
cons: Less flexible and fine-grained than capability-based model.
Harder to support revokable and transferable tokens.
May not support cross-zome and bridging calls securely.

alternatives.description: Rely solely on cryptographic signatures and public key infrastructure without capability tokens.
pros: Simplifies token management.
Leverages existing cryptographic mechanisms.
cons: Lacks fine-grained access control.
Difficult to revoke or transfer access rights.
Does not easily support complex access policies.

template_adherence.title: 2. NOSCRIPT nodes
template_adherence.context: HTML pages can contain `noscript` nodes, which reveal their contents only in case when JavaScript is not available. Most of the time they contain hidden messages that inform about certain JavaScript-dependent features not being operational, however sometimes can also feature media assets or even iframes.
template_adherence.decision: When the document is being saved with or without JavaScript, each `noscript` node should be preserved while its children need to be processed exactly the same way as the rest of the document. This approach will ensure that even hidden remote assets are embedded — since those hidden elements may have to be displayed later in a browser that has JavaScript turned off. An option should be available to "unwrap" all `noscript` nodes in order to make their contents always visible in the document, complimenting the "disable JS" function of the program.
template_adherence.consequences: Saved documents will have contents of all `noscript` nodes processed as if they are part of the document's DOM, therefore properly display images encapsulated within `noscript` nodes when being viewed in browsers that have JavaScript turned off (or have no JavaScript support in the first place). The new option to "unwrap" `noscript` elements will help the user ensure that the resulting document always represents what the original web page looked like in a browser that had JavaScript turned off.

template_adherence.title: 8. Base Tag
template_adherence.context:
HTML documents may contain `base` tag, which influences resolution of anchor links and relative URLs as well as dynamically loaded resources.

Sometimes, in order to make certain saved documents function closer to how they operate while being served from a remote server, the `base` tag specifying the source page's URL may need to be added to the document.

There can be only one such tag. If multiple `base` tags are present, only the first encountered tag ends up being used.
template_adherence.decision:
Adding the `base` tag should be optional — saved documents should not contain the `base` tag unless it was specified by the user, or the document originally had the `base` tag in it.

Existing `href` attribute's value of the original `base` tag should be used for resolving the document's relative links instead of document's own URL (precisely the way browsers do it).
template_adherence.consequences:
#### If the base tag does not exist in the source document

- If the base tag does not exist in the source document
- With base URL option provided
- use the specified base URL value to retrieve assets, keep original base URL value in the document
- Without base URL option provided
- download document as usual, do not add base tag
-  If the base tag already exists in the source document
- With base URL option provided
- we overwrite the original base URL before retrieving assets, keep new base URL value in the document
- Without base URL option provided:
- use the base URL from the original document to retrieve assets, keep original base URL value in the document

The program will obtain ability to retrieve remote assets for non-remote sources (such as data URLs and local files).

The program will obatin ability to get rid of existing base tag values (by provind an empty one).

template_adherence.title: Use `public final` instead of getters to offer access to immutable variables

template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "Offer public static field", because getters used to be a convention which was even more manifested due to libraries depending on the existence on getters/setters. In the case of immutable variables, adding public getters is just useless since one is not hiding anything.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Shorter code

Negative Consequences:
* newcomers could get confused, because getters/setters are still taught

alternatives.description: Offer public static field
pros: Shorter code
cons: Newcomers could get confused, because getters/setters are still taught

alternatives.description: Offer getters
pros: Follows common Java convention
Compatible with libraries expecting getters/setters
cons: Adds unnecessary code for immutable variables

template_adherence.title: Handle different bibentry formats of fetchers by adding a layer
template_adherence.context: All fetchers (except IDFetchers) in JabRef return BibEntries when fetching entries from their API. Some fetchers directly receive BibTeX entries from their API, the other fetchers receive their entries in some kind of exchange format such as JSON or XML and then parse this into BibEntries. Currently, all fetchers either return BibEntries in BibTeX or BibLaTeX format. This can lead to importing BibEntries of one format in a database of the other format. How can this inconsistency between fetchers, and their used formats be addressed?
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to handle inconsistencies between different bibentry formats returned by fetchers, to ensure separation of concerns, minimize code changes in fetchers, centralize conversion logic, and maintain extensibility and testability of the import process.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to introduce a new layer between fetchers and caller, such as a FetcherHandler, that manages the conversion. This approach composes all steps required during importing, not only format conversion of fetched entries, and isolates conversion logic from fetchers and callers.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include separation of concerns, no need for fetchers or other code to handle conversion, extensibility for future import procedure changes, and centralized management of conversion steps. Negative consequences include the requirement for significant code changes and the need for extensive testing of the new layer.

alternatives.description: Pass fetchers the format, they have to create entries accordingly (in the correct format).
pros: Fetchers handle BibEntry creation in their format of choice, which is part of their responsibility.
Fetchers only create BibEntries of the correct format, reducing chances of wrong format propagation.
Conversion does not have to take place.
cons: Fetchers must know all differences of the formats, cluttering the code.
This code has to be tested, and conversion already exists.

alternatives.description: Pass fetchers the format, they have to call a conversion method if necessary (in the correct format).
pros: Less code has to be written than the option where fetchers create entries accordingly.
Code is already tested.
Keeps all conversion code centralized, promoting code reuse.
cons: Fetcher first creates the BibEntry in a possibly wrong format, which can lead to bugs due to code changes.
Adds dependency.

alternatives.description: Let the caller handle any format inconsistencies and the conversion.
pros: Fetcher code does not have to change.
Fetcher only has to fetch and does not need to know anything about the formats.
cons: Programmers might assume a certain format is used, which may not be true, causing issues.
At every place where fetchers are used and format matters, conversion has to be used, creating more dependencies.

alternatives.description: Introduce a new layer between fetchers and caller, such as a FetcherHandler, that manages the conversion.
pros: Fetchers do not have to think about conversion (Separation of concerns).
No other code that currently relies on fetchers has to do the conversion.
This layer can be used for any kind of import to handle all conversion steps, not only format.
This layer can easily be extended if the import procedure changes.
cons: Requires a lot of code changes.
Has to be tested extensively.

template_adherence.context:
All libraries use their own query syntax for advanced search options. To increase usability, users should be able to formulate their (abstract) search queries in a query syntax that can be mapped to the library specific search queries. To achieve this, the query has to be parsed into an AST.

template_adherence.title: Only spread props on "form-like" components
template_adherence.context:
When should we spread props in components?

Example:

const Component = ({ foo, bar, ...restProps}) => {
<element foo={foo} bar={bar} {...restProps} />
}

If we spread rest props on every component, we create an opportunity for developers to customize components via code instead of explicitly defined props.

For components that render attribute-heavy DOM elements (like `button`), it may make sense to spread props. For more complex components, spreading props could lead to bugs, side effects, and unnecessary customization.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the need to balance flexibility and explicitness in component props, avoiding bugs and side effects from overusing spread props, and maintaining clear and maintainable prop interfaces especially for complex components.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen option is "Only components that render attribute-heavy DOM elements spread rest props". This compromise allows creating the right prop interface for each component's job. Components mapping to attribute-heavy DOM elements (like HTML form elements) will allow spread props to keep explicitly defined props easier to reason about, while other components (e.g., Toast) will define explicit prop interfaces without spreading props.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include clearer and more maintainable prop interfaces for complex components and flexibility for form-like components. Negative consequences include inconsistent behavior across components and the need to document when a component supports spread props.

alternatives.description: Every component spreads rest props.
pros: Maximum flexibility for developers to customize components via code.
cons: Can lead to bugs, side effects, and unnecessary customization.
Makes it harder to reason about component props.

alternatives.description: No components spread rest props.
pros: Explicit prop interfaces for all components.
Easier to reason about component behavior.
cons: Less flexible for components that could benefit from spreading props, such as attribute-heavy DOM elements.

alternatives.description: Only components that render attribute-heavy DOM elements spread rest props.
pros: Balances flexibility and explicitness.
Allows form-like components to spread props for convenience.
Keeps complex components explicit to avoid bugs.
cons: Not all components behave the same way regarding prop spreading.
Requires documentation to clarify which components support spread props.

template_adherence.title: Components Ignore `classNames`
template_adherence.context: Some components in FDS would suffer from accepting a `classNames` prop. `Flex`, for example, would no longer guarantee it would work as a basic layout utility if we allowed arbitrary style overrides on the component. template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to maintain layout utility guarantees and consistent prop interfaces across all components, and to avoid risky style overrides via arbitrary class names.
template_adherence.decision: No components accept a `className` because it's too risky to introduce style overrides to low-level layout components, and style customization should happen via props, where the component can be responsible for style changes and variations.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include prop API consistency across all components. Negative consequences include that consumers of FDS components must handle the breaking change, moving any custom `className` props to a direct parent or child of the component.

pros: Allows style overrides via class names on components.
cons: Risky to introduce style overrides to low-level layout components.

pros: Maintains layout utility guarantees.

cons: Breaking change for consumers who use `className` props.

template_adherence.title: When to build a utility class
template_adherence.context: We take a utility class based approach (aka "functional CSS" aka "expressive CSS") in FDS. We have a lot of utility classes that do only one thing (e.g. `display--none`). At one point, we discussed adding a `position--relative` class, which led us to a key question we needed to clarify: When does it make sense to add a utility class?
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to clarify when it makes sense to add a utility class, balancing between adding any property/value combination and only adding utility classes that are useful on their own, considering the utility and API surface area.
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "Only add utility classes that are useful on their own". This decision was made because utility classes should be useful as a single unit, keeping the API surface smaller and avoiding functionally useless classes.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a smaller API surface area and utility classes that are useful on their own. Negative consequence is that it requires a judgment call on each candidate utility class, which may add some decision overhead.

alternatives.description: Add a utility class for any property/value combination as needed.
pros: It's a rule that can be universally applied without any additional decision making.
cons: Would eventually lead to a large number of functionally useless classes.

alternatives.description: Only add utility classes that are useful on their own.
pros: Utility classes will only be introduced when they're useful as a single unit.
The utility class API surface area will remain smaller.
cons: It takes a judgment call on each candidate for a utility class.

template_adherence.title: Utilize relative spacing through tshirt sizes
template_adherence.context: We'd like to change the spacing system to something more generic.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The current pattern of relative spacing (half, double) that's based on a default, is deficient in a couple of ways:

- We'd like to add additional spacing values that don't map cleanly to these words. If default spacing is 16, there's no clean word to describe the jump to 24.
- The current model makes it impossible to ever cleanly change the default value. Given the model of default, half, and double, if we decided to make double the new default, the current default would have to be renamed to half, and half would need to be renamed to half/half.
template_adherence.decision:
Generic tshirt system was chosen over the other options.

- Coding a direct "arbitrary value" into a CSS class (color, number representing a unit) is generally considered an anti-pattern for reasons that are too long to cover in this ADR.
- We like the numbering system but we use t-shirt sizes everywhere else in our system so it makes sense to skew towards alignment with the larger system.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
- By doing this we were able to add additional spacing classes without any friction and we'll be able to add / remove these easily in the future.
- It's very easy to change what our default spacing is now if we so choose.

Negative Consequences:
- The jumps are arbitrary and it's not always immediately clear to an engineer how a relative jump maps to the raw spacing value.

alternatives.description: Encode the value directly in the class. padding-16 / margin-x-32
Use generic numbering system (padding-2 / margin-x-4)
Use generic tshirt system (padding-s / margin-x-l)

template_adherence.title: ADR002 - Concourse pool resource
template_adherence.context: When building pipelines using concourse, we investigated using the pool resource in order to control flow through jobs. This was an alternative to the use of the semver resource. These 2 resources are both workarounds to solve the problem of triggering jobs when we haven't made changes to a resource. The problem is that the pool resource relies on write access to a github repo, which means we must pass public keys that allow this access into the pipeline and deployed concourse instance - we want to minimise the number of credentials we pass, and the semver resource relies on AWS credentials that are already passed.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to control flow through jobs in concourse pipelines without triggering jobs unnecessarily. Minimizing the number of credentials passed into the pipeline and deployed concourse instance. The pool resource requires write access to a GitHub repo (public keys), which is a security concern. The semver resource relies on AWS credentials that are already passed, making it preferable.
template_adherence.decision: We will not use the pool resource for flow between jobs - instead we will use the semver resource.
template_adherence.consequences: This was an investigation into a different approach, so no consequences.

alternatives.description: Use the pool resource to control flow between jobs.
pros: Provides a mechanism to control job flow in concourse pipelines.
cons: Requires write access to a GitHub repo, necessitating passing public keys into the pipeline and deployed concourse instance, increasing credential exposure.

alternatives.description: Use the semver resource to control flow between jobs.
pros: Relies on AWS credentials that are already passed, minimizing additional credential exposure.
Provides a workaround to trigger jobs without changes to a resource.
cons: May have limitations compared to the pool resource in some scenarios.

template_adherence.title: ADR003 - AWS credentials
template_adherence.context:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) are our current Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) provider. Our deployment tooling (Concourse, Terraform, BOSH, etc.) and Cloud Foundry components (Cloud Controller, RDS broker, blobstore clients, etc.) use the APIs to manage or access IaaS resources.

The most common mechanism for authenticating the API calls is to create an Identify and Access Management (IAM) user with the appropriate permissions, generate an Access Key ID and Secret Access Key for that user, and export those as environment variables. `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` are the standard environment variable names used by most utilities and libraries.

The problem with this approach is that it's very easy to accidentally leak the plain text keys. They can appear in output from your shell, which you might copy+paste into a gist or email when debugging a problem. You might add them to your shell configuration or include them in a script, which can be pushed to a public code repository.

Our team have leaked keys like this on more than one occasion. It's worth noting that even if you realise that you've done this, delete the commit and revoke the keys, they may have already been used maliciously because automated bots monitor sites like GitHub using the [events firehose][] to detect any credentials.

[events firehose]: https://developer.github.com/v3/activity/events/

As an alternative to using pre-generated keys, AWS recommends that you use [IAM roles and instance profiles][] when accessing the API from EC2 instances. You delegate permissions to the EC2 instance and temporary credentials are made available from the instance metadata service. Most tools and libraries automatically support this. The credentials are regularly rotated and never need to be stored in configuration files.

[IAM roles and instance profiles]: http://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html#use-roles-with-ec2
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce the likelihood of leaking AWS keys.
- Need to reduce the impact of leaked AWS keys.
- Use of AWS IAM best practices and recommendations.
- Compatibility with existing deployment tooling and Cloud Foundry components.
- Security concerns about storing plain text keys.
- Operational considerations for managing credentials.
- Limitations of IAM roles and instance profiles in containerized environments.
- Requirement to manage IAM roles, profiles, and policies centrally.
template_adherence.decision:
To reduce the likelihood of us leaking AWS keys we will use IAM roles and instance profiles for all operations that run from EC2 instances. This includes everything that happens within Concourse and Cloud Foundry.

To reduce the impact of us leaking AWS keys we will use an IAM policy with an [`aws:SourceIp` condition][condition] to enforce that IAM accounts for team members are only used from the office IP addresses.

The IAM roles, profiles, and policies will be managed by our [aws-account-wide-terraform][] repo.
template_adherence.consequences:
- AWS keys will still be needed for operations outside EC2, requiring careful handling.
- Using IAM profiles means any process on the VM can access the same credentials, which is a drawback for assigning credentials to specific processes in different containers.
- Maintenance of forks of some Concourse resources to add support for IAM roles and instance profiles.
- Requirement to use office VPN to administer AWS from outside the office, with disaster recovery provisions for VPN connectivity.
- Overall improved security posture by reducing plain text key exposure.

alternatives.description: Continue using pre-generated AWS Access Key ID and Secret Access Key as environment variables for authentication.
pros: Simple and widely supported method.
No changes needed to existing tooling or processes.
cons: High risk of accidental key leakage through shell output, scripts, or public repositories.
Keys are static and require manual rotation.
Leaked keys can be used maliciously before revocation.

alternatives.description: Use IAM roles and instance profiles for EC2 instances to provide temporary credentials automatically.
pros: Credentials are temporary and rotated automatically.
No need to store keys in configuration files.
Reduces risk of key leakage.
Supported by most AWS tools and libraries.
cons: All processes on the VM share the same credentials, which may not be ideal for containerized environments.
Requires changes to tooling and processes.
Some Concourse resources do not support IAM roles out of the box, requiring forks.

template_adherence.title: ADR004 - Domain naming scheme
template_adherence.context:
As part of our deployment we have a pipeline, where changes that are made can move from a development environment through to production illustrated thusly:

![pipeline image](../images/pipeline.jpg)

There are a number of externally available endpoints that are accessed to manage and view information about the platform, as well as issue commands via the Cloud Foundry API. In addition to this, a URL also needs to be available to access Apps hosted on the platform. These need to be accessed via some sort of sensible URL.

The reason for splitting system domains from app domains was to prevent applications from stealing traffic to CF components (for example, api.<domain>) or masquerading as official things of the platform (for example, signup.<domain>).

### Naming considerations
A number of aspects were considered as part of the naming process.

* Clear sense of purpose
* Clear distinction between Production and other Environments
* No overly technical names (for example, hosting/paas/scalable-elastic-public-government-hosting)
* Prevent possibility of domains suggesting 'live' service, for example if we allowed [app name].paas.gov.uk it could appear as thought they were live services.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for clear and sensible URL naming for different environments and apps.
- Separation of system domains from app domains to prevent security and impersonation issues.
- Clear distinction between production and non-production environments.
- Avoidance of overly technical or misleading domain names.
- Support for pipeline stages from development to production.
template_adherence.decision:
For non-production environments, use domains like [environment name].cloudpipeline.digital and [app name].[environment name].cloudpipelineapps.digital.

For production, use cloud.service.gov.uk and [app name].cloudapps.digital.

Live services will use 'Bring Your Own' domains; apps on cloudapps.digital are not live production applications.
template_adherence.consequences:
Certificates and domains had to be purchased and registered.
Automated deployments were configured to specify domains for each pipeline stage.
Clear domain naming helps prevent security issues and confusion.
Potential overhead in managing multiple domains and certificates.

alternatives.description: Use a single domain for all environments and apps, differentiating only by subdomains or paths.
pros: Simpler domain management.
Easier to remember base domain.
cons: Higher risk of confusion between environments.
Potential security risks if apps can masquerade as system components.
Less clear distinction between production and non-production.

alternatives.description: Allow apps to use production domains directly without 'Bring Your Own' domains.
pros: Simplifies app deployment in production.
No need for customers to bring their own domains.
cons: Risk of apps appearing as official platform components.
Security concerns with domain impersonation.
Less control over domain usage.

template_adherence.title: ADR0048: Include record for services/resources provisioned for tenants
template_adherence.context:
The GOV.UK PaaS billing system receives a series of events from Cloud Foundry notifying, for each tenant, whether services or resources have been created, renamed, or deleted.

The original GOV.UK PaaS billing system translated the Cloud Foundry events into records of services/resources by calendar month before calculating the final monthly bill for each tenant. This process, called billing consolidation, was done at the start of every month and there was no persistent record of the results of each stage of processing, including what services or resources tenants had provisioned. After each stage of processing database tables were populated but the contents of these tables were impermanent, being refreshed the next time billing consolidation was run.

If there is a problem with a tenant's bill it was very difficult to find the source of the problem.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for persistent record of tenant services/resources to avoid regenerating historical data each billing run; improve ability to investigate billing discrepancies; enable more flexible billing calculations (e.g., between any two dates/times).
template_adherence.decision:
We need to have a persistent record of the services or resources each tenant has provisioned with dates indicating when the service or resource was/is being used. This persistent record is in the new `resources` table.

The reason for this is that there is no need to regenerate historical records of services or resources provisioned for tenants each time billing is run each month since this information does not change. Furthermore, recording this information for each month makes it difficult for us to calculate bills between any two dates and times.

The `resources` table also acts as an audit point within GOV.UK PaaS billing. It makes investigation of discrepancies in tenant bills easier to investigate. Anyone supporting GOV.UK PaaS billing can first look at the contents of `resources` and see whether the discrepancy arose in the population of `resources` or afterwards in the actual calculation of the bill.
template_adherence.consequences:
This makes billing easier to support. It also makes billing run much more quickly since we do not need to go through all the Cloud Foundry events whenever we need to calculate tenant bills. With this method we can calculate tenants' bills on-demand, rather than calculating all bills in advance as original GOV.UK PaaS billing system did, so it opens up the possibility of the following:
- Calculating bills between any 2 dates and times quickly
- It is easier to break down bills by org, space, etc., or, later on, by annotation

template_adherence.title: Decouple what we're calculating bills for from how the bills are calculated
template_adherence.context:
Tenants provision a wide variety of services and AWS/Aiven resources via GOV.UK PaaS. We need to calculate bills for these services/resources. GOV.UK PaaS billing receives notifications of when services or resources are created, renamed, or deleted from upstream in the form of events from Cloud Foundry.

The original GOV.UK PaaS billing system translated the Cloud Foundry events into records of services/resources by calendar month before calculating the final monthly bill for each tenant. This process, called billing consolidation, was done at the start of every month and there was no persistent record of the results of each stage of processing, including what services or resources tenants had provisioned. After each stage of processing database tables were populated but the contents of these tables were impermanent, being refreshed the next time billing consolidation was run.

In the GOV.UK PaaS billing rewrite, this has been changed. We want to calculate bills for variable time periods and also to forecast bills for the future (for the web-based billing calculator). However, the method to calculate the actual bill always needs to be the same.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to calculate bills for variable time periods and forecast future bills.
- Maintain a single source of truth for bill calculation.
- Decouple the data about what is being billed from the calculation method.
- Support different code entry points for billing (e.g., tenants, prospective tenants).
- Enable tailored billing reports and filtering capabilities.
template_adherence.decision: The code to calculate the bill has been decoupled from the code used to determine what is being billed. The approach is to first populate a temporary database table with the resources and time intervals to be billed, then call a stored function to calculate the bill using only the contents of that temporary table. This allows the same calculation code to be used for all billing scenarios, ensuring consistency.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Single source of truth for all bill calculations.
- Ability to calculate bills for tenants and prospective tenants using the same code.
- Flexibility to have different code entry points into billing by varying how the temporary table is populated.
- Easier tailoring of billing reports and filtering by input fields.
- Simplifies the billing calculator on the GOV.UK PaaS website by reusing calculation logic.

alternatives.description: Keep the original monolithic billing consolidation process that runs monthly and does not persist intermediate results.
pros: Simplicity in the existing process.
No need to redesign the billing system.
cons: Inflexible billing periods (only monthly).
No support for forecasting future bills.
No persistent record of intermediate processing stages.
Difficult to tailor billing reports or support different billing scenarios.

alternatives.description: Use a fully embedded SQL approach without stored functions for bill calculation.
pros: Potentially simpler codebase without stored procedures.
Easier to modify calculation logic in application code.
cons: Risk of code duplication if calculation logic is repeated.
Harder to ensure a single source of truth for bill calculation.
Potential performance issues compared to stored procedures.

template_adherence.title: ADR005 - Pingdom healthchecks
template_adherence.context:
We wanted to open up access to tenant applications in our production environment.

As part of an earlier story, Pingdom checks were set up for a healthcheck application in CI, Staging, and Production. At this stage applications were not accessible from non-office IP addresses.

The problem we faced was a need to test the code introduced to make our production environment accessible to the world. Initially, we suggested applying the same change to our staging environment. However, this approach means all applications in staging will be accessible from anywhere.

If we use Pingdom to assert an application is accessible from the outside world then we need to remove the explicit rules (security groups) allowing Pingdom traffic. This means our CI environment would not be accessible to Pingdom probes.

* [#116104189 - set up Pingdom](https://www.pivotaltracker.com/story/show/116104189)
* [#115347323 - allow public access to tenant applications](https://www.pivotaltracker.com/story/show/115347323)
template_adherence.decision:
It was decided we would make the staging environment accessible to the outside world as well as production, and define future work for removing the CI Pingdom check and security groups allowing Pingdom probes, and setting up tests from the pipeline which use the Pingdom API.

Given that the advantages relate to the availability of our production environment, they outweigh not having an automated healthcheck on an application in our CI environment. However, we remain open to hearing solutions to providing healthchecks for CI in future.
template_adherence.consequences:
A story is now required to remove the Pingdom health check for our CI environment, and the security groups allowing Pingdom probes.

### Positive
* We are now able to test accessibility using the staging environment
* We are now able to use Pingdom to assert not just application health, but routing as well.
* We have maintained consistency between staging and production

### Negative
* Any applications in our staging environment need to be considered for whether they are suitable to be public.
* We would no longer have healthchecks via Pingdom for our CI environment.
