template_adherence.title: ADR007 - Terminating TLS at ELBs
template_adherence.context:
We needed to decide where to terminate TLS connections for public and tenant facing endpoints and how to manage the corresponding private keys.

We had previously decided to only support HTTPS to both deployed applications and Cloud Foundry endpoints.

At the time of writing there were 4 endpoints to consider:

- Deployed applications (gorouter). Accessed by the public.
- CF API. Accessed by tenants.
- UAA. Accessed by tenants.
- Loggregator. Accessed by tenants.
- SSH proxy. In theory accessed by tenants, but not working in our environment.

We had an existing credentials store suitable for storing the private keys at rest. Only a small number of engineers within the team can access; the same ones that can make IAM changes using our account-wide terraform config.

Placing ELBs in front of public-facing services is an architectural pattern advised by Amazon [in order to reduce attack surface](https://d0.awsstatic.com/whitepapers/DDoS_White_Paper_June2015.pdf). Specifically they advise that it helps withstand volumetric Denial of Service attacks; the ELB handles TCP connections and therefore the responsibility for handling DDOS at Layer 4 and below resides with the ELB team.

We did a spike, where we attempted to place everything public-facing or tenant-facing behind ELBs. We found that:

- In HTTP mode the ELBs do not support web sockets. This is known to break loggregator, which relies on them for log streaming. It would also prevent tenants from using web sockets within their applications.
- When the ELB is in TCP mode, we have no way of communicating the client IP address to the downstream service. Practical consequences of this would be that tenants would be unable to see in their logs who is using their service or do any access control based on client IP address.

In attempting to solve the second problem, we explored some options:

- ELB has support for the [Proxy Protocol](http://www.haproxy.org/download/1.5/doc/proxy-protocol.txt), but unfortunately none of the downstream services, such as gorouter, support it. It seemed simple to add support to gorouter.
- We could introduce another intermediary proxy such as HAProxy, which understands the proxy protocol and adds or appends to an `X-Forwarded-For` header with the client IP address as provided via the proxy protocol.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to decide where to terminate TLS connections for public and tenant facing endpoints.
- Requirement to manage private keys securely.
- Support HTTPS for deployed applications and Cloud Foundry endpoints.
- Architectural best practices to reduce attack surface and handle DDoS attacks.
- Technical limitations of ELB modes (HTTP mode lacks websocket support; TCP mode lacks client IP forwarding).
- Need to preserve client IP information for logging and access control.
- Feasibility of adding proxy protocol support to downstream services.
- Use of existing credentials store and limited engineer access for security.
template_adherence.decision:
We decided to:

- use the ELB to terminate TLS
- use the ELB in TCP mode
- submit proxy protocol support to gorouter
- use S3 logging to ensure we have the IP addresses of clients using the CF endpoint
template_adherence.consequences:

template_adherence.title: ADR008 - Haproxy for request rewriting
template_adherence.context: We want to serve HSTS headers for all HTTPS requests to the apps domains, but it will safeguard existing users from being MITMed over insecure connections and it will improve the user experience when they select a hostname that doesn't have a protocol. We want to leave open the option of able to override these headers from the tenant application if they wish. This feature requires conditionally process and modify the request headers. There are several possible implementations: 1. Implement the logic in the gorouter itself; 2. Add some intermediate proxy (for example nginx, haproxy) in front of the go-routers and after the ELB; 3. Implement it in a external CDN in front of PaaS origin; 4. AWS ELB does not support this logic and will not in the short term.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to serve HSTS headers for HTTPS requests, safeguard users from MITM attacks, improve user experience, allow tenant application overrides, and the limitations of existing components (gorouter, ELB, CDN). Also, considerations about development effort, simplicity, and performance.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a proxy in front of the gorouter, specifically HAProxy, as a short-term solution. HAProxy will be colocated with the gorouter, handle SSL termination, and proxy to localhost. The gorouter will not be modified immediately, but future work includes proposing a PR to add header logic to gorouter. CDNs are excluded as they are optional and to keep the platform simple.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to add more logic to rewrite HTTP communication, better SSL termination performance, support for web-sockets and HTTP multiplexing, and ability to implement HTTP to HTTPS redirects. Negative consequences include added latency, maintenance of a custom HAProxy release, and an additional component to monitor.

pros: Powerful and flexible proxy solutions available.

cons: Adds additional latency to requests.

template_adherence.title: ADR009 - X-Forwarded- headers
template_adherence.context:
We need to pass correct client IP and requested protocol to applications deployed to the platform. To achieve this we want to use X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto headers.
In the current setup we've got HAProxy behind ELB to allow insert HSTS headers, and ELB is configured in SSL mode (not HTTPS) because it does not support WebSockets. In SSL/TCP mode ELB is not able to set any `X-Forwarded` header.

The solution is to use ProxyProtocol to pass information about recorded client IP and protocol to HAProxy which can set required headers for us. Unfortunately [ELB sets ProxyProtocol header inside SSL stream and HAProxy expects it outside](http://serverfault.com/questions/775010/aws-elb-with-ssl-backend-adds-proxy-protocol-inside-ssl-stream).

There are two options to workaround this:

* Use a more complex configuration of HAProxy with two frontends/listeners chained
* Disable SSL between ELB and HAProxy
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to pass correct client IP and protocol to applications; limitations of ELB in SSL mode not supporting WebSockets and inability to set X-Forwarded headers; ProxyProtocol header placement incompatibility; security considerations of disabling SSL internally.
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided to disable SSL encryption between internal IP of ELB and HAProxy to allow us to use ProxyProtocol.
We don't think this has any significant increase in risk because:

* gorouter to cell traffic is already HTTP (it has to be because we can't do termination in app containers)
* the inner interface of the ELB is on an internal network in our VPC
template_adherence.consequences: The http traffic between ELB and HAProxy will not be encrypted.

alternatives.description: Use a more complex configuration of HAProxy with two frontends/listeners chained
pros: Allows keeping SSL encryption between ELB and HAProxy
Maintains security of internal traffic
cons: More complex HAProxy configuration
Increased operational complexity

alternatives.description: Disable SSL between ELB and HAProxy
pros: Simpler configuration
Allows use of ProxyProtocol as required
cons: Traffic between ELB and HAProxy is unencrypted

template_adherence.title: ADR010 - Postgres bind behaviour
template_adherence.context:
We use RDS for tenant databases. Tenants can bind more than one application to a database instance created via the services console. Database migrations were broken when a binding was removed and re-added, or when another bound application other than the one that created the database tables attempted to modify them.

Previously the RDS broker PostgreSQL engine copied the MySQL engine and granted all rights on the database to the newly created user. In PostgreSQL this will give the user rights to create tables, but because it has a more finely-grained permission model than MySQL this does not give the user rights on existing tables, or tables newly created by other users.

Only the owner of a table can alter/drop it, and you cannot grant this permission to other users. Users who are the owners of tables cannot be removed until the table ownership is changed.

We attempted to work around the PostgreSQL permissions system in the following ways:

* Using [`ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/static/sql-alterdefaultprivileges.html) on every newly created user to `GRANT ALL ON PUBLIC` - this means that every user can `SELECT`, `INSERT`, and `DELETE`, but because only the table owner can `ALTER` or `DROP` this will not allow other bound users to run migrations. This is also limited to the `PUBLIC` (default) schema, so would fail to work for any applications that have custom schemas.

* Making the group the owner of the `PUBLIC` schema. This allowed members of the group to `DROP` tables within the schema, but still did not allow them to `ALTER` these tables.

* Creating a "parent" group that is given ownership of all tables, sequences, and functions. New users are granted rights on this group and thus can carry out all owner actions on group-owned items. A [DDL event trigger](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/static/event-trigger-definition.html) using the built-in `REASSIGN OWNED BY` command handed over ownership of all resources owned by the current user to the parent `$DBNAME_owner` group. This worked perfectly on all the PostgreSQL databases we tested with, however RDS does not allow use of event triggers so it was unworkable in production.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support multiple applications bound to the same PostgreSQL database instance.
- PostgreSQL's permission model restricts altering/dropping tables to their owners.
- Previous approaches to work around permissions were insufficient or incompatible with RDS.
- Desire for a simple, workable solution that avoids ownership conflicts.
- Security concerns: credentials should be changeable and encrypted to mitigate breach risks.
- Potential future extension to support read-only or limited permission credentials.
template_adherence.decision:
The chosen solution is to issue the same credentials to all applications bound to the database, so they share a single user and avoid ownership conflicts when altering or dropping tables.

Credentials are stored in the backing database and encrypted with a symmetric key held by the broker, allowing credential rotation and protection against breaches.

Future plans may include issuing credentials with limited permissions (e.g., read-only).
template_adherence.consequences:
- All applications bound to the same PostgreSQL database instance receive the same credentials.
- This eliminates ownership problems related to `DROP` or `ALTER` commands.
- Credentials are stored encrypted, enhancing security.
- Credential rotation is possible.
- Potentially less granular permission control until future extensions are implemented.

alternatives.description: Using `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` on every newly created user to grant all on PUBLIC schema.
pros: Allows users to `SELECT`, `INSERT`, and `DELETE` on public schema tables.
cons: Does not allow users to `ALTER` or `DROP` tables owned by others.
Limited to the PUBLIC schema, failing for custom schemas.

alternatives.description: Making the group the owner of the PUBLIC schema.
pros: Members of the group can `DROP` tables within the schema.
cons: Does not allow members to `ALTER` tables.

alternatives.description: Creating a parent group owning all tables, sequences, and functions, with event triggers to reassign ownership.
pros: Allows group members to perform all owner actions on group-owned items.
Works perfectly on tested PostgreSQL databases.
cons: RDS does not allow event triggers, making this unworkable in production.

template_adherence.title: ADR011 - Security group structure
template_adherence.context:
In https://www.pivotaltracker.com/story/show/115252309 we described a pattern for defining security groups between services and the VMs that connect to them. This involved creating a client security group for each service that the service allowed connections from. This client security group was then applied to the VMs that needed to be able to connect.

This has the problem that in some cases we would need to add several client security groups to a given VM, and we are at risk of running into the AWS limits (by default it's a max of 5 groups per interface).
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the context and decision sections imply drivers such as AWS security group limits, clarity of connections between components, and ease of managing security groups when moving components between VMs.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use an alternative approach where a security group is defined for each component (or component group) in the system. Services then define rules allowing connections from the components that need access. There are some instances where a component will be both a client of other services and a provider of a service. We will use the same security group for both of these roles.

This approach has a number of advantages:

* The number of security groups applied to a VM is driven by the number of components on that VM, not the number of things that they need to connect to. The number of components is likely to be small, and we're better able to control this that we can control the number of things a  component talks to.
* It's easier to see what components connect to a given service by looking at the rules for that service's security group.
* When moving a component between VMs it's much clearer which security groups need to move with it.
template_adherence.consequences:
* This will enable us to avoid hitting the AWS limits for the number of security groups applied to a given interface.
* It will make it clearer which components are allowed to connect to a given service.
* There will be some work to update our existing groups to use this pattern.

There are some potential issues:

* There's the possibility for cycles in the Terraform dependency graph when we have 2 components that both initiate connections to each other. This can be avoided by using the `aws_security_group_rule` Terraform resource instead of defining the rules inline in the `aws_security_group`.

* When looking at a given VM, it's harder to see what services it connects to. This is not seen as a major problem because it should be possible to create tooling to visualise this without much effort.

alternatives.description: The original pattern described in the linked story where a client security group is created for each service that the service allowed connections from, and this client security group was applied to the VMs that needed to connect.
pros: Simple to understand and implement initially.
cons: Risk of hitting AWS limits on max security groups per interface (default max 5).
VMs may need multiple client security groups, increasing complexity and limits risk.

template_adherence.title: ADR012 - Haproxy healthcheck
template_adherence.context:
Stories: [#123490171](https://www.pivotaltracker.com/story/show/123490171) & [#121933113](https://www.pivotaltracker.com/story/show/121933113)

We were investigating how to avoid downtime to deployed applications when we
made changes to the platform. We had discovered that short outages occurred
when the gorouter was taken out of service.

gorouter has drain functionality to allow upstream load balancers to gracefully
take instances of the gorouter out of service before any requests start to
fail.

When a USR1 signal is sent to instruct the gorouter to start draining,
healthchecking requests, identified by the header `User-Agent: HTTP-Monitor/1.1`
start failing with HTTP 503. User requests are allowed to continue.

Two things prevented us from using drain mode:

- we had the ELB configured to use TCP healthchecks, not HTTP
- the ELB sends HTTP healthcheck requests with `User-Agent:
ELB-HealthChecker/1.0`, which means they were not recognised as healthcheck
requests by gorouter, they returned HTTP 200 and the ELB did not take the
draining gorouter out of service.

The result was a very small amount of downtime for deployed apps that received
requests during a short window of < 1 second.
template_adherence.decision:
We decided to:

- submit a change upstream to [allow the gorouter to recognise ELB
healthchecks](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/gorouter/pull/138)
- implement a healhchecking port 82, in the HAProxy we introduced in ADR008,
which appends the `User-Agent: HTTP-Monitor/1.1` that gorouter expects

template_adherence.title: ADR014 - HSTS preload using api gateway
template_adherence.context: We will only serve HTTPS traffic, keeping TCP port 80 (HTTP) closed and use HSTS preload lists. To add our domains to HSTS preload lists, there are requirements such as serving a valid certificate, redirecting HTTP to HTTPS on the same host, serving all subdomains over HTTPS, and serving an HSTS header on the base domain for HTTPS requests. Our Cloud Foundry app endpoint already serves the right HSTS Security header with HAProxy but cannot be used because port 80 is closed. Implementing a second ELB to listen on HTTP and HTTPS and use HAProxy would increase dependency. Serving from the root domain is required but CNAME records are not allowed at the apex domain, which can be an issue with ELB or CloudFront.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to serve HTTPS traffic exclusively, meet HSTS preload list requirements, avoid opening port 80 on the Cloud Foundry app endpoint, minimize dependencies on HAProxy, and handle DNS constraints at the apex domain.
template_adherence.decision: Implement a basic AWS API Gateway with a default MOCK response returning the correct Strict-Transport-Security header. Use a Custom Domain Name to create an AWS Cloud Front distribution for public access. Use AWS Route 53 ALIAS resource record to serve the IPs of the Cloud Front distribution as A records.
template_adherence.consequences: Setting up AWS API Gateway Domain Names requires access to SSL certificates. Certificates can be uploaded separately and the AWS Cloud Front distribution can be created manually. This approach avoids opening port 80 and reduces dependency on HAProxy but introduces AWS API Gateway and Cloud Front into the architecture.

alternatives.description: Use the existing Cloud Foundry app endpoint with HAProxy to serve the HSTS header including preload and includeSubDomains flags.
pros: Leverages existing infrastructure and configuration.
No need to introduce new AWS services.
cons: Cannot use because port 80 (HTTP) is closed on this endpoint.
Does not meet the requirement to redirect HTTP to HTTPS on the same host.

alternatives.description: Implement a second ELB listening on HTTP and HTTPS and use HAProxy to do HTTP to HTTPS redirect and serve the right header.
pros: Meets the HSTS preload requirements.
Uses familiar HAProxy service for request rewriting.
cons: Increases dependency on HAProxy service.
Adds complexity with an additional ELB.

template_adherence.title: ADR016 - End-to-end encryption
template_adherence.context:
In order to ensure the confidentiality of private tenant data processed on the platform we need to ensure that requests and responses for traffic between the user and application instances are encrypted so that it is not possible for a network eavesdropper to access private tenant data.

There are 3 main network sections between the user and the application:

* User to ELB
* ELB to router
* Router to cells
template_adherence.decision:
* The traffic between the user and the ELB is encrypted by using an TLS listener on the ELB. A certificate issued by a certificate authority is set on the ELB and access to the private key is very restricted.
* The ELB connects to the router VM via TLS. The router VM must, in consequence, serve TLS.
* The router to application instances traffic is plain HTTP because the Cloud Foundry doesn't support TLS between gorouter and the application instances and the application instances may not talk TLS. We've decided to use IPSec on router and cell so the traffic will be encrypted transparently.
template_adherence.consequences: The traffic is encrypted end-to-end between the user and the applications.

template_adherence.title: ADR022 - web app language and framework selection
template_adherence.context:
We are starting to develop a number of user-facing applications with web interfaces that need to be styled to look like GOV.UK etc. In order to keep things consistent we want to pick a single programming language and framework to write these in.

We've previously used Sinatra for this, but ran into issues with its default configuration which isn't secure, leading to an XSS vulnerability. We therefore want to choose something that comes with secure defaults, and makes it easier to avoid this sort of issue.

Requirements:

* Must be well supported by govuk_template and govuk_frontend_toolkit (as well as the future govuk-frontend project)
* Must be understood broadly by members of the team.
* Must be understood broadly by members of the frontend developer community within GDS.

After dicsussion with the head of the frontend community and members of the team, the choice seems to be Rails for the following reasons:

* Most of www.gov.uk is written in Rails, as is the Verify frontend, and therefore is well known within the frontend developer community.
* It's well supported by the frontend toolkits (both projects are available as gems that provide a Rails engine). Given the wide use of Rails with GDS, the future govuk-frontend project is likely to support it.
* It's the framework that's most familiar to our team.
* It is opinionated, and comes with secure defaults making it much easier to create a secure web app.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a single programming language and framework for user-facing web applications.
- Security concerns with previous framework (Sinatra) due to insecure defaults leading to XSS vulnerabilities.
- Requirement for good support by govuk_template, govuk_frontend_toolkit, and future govuk-frontend.
- Broad understanding within the team and frontend developer community.
- Preference for a framework with secure defaults and opinionated design.
template_adherence.decision: We will use Ruby and Rails to create new user-facing applications with web frontends.
template_adherence.consequences: We should consider porting some of our existing applications over to Ruby and Rails.

pros: Familiarity with Sinatra from previous use.
cons: Default configuration is insecure, leading to XSS vulnerabilities.

cons: May not be well supported by govuk_template and frontend toolkits.

Uncertainty about future support from govuk-frontend project.

template_adherence.title: ADR025 - Service plan naming conventions
template_adherence.context:
Our service plans have evolved incrementally over the last few years and are in need of some attention. Names are inconsistent, potentially confusing and in many cases contain irrelevant redundant information that is of no practical use to the platform operators or to tenants consuming the service.

Adding additional versions of services has the potential to compound the problem by multiplying plans of different characteristics with different versions.
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided to use the following naming convention for naming plans going forward:

```
SIZE[-HA][-LABEL,-LABEL,...]-VERSION
```

Where:

* `SIZE` is a string describing the scale one of the plan, it should be one of: `xlarge` `large` `medium` `small` `tiny`.
* `HA` is the string `ha` to indicate highly available if relevent.
* `LABEL` is a string describing some specific variant of the service if relvent.
* `VERSION` is the version number of the service plan.

### For example:

A large multi-az postgres plan for version 9.6 would be `large-ha-9.6`.

A small not multi-az, unclustered, redis 3.2 plan would be `redis-unclustered-3.2`.

### Example migrations of some existing plans:

```
L-HA-enc-dedicated-9.5 => large-ha-9.5
M-HA-enc-dedicated-9.5 => medium-ha-9.5
tiny-clustered => tiny-clustered-3.2
tiny-unclustered => tiny-unclustered-3.2
```

### Additionally:

* We will avoid use of the word "free" in names.
* We will avoid using redundent words (like 'dedicated') in names to reduce noise.
* We will avoid use of uppercase characters in names.
* We will avoid abbriviations where possible ("medium" instead of "M", "large" instead of "L").
* We will avoid offering unencrypted plans where an encrypted version is available (legacy unencrypted plans will be explicitly labelled with `-unencrypted` and hidden from the marketplace).
template_adherence.consequences: Renaming exisiting plans to conform to this format may be disruptive to tenants who may rely on the old names in scripted deployements.

template_adherence.title: ADR027 - Pipeline locking
template_adherence.context:
In our Concourse pipelines a locking mechanism was required to prevent concurrent deploys. Concurrent deploys cause problems because:

* one deployment may make changes which break another
* we have availability tests which tell us if a specific change causes app or API downtime
* Bosh has its own locking mechanisms, which mean concurrent deploys will fail.
* concurrent testing puts extra load on the platform and Concourse
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to prevent concurrent deploys due to potential deployment conflicts, availability test failures, Bosh locking conflicts, and platform load concerns. Also, the desire to use a Concourse-native locking solution, leverage mature client libraries, avoid managing additional user credentials, and maintain repository privacy.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to implement locking using the Concourse pool resource, AWS CodeCommit, and Terraform. The Concourse pool resource was chosen as it is the native solution for locking in Concourse, requiring a Git repository for the lock. AWS CodeCommit was selected over GitHub due to more mature client libraries, ability to use existing instance profiles instead of managing SSH keys or tokens, and to keep the repository private. Terraform was used to allow pipelines to manage AWS CodeCommit permissions securely via IAM users and groups.
template_adherence.consequences: We have to store an SSH private key for Git in an environment's S3 state bucket. This key must be created in the pipeline and used as an input to Terraform configuration which generates the CodeCommit repository.

alternatives.description: Use GitHub instead of AWS CodeCommit for the Git repository backing the Concourse pool resource.
pros: GitHub is a widely used and familiar platform.
Potentially easier integration with existing GitHub workflows.
cons: Would require managing users and SSH keys or tokens separately.
The repository containing locks would have to be public or require additional access management.
Client libraries for the necessary APIs were less mature, increasing work.

alternatives.description: Use a different locking mechanism other than the Concourse pool resource.
pros: Might avoid dependency on Git repositories for locking.
Could potentially simplify or improve locking performance.
cons: Would not be Concourse-native, possibly requiring more custom work.
Might lack mature tooling or community support.
Could introduce new dependencies or complexity.

template_adherence.context:
Aiven provides hosted Elasticsearch for the Elasticsearch backing service.

The PaaS has several environments which will need to use Aiven. These
environments should be isolated from each other so that changes made in testing
and development environments do do not affect production users.

Aiven provide a "Project" abstraction where a user can be a member of several
projects. API tokens are user specific. By creating one user per project it's
possible to scope API tokens to a project.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to isolate environments (CI, dev, staging, prod) to prevent changes in one environment affecting others.
The requirement to manage API tokens scoped per project for security.
The need for team members to have management access across projects.
Credential management and storage considerations.

We'll use separate projects for separate environments, initially using the following Aiven projects:

* ci-testing (for the CI environment for the elasticsearch broker itself)
* paas-cf-dev
* paas-cf-staging
* paas-cf-prod

For staging and prod we will use separate API tokens within the same project to separate credentials between the London and Ireland regions.

We will have the following per-project users to hold API tokens:

the-multi-cloud-paas-team+aiven-ci@digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk
the-multi-cloud-paas-team+aiven-dev@digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk
the-multi-cloud-paas-team+aiven-staging@digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk
the-multi-cloud-paas-team+aiven-prod@digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk

The credentials for the ci and dev users will be stored in the `paas-credentials` passwordstore. staging and prod will be stored in `paas-credentials-high`.

Members of the PaaS team will each have their own user which will have access all of the projects for management purposes.
template_adherence.consequences:
Members of the PaaS team will need their own Aiven accounts.

The Aiven credentials of the four service users will be managed in the PaaS team's passwordstores.

We will be able to interact with elasticsearch on a given environment without risk of affecting other environments.

template_adherence.title: ADR030 - Single staging environment in London
template_adherence.context:

In addition we need to manage the use of Amazon Web Service resources to reduce our running costs. Having staging environments in both Ireland and the UK increases the total infrastructural costs, which is not justified by the benefit of the additional tested cases.

The London region is newer than the Ireland and currently offers a subset of services compared to the Ireland region. Hence, having the staging environment in London should allow us to capture the cases that may cause failure due to the unavailability of services.

Therefore, the risks of running a single staging environment are offset by the cost savings and simplification of deployment pipelines.

- London region is newer and offers fewer services than Ireland, so testing there captures potential failures.
- Simplification of deployment pipelines is desired.
- Risks of single staging environment are offset by cost savings and simplification.

template_adherence.consequences: We will have one staging environment for testing both London and Ireland production environment. This ADR does not affect the setup of the dev or production environment.

template_adherence.title: ADR032 - SSL-only for applications and cf endpoints
template_adherence.context:
It is expected for the government websites to be secure and keep the user interactions private. Because that we want to enforce all communications to any application and to the platform endpoints to use only and always HTTPS, as it is described in the Gov Service Manual.

When a user inputs a website name without specifying the protocol in the URL, most browsers will try first the HTTP protocol by default. Even if the server always redirect HTTP to HTTPS, an initial unprotected request including user information will be transferred in clear: full URL with domain, parameter, cookies without secure flag or browser meta-information.

HTTP Strict Transport Security mitigates this issue by instructing modern browsers that support it to always connect using HTTPS. This is also a requirement in the service manual.

There is still a potential initial unprotected HTTP request that might happen before retrieve the HSTS headers or after the specified HSTS max-age. To solve this issue, the root domain can be added to HSTS preload list which will be used by most common browsers.

Currently the only way to avoid any clear text HTTP interaction is closing or dropping any attempt to connect to the port 80 at TCP level.

Although not all application deployed on the PaaS will be services as in the service manual meaning, we must not allow HTTP to make it easier to service owners to comply with this requirements.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to ensure government websites are secure and user interactions are private.
- Requirement to enforce HTTPS for all communications.
- Browsers default to HTTP if protocol is not specified, causing potential unprotected requests.
- HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a mitigation but has limitations.
- Need to handle initial unprotected HTTP requests before HSTS headers are received.
- Compliance with Gov Service Manual requirements.
- Simplify compliance for service owners by disallowing HTTP.
template_adherence.decision:
We will only open port 443 (HTTPS) and drop/reject any TCP connection to TCP port 80 (HTTP).

We will implement and maintain HSTS preload lists for our production domains.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Must configure and maintain our domain in the HSTS preload lists.
- Users of browsers which do not support HSTS, or HSTS preload lists, will not be able to connect to the sites without specifying the protocol https:// in the URL.
- This only happens when the user manually inputs the URL in the browser.

alternatives.description: Allow both HTTP and HTTPS connections, redirecting HTTP to HTTPS.
pros: Users can connect using HTTP and be redirected to HTTPS automatically.
Compatible with browsers that do not support HSTS or preload lists.
cons: Initial HTTP requests are unprotected and can leak sensitive information.
Does not fully enforce HTTPS-only communication as required.
Increases risk of man-in-the-middle attacks during initial HTTP connection.

alternatives.description: Use HSTS without dropping port 80 connections.
pros: Simpler to implement without firewall or network changes.
Allows gradual enforcement of HTTPS via HSTS headers.
cons: Initial HTTP requests still occur and can leak information before HSTS is applied.
Does not fully prevent unprotected HTTP connections.
Relies on browser support and user behavior.

template_adherence.title: ADR033 - Redirect HTTP for applications
template_adherence.context: In ADR032 we decided that we would only support https for applications on the PaaS, and that we would drop plain http connections (port 80). Since then, we've observed this causing confusion for users on numerous occasions where they think their app isn't working after being pushed. The situation is improved with the inclusion of the cloudapps.digital domain in the HSTS preload list, but this only helps users with recent versions of modern browsers. As a result of the continued confusion for users we should revisit the decision from ADR443. There are a number of things that could be done to address this: Update the CF CLI to include the scheme and Redirect http to https.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include user confusion caused by dropping plain HTTP connections, the limitations of HSTS preload support in browsers, the need to improve user experience after pushing apps, risks of misconfiguration allowing non-encrypted traffic, and the effectiveness and feasibility of potential solutions such as updating the CF CLI or redirecting HTTP to HTTPS.
template_adherence.decision: We will redirect http traffic to the corresponding root https endpoint. We will continue to maintain HSTS preload lists for our production domains.
template_adherence.consequences: We must configure and maintain an endpoint on the routers that accepts http connections and redirects to the corresponding base https endpoint.

alternatives.description: Update the CF CLI to include the scheme in the output after pushing an app to reduce user confusion.
pros: Helps users immediately after pushing an app by clarifying the URL scheme.
Improves user experience in a specific scenario.
cons: Unclear how much work is involved due to lack of HTTP/HTTPS modeling in CloudFoundry.
No guarantee users will upgrade their CLI to benefit from this change.
May only fix some cases and not cover all user confusion scenarios.

alternatives.description: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS by adding an endpoint that listens to all HTTP requests and redirects them to the corresponding HTTPS URL.
pros: Provides a seamless redirect for users accessing HTTP URLs.
Mitigates user confusion by ensuring HTTP requests are redirected to secure endpoints.
Can strip path and query to avoid unnoticed incorrect HTTP links.
cons: Risk that services could link to HTTP URLs and not notice due to the redirect.
Risk of misconfiguration allowing non-encrypted traffic through to applications.
Requires configuration and maintenance of an additional endpoint on routers.

template_adherence.title: ADR034 - Continuously deploy platform CF applications
template_adherence.context: As part of GOV.UK PaaS we have a number of applications that we consider to be an essential part of the platform deployed as cloud foundry apps. These include: paas-admin, paas-billing, paas-accounts. Prior to July 2019 the versions of these applications were pinned in paas-cf, and they were only deployed along with the whole platform. This had a couple of negative consequences: manual changes required to deploy apps after source changes, and deployments had to wait for unrelated slow pipeline steps. There were also advantages of specifying versions explicitly: record of working versions and controlled deployment permissions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve deployment speed and automation, while maintaining security controls such as requiring signed commits, and balancing the loss of explicit version records.
template_adherence.decision: Update the pipeline to require GPG signatures on git commits before deploying applications in staging and production; automatically deploy every build of the master branch of the applications to staging; tag the application repo in staging when deployment passes acceptance tests; and in production, automatically deploy any build tagged by staging.
template_adherence.consequences: Deployments to paas-admin, paas-billing and paas-accounts will take minutes instead of hours; enforcement of signed commits for production code continues; loss of a single record of which versions of applications were deployed with which platform version.

template_adherence.title: ADR035 - Do not use HAProxy ; Use AWS ALBs
template_adherence.context:
In ADR008 and ADR014 we decided to use HAProxy, for three reasons:

- Writing HSTS header if they are not present in the upstream request
- Implementing HTTP -> HTTPS redirect
- Custom health check for Gorouter

These problems have since been fixed:

- Header rewriting was implemented in [v0.183.0](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/routing-release/releases/tag/0.183.0)
- HTTP healthchecking was implemented in [v0.139.0](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/routing-release/releases/tag/0.139.0)
- HTTP -> HTTPS redirect can be done using AWS ALBs

We currently use multiple ELBs (classic) which we want to replace with ALBs.
We want to use ALBs because:

- ELBs are deprecated in terraform and cause crashes
- ALBs can give us more metrics in CloudWatch
- ALBs have better support for X-Forwarded-For
- ALBs support fixed-response which can be used for HTTP -> HTTPS rewriting

HAProxy adds significant complexity to our routing deployment and maintenance:

- Proxy Protocol is non-standard and hard to understand
- HTTP -> HTTPS rewriting is hard to understand
- HAProxy config is rarely touched
- We have to maintain our own HAProxy BOSH release
- HAProxy duplicates the number of logs we receive because every platform request is written twice
- HAProxy adds an extra network hop for every request
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to replace deprecated ELBs
- Desire for better metrics and support (CloudWatch, X-Forwarded-For)
- Simplify routing deployment and maintenance
- Remove complexity and overhead introduced by HAProxy
template_adherence.decision:
- Replace ELBs with ALBs
- Use ALB fixed-response to redirect HTTP -> HTTPS
- Use Gorouter directly for TLS termination, HSTS header rewriting, and healthchecking the router instance
- Remove HAProxy
template_adherence.consequences:
- Archive alphagov/paas-haproxy-release
- Use Gorouter's /health endpoint for drained healthchecking
- Communicate to tenants about changes in X-Forwarded-For header contents
- No longer have HAProxy logs, saving money on log ingestion/storage

alternatives.description: Continue using HAProxy as previously decided in ADR008 and ADR014.
pros: Existing setup already in place
HAProxy provides HTTP -> HTTPS redirect, HSTS header rewriting, and custom health checks
cons: Adds significant complexity to routing deployment and maintenance
Proxy Protocol is non-standard and hard to understand
HAProxy config is rarely touched and requires maintenance
Maintaining own HAProxy BOSH release
Duplicates logs, increasing storage costs
Adds extra network hop for every request

alternatives.description: Use classic ELBs instead of ALBs.
pros: Existing infrastructure in place
Familiarity with ELBs
cons: ELBs are deprecated in terraform and cause crashes
Lack of advanced metrics compared to ALBs
Less support for X-Forwarded-For headers
No fixed-response support for HTTP -> HTTPS rewriting

template_adherence.title: ADR037 - Automated certificate rotation
template_adherence.context:
Our certificate rotation was a largely manual process, involving an operator triggering a series of Concourse pipeline jobs in a particular sequence. We did not have a routine for doing rotations, and would typically only do them as part of a CF upgrade.

The only means we had for knowing if a cert rotation was necessary was the `check-certificates` job, in the `create-cloudfoundry` Concourse pipeline, which would fail if any certificate had less than 30 days until it expired.

In Q2 2019 (August/September) we moved all of our platform secrets from AWS S3 to [Credhub](https://docs.cloudfoundry.org/credhub/). This covered third-party service credentials, platform passwords, and certificates. Since Credhub supports [certificate rotation](https://github.com/pivotal-cf/credhub-release/blob/master/docs/ca-rotation.md), we chose to implement automatic certificate rotation. This ADR contains details of how we did it.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to automate certificate rotation to avoid manual, error-prone processes.
- Use of Credhub's certificate rotation capabilities.
- Avoid downtime during certificate rotation.
- Integration with existing Concourse pipeline.
- Early detection of rotation failures via certificate expiry checks.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to implement automatic certificate rotation using Credhub's transitional certificate feature. The rotation process is implemented as a job at the end of the `create-cloudfoundry` pipeline, consisting of three tasks (`remove-transitional-flag-for-ca`, `move-transitional-flag-for-ca`, and `set-transitional-flag-for-ca`) executed in reverse order to avoid downtime. The existing `check-certificates` job was also modified to detect certificates expiring in less than 15 days to catch rotation failures early.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Certificate rotations will happen more frequently.
- Documentation related to certificate rotation and its references will need updating.
- Reduced manual intervention and potential for errors.
- Improved reliability and automation of certificate management.

alternatives.description: Continue with manual certificate rotation triggered by operators.
pros: No changes to existing pipeline or processes.
Operators retain full control over rotation timing.
cons: Manual process is error-prone and inconsistent.
Higher risk of downtime or expired certificates.
No automation benefits.

alternatives.description: Implement partial automation without using Credhub's transitional certificates.
pros: Simpler implementation without relying on transitional certificates.
May require fewer changes to existing infrastructure.
cons: Potential for downtime during rotation.
Less robust and reliable than full automation.
Does not leverage Credhub's built-in features.

template_adherence.title: ADR040 - BOSH access without SOCKS5 or SSH
template_adherence.context: To comply with Payment Card Industry (PCI) Requirements we will remove the use of shared credentials anywhere in the platform. We will use Google Single Sign On (SSO) to avoid credential sharing. To enable SSO we will expose some of the APIs on the BOSH instance without using a SOCKS5 proxy. This is due to the SOCKS5 proxy not being compatible with our VPN, which in turn creates a support risk. We discussed proposed methods with IA and Cyber after reviewing the RFC created as part of #169915408.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Compliance with PCI requirements, removal of shared credentials, compatibility issues with SOCKS5 proxy and VPN, support risk reduction, enabling Google SSO, and security considerations involving IA and Cyber teams.
template_adherence.decision: We will remove the reliance on SOCKS5 or SSH tunnels for the User Account and Authentication Service (UAA) API endpoint so that we can remove the use of shared credentials. The current method will be replaced with SSO to obtain a UAA token, which is then used to interact with the rest of the APIs on the BOSH instance.
template_adherence.consequences: We will no longer rely on IP allow lists or SSH tunnels and have individual credentials for accessing UAA on the BOSH Director. Cyber can set up full alerting for this component. We will not be using SSH tunnels to obtain UAA tokens.

cons: Does not comply with PCI requirements.

SOCKS5 proxy is incompatible with VPN, creating support risks.

pros: Maintains current security model with SOCKS5 proxy.
cons: VPN incompatibility causes support risks.

template_adherence.title: ADR041 - BOSH access with mTLS

template_adherence.consequences: We will no longer rely on IP allow lists when accessing the components on the BOSH Director. Cyber can implement full alerting for this component. We will not be using SSH access to the BOSH Director when carrying out daily operator tasks, which should reduce false alerting within Cyber.

No immediate need to implement new technology.
cons: Less secure compared to mTLS.
Contradicts the move towards zero trust network model.
Does not authenticate both user and machine.

template_adherence.title: ADR042 - Isolation segments
template_adherence.context: GOV.UK PaaS would like to be able to isolate specific tenant apps and tasks to different pools of virtual machines (VMs). GOV.UK PaaS would like to be able to prevent specific tenant apps and tasks from egressing to the internet. Apps running inside the separate pools of VMs should be able to discover and access other apps running within the platform, providing that the correct Cloud Foundry Network Policies have been created. Apps running in the shared pools of VMs should be able to discover and access apps running inside an isolation segment, providing that the correct Cloud Foundry Network Policies have been created.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to isolate tenant apps and tasks to different VM pools, prevent egress to the internet for specific apps, maintain app discoverability and access within the platform, and implement egress restrictions without interfering with existing networking or requiring network topology changes.
template_adherence.decision: GOV.UK PaaS will implement egress-restricted isolation segments configured by a developer, using IPTables rules to achieve egress restriction. Isolation segments will be implemented as new instance groups with placement tags in the BOSH deployment manifest, supporting variable properties such as number of instances, instance type, and egress restriction.
template_adherence.consequences: Isolation segments will enable hosting apps without internet access, hosting apps on separate VMs, provisioning different instance types, and not interfere with normal container networking. Egress restrictions will not interfere with VPC peering or internal services but may affect communication with external brokered services. No network topology changes are required, only VM network configuration. Maximum capacity of isolation segments is smaller than shared pools, requiring support contact for capacity changes.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR text, but implicitly alternatives could be not implementing isolation segments or using different network isolation techniques.
pros: Implicitly, simpler architecture if not implemented.
cons: Does not meet the requirements for isolation and egress restriction.

template_adherence.title: ADR043 - new product pages language and framework
template_adherence.context:
[PaaS product pages] have been reviewed and a number of accessibility issues have been identified. To resolve those we, would need to make an upgrade and and review if any additional changes are needed to align with the GOV.UK Design System.

As those pages are built in Ruby and in [ADR024] we've made the decision to develop our user-facing applications on Node, it's a good opportunity to look at rebuilding the product pages.

We've discussed user needs and it emerged that:

* anyone in the team (developer and non-developer) should be able to update pages with less effort
* pages should be performant for end users
* pages should be rendered by the server
* keeping pages up to date with GOV.UK Design System releases should be quicker and easier
* alignment of technologies for our user-facing web products should provide better developer experience and give us the option to have shared component libraries

With the above in mind we researched options. Our admin interface is built in React, so we narrowed the scope to React-based static site generators.

We ended up comparing two: [NextJS] with static page export and [GatsbyJS] which exports static pages by default.
For page content we agreed that writing pages in [Markdown] is a good option, so we tested both with [MDX] which can also embed React components inside content pages.

[NextJS] and [GatsbyJS] have different approaches to development and there are minor performance differences between them.

Our use case for now is narrow enough, and with the primary need of anyone in the team being able to update pages, [NextJS] marginally gets more votes as Gatsby cannot be installed and run on non-developer machines.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to resolve accessibility issues and align with GOV.UK Design System
- Pages currently built in Ruby, but decision to develop user-facing apps on Node
- User needs: ease of update by anyone in team, performance, server-side rendering, ease of keeping pages up to date, alignment of technologies for better developer experience
- Research narrowed to React-based static site generators
- Comparison between NextJS and GatsbyJS
- Primary need: non-developers able to update pages easily
template_adherence.decision: We will use [NextJS] together with [MDX] to author PaaS product pages content in [Markdown] and deliver them to users as static pages.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Faster content iteration as non-developers can make changes easily
- Easier to keep pages updated with GOV.UK Design System releases
- Both user-facing products on the same platform
- Possibility to have shared components if needed

alternatives.description: Use GatsbyJS as the static site generator for product pages.
pros: GatsbyJS exports static pages by default.
Minor performance differences compared to NextJS.
cons: Cannot be installed and run on non-developer machines, limiting ease of updates by non-developers.

alternatives.description: Continue using Ruby for product pages without rebuilding.
pros: No need to rebuild existing pages.
cons: Does not resolve accessibility issues.
Does not align with decision to develop user-facing apps on Node.
Does not improve ease of updates or alignment with GOV.UK Design System.

template_adherence.title: ADR047 - Postgres allowed-extensions approach
template_adherence.context: Up to the release of postgres 13 plans to tenants, the policy for choosing the set of postgres extensions we allow for a certain major version was ad-hoc. A mixture of "allow everything", simply copying the list from the previous postgres version and not actually trying any of these extensions had lead to an extensions list with misnamed entries, entries removed from earlier postgres versions, missing newly-offered extensions, extensions that could never be used without superuser access, and extensions that could never be used with the VPC restrictions we have in place for our RDS instances. Some of these extensions had been omitted from the list in the documentation, but it was unclear how these decisions had been made and where we stood on each extension. This is confusing for tenants and could lead them down a path of trying to use an extension which will never work, or even start designing a system that relies on functionality in a listed extension only to find it unusable.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have a clear, reliable, and feasible list of allowed postgres extensions for each major version to avoid confusion and misconfiguration by tenants. The desire to ensure extensions can be enabled without superuser privileges and within VPC restrictions. The importance of maintaining an up-to-date and accurate document tracking extension feasibility and dependencies. The need to balance thorough testing with reasonable time commitment.
template_adherence.decision: For postgres 13 onwards, offer a selection of extensions limited to those we know can be successfully enabled and think are feasible to use given the limitations of our platform. Maintain a document tracking conclusions on each extension by postgres major version. When preparing a new major version, copy and adjust the previous release's sheet according to new extensions, researching feasibility. Use a dev environment and scripts to check each extension can be enabled and disabled, noting dependencies and shared_preload_libraries requirements. Actual functional testing of extensions is deferred for now, with documentation noting the semi-supported nature of extensions.
template_adherence.consequences: Adding a new major postgres version will take more work than before. There is a risk of mistakenly disabling useful extensions, but tenants can request reassessment. Extensions are not removed from current databases, so impact is limited. The approach improves clarity and reliability of allowed extensions, reducing tenant confusion and misconfiguration.

alternatives.description: Continue with the previous ad-hoc approach of allowing all or copying previous lists without thorough testing.
pros: Simpler and less upfront work when releasing new postgres versions.
No need to maintain a detailed document or perform testing.
cons: Leads to confusion due to misnamed, removed, or unusable extensions.
Tenants may try to use unsupported extensions, causing failures.
Lack of clarity and reliability in extension support.

alternatives.description: Allow only a minimal set of well-known extensions without attempting to test or document others.
pros: Simplifies maintenance and testing.
Reduces risk of unsupported extensions being used.
cons: May unnecessarily restrict tenants by excluding feasible extensions.
Lacks transparency and documentation for tenants.
May require frequent exceptions or requests for additional extensions.

template_adherence.title: Enforce HTTPS and Drop HTTP Connections on Government Websites
template_adherence.context: It is expected for the government websites to be secure and keep the user interactions private. Because that we want to enforce all communications to any application and to the platform endpoints to use only and always HTTPS, as described in the Gov Service Manual. Browsers default to HTTP if no protocol is specified, which can expose user data in an initial unprotected request. HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) mitigates this by instructing browsers to always use HTTPS, and adding domains to the HSTS preload list further prevents initial HTTP requests. Currently, the only way to avoid any clear text HTTP interaction is to close or drop any attempt to connect to port 80 at the TCP level. Although not all applications deployed on the PaaS will be "services" as defined in the service manual, HTTP must be disallowed to help service owners comply with these requirements.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Security requirements to keep user interactions private and secure.
- Compliance with the Gov Service Manual's HTTPS usage guidelines.
- Browser behavior defaulting to HTTP when protocol is unspecified.
- Limitations of HSTS and the need for HSTS preload lists.
- Need to prevent any clear text HTTP interactions at the network level.
- Applicability to all applications on the platform, not just services.
template_adherence.decision: We will only open port 443 (HTTPS) and drop/reject any TCP connection to TCP port 80 (HTTP). We will implement and maintain HSTS preload lists for our production domains.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to configure and maintain our domains in the HSTS preload lists.
- Users with browsers that do not support HSTS or HSTS preload lists will need to specify the protocol explicitly (https://) to connect.
- This may affect user experience for manual URL inputs in unsupported browsers.

alternatives.description: Allow both HTTP and HTTPS connections, redirecting HTTP to HTTPS at the application level.
pros: Simpler network configuration, allowing HTTP connections.
Users typing URLs without protocol are automatically redirected to HTTPS.
cons: Initial HTTP requests are unprotected and can expose user data.
Does not fully comply with Gov Service Manual requirements.
Relies on application-level redirects which may be bypassed or delayed.

alternatives.description: Use HSTS without dropping port 80 connections, relying on browser support to enforce HTTPS.
pros: Allows legacy browsers to connect without issues.
Simpler to implement initially.
cons: Initial HTTP requests before HSTS headers are received remain unprotected.
Does not prevent clear text HTTP traffic at the network level.
Less secure and not fully compliant with security requirements.

template_adherence.title: ADR001: Support Model
template_adherence.context:
How we structure our support model has a large impact on the design of any systems we put in place or services we provide.

The different models could be considered on a spectrum:

* A **Platform as a Service** model:
* A larger dedicated team of SREs provide a centralised full end-to-end service for building, deploying, running applications and required services for Service Teams to consume
* Usually implies centralised infrastructure and benefits from the economies of scale that such an architecture brings
* Requires little to no ops knowledge from Service Teams
* Evolution of the system is dependent on the platform team
* A **shared responsibility** or **supported workflow** model:
* A smaller team of dedicated SREs provide the lower-level infrastructure primitives, and – by regularly rotating/embedding/consulting within teams – work to identify common needs, and improve the re-usability and reliability of shareable solutions and maintain best-practice documentation
* Makes no assumptions about what is "centralised"
* Requires some knowledge of the ops side from service teams or a structure for support from the dedicated SRE team
* Evolution of the system is a shared responsibility
* A **Paved Path** model:
* Teams have their own dedicated SREs focused solely on their team's needs and knowledge sharing is achieved by regularly contributing to organisation best-practices, guidance documents or reusable code where and when possible
* Usually implies de-centralised infrastructure with each team running their own
* Requires strong knowledge of ops side within Service Team
* Evolution of the system is dependent on the Service Team

The table below aims to illustrate where responsibility for the maintenance, evolution and iteration of various parts of such a system lie in each of these models.

| Responsibility  | PaaS Model | Supported Workflow Model | Paved Path Model |
|---|---|---|---|
|  | Give us your code, we'll keep it running for you | Use our tools and follow our guidance, and we'll support you | Here's some examples and guidance, do it yourself |
| Application lifecycle (HA, Capacity) | RE | RE/ServiceTeam | ServiceTeam |
| Observability etc | RE | RE/ServiceTeam | ServiceTeam |
| Backing services | RE | RE/ServiceTeam | ServiceTeam |
| Iterating new features | RE | RE/ServiceTeam | ServiceTeam |
| Workflow/Process | RE | RE | ServiceTeam |
| Productionising common features | RE | RE | ServiceTeam |
| Infrastructure Responsibility | RE | RE | ServiceTeam |

Traditionally GDS teams were operating closest to a "paved path" model where teams took complete control over their own infrastructure. GDS also operates the [GOV.UK PaaS](https://cloud.service.gov.uk), a platform targeting other government departments with limited operations capability.

More recently GDS has created a Reliability Engineering team (RE) to provide support for common needs of Service Teams and reduce duplication of effort around areas like infrastructure, build tooling and observability.

With more of the operations skills centralised in Reliability Engineering, models on the "paved path" end of the spectrum become more difficult to sustain. This leaves us with two choices:

* provide a full-stack PaaS model, growing the size of the PaaS team as required to keep up with demand for new features.
* provide only the lower-level building blocks, guidance and let service teams contribute to the development of new features
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to balance operational support and service team autonomy
- Desire to reduce duplication of effort and improve reusability
- Constraints on team size and skills distribution
- Need for flexibility in deployment and evolution of features
- Importance of shared responsibility and collaboration between Reliability Engineering and Service Teams
template_adherence.decision:
We will design a system around a shared responsibility between Reliability Engineering and Service Teams.

We believe that the middle ground where service teams have a high level of responsibility over their deployments but Reliability Engineering takes most of the responsibility for the lower-level deployment primitives as well as providing solutions to the common needs of service teams (such as deployment workflows, monitoring, deployment patterns) will maintain the flexibility service teams need when iterating new features as well as providing the framework for getting support from Reliability Engineering when such new features could benefit from hardening or sharing with the organisation as a whole.

* We should provide, promote and support the use of a common language for declaratively describing infrastructure and deployments
* We should provide, promote and support low-level deployment primitives suitable for service teams to build upon
* We should work closely and continuously with service teams to reduce duplication of effort by identify common needs and providing reliable, reusable solutions
template_adherence.consequences:
* Implies a framework for embedding/loaning/floating SREs within Service Teams so that knowledge can be shared and common needs can be identified and improved upon
* Will require a migration to a common declarative deployment language
* Gives more control/flexibility to Service Teams than a PaaS model at the cost of potentially more complex deployment patterns
* Keeping Service Teams converging on a smaller set of best-practice solutions would be harder than with a centrally enforced PaaS model

alternatives.description: Provide a full-stack PaaS model, growing the size of the PaaS team as required to keep up with demand for new features.
pros: Centralized infrastructure management
Economies of scale
Little to no ops knowledge required from Service Teams
cons: Requires large PaaS team
Less flexibility for Service Teams
Evolution dependent on platform team

alternatives.description: Provide only the lower-level building blocks, guidance and let service teams contribute to the development of new features.
pros: Empowers Service Teams
Encourages innovation and flexibility
Shared responsibility model
cons: Requires ops knowledge in Service Teams
Potential duplication of effort
Harder to enforce best practices centrally

template_adherence.title: ADR004: Tenant Isolation
template_adherence.context:
The two main isolation models for Kubernetes are:

* Namespaces within a single cluster
* Running multiple clusters

All Service Teams currently have separate AWS accounts.

Some Service Teams have separate AWS accounts for separate environment (ie. Staging, Production etc)

Many Service Teams have micro-service architectures

Some Service Teams have unique network isolation requirements that may be hard to implement in a shared environment.

To ensure "smooth transition" during a migration it would be preferable to have clusters deployed to Service Team's VPCs.

To ensure separation of billing it would be preferable to deploy clusters to Service Team's AWS accounts.

To ensure strong network/compute isolation between Service Teams it would be preferable to deploy separate clusters for separate environments.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for strong network/compute isolation between service teams
- Clear separation of billing
- Ability to deploy clusters into target VPCs for smooth migration
- Existing use of separate AWS accounts and environments
- Complexity considerations in managing multiple clusters/accounts
template_adherence.decision:
We will manage multiple Kubernetes clusters, one per environment per tenant.

This should provide:

* Strong network/compute isolation between service teams
* Clear separation of billing
* Ability to deploy into target VPCs to make piecemeal microservice migration practical
template_adherence.consequences:
* Managing multiple clusters across multiple accounts may be more complex than managing a single big one
* Lack of direct control over the target account/environment may introduce complexities

alternatives.description: Use namespaces within a single Kubernetes cluster for tenant isolation.
pros: Simpler management with a single cluster
Lower operational overhead
cons: Weaker network/compute isolation
Billing separation is less clear
May not meet unique network isolation requirements

alternatives.description: Run multiple Kubernetes clusters, one per environment per tenant.
pros: Strong network/compute isolation
Clear billing separation
Ability to deploy into target VPCs
cons: More complex management
Potential lack of direct control over target accounts/environments

template_adherence.title: ADR005: Ingress
template_adherence.context:
Creating a [`Service`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service) resource of type [`LoadBalancer`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#loadbalancer) will result in cloud provider specific infrastructure – for example an [Elastic Load Balancer](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/) on AWS – being provisioned to expose the Service to the public.

This is unfortunately a bit of an anti-pattern as:

* Provisioning one load balancer per exposed service would be unnecessarily expensive.
* Provisioning a load balancer takes time, which can result in significantly slower deployment times.
* LoadBalancer types of Service require vendor specific extensions and have often have vendor specific configuration that is not portable
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Avoid unnecessary expense of provisioning one load balancer per service
- Reduce deployment time delays caused by provisioning load balancers
- Avoid vendor-specific extensions and non-portable configurations associated with LoadBalancer type Services
template_adherence.decision:
- Provide a single load-balancer to provide ingress to each cluster.
- Provide an ingress controller as part of managed cluster deployments to enable Ingress resources.
- Provide guidance to promote the use of Ingress over LoadBalancer types of Service for routing.
- Not support and may disable the use of LoadBalancer types of Service entirely.
template_adherence.consequences: - The LoadBalancer Service type is well documented and provides a convenient way to expose a Service that people may expect to be enabled.

alternatives.description: Use LoadBalancer type Services for each exposed service, provisioning cloud provider specific load balancers per service.
pros: Convenient and well documented way to expose services.
Familiar to users expecting LoadBalancer type Services.
cons: Provisioning one load balancer per service is expensive.
Provisioning load balancers takes time, slowing deployments.
Requires vendor specific extensions and configurations, reducing portability.

template_adherence.title: Continuous delivery workflow
template_adherence.context:
If a Reliability Engineer on support has to make a change to a Service Team's deployment or cluster to resolve an issue or perform a critical upgrade, they need to know how to perform a release, where to look for the code and need confidence that any changes they make have not broken the deployment.

Traditionally this problem has been addressed with the use of "Team Manuals" that document release processes, locations of project repositories and who should have access. These manuals can get out of sync with processes, and processes often differ significantly between teams.
template_adherence.decision:
We will provide the tools and guidance for teams to practice [continuous delivery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_delivery)

We expect this to improve the efficiency of supporting multiple services by:

* promoting a consistent pattern for deployment across teams (merging PRs)
* giving confidence to those making changes to deployments (culture of testing/staging releases)
* giving confidence that the desired state of deployment is what is commited to git
template_adherence.consequences:
* We will likely have to run and maintain CI/CD tools
* CI/CD tooling is an area where people have quite strong opinions
* Some teams may have complicated "gated" pipelines where human approval is required

template_adherence.title: Multi-tenancy for CI and CD
template_adherence.context:
Two models have been proposed concerning CI and CD tool sets:

1. Multi-tenant: all tenants, including Reliability Engineering, share that same CI and CD instance
2. Per-tenant: each tenant has their own CI and CD cluster
template_adherence.decision: - There will be a single CI and CD toolset used by all tenants of the new service
template_adherence.consequences:
- With a single CI and CD toolset used by all tenants, there will be a need for those tools to have strong RBAC to prevent cross-tenant pollution
- The decision to use a single tool for all tenants could easily be adapted in the future to allow per-tenant CI and CD tool deployments should requirements change
- Authentication for the CI and CD toolsets should align with [ADR007](ADR007-identity-provider.md)
- It is believed that by having the CI and CD toolset sitting within a kubernetes cluster, rather than on puppetised and terraformed EC2 instances, it will allow for easier updates and upgrades to occur, and reduce the need for extra technology to handle configuration management (Puppet, Chef or Ansible) and infrastructure as code tools (Terraform)
- By having a single CI and CD toolset used by all tenants, it will enable Reliability Engineering to centrally manage and upgrade the toolset, rather than having tenants own the management and maintenance responsibility

template_adherence.title: ADR012: Docker image repositories
template_adherence.context: Artefacts that we build must be published somewhere that a Kubernetes cluster can pull from. This can be solved by using an image repository. Multiple options exist including Docker Hub, Vendor Managed Registry (e.g., AWS ECR or Google Cloud Container Registry), and Self-hosted Docker Registry (e.g., Docker Registry or Harbor). All implement the Docker registry API and are broadly equivalent. Docker Hub requires managing authentication and authorization separate from existing IAM setup. Managed Registry from a vendor saves dealing with authentication or authorization if running Kubernetes nodes with that vendor. Self-hosted Docker registry involves maintenance and operational work but offers flexibility. Since targeting AWS, it makes sense to delegate extra work to AWS, allowing restriction of access with IAM policies.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for a reliable image repository accessible by Kubernetes clusters, ease of managing authentication and authorization, operational maintenance considerations, flexibility, and alignment with the current cloud provider (AWS) to leverage IAM policies for access control.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a Managed Registry from the vendor currently in use, specifically AWS ECR.
template_adherence.consequences: Images must not contain sensitive data even if published to private registries. ECR requires creation of repositories ahead of time, so the build process must include repository creation.

alternatives.description: Use Docker Hub as the image repository.
pros: Widely used and supported.
No need to manage own infrastructure.
cons: Requires separate management of authentication and authorization outside existing IAM setup.

alternatives.description: Use Vendor Managed Registry such as AWS ECR or Google Cloud Container Registry.
pros: Saves dealing with authentication and authorization if Kubernetes nodes run with that vendor.
Integration with existing cloud IAM policies.
cons: May be vendor lock-in.
Dependent on vendor availability and pricing.

alternatives.description: Use Self-hosted Docker Registry such as Docker Registry or Harbor.
pros: High flexibility.
Full control over the registry and its configuration.
cons: Requires maintenance and operational work from the team.
Additional infrastructure to manage.

* A per-cluster key pair may lead to more complex deployment charts that require selecting secrets based on environment.

template_adherence.title: ADR016: Code Verification
template_adherence.context:
All of our deployment processes start with code in git repositories hosted on Github and continuous delivery pipelines automate the build and deployment of applications out to production. Git supports GPG signing of commits.

Code changes should not be able to make it out to a production environment without being exposed to at least two authorised code owners.

Our aim is to improve on process-based approval methods by being able to digitally verify that code has been exposed to at least two authorised code owners without adversely affecting developer workflow.

Some potential solutions involve:

1. Enforcing that two unique developers each an add empty signed commit at the tip of the branch for PRs before being merged, and verifying the existence of these empty signed commits as part of the delivery pipeline.
2. Enforcing that two unique developers each sign the commmit at the tip of the branch for PRs using [git-signatures](https://github.com/hashbang/git-signatures) and verifying that at least two trusted developer keys are present as part of the delivery pipeline.
3. Verify that at least one (non-PR-authoring) trusted Github user has approved the commit from the delivery pipeline using the Github API (rather than the web UI, which is vulnerable to manipulation by a single Github "owner").
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the 'Context' section includes some drivers such as the need to improve process-based approval methods, the desire to digitally verify code exposure to authorized owners, and the consideration of developer workflow impact. These can be interpreted as decision drivers influencing the choice of solution.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is clearly stated under the 'Decision' section. It explains that solutions (1) and (2) introduce significant changes to developer workflows and that their benefits do not warrant the reduced usability. Therefore, solution (3) is implemented.
template_adherence.consequences: The 'Consequences' section is present and lists the impacts of the decision: developer workflow is largely unaffected, and there is a risk that compromise of multiple developer laptops could mitigate the 'two-eyes' process.

alternatives.description: Enforcing that two unique developers each add empty signed commits at the tip of the branch for PRs before merging, and verifying these commits in the delivery pipeline.
pros: Provides strong cryptographic proof of code approval.
Enhances security when combined with hardware security devices like Yubikey.
cons: Introduces significant changes to developer workflow.
May reduce usability for developers across GDS.

alternatives.description: Enforcing that two unique developers each sign the commit at the tip of the branch for PRs using git-signatures and verifying trusted developer keys in the delivery pipeline.
pros: Provides cryptographic verification of code approval.
Can be combined with hardware security devices for enhanced security.
cons: Significant changes to developer workflow.
Potentially reduces usability for developers.

alternatives.description: Verifying that at least one (non-PR-authoring) trusted Github user has approved the commit from the delivery pipeline using the Github API.
pros: Largely unaffected developer workflow.
Uses existing Github features familiar to teams.
cons: Relies on Github API which may have vulnerabilities.
Less cryptographic assurance compared to solutions (1) and (2).
